# A life of unalloyed devotion

## A life of unalloyed devotion

Part One: Preparing an Offering of Love. Dinatarini Devi

With eternal gratitude to His Divine Grace A. C Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada

Had you not come, Who had told  
The message of Krishna, forceful and bold,  
That’s your right, you have the mace.  
Save me a fallen, Your Divine Grace.

The line of service as drawn by you  
Is pleasing and healthy like morning dew.  
The oldest of all but in new dress.  
Miracle done, Your Divine Grace.

“ADORE YE ALL” BY SR1LA PRABHUPADA 1936 VYASA PUJA OFFERING

## Foreword

UNALLOYED—“LOVE THAT is pure, untainted by any trace of egoism or selfishness — the realm of consciousness where every thought, word and deed is an offering for the pleasure of ones beloved”—this is the story of Yamuna devi’s life.

In March of 1971, I first met with Yamuna devi. She was sitting on a stage in a giant tent in a park in downtown Bombay. She sat alone, with her eyes closed, singing into a microphone with a devotion that deeply affected my life. It was so deep and so real. It was late morning, and only a few people were scattered in the tent; most were talking or walking about. I was alone, sitting on the ground in a far corner of the park, listening and observing. She seemed to be oblivious to the noisy, inattentive audience and the blaring horns and yelling people close by. She was totally absorbed, blissfully singing for the pleasure of the Lord within her heart. Witnessing her devotion inspired me to stay till evening to hear from the guru who could inspire this kind of love. Her guru was Srila Prabhupada.

Yamuna devi first met Srila Prabhupada in 1966, after traveling from her home in Oregon to the Lower East Side of New York for her sister Janaki’s marriage. From that moment in her life, she began her magical journey of transformation. In the pages of Yamuna Devi: A Life of Unalloyed Devotion we will join her on that journey and witness how almost everything Srila Prabhupada encouraged her to do, which was like the planting of a seed, soon blossomed into a flower that spread its fragrance across the world and created history.

At that first meeting in New York, Srila Prabhupada was personally cooking the wedding feast for her sister. He invited Yamuna to help him cook. She took that initial connection so seriously, and valued so deeply the opportunity to please her guru, that she was soon invited to be Srila Prabhupada’s cook. Bhakti means that everything we do, we do our very best, with a sincere intent to please Krishna. Taking this spirit to heart she dove deeper by studying and perfecting the culinary arts, all for the pleasure of her guru and Lord Krishna. Wishing to share this gift with everyone, she authored what became one of the most popular cookbooks of all time, awarded international cookbook of the year. Along with teaching hundreds of precise recipes, the book, in a gentle, gracious way, guides us into the internal world of pure devotion.

In 1967, in San Francisco, Srila Prabhupada encouraged her to lead others in kirtan, the chanting of Krishna’s names. Kirtan became her very life and soul. Having witnessed the profound humility and intense love of Srila Prabhupada as he chanted devotional prayers greatly impacted her. She chanted from the depths of her heart, calling out to Radha-Krishna for unalloyed loving service. Later, in London with her husband Guru das and friends Mukunda, Janaki, Shyamasundara, Malati and baby Saraswati, they chanted kirtan wherever they were allowed to do so. In those days they had little money, no fixed residence and were totally unknown.

When the Beatles were at the peak of their popularity, George Harrison had disguised himself and secretly attended their kirtan at an underground venue. When he first met Yamuna devi, he told her that her chanting mesmerized him. George invited Yamuna and her dear friends to record the “Hare Krishna Mantra” with Apple records. With Yamuna leading the chant, the record climbed to the top of the charts and was played everywhere. The devotees were invited on television, radio and to perform concerts. This was the first time in history that kirtan reached a vast audience of millions in the West.

Srila Prabhupada was immensely pleased. His pleasure was Yamuna’s most valued purpose and joy, in every aspect of her life. It was actually all she wanted. George was eager to make her a famous star, but she soon departed for India, preferring to do whatever meager service her guru asked of her. Throughout the world, in all ISKCON temples, the Supreme Lord is ceremoniously greeted just after sunrise with a recording of Yamuna devi sweetly singing, govindam adi purusham tarn aham bhajami. Srila Prabhupada called it a symphony of pure devotion.

Yet, despite the historic proportion of these and many more of her accomplishments, she gracefully shied away from receiving any honor or respect for herself. Her humility was genuine. Her greatest joy was to give all credit to her beloved guru and to all others.

Srila Prabhupada accepted her as one of his most trusted leaders and gave her essential responsibilities. He recognized her brilliant intelligence, incredible talents and total dedication. Yet, as you will read in this book, she was at times repressed, insulted and neglected. It was initially heartbreaking for her. Yet she internalized the experiences and went deeper and deeper into her own devotion, where she found the pure joy of Krishna’s love. Her life was a celebration of that love. With grace, dignity and respect for all, she strived to enlighten her devotional society with the true spirit of Srila Prabhupada’s compassion, for everyone.

Yamuna devi was extremely concerned for the future of her guru’s mission and the need to safeguard the purity of his teachings and practice. In this mood she was especially concerned for the youth. Although she had no biological children herself, as a loving spiritual mother she dedicated much of her time to inspire faith and provide clear direction for the second generation as no one else could do. I recall, during one of her visits to Mumbai, whenever she was asked to sing, in large or small gatherings, she excitedly arranged for the youth to sing instead. “Their devotion and their singing is far better than mine,” she would say, with all honesty. And when they sang she would close her eyes, smile and enter into a trance of spiritual joy. With her gravity, wisdom, humor, affection and soul-stirring kirtans she gave these young men and women an entrance into the magic of pure bhakti.

Yamuna devi deeply cared for every soul she encountered. In 2011, when she was about to leave the Bhaktivedanta Hospital after several months of treatment, she arranged a wonderful feast and personally crafted unique gifts for each and every person who had done anything for her. With tearful eyes she shared the message of her life—how by a sincere attempt at practicing devotional service and associating with a pure devotee, any life can be transformed and joyful. There was infinite hope for anyone who connected to the current of divine grace. Her words, infused with wholehearted faith and a lifetime of realizations, penetrated deeply. To bring her message deeper into their hearts, she then shared beautiful stories of her relationship with Srila Prabhupada. Her compassion, humility and truly nonenvi-ous nature transformed all present, who were unable to do anything but weep with joy and gratitude.

Over the years, hundreds of devotees appealed to Yamuna devi to write her memories. Feeling obliged, she did. But she anticipated that Srila Prabhupada would soon call for her. At that time she requested Dinatarini devi to complete the book in the event of her physical departure. Dinatarini was Yamuna’s closest associate for over thirty years. They shared one heart in their pure devotion to Srila Prabhupada, their appreciation of devotees and their compassion for all. It seems that Krishna personally orchestrated the relationship between these special souls as a blessing for everyone. Dinatarini devi accepted the service with humility and gratitude. We offer our eternal gratitude to her, along with Yamuna’s very dear spiritual children Kartamasa and Radhakunda, for seeing through this masterpiece of devotional literature.

"Yamuna Devi: A Life of Unalloyed Devotion" is an honest and sincere attempt to bring us into Yamuna devi’s extraordinary life. In every situation she sought the essence, and she offered her heart and soul to that essence. Please open your hearts and, through this book, allow Yamuna devi to share that essence with you.

Radhanath Swami

## Preface

IT WOULD NOT be an understatement to declare that Yamuna devi was reluctant to write both of her life and her years of service v as a beloved disciple of His Divine Grace A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada, and yet at each opportunity during his manifest presence she assiduously chronicled his teachings through her journals and recordings. Unfortunately, most of the journals were later lost, yet those that remain reveal a depth of sincerity of purpose and dedication to the practice of Krishna Consciousness which dehned and characterized her throughout her life. The reasons for this reluctance changed marginally over the years, and in one earlier writing attempt, she expressed her hesitancy:

**In the field of writing, I have been known as a cookbook author and food writer. Though often encouraged by others and yes, even prompted from within to write, for over thirty years the autobiographical book project has been placed on the metaphorical back burner. Even though my reasons not to write the book changed over time, some excuses seem as if chiseled in stone. A few enduring ones are: I may not be a good storyteller; I may be unable to write with resonance; I may be incapable of doing justice to its principal character, Srila Prabhupada; and finally, the most daunting—I may end up writing a stolid, egocentric “I-Me-My” book.**

Periodically over the last twenty years, Yamuna would become emboldened and enthusiastic to write. These endeavors were often preceded by her perusing books on writing techniques, followed by hours, days and weeks laboring at the computer, only for her to lose momentum when the result did not meet her expectations or if another “service” required her attention. Yamuna was always a perfectionist in every endeavor she undertook, and I often suspected that some of the other “services” were a means of avoidance. Then a very dramatic event occurred in 2003 at the Saranagati farm community in British Columbia where we then lived that again gave immediacy to the project. A massive forest fire threatened to decimate the entire 2,000-acre valley and its residences.

Initially Yamuna had gone to the Rathayatra festival in Vancouver, while I stayed back at our ashram, Radha-Banabehari Mandir. It was one of those magical, sunny days of summer, and I sat peacefully sewing while absorbed in Bada Hari prabhu’s lyrical prayer of Vasudeva Ghosh, “Gauranga tumi more”—the heartfelt plea of the devotee to Lord Chaitanya not to withhold His mercy. It is a prayer of sincere and deep urgency. At that moment I was interrupted by a persistent knocking on the door. On opening it, I found myself confronted by a policeman from the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, his stoic demeanor and starched and badged uniform almost comically at odds with the thick black column of choking smoke rising on the mountain directly behind him. He calmly informed me that I had 30 minutes to take whatever was important and immediately evacuate. I went from peaceful and absorbed to frantic in less than 30 seconds, and in a totally disoriented state I took our beloved Deities, Sri Sri Radha-Banabehari in Their traveling case, some of Their jewelry and clothes, and a few totally incongruous things, put everything in the truck, and left. The next day, Yamuna came back from Vancouver and, because the fire had temporarily shifted, the police allowed us to return to our homes to retrieve more valuables. Yamuna later wrote about that return trip:

**I arrived home to an August clear blue sky, with east and west mountain ridges that paralleled each other in our rectangular-shaped valley. Down its center, three glassy-smooth lakes mirrored the images of thick Douglas fir and pine forests. No man-made sounds, just nature, pretty much as it had been for thousands of years. When I was allowed to return to collect valuables, I saw—maybe a thousand yards away from our ashram behind the east ridge—a tsunami-like wall of crackling, jittery red, orange and yellow fire. A giant plane flew low, almost touching the treetops, and dropped blood-red retardant powder in huge swathes, and then, as if on cue, two helicopters appeared and dropped water on the flames. The firefighters were true heroes, working tirelessly around the clock to contain the massive blaze (one of hundreds that year in British Columbia), yet the fires continued to accelerate in almost predictable bursts. At the same time, the police were waiting for us to collect our valuables and evacuate. What items should I save? I surprised myself when I filled three garden-sized plastic bags with everything. I had collected over the years to write a memoir—the journals, taped interviews, original letters, boxes of photos and slides, unedited videotape footage, and a few stabs at chapter first drafts. Along with a pillow and quilt, I threw the bags into the back of the pickup and drove off to safety through clouds of choking black smoke. For the next two weeks neighbors helped neighbors, and everyone helped the firefighters, but in the end, it was the wind that saved the valley. Amazingly, it continually blew in a northward direction away from us. This incident helped me to understand that the memoir project meant more to me than I had been willing to acknowledge.**

From this point on, Yamuna became more invested in writing her memoirs, even as our lives became ever-increasingly engaged with programs and services in our ashram and community. Sometimes I would ask to read what she had written, and she would deftly evade my request by commenting that it was not yet ready to be seen or that she was only working on writing exercises. It was only after Yamuna passed away that I was finally able to read her precise and deeply devotional passages and then realized why she had so stealthily denied me access to them. I found, not surprisingly, that in almost every exchange or pastime with Srila Prabhupada she had featured in, or any programs, kirtans or ISKCON historical events at which she was a central participant, she had invariably minimized her importance in them. For instance, in her telling of the “Govindam” recording sessions, she became merely one of a choir of voices, or when Srila Prabhupada praised or recognized her in some way, she neatly ascribed it to another person. Knowing that I might read those entries and then vehemently object to her lack of specificity as to her own prominence in these pastimes, she kept them from me. This in itself speaks volumes about Yamuna’s character and qualities. Her nature was at once devoid of the desire for honor and recognition and relentlessly compassionate toward others. She would find ways to honor others for even the slightest service, and her character personified the devotional maxim of para dukha dukhi—unable to tolerate the discomfort of others. In one of her mice-eaten notebooks from Vrindavan, Yamuna carefully highlighted Srila Prabhupada’s comments from his Nectar of Devotion lectures describing a devotee’s nature:

**Pure devotional service automatically puts one in transcendental pleasure. In the material pleasure, if I see you happy, I am unhappy; if I see you unhappy, I become happy. This is nature. I may say otherwise, but material nature is, if one is put into difficulty, then I become very happy, and if I am happy, others become envious. This is material pleasure. Whereas spiritual pleasure means that when one sees Krishna is happy or a devotee is happy, the other devotee becomes happier.... This is the difference between spiritual pleasure and material pleasure. It is not difficult to understand. Material pleasure means if you are happy, I become unhappy; if you are unhappy, then I become happy. This is material pleasure. And spiritual pleasure means by seeing your happiness, I become happy.**

**— LECTURE, NOV. 3, I972**

As Yamuna’s health steadily deteriorated during the last few years of her life, it became apparent that she might not be able to complete the memoirs with the determination that she had committed to. Less than a month before her passing, she requested me to take up this mammoth project if she were unable to do so. Although I felt unqualified on many fronts, I agreed to her request, never thinking that I would actually have to do it. Yet the plan of the Lord is often inconceivable, and because I had given my word, I saw this project as my opportunity to honor and memorialize this extraordinary devotee from the vantage point of being her companion of the last 37 years.

More importantly, I began to see this as a blessing in disguise for several reasons. Had Yamuna written this as her personal memoir, it would only have detailed her years during Srila Prabhupada’s manifest presence with us. And yet Yamuna devi’s contribution to Srila Prabhupada’s mission reached far beyond those twelve years, for she not only served him and assimilated his teachings, but she unreservedly dedicated the remainder of her life to their practice and dissemination. I began to see this memoir/biography as an opportunity to exalt the process of Krishna Consciousness through the extraordinary devotional journey of Yamuna devi, who personified not only how to live a life of dedication, but how to lovingly and compassionately give it to others.

Yamuna always stressed to others that Krishna Consciousness is a “process,” and not an expression of mundane sentiment. She emphasized in her writings, emails, classes, conversations and at every possible opportunity that we have been given such a unique and unequalled gift by Srila Prabhupada, our lineage of great Acharyas and Sri Chaitanya Maha-prabhu, and that we have to take this gift to heart through its practice. Yamuna often mentioned that sometimes after giving her an instruction, Srila Prabhupada would punctuate it by telling her to just “Take it.” He emphasized that he had given us everything required to become perfected in devotional service, but we needed to sincerely engage in the practice of bhakti—not just for our own advancement, but so we could pass on this great treasure of Krishna Consciousness to others.

Yamuna was the living embodiment of those two words of Srila Prabhupada. She deeply imbibed the teachings of Srila Prabhupada. Taking them as her life and soul, she practiced Krishna Consciousness throughout the remainder of her life, and then with great feeling, selflessness and open-hearted love, she freely gave the gift of bhakti to others.

The lives of so many people around the world were touched by Yamuna devi. She had that inexplicable ability to make every person she connected with feel as though she had known and cared for them forever. Whether it was those she personally interacted with or those who were transformed through her kirtans, her cookbooks or by her living example, she tirelessly enthused others through her own simple yet compelling presentation of Krishna bhakti.

Throughout her Krishna Conscious life, but especially during the last ten years, Yamuna made a special effort to connect with the younger generations. She had an enduring empathy for the difficulties they faced in trying to become Krishna Conscious in a world with multiple attractions, not just in the material sphere, but also in the often-confusing spiritual one. Every one of the younger “friends” she mentored over the years heard her message about making the process of Krishna Consciousness real and heartfelt. Yet I feel equally certain that they would all say that it was by actually seeing in her the living process of Krishna bhakti—through her personal example—that most inspired and encouraged them. Simply put, Yamuna embodied everything we are promised if we honestly and sincerely take to the process of Krishna Consciousness—joy, an impassioned love for chanting the Holy Names, selflessness, compassion, mercifulness, humility, the quality of being nonjudgmental—she personified what it meant to “preach by example.”

This memoir and biography is not intended as a history of ISKCON itself, although we have tried to be accurate as to time and place. Neither is it intended as a revisiting or retelling of other histories and remembrances already written. Rather, it is a chronicle of the extraordinary devotional odyssey of Yamuna devi—a journey of the spirit from curiosity-seeker, to knowledge-seeker, to transformation through meeting Srila Prabhupada, to commitment to the process, to assimilation of Srila Prabhupada’s teachings, to dedication to the practice, to devotional maturation, and finally to disseminating bhakti to others. It is my sincere wish that those who read this offering will be encouraged in their own practice or, if new to the great treasure of Krishna Consciousness, will dive into the nectarean ocean of its possibilities. In advance, I apologize for any unintentional inconsistencies or offenses. In the mood of trying to thread a camel through the eye of a needle, this project is a humble attempt to memorialize the life of an extraordinary devotee, Yamuna devi, with whom I had the great blessing of her association and companionship for most of my adult life.

Much of the source material not written specifically by Yamuna devi for the memoirs comes either from informal talks, lectures, letters, remembrances or personal reflections given by her which were recorded. Also included are personal recollections of devotees and material gathered from her journals, drafts of earlier books and emails. What is not included in the written text will be added to the website, along with her songs, pictures, some of her calligraphy, design work and email exchanges.

Your servant with gratitude, Dinatarini devi dasi

I freely gave my assurance, while fully believing that I would never actually be called upon to honor it. Yet almost immediately after her death, despite my grief, feelings of inadequacy and lack of qualification, I felt compelled to share her inspirational journey of unalloyed devotion with others. The small seed of that promise, watered through incessant prayer and nurtured by the encouragement and assistance of friends and well wishers, has grown into the tree of the Unalloyed: The Yamuna Devi Legacy Project.

## Chapter 1

**A Gathering of Ingredients. Earle life 1942-1965**

SRILA BHAKTISIDDHANTA SARASWATI Thakur was once asked why the Lord’s devotees sometimes come from undistinguished backgrounds or are poor, uneducated or physically challenged. He replied:

**Devotees are never subject to the results of their karma. It is by the will of the Lord that they take birth and perform other pastimes. But when it is seen that they are born in low-class families, are illiterate, or are disease-ridden, we should know that there is a great or noble purpose behind it. If people saw that devotees were always born in high-class families or were always strong or educated, then they would become discouraged. So the merciful Lord, in order to benefit people of all classes, sends His devotees to different classes of society to give His mercy to other living entities.... Srila Vrindavan das Thakur has said in the Chaitanya Bhagavat that a Vaishnava delivers everyone just by taking birth. In a land and in a family where a Vaishnava descends, many hundreds of miles around that place become purified by his influence.**

**— SRILA SARASWATI THAKUR**

## Sowing the Seeds of Devotion— Butte, Montana

This statement of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati can manifestly be seen in Yamuna devi’s derivation. Born in a remote mining community in Montana— her father’s occupation is listed as “butcher” on her birth certificate—she remembered a rugged existence meager in material amenities yet rich in familial love. Reflecting fondly on those years, she recalled being nurtured by a mostly female coterie of relatives who kindled her imaginative spirit from infancy using the richness of the natural landscape as their palette. She thrived in this environment and derived from it a deeply affecting appreciation of nature that endured throughout her life.

In 1996, during one of our cross-country forays, Yamuna and I stopped in Butte, Montana, the place of her birth. She had not returned since 1949, and as we drove up and down the eerily vacant streets, Yamuna stared in wideeyed amazement at the still-standing buildings familiar from her youth.

**Yamuna**: *I was shocked to see Butte for the first time since my childhood, and felt like I had entered a land where time stood still. The brown brick and stone buildings in the town center, their walls bearing faded advertisements for long-forgotten businesses, stood as empty reminders of former prosperous times. Dozens of abandoned mining derricks still dotted the landscape around Butte just as I remembered them through my child’s eye a half century ago. And yet, where were the rich and vibrant hills full of natural wonders I so cherished in my childhood—those undulating meadows full of wildflowers where I first felt the presence of God in His creation? I knew that what had appeared as mountains in my childhood would in fact be much smaller in adulthood, and even toyed briefly with this as an explanation for the complete topographic changes before me. Had I created the landscape I remembered as a child in my fertile imagination as one creates an imaginary friend? I did not think so, and Dina and I spent the next day researching the history of Butte to find the truth.*

Butte had long been known as a mining town, the hills or “buttes” surrounding it filled with gold, copper and silver ore. During the years Yamuna lived there, mining was done the old-fashioned way by digging and drilling underground, a process considered expensive and labor-intensive by the big mining companies. To remedy this, in the early fifties they started strip mining—literally blasting away the hilltops with explosives to expose the rich ore veins—thereby leaving the topography surrounding Butte virtually unrecognizable to Yamuna. Although this new mining technology leveled many of the surrounding neighborhoods of Butte, the residents basically accepted it as a necessary concession to the job opportunities it provided. We left Butte after two days, and whenever Yamuna referenced it later on, she would say that in this material world there is constant change, but in the midst of such changes, we have to remain unchanged in our dedication to Guru and Krishna—they are the only true constants.

## An Unheralded Lineage

Photographs from her early childhood paint a colorful and enigmatic portrait of Yamuna’s family. In one, her parents, Mary Lee and Sam Campanella, sit on a manicured lawn with infant Joanie, her mother’s smiling countenance at odds with her father’s stern, almost forbidding glare. Another, taken a year later, shows Yamuna standing between her father and grandfather against the backdrop of their roughhewn log cabin. Although primitive by Western standards, with no running water or electricity, Yamuna remembered it as being solid and cozy, with the ever-present wonderful scent of bread baking in the wood cook stove:

**Yamuna**: *My mother and her sister Agnes were camping in Yellowstone National Park when mom went into labor with me. When both of them figured that mine might be a difficult birth, Agnes drove mother to a hospital in Butte. Within two hours of my mother arriving there, I was born on May 19,1942, and named Joan Agnes Campanella. Two hours after that all three of us went home to the log cabin my father and grandfather had built the year before.*

*Many children born during the World War II* *years experienced a freedom derived from the fact that their parents were in some way engaged in the war effort. At a very young age we took on grown-up responsibilities and learned to sense the difference between what was safe and what was dangerous. I had the added benefit of living close to nature, my friends, the grand energies—the earth, trees, creeks, sky, meadows, mountains, caves, animals, birds and insects. We had our secret, private “hidey” spots known to no one. I lived the first six years of my life in such an idyllic environment, oblivious to the perilous condition of the world and even within my own family.*

*My first memory was at age two, sitting on my aunt’s lap in a rocking chair by the wood cook stove. Our woodstove served three purposes: heat, cooking our meals, and our livelihood. To support us, almost every evening mother baked batches of Cornish potato pasties. They were then sold to single Welsh and Irish miners who appeared early in the mornings and carried them off in their lunchboxes to the mines.*

*My father, Sam Campanella, went off to fight in World War 1I shortly after I was born, returned for a brief period that produced my younger sister Janice Marie, and then came back to divorce my mother when I was seven. There always remained a furtive mystery surrounding their marriage and subsequent separation, one that neither my sister nor I were ever able to elicit from our tight-lipped aunts. We were simply informed that he died and accepted it without question, until he turned up very much alive in our adulthood. But that is another story.*

*Without electricity in the log cabin, we had no radio for news or entertainment. Television was not around yet and movies beyond our reach. We had few toys and virtually no other childhood friends. In this setting, my sister and I lived in a richly-constructed imaginative world. We played outdoors in the fresh air and were comfortable creating our own amusements and excitements. I confidently pulled my sister in a little red wagon the half-mile to visit our grandmother; we helped her cook and do chores, ate sweet cookies and drank fresh milk. We knew paths hewn in rock that would lead us to spots where mountain goats with curved horns played. We knew where and when the prettiest spring wildflowers bloomed in the meadow above our house, and we learned how to make lovely flower garland chains to give as gifts to mother and Aunt Agnes. We had no money for bicycles, so we walked everywhere. We climbed trees and swam when it was warm enough. These formative years nurtured within me a lifelong appreciation of the peaceful and sonorous rhythms of nature.*

In her later years, whenever she felt overwhelmed or overextended, Yamuna could often be found working in the gardenplanting, weeding, raking, harvesting flowers and vegetables or just sitting outside in her rocking chair, beads rhythmically clicking in her hand, taking solace in the same sonorous rhythms in this time-honored way. Almost invariably after the morning program she would make her way outside, whether winter, spring, summer or fall, and do everything from building rock walls, to enticing flowers to grow in recalcitrant soil. She was tireless in her outdoor pursuits and when she was no longer physically able to exert the energy she once had, she would pace herself, sitting and chanting, then again doing “outdoor meditation,” as she called it. I learned long ago never to challenge her by declaring a task too difficult or beyond the capabilities of her age or health. If she decided to build a rock-walled garden at 65 years old, she would drive our old truck repeatedly up into the hills, filling its bed each time with massive rocks. She would then unload them and build the walls with each rock neatly intersected into the next like a mosaic. With every outdoor project, she would work for days or weeks on end until it was done to her satisfaction. In fact, to the very end, she somehow always found remarkable reserves of energy. When the doctors told me that all of the arteries in her heart were blocked and she had been living on what they call coronary collaterals, no one was more stunned than I because she always worked longer and harder, with more dedication and determination than any of us.

## First Tenuous Steps in Spiritual Life

In looking back through the prism of her life, Yamuna would sometimes comment on how propensities and talents which emerged with apparent randomness in her early years later proved to be useful or necessary components of her devotional life. A natural and gifted inquisitor, she would spontaneously ask others to comment on the awakening of their spiritual propensities. “How did you first become interested in spiritual life?” was an often-heard query.

**Yamuna**: *My family came from the Catholic tradition and, as is so often the case, the elder women of the family were the most devout. They would tell us stories about saints and martyrs, about people who were noble and sacrificed themselves for God and mankind. I was fascinated by these stories, and my interest in God—in dedicating myself to serving God—manifested at an early age with the determination to become a nun. To humor me, my mother even made a nun’s habit for me. More than anything this highlighted the character of my mother in those days—that despite our penury, despite her marital and other problems, she always tried to nourish the creative propensities of my sister and myself by allowing our dreams and fantasies to take flight.*

*I don’t have a specific memory of Holy Communion, but I remember attending church with a group of young children where we were asked to confess our sins before God and His representative, the priest. Since I could not remember committing any sins, when I entered the smoothly-polished confession booth, I frankly told the priest I had nothing to confess. To my dismay he sternly assured me that each of us has sins to confess and I was certainly no different. So in my desire to be obedient, I made up a few perceived “sins.” It didn’t occur to me at the time that now I had actually committed the sin of untruth, but I was far more worried about displeasing the priest.*

Later, in her early years with Srila Prabhupada, on more than one occasion Yamuna committed the same transgression by embroidering the truth rather than incurring his displeasure with either herself or anyone else. An early example Yamuna remembered with some remorse was her deflection of Srila Prabhupada’s queries as to the whereabouts of her sister Janaki. “Why was Janaki not at the temple today?” he would ask. Yamuna would reply that she was sick or shopping or encumbered in some other way, which prevented her from coming. In truth, she did not want Srila Prabhupada to think that she was purposely avoiding the programs, nor did she want Janaki to be chastised. Of course, she later realized that Srila Prabhupada had always known the situation perfectly.

## Emergence of the Creative Spirit

**Yamuna**: *When I was seven, my mother moved us to Klamath Falls, Oregon, to live with our Aunt Edna and Uncle Dean Howell. Aunt Edna owned the Normadean Dance Studio, and I immediately became a dedicated and disciplined student of ballet. This was prompted by my having seen my first movie, a ballet film called “The Red Shoes.” I practiced for hours each day, seven days a week, the same ballet positions again and again, determined to become a prima ballerina like the heroine of the film.*

In a picture from this time, Yamuna stands in a ballet pose, a look of serious determination on her face. She is graceful, poised, with a maturity far beyond her years. In fact, she was so gifted that she won successive summer scholarships to the famed San Francisco Ballet Company with the assumption that upon graduation she would join their corps de ballet. And yet, as she grew, it became apparent that she would not have the physical body type required of a ballet dancer, and reluctantly she was forced to relinquish that dream.

Throughout her life Yamuna was a perfectionist, and the patience and determination to do something over and over again until it was acceptable to her high standards was a well-known feature of her personality. This would later be evidenced not only in the standard of her service to Srila Prabhupada, but in virtually everything she did. I witnessed many occasions over the years where Yamuna would painstakingly work on something for long periods only to take it apart over a perceived defect no one else could see. She wanted her service to be of the highest quality, and if she saw a flaw, she would say that Krishna would see the flaw as her insincerity.

When Yamuna was eleven, her mother married Bob Oslund, a lawyer, and the family moved to Salem, Oregon. The marriage and move dramatically enhanced their financial and social positions. Mary Lee went from working full time as a struggling single mother to a life of privilege—entertaining lavishly, joining the country club, and golfing with her friends. Yamuna was enrolled at Salem Junior High School, where she met Sam Speerstra, later Shyamasundara das, a friend whose life would take a similar spiritual trajectory to her own:

**Yamuna**: *I remember meeting Sam on fall orientation day at school. As fate would have it, he sat in an adjoining desk behind mine. Being somewhat mischievous by nature, Sam decided to dip my braids in his inkwell. When a nearby classmate whispered that trails of ink were dripping off my braids and down the back of my sweater, I froze, stunned, and whipped my head around to see who had done this to me. At the same moment that I felt ink seeping onto my bare skin, I saw Sam’s astonished face—open-jawed, wide-eyed, and splattered with ink that had jetted off my soaked braids. It was such a ludicrous sight that I began to laugh, then he laughed, then the whole class laughed. We all continued to laugh at laughing itself, all except the teacher, who of course found no humor at all in this disruptive behavior.*

The next year the family moved to Lake Oswego, Oregon. Yamuna and her sister had taken the last name “Oslund,” realizing much later that their new stepfather had never officially adopted them. Although this marriage was already fraught with difficulties, Mary Lee was determined to somehow make it work, if only to give her daughters the opportunities their social position now afforded. In later life, Yamuna revisited those years infrequently, but her school yearbooks reveal a popular and charismatic student. She was a member of the cheerleading squad and the Homecoming Court, the French Club and American Heritage Society. Summers were spent picking strawberries and green beans on farms in the Willamette Valley for “clothes money,” an activity both parents felt to be character-building. Mary Lee also taught her daughters the all-important domestic skills expected of all proper young girls—how to keep house and how to cook. It was from her mother that Yamuna imbibed the neatness, cleanliness and love of order that were her prominent character traits. These qualities in Yamuna were often noted or acclaimed by Srila Prabhupada in later years.

Throughout our travels over the years, whatever Yamuna filled any drawer, pantry, cabinet or closet with was always perfectly and even artistically arranged. One example was her famous collection of “sweetie jars” from England. We carried this collection of about 50 two-liter glass jars around the world for over 30 years because Yamuna liked the size and square shape of them. She even designed and built her kitchen pantry at our Saranagati ashram to exactly fit their dimensions.

**Yamuna**: *My mother was an instinctive and creative cook, often having special ingredients flown in from all over the country to create her culinary masterpieces. She was also meticulous and emphasized the necessity of cleaning as we cooked. She taught us how to make different types of dough for baking, basic sauces that could be universally used in a multitude of preparations, and a variety of jams and jellies. I learned from her not only the basic elements of the cooking art, but also the importance of cleanliness and quality, two principles later affirmed by Srila Prabhupada.*

## Nascent Philosophies

The religious ardor so deeply felt in Yamuna’s early years became submerged by the complexities of student life in the 50’s. It was a time rigidly circumscribed by its hierarchical social structure, its etiquettes and its stigmas. Young ladies wore angora sweaters, poodle skirts and bobby sox, and attended carefully chaperoned school dances, or “hops.” There was little opportunity for nurturing ideas antithetical to the social and cultural ethos of the times. With her warm, engaging personality, attractive appearance and quick wit, Yamuna prospered during these years, yet she was beginning to question the social mores, considering them shallow and elitist. She made a conscious effort not to exclude others and was naturally friendly and broad-minded.

Although an avowed agnostic, Yamuna’s mother Mary Lee was intelligent and philosophically inclined. She encouraged her daughters to expand their metaphysical horizons and was especially enamored by the poetic credo of Khalil Gibran, often reading to them at night from his opus, The Prophet:

- Is not religion all deeds and all reflection?
- And that which is neither deed nor reflection, but a wonder and a surprise ever springing in the soul, even while the hands hew the stone or tend the loom?
- Who can separate his faith from his actions, or his belief from his occupations?
- Who can spread his hours before him, saying, “This for God and this for myself; This for my soul, and this other for my body?”

This was perhaps Yamuna’s first exposure to unorthodox expressions of spirituality. Though she was receptive, it would not be until her first year in college that she would become a true “seeker.” It was then that the pivotal questions in life of “Who am 1?", “Who is God?”, and “Why am I here?” sprang to the forefront of her consciousness. In the meantime, she continued to develop her interest in practical arts and crafts, which would later serve her well in her devotional life:

**Yamuna:** *Between my junior and senior year at Lake Oswego High School, I won a summer scholarship to travel on the East Coast with the American Heritage Tour. One of the destinations was the Smithsonian Institute in Washington DC, which was hosting an exhibition of some of the world’s finest examples of ancient and contemporary calligraphy. While perusing the calligraphy contained in several rooms, I became fascinated by this elegant and enduring art, determining on the spot to try and learn it, study it, become good at it—maybe even make a living with it.*

In 1960, Yamuna graduated from high school and enrolled in the University of Oregon in Eugene. In the yearbook from Lake Oswego High School, she was given the honor of “Most Witty” by the student body. Although she had never mentioned this in all the years I knew her, it did not surprise me, for she had an insatiable and subtle wit that was simultaneously self-effacing and profound. In her later years, even with her health declining at an impossibly alarming rate, she often found humor in it. Throughout her prolonged stay at the Bhaktivedanta Hospital in Mumbai and during her last months in Florida, she would often spontaneously mimic or express something with such humor that those around her would be reduced to tears of laughter. And yet, she could revert from such light humor to become sober and grave at a moment’s notice, especially when speaking of Srila Prabhupada.

As a graduation gift, Yamuna was given a blue MG sports car as a reward for her achievements. She had always been an obedient daughter and had every intention of fulfilling the wishes of her parents by furthering her education. And yet, unbeknownst to anyone, her future was to take a course no one could have imagined. She wrote of this time:

**Yamuna:** *I drove down the Interstate to my first semester at the University of Oregon full of the anticipation that springs from hope for the future. There was some trepidation because, externals aside, I didn’t quite fit into the mold of collegiate womanhood despite my well-turned-out look. My first two weeks in a female freshman dormitory felt as a kind of hell to me; the second two weeks were worse. My core distaste arose from the intrinsic sorority subculture. Everyone went through a sort of evaluation process called “rush,” where you visited many sorority houses and, if you were among the chosen, you “pledged” their ranks. The whole process seemed shallow, artificial and elitist to me. By the end of six weeks of this, I clearly understood that I was not meant for the life of a sorority girl, living the sorority way. It intensified within me my growing dissatisfaction with the status quo, along with an inner yearning to find real meaning and purpose to my life. My internal mantra became “Why am I here?” a mantra that applied both to my collegiate experience and life in general. I found myself driving to Portland on weekends, staying with friends, and visiting offbeat coffee houses, going to offbeat poetry readings and listening to offbeat music.*

After one semester, Yamuna dropped out of university, her first major act of rebellion, and one that had immediate repercussions. Her parents, deeply disappointed, withdrew their financial support, and for the first time she was on her own:

**Yamuna***: Although I promised my parents that I would continue my education in Portland, they calmly informed me that I would have to pay for it myself. That meant immediately finding a job, a place to live, and looking into school options. It was then that I remembered my previous determination to study calligraphy. I got a night-shift job working for a bank and a part-time day job as a sales clerk in Portland’s largest department store. To save money, I shared a basement studio apartment with Eve, my best high school friend. One day, while browsing through a book store looking for names of nearby calligraphy teachers, I stared in stunned disbelief when I found that one of the world’s most renowned calligraphy teachers, Lloyd J. Reynolds, lived and taught in Portland at Reed College and the Portland Art Museum. Then and there I determined to become his student.*

During this time Yamuna cultivated new friendships and again met her friend from the seventh grade, Sam, now part of the Reed College student community, along with his friend Michael Grant, who would later marry her sister Jan. Who could have imagined that within a few years destiny would bring all four together under the shelter of His Divine Grace A. C. Bhaktivedanta Swami Prabhupada? Yamuna used to say that looking back in retrospect at these seemingly coincidental happenings, and seeing so clearly the loving hand of the Lord gently guiding her closer to Him, always brought tears of gratitude and increased her faith and conviction.

**Yamuna:** *That winter I began taking calligraphy, graphic arts and pottery courses at Reed College. The following year, in 1962,I continued this type of education at the Portland Art Museum and Portland State College, adding weaving to my craft-heavy curriculum.*

Over the course of two years, Yamuna devoted herself to the study of calligraphy under Lloyd Reynolds, a brilliant and charismatic teacher who inspired his students to such an extent that even reports and theses on disparate subjects at Reed College were often submitted beautifully hand-calligraphed. Reynolds, with his wide-ranging interests in philosophy and spirituality, encouraged Yamuna not only in the calligraphic arts, but also in her first serious exploration of countercultural religious thought, specifically that of Zen Buddhism.One well-known student of calligraphy at Reed College later spoke about the program there:

**Reed College at that time offered perhaps the best calligraphy instruction in the country. Throughout the campus, every poster, every label on every drawer, was beautifully hand-calligraphed. Because I had dropped out and didn’t have to take normal classes, I decided to take a calligraphy class to learn how to do this. I learned about serif and sans serif typefaces, about varying the amount of space between different letter combinations, about what makes great typography great. It was beautiful, historical, artistically subtle in a way that science can’t capture, and I found it fascinating. None of this had even a hope of any practical application in my life. But ten years later, when we were designing the first Macintosh computer, it all came back to me. And we designed it all into the Mac. It was the first computer with beautiful typography.**

**— STEVE JOBS, STANFORD COMMENCEMENT ADDRESS 2005**

Later, when Srila Prabhupada first saw examples of Yamuna’s calligraphic skill, he immediately engaged her in making invitations, membership certificates for 1SKCON, life membership forms, posters, and sometimes letters. He would, on occasion, show guests something she had calligraphed, proudly displaying her elegant handwriting in the same way he would later highlight her consummate culinary and kirtan abilities.

Another friend of Sam’s was David, a brilliant crafts-man who Yamuna met in a pottery class at Reed College. A man of many skills, including ceramics, sandal making and wood-working, he shared many of Yamuna’s artistic visions and would become her first partner in life.

Yamuna entered into the study of the ceramic arts with the same single-minded determination and intensity she had dedicated to the study of calligraphy. After initial pottery courses in Portland, she determined to continue her studies by seeking out the best teachers, eventually studying under famed ceramic artist Marguerite Wildenhain at her Pond Farm studio near Guerneville, California.

**Yamuna**: *We rarely kept any of the pots we made while studying under Marguerite Wildenhain. For eight hours a day we threw the same style of pot, each a little piece of perfection to our eyes, and then she had us destroy them and perform the same task again. Though onerous, this teaching style was so effective that each of us eventually felt that we could create our ceramic masterpieces blindfolded. I became even more determined that I would use my love of pottery and calligraphy to somehow make my way in life by showcasing these ancient and exquisite arts that were fast becoming lost to modernity.*

## A Death in the Family — The Passing of Mary lee

Despite holding down two jobs and maintaining a heavy load of studies in Portland, Yamuna often visited her mother and sister in nearby Lake Oswego. Mary Lee had developed a severe form of colitis that eventually devastated virtually all of the organs in her body. Practical and scientific to the end, she requested that when she died her body be donated to science to help in finding both a cause and cure for this wasting disease. Yamuna remembered both she and her mother becoming more philosophical as the disease progressed:

**Yamuna**: *My mother was feeling great pain and discomfort, yet to some degree she remained stoic. With each visit I noticed that her perspective was becoming more philosophical. Knowing that death was near, she realized that everything she had aspired for and achieved materially had not made her happy. I had no answers for her—only ineffectual attempts to comfort her and ease her pain. Seeing my once vibrant and so alive mother in this wasted and painful condition made me feel helpless and disturbed, yet looking down at the emaciated and diseased body before me, I became convinced that my mother was not this body—that it was only a shell meant to be donated to science, and that she would continue to exist, at once vibrant and so alive, somewhere else. This conviction astonished me because I had never before given much thought to reincarnation. And yet it was as real and conclusive to me as the certainty of the sunrise.*

Mary Lee passed away when Yamuna was still 20 and \]an only 17. It was a time of great upheaval. Jan lived with her stepfather for a short time, then moved to Los Angeles with their Aunt Ricky, who was going through an acrimonious divorce. In a state of continuous flux, she eventually returned to Portland where her stepfather had found another wife and new stepchildren. Jan, still traumatized by her mother’s death and stepfather’s remarriage, got a job at a bank and tried to adjust to the new reality, yet she increasingly felt like an outsider.

In 1963, Yamuna’s dream to use her pottery, calligraphic and weaving skills to make a living became a reality when she moved to San Francisco and became co-owner of a craft shop on Grant Avenue in North Beach with her partner, David.

**San Francisco in the Early 60s**

In the early 60s, before the hippies, before the flower-power generation, the North Beach area of San Francisco was the dynamic hub of the “Beat Generation” (whose iconic name was derived from the writings of Jack Kerouac). An eclectic domicile of bohemian thought, this phenomenon both inspired and nurtured writers, poets, artists and musicians alike. The ubiquitous “beatniks,” in their stereotypical uniform of black turtleneck shirts and pants with accompanying berets, met to share ideas and listen to bebop jazz or folk music at so-called “discovery clubs” like Coffee and Confusion, the Hungry I and the Purple Onion, or congregated at the City Lights Bookshop or Coexistence Bagel Shop to expound esoteric philosophy, poetry, literature, or anti-establishment political dogma. It was an era defined by its promulgation and open-armed acceptance of freedom of thought, and two oft-discussed themes were Eastern religion and the rejection of materialism.

Yamuna, already questioning material stereotypes and values, felt at home in this environment and was allured by its creative magnetism and utopian ideals. Here she rekindled her previous interest in Zen Buddhism and began reading books on yoga, particularly Paramahamsa Yogananda’s Autobiography of a Yogi. In rereading this book many years later in preparation for her own memoir, she recalled:

**Yamuna**: *Until I read Autobiography of a Yogi, I did not know what “guru” meant, nor did I understand the importance of finding a self-realized soul to act as one’s guide along the spiritual path. Though I could not put it into context at the time, this telling of Yogananda’s search for a guru kindled in me the spark of a smoldering fire to find the highest spiritual truth—to go to the highest place. When I later met Srila Prabhupada, that smoldering fire in the heart ignited into a conflagration of purpose and determination. In him I had found that spiritual guide so many have searched for in vain.*

Yamuna’s apartment above the shop on Grant Avenue became a popular gathering place for artists, musicians and intellectuals. In contrast to the prevailing laxity of the times, Yamuna kept a very clean and orderly apartment, with abundant flowers and examples of her crafts prominently displayed. She would cook delicious meals, freely serving them to anyone who came, and was already becoming known for her cooking skills. The gracious and empathetic nature which defined and characterized her throughout her life drew people to her, and she in turn nurtured and fed them. Many of the musicians and artists who later became famous ate at Yamuna’s generous table during their leaner times.

Still, the early idealism of bohemian San Francisco that initially so charmed Yamuna all too quickly became overshadowed by its emphasis on drugs and promiscuity as its means of free expression and self-realization. Though she later remembered these times as pivotal, especially in evoking her latent spirituality, Yamuna became disgusted with the baser aspects of the prevailing subculture and eventually returned to Portland. She moved into an old Victorian house next door to her old friend Sam and his girlfriend Melanie.

## New Awakenings

Meanwhile Yamuna’s sister Jan, unable to cope with the onslaught of tragic and disorienting events of the last few years, attempted suicide. Under Oregon law, she was remanded to the state psychiatric hospital, and on her release, Yamuna, now her only immediate family, brought her home to live with her.

**Yamuna:** *On the day of her release, Jan was coiled up inside herself, tenuous, but eager to champion a new life. She suggested that we celebrate sisterhood and cook an Italian meal together. So that’s what we did. We harvested herbs, tomatoes, peppers and zucchini from the garden, made bread dough, and got a vegetable tomato sauce going. In the crisp air of early fall, we strolled up to the grocery and shopped for other staples— mozzarella, ricotta, lasagna noodles, and fresh fruit for dessert. Jan was a creative, natural cook, and I enjoyed our shared bonding experience.*

When we arrived home from the store, Michael Grant, my friend from Reed College days, was sitting on the porch. A talented musician and composer, he had come from New York to visit family in Portland. He stayed for our special dinner and immediately connected with Jan. She had been engulfed in sadness and tumult over the last years, and the bohemian-looking jazz musician with pierced ear and an adventuresome spirit seemed just the antidote she needed. Within a week she had driven off with him to New York to begin a new life.

## Chapter 2

**On Winget Feet (New York 1966)**

OVER THE YEARS Yamuna often spoke about the inconceivable sacrifices Srila Prabhupada made to pioneer the Krishna Consciousness Movement in the West. Barely two months before she passed away, we reread his letters from 1965 and 1966, which describe in sometimes excruciating detail the hardships he faced in coming to the West. She found reminiscing and speaking about those trying times enhanced both her faith and strength. “What if he had gone back to India, as he hinted in several of his late 1965 letters?” Such reminiscences could cause Yamuna to burst into a spontaneous singing of Srila Prabhupada’s “Had you not come, who would have told, the message of Krishna, forceful and bold” verse from his “Adore ye” homage to Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakur.

## The Bowery—"A Kind of Hell to Me”

**Yamuna**: *After she moved to New York, Jan and I maintained a sometimes thoughtful, often amusing exchange of letters. When I thought of her new life there, I conjured up visions of the New York I had seen in sleek magazines like the New Yorker and Harper’s Bazaar. Yet Jan’s New York was quite different from what I envisaged. To my increasing dismay, she painted in broad strokes the colors and textures of their lives there. Comparing their Bowery neighborhood to an amplified version of Portland’s wino district on Burnside, she vividly evoked its heavy liquor smells and juke box music oozing out of the many taverns and bars on each block. Their third floor walk-up loft fronted Bowery Street, and she casually wrote of having to step over sleeping drunks to enter her building. It seemed a kind of hell to me.*

The Lower East Side of New York in the early to mid-1960s, though gritty and unfashionable, was a haven for artists and bohemians, who crowned it the “New Bohemia.” It can only be imagined how those free spirits appeared to the immigrant Ukrainians, Poles and other ethnic minorities who also called this home. Somehow they peacefully coexisted in low-rent buildings, the artists, poets and musicians seeing it as a fusion of creative minds, and the immigrants as their ticket to a better life.

Yamuna, the ever-protective older sister, was alarmed that they lived in New York’s infamous Bowery neighborhood, the acknowledged “skid row” of Manhattan, teeming with drunks, drug addicts and vagrants—an area considered squalid even by Lower East Side standards.

**Jan**: *We lived in a third floor loft apartment in the Bowery section of New York. This was before it became a “hip” place to live. I remember the strong smell of urine, and intoxicated men with bottles in brown bags staggering or simply lying in alcoves and doorways, either sleeping, passed out or dead. It was surreal.*

*Our loft was one big room, no dividers or separations, and so I made rice paper walls and divided it that way. It was essentially a music studio. Mike had two pianos, a harpsichord, drums, several brass and other kinds of instruments. I remember it always being filled with people—musicians jamming or people just hanging out. These were not ordinary musicians but professionals, some of them legends in their field, and in that way it was a happening place. Mike had an arrangement with the tavern next door, and so when I needed space, I would go there with a book and they’d sit me in a back booth with a coke and keep a kind of protective eye on me.*

Mike was a talented jazz musician and composer, and so this loft seemed suited to his lifestyle and budget. But Yamuna worried about Jan, who had only recently overcome serious mental health issues. Her worries were in no way alleviated by Jan’s letters, which continued to paint ever more vivid portraits of their neighborhood.

**Yamuna**: *Jan writes that the Bowery is covered in a patina of grime—grimy buildings, grimy dress, grimy food. The foul-smelling winos, or street drunks, with their hollow, sunken eyes, are everywhere, their only possession the ubiquitous brown bags of cheap liquor. This does not sound like a place she would be comfortable in at all. Why would anyone choose to live in such a place?*

Yamuna, though troubled by concerns over her sister’s life, was herself at an impasse. Her creative and brilliant partner, David, in whom she had invested her future hopes, became heavily involved in the drug culture, and she became disillusioned that the once progressive idealism of the early 60s was now becoming debased by drug-taking, promiscuity and indolence. She was ready for a change in her life, but had no idea how or in what way it would manifest. I can only imagine her at this crossroads, as Yamuna was nothing if not steady and resolute, and change did not come easily to her.

## An Invitation to a “Hindu” Wedding

In the summer of 1966, Yamuna received two letters in quick succession from Jan. The first informed her that she and Mike had met an Indian “holy man” and were taking classes from him; the second was an invitation of sorts to their “Hindu” wedding.

**Yamuna**: *In her last missive, Jan informed me that she and Mike had met an Indian holy man, an elderly Bengali gentleman who wears saffron robes, white plastic shoes, and strange hats, and they’ve been going to his storefront temple to learn Indian music and philosophy. She matter-of-factly said that he was a “bona fide swami” who teaches something called bhakti-yoga, and they were going to be “initiated” as his students. I was taken back, to say the least. What does this mean? What kind of holy man? What was a “bona fide swami”? Does he speak in mystical parables? Perform miracles? Zap people with currents of wisdom? My only prior references to Indian holy men were the Dalai Lama and Yogananda. Needless to say, I was intrigued and anxiously awaited the next installment.*

In fact, Srila Prabhupada was already drawing eager seekers to the small storefront temple on Second Avenue. Years later he reminisced about the Bowery and how he had seen his first humble temple in the United States as a blessing rather than a curse:Mukunda suggested this (26 Second Avenue) as a good place. And actually it happened to be a good place.... So I had no disturbance. I was living in the Bowery, and on my door these bums were lying with urine and wine bottles and everything. Still, they were so respectful.... I had no quarrel with them. They were very kind. They welcomed me; they opened the door:

**Mukunda suggested this (26 Second Avenue) as a good place.  And actually it happened to be a good place.... So I had no disturbance. I was living in the Bowery, and on my door these bums were lying with urine and wine bottles and everything.  Still, they were so respectful.... I had no quarrel with them.  They were very kind. They welcomed me; they opened the door:“Please go.” So ... if you remain on the spiritual platform, this material condition cannot hamper you.**

**— CONVERSATION, AUG. 10, 1976**

Reed Collins, who made a short film called “Happiness on Second Avenue,” describes the mood and message of the little storefront temple in his introduction to the film:

**Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. A hypnotic rhythmic chant of sixteen words has replaced LSD and other drugs for some in New York’s East Village. On Second Avenue and First Street is a storefront in which a Hindu swami has set up shop. There his American disciples are learning about Krishna Consciousness.**

**— HAPPINESS ON SECOND AVENUE**

**Yamuna**: *A week later my sister sent a letter that arrived during one of those tumultuous Portland storms where trees were splitting in the front yard. In the midst of the storm, the mailman came around the corner, bounded up the front steps, pulled a little blue envelope out of his mail pouch and said, “This looks like it’s something big. You better open it now.” And there it was—the invitation to her wedding. It was not the typical copperplate-scripted invitation for a church wedding and family reception, but rather a handwritten note from my sister explaining that she and Mike were getting married on September 13,1966, in a “Hindu” wedding.*

**I know you will come. I can’t wait to speak face to face again. I’ve missed that so much. Now that Mom is dead and Bad Dad Bob has abandoned us to a new family, we only have each other. Make plans to come here immediately, if not sooner. I’m really sorry for such short notice, but things have been happening fast. As I explained to you, a few days ago Swamiji held an initiation ceremony for eleven students, and amazingly, I’m Swamiji’s first and only initiated woman student.**

**Further, since Mike and I are the only couple in the group, Swamiji offered to marry us, and we agreed. It will be the first marriage ceremony in this temple. This is all just amazing to me, though you predicted we would get hitched up.**

**So, if the wedding ceremony is anything like the initiation ceremony, get ready for something unlike you have ever seen before. It won’t resemble anything like a familiar Catholic Church wedding with groom in a black tux and bride in a white gown and white lace mantilla. Be ready for something entirely different.**

**— LETTER FROM JANAKI DEVI, SEPT. 1966**

**Yamuna**: *Jan also informed me that she and Mike had new names; she was now “Janaki devi” and he was “Mukunda das.” I took in this new development smoothly—I was now beyond being shocked and expected the unexpected. She wrote that not only would the ceremony be performed by their “bona fide swami,” but there would be a “fire sacrifice.” Good Lord, what is a fire sacrifice? And there’s that word “bona fide” again. One sentence suggested that I would be the only family member to attend. Two words— MUST COME—were scrawled across the envelope.*

*Yes, I’ll come. Western Union was the only fast way to confirm it, so it read: J AND M, ARRIVING AT LOFT MID-MORNING OF 12TH. JOAN.*

## Yamuna Meets the Swami: A Golden, Radiant Holy Man”

After arriving in New York’s Lower East Side the morning before the wedding, Yamuna was immediately whisked to the Swami’s apartment at 26 Second Avenue. She felt exhausted from the long trip, and although somewhat prepared by Jan’s letters on what to expect of the neighborhood and its eclectic inhabitants, she was still wide-eyed with amazement.

**Yamuna**: *Jan, Mike and I walked from their loft to the storefront temple. City noises were intense—the rattle of wheels over potholed pavement, the screech of brakes, the shout of irate voices—everyone on the move. I was barely aware of the building facades as we walked to the Swami’s apartment. Just after passing the Matchless Gifts storefront temple at 26 Second Avenue, we turned down a walkway, passed through a small, mostly concrete courtyard, and then climbed up two flights of stairs. It was obvious which apartment was the Swami’s, for the door was ajar and a dozen or so pairs of shoes blocked the entrance. Once inside, I was led down a short hallway into what I presumed to be a living room. It was unfurnished— apart from the low shelves under the windows on the outside wall—with white walls and polished hardwood floors. This was the room where the wedding would take place tomorrow; today it served as a dining room.*

*All the lunch guests were men, and all were seated on the floor in an open-ended rectangle. Several pots of food sat on shelves in one corner. The room was hot, the air filled with unidentifiable smells. Lunch was underway, the diners eating with the fingers of their right hand from an odd assortment of plates, cups and bowls placed directly on the floor. On the walk over, Jan explained about the custom of eating a meal without cutlery. Rich or poor, this was the practice of millions in India. Bite-size portions of food were scooped up either with the tips of the thumb and next three fingers of the right hand or using a small piece of chapati flat bread. The food was then brought to the mouth as one would using a fork or spoon, and relished in a “genteel” manner. I assumed that genteel meant neatly, not messily. Soup seemed to be sipped from cups like tea.*

*Only one person was standing, serving the meal, and it was obviously the Swami. I had the sudden awareness of this golden, radiant holy man bathed in sunlight. His frame was small and Gandhi-like, his luminous skin cafe-au-lait, and his eyes a sparkling gray. With a clean-shaven head and wearing only a thin cotton dhoti, he still projected an aristocratic aura, yet at the same time a humble, unassuming one.*

*As instructed, I greeted him by placing upright palms together at chest level and awkwardly repeated four new words, “Namaste. Hare Krishna, Swamiji.” With an immediate smile and an almost intimate glance, he shook his head and in a thick Bengali accent said, “So you are Janaki’s sister and you are coming from so far—very nice. And when will the other members of the family arrive?” “I am the only one who has come for the wedding,” I reply. He chuckles: “Mmm. Oh, this is most unusual—most unusual. In India, the bride’s family makes all arrangements for the wedding. Sometimes the wedding festivities go on for days. Never mind. Please come. Sit down and take some nice Krishna prasadam.*

*Looking at the various pots, I was concerned. I followed a strict macrobiotic diet. My meal plan centered on a strict theme: brown rice with gomasio and pickled ginger and steamed greens or a veggie dish sprinkled with tamari. I was extremely reluctant to even try Indian food.*

*At the same time, I was hungry and wanted to be amenable. He served each dish to us with precise care. Maybe because of my past in dancing, I was mesmerized by the grace of his fluid movements, even in something so prosaic and repetitive.*

*I had never tasted anything like these dishes—one or two were identifiable, but the others were completely new. The most familiar were chapatis— whole wheat flat breads. The Swami’s were the best I had ever tasted: made from scratch, first griddle-baked and then flame-toasted, they were thin, tender, aromatic and slathered with clarified butter, called ghee. He had made a stack of chapatis over a foot high, enough for big eaters to chow down six or more at a sitting. His rice was steamed, but drizzled with ghee just before serving.*

*My eyes watered from the chilies and my throat burned. The vegetable dishes were bold and spicy, with assertive rather than hinted flavors. This was a far cry from macrobiotic simplicity. But I kept looking over at the Swami, smiling and radiant, who seemed so eager for me to eat this food. Throughout the meal he was overseeing everything and said: “You want more? You want more?” And I politely replied, “No thank you, I am so full; I simply can’t eat another bite.” So I ate it all. But I decided then and there that this would be the last time I ate here. I did not yet know that this was not ordinary food, but prasadam, food for the soul.*

*After the meal Swamiji asked to talk to Mukunda, Janaki and me about arrangements for the wedding the next day. I couldn’t help but notice the coffee can in the corner with large globules of crystallized sugar drizzling down its sides. As an anti-sugar macrobiotic, I feared what was coming. Sure enough, he gracefully picked up the can, reached an elegant hand into it, and lifted out a syrupy, dripping, round gulab jamun. With a warm smile, he said to me, “Take.” I protested as forcefully as I could: “Swamiji, I am so full; I can’t possibly eat any more.” But he somehow made me hold out my hand and then again said, “Take, take.” I took. It was like biting into a sugar explosion. By the time I finished the gulab jamun, I was even more convinced that this would be the last time I ate there.*

*Then Swamiji turned to the wedding. He reiterated that in the Vedic tradition the woman’s side of the family makes lavish arrangements for the festivities. Since I was the only member of either side of the family there, then tomorrow I should come to assist him in making the wedding feast. Janaki and Mukunda would decorate the room by stringing leaves and flower garlands across it, as well as arrange for the fire sacrifice, and I would meet the Swami at 9:00 am the next morning to assist in cooking.*

## The Wedding Feast—First Instructions in Cooking for Krishna

**Yamuna**: *I arrived at Swamiji’s apartment promptly at 9:00 am, and he immediately sent me off with a list of five or six items to purchase. One of the items, “huld”, was not available anywhere in the market despite my repeated attempts to find it. When I returned, Swamiji said, “You have obtained all the items on the list?” and I replied: “Well, no one knows what ‘huld’ is.” I was both captivated and intimidated by his penetrating inquiry. “Oh? Kirtanananda always finds turmeric,” he said. So that was haldi, or turmeric. And it’s very difficult to make an Indian feast without this essential spice. But with a quick “Never mind,” he entered his matchbox-size kitchen and carefully lined up the ingredients.*

*Returning, he asked me to wash my hands and sat me on the floor of the front room with a five-pound bag of flour, a pound of butter and a pitcher of water. Looking down at me, he said, “Can you make a medium-hard dough?” I replied: “Do you mean a pastry or pie-crust dough? Or a short-crust or filo pastry dough? What kind of dough do you want?” And he pointedly said: “How old are you?” “I’m twenty-five, Swamiji.” With a look of surprise, he said: “You are twenty-five and you can’t make a medium-hard dough? In India any young girl from the age of five years can make a medium-hard dough. Never mind, I will show you.”*

Over the years, Yamuna often spoke about this first experience of being mildly “chastised” by Srila Prabhupada. An early account is found in Srila Prabhupada-lilamrta, yet including it here is central to the understanding of how she assimilated his instructions throughout her life—with unshakable trust and humility. In looking back, she was amazed that somehow she never took offense or felt slighted by his corrections. Though not knowing anything about Srila Prabhupada or his “Hare Krishna” Movement, from this pivotal first meeting to the end of her life, she always held his instructions, corrections, directions and praises at the very core of her being, bringing them out like golden nuggets of wisdom for her own benefit or for the encouragement of others in their spiritual life. In some of her later tellings of this exchange with Srila Prabhupada, Yamuna would allude to statements made by disciples of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati that they considered it a matter of honor to be chastised by their guru because it demonstrated that he cared enough about them to correct them. In all of the corrections to come, Yamuna strongly felt this caring from Srila Prabhupada, and redoubled her efforts to correct whatever he found in need of improvement.

**Yamuna**: *So he deftly emptied the contents of the bag of flour and broke up the butter with his fingertips to the consistency of course meal; he made a well in the center of the flour, poured in just the right amount of water, and very quickly and expertly had a velvety-smooth, medium-hard dough. He then brought in a tray of potatoes, mashed them with his fingertips and began to sprinkle in spices. I asked, “Swamiji, what are these spices?” So he explained, using the Hindi terms for the spices, which I didn’t understand at all. Not wanting to appear more incompetent than I already felt, I said nothing. I soon found out that my cooking duty for the entire day was to make something called “aloo kachori,” a fried potato pastry which is a staple of festive occasions in India and, as anyone who has made them knows, one of the more difficult savories to master. Swamiji then showed me how to shape and stuff the kachoris, and from n:oo am until 5:00 pm I sat in the room making this one preparation. During that time, Swamiji routinely and effortlessly swept into the room with about 13 cooked preparations for at least 100 persons that he single-handedly made in his narrow, sauna-like apartment kitchen. Even though there were about 40 people there, still he easily made enough food for 100.*

*Throughout the course of that day, Swamiji instructed me on some of the fundamental aspects of Krishna Consciousness philosophy. It was an excruciatingly hot New York day, and after sitting in the airless room for what seemed like hours to me, I asked, “Swamiji, may I please have a glass of water?” He peeked around the kitchen door and said, “Go wash your hands.” Although baffled, I immediately did so. When I came back into the hallway, he was waiting with a glass of water for me. He then explained that while preparing this special kind of food meant to be offered to the Supreme Lord, one does not think of eating or drinking for oneself. So after drinking the water, I again washed my hands and sat down to my kachori task.*

*After some time Swamiji came out with a batch of broken-open, cooked kachoris and said, “They are all falling apart because you are not sealing them properly.” So he again showed me how to shape and seal them, and throughout my life I would always judge kachoris as the piece de resistance in the kitchen, because I learned what perfection was from the very beginning by watching Swamiji’s graceful and beautiful hands shaping and making kachoris.*

*At about 2:00 pm I asked, “Swamiji, may I go have a cigarette?” He peeked around the door again and replied, “Go wash your hands.” So I again took my baffled self to the bathroom, washed my hands, and returned to the ever-present kachoris. Swamiji then came in and explained to me the four regulative principles of Krishna Consciousness—no meat eating, no illicit sex, no gambling and no intoxication (e.g. smoking). I continued to make the kachoris, all the while marveling as Swamiji paraded preparation after preparation by me and lined them up for the wedding feast.
