Despite the almost unbearable heat in the apartment, he appeared unburdened by his efforts and was not even perspiring. I, on the other hand, was quite literally drenched in perspiration and miserable in the extreme heat. Sometime near 4:00 pm, as Swamiji brought yet another preparation into the room, he saw me wipe my arm and hand across my forehead. He looked down and said the now familiar words: “Go wash your hands.” Again I did so, and when I returned, he handed me a moistened paper towel. He then patiently explained that cooking for the Supreme Lord requires standards of cleanliness and purity that are different from what I am accustomed to, and that while cooking one should not touch the body or clothing. In this way, Swamiji, using the medium of cooking, gave me my first fundamental instructions in Krishna Consciousness.*

Yamuna always told this story with both humor and gravity, a unique combination. An engaging and consummate storyteller, she often used the humorous aspects of her association with Srila Prabhupada to delight the listeners so that she could ultimately evoke the deeper, underlying message of Krishna Consciousness within. As cooking would become one of her principal services to Srila Prabhupada, over the years it became the nexus of so many valuable devotional instructions. Whether he was comparing the quality of spices or showing a cooking technique, Srila Prabhupada somehow always gave some philosophical instruction as well, inevitably reminding her that she was not merely cooking, but rather performing an act of devotion.

## The Wedding—A Ceremony of Contrasts

When it came to the wedding ceremony itself, Yamuna recalled watching it through eyes fogged with exhaustion and sensory overload. Janaki, looking distinctly uncomfortable in her red silk sari, jewelry and heavy makeup, had a deer-in-the-headlights look that Yamuna understood and empathized with. It was not that she did not want to marry; rather, she felt as though pulled from introduction to initiation to wedding without a real understanding of what it all meant. And yet, Srila Prabhupada could not have been more kind and accommodating. Janaki later recalled that he personally put flowers in her hair. He then tore off a piece of his own dhoti, wrapped it like a shawl on Mukunda, and then after the ceremony tied it to her sari, saying that they now had to remain together.

Following her recent initiation ceremony, Janaki, already vulnerable and overwhelmed by the accelerated pace of commitment to their newly spiritualized lives, had immediately slipped out of the building, flagged down a cab and asked the driver to simply drive until she could compose herself. Of course, she had no money, so when they finally reached her apartment, she had the added burden of having to deal with the justifiably furious cabdriver.

For Janaki, who had been abandoned first by her biological father and then her stepfather, Srila Prabhupada, through his unreserved affection and kindliness, became a father figure to her. Her connection to Krishna Consciousness was her affection for him, and whatever service she did was a direct expression of that affection.

Yamuna, on the other hand, spent the ceremony thinking how she would describe the esoteric event to her staunchly conservative Roman Catholic relations. She amused herself drafting the post-wedding announcement. “They were married by an Indian Swami in a smoke-filled room with a large fire in the center into which they threw bananas.” No. That would never do. Because their extended family embodied all that was admirable in their Catholic faith, they would try to lend support; they would offer heartfelt congratulations, but they would never understand.

## First Impressions of Swamijis Chanting— The Grace of the Supreme Father

**Yamuna**: *Toward the end of the ceremony, Swamiji, smiling broadly, picked up a small bongo drum and said, “Now we will have kirtan.” His chanting started off slowly, and he appeared fully absorbed in it. His voice was vibrant and clear, the melody simple, the cadence strong and steady. I was relieved because this part seemed easy enough—quite unlike the Sanskrit recited throughout the wedding ceremony. After a couple of repetitions of*

*Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare, Swamiji nodded his head and other voices joined in. Over and over they repeated the three-worded mantra. When Swamiji closed his eyes, I noted that many others did so as well. I speculated that this fostered a trance-like state, but I still kept my eyes wide open so as not to miss anything. I did not chant, fearing that if I were to add my voice to the mix, it might disturb its cohesiveness, its balance.*

*In this way, I observed and listened to the chanting for a good five minutes or so. Chanting the mantra seemed different from any group singing I had ever experienced. The first thing that struck me was its simplicity: a simple melody, an easy rhythm, and only three words. When I too closed my eyes and joined the others, it was as though I had been chanting this simple song to God forever. I soon found myself soothed and relieved of all my anxieties, though I could not understand how or why this was happening. I just surrendered to the sound and let it envelop my senses, allowing myself to trust, to call out—to open my heart to its promise.*

*Even as a beginner, I found myself leaving the world of the temporal senses. Swamiji varied the tempo of the chanting, allowing us to experience different emotions. Sometimes he increased the tempo slowly, at other times quickly. He brought the chanting to an intense crescendo, and then again slowed the pace and the kirtan manifested in an entirely different way. It was akin to the pure improvisation of an experienced classic or jazz master, but its purpose and intent were still inexplicable to me. What I did know was that the experience of first chanting with Swamiji created an impression in my heart. I didn’t know it yet, but this small beginning would grow to encompass my whole being, and the chanting would become the fulcrum around which every other aspect of my devotional life would revolve.*

*Even though I was shy and reluctant to say anything, I later asked, “Swamiji, what is the effect of chanting?” He answered: “Chanting cleanses the heart of all dirty things and brings about love of God.” I thought it a mystical answer, for what could possibly be dirty in the heart?*

Srila Prabhupada in those early days defined the meaning of the Hare Krishna mahamantra in simple language. In a masterful and relatable way, he piqued the interest of the young attendees and encouraged them to explore the chanting—to dive deeply into its potency. The combination of the power of the mantra, his obvious immersion in it, as well as his musicality, captivated his young audience. Yamuna, though not yet convinced by the food or prasadam, was moved and impressed by the chanting and therefore wanted to know more about this philosophy he so resolutely wanted them to explore.

**The chanting is exactly like a genuine cry by the child for the mother. Mother Hara helps in achieving the grace of the Supreme Father, Hari, or Krishna, and the Lord reveals Himself to such a sincere devotee. No other means, therefore, of spiritual realization is as effective in this age, as chanting the mahamantra, Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare.**

**— ADDRESS BY SWAMI А. С. ВHАКTIVEDANTA , KRISHNA CONSCIOUSNESS ALBUM**

After the kirtan, the much anticipated wedding feast was served—again by Srila Prabhupada. Yamuna sometimes mentioned how she felt that he must have had superhuman powers because here he was, an elderly man in a sweltering apartment crowded with people, having cooked all day while giving instructions and attending to hundreds of details, yet still showing no signs of exhaustion or heat affectation. It seemed to her simply beyond any human capacity.

**Yamuna**: *The wedding feast was served with great care and attention by Swamiji. While we may not have been aware of the mystical nature of prasadam, he most certainly was, and he took obvious pleasure in seeing that we all ate to our heart’s content.*

*I  was in awe of this effulgent and selfless personality. He had cooked all day in an oven-like kitchen and now, showing no signs of exhaustion, he performed the wedding ceremony, engaged everyone in chanting kirtan, and served the wedding feast, all the while encouraging, supporting and accommodating. He was an elderly man, yet he had more energy than anyone there. I wondered where he drew such reserves from. I thought he must definitely have the magical yogic powers I had been reading about in my books on Eastern mysticism.*

The magnitude of Srila Prabhupada’s physical presence—his aristocratic bearing and graceful movements—were often recalled and spoken about with deep feeling to others by Yamuna. Once, in 1994, we were riding a train from Calcutta to Puri and a man entered our compartment. He must have felt so uncomfortable because both Yamuna and I were staring at him with unblinking eyes. Then Yamuna began crying, tears pouring from her eyes, because this man not only looked like Srila Prabhupada, but had the same dignified and aristocratic bearing, and she was immediately transported to the time of Srila Prabhupada’s manifest presence.

Many years later, Yamuna still remembered her first personal association with Srila Prabhupada with a deep and pervasive gratitude. In her 2002 Vyasa Puja homage, she prayed:

**Yamuna**: *I remember you asked me to grocery shop for my sister’s wedding feast in the morning, and then assist you in cooking for the remainder of the day. First I bungled the shopping, and then made numerous blunders trying to make aloo kachori for the next several hours. By this time I thought I might not be capable of anything you asked me to do. But you were so patient, and in the course of that day imparted many basic Vaishnava cooking and kitchen precepts. Further, while you single-handedly prepared a multi-course wedding feast, I watched you chop, peel, mince, stir, mix, fry, bray and so on—often using your hands rather than tools as equipment, and noted your kitchen ease, focus and expertise. I was fascinated by everything about you. In this connection, I pray to share these things that you have taught me, especially with the younger generation now poised on the launching pad, in hopes that they may take these instructions to heart.*

*I also remember the wedding ceremony that evening—a fire blazed in the dead center of your small living room that we had met in only 24 hours previously—with smoke so thick I was coughing. Again I watched you, this time in a “Swamiji” role of officiating priest chanting Sanskrit prayers and hymns, as you lovingly gave away my only sister in marriage to an old friend—both only initiated devotees for two weeks. In this connection, I pray that all vows and prayers spoken by me to you at a sacred fire yajna be followed purely.*

## Swamiji Speaks on Love and Lust — Liquid Beauty

Up to this point in her life, in religious terms Yamuna would describe herself as a casual seeker. Though she had become an avid reader of Indian and Buddhist texts, such as The Tibetan Book of the Dead, Siddhartha, and her much perused Autobiography of a Yogi, she still remained philosophically noncommittal. She did not envision her life in terms of a full immersion in any ideology and yet felt pulled from within towards the East. In her first meeting with Srila Prabhupada, she was attracted by his demeanor and impressed by the way he openly accepted and cared for those who came to the small temple storefront of “Matchless Gifts.” And yet she still knew very little of the philosophy he was representing and wanted to know more.

**Yamuna**: *After the festivities, when I approached Swamiji to thank him, he asked how long I would stay in New York, and then requested that I come to the morning and evening kirtans and classes. He said, “If you chant Hare Krishna every morning and evening and follow the rules and regulations, you will advance quickly in Krishna Consciousness.” I was anxious to come, as I was not only spellbound by his presence, but I felt that he was sincerely concerned for my spiritual well-being. The very first morning, he told the story of the young man of doubtful character who fell in love with a beautiful girl. The girl was very saintly and thus rejected his advances. Because he was insistent, she requested him to wait seven days and then she would submit to him. During those seven days, she took strong laxatives and purgatives and stored all of the vomit and loose stool in jars, which she carefully lined up in a row. She thus became skeleton-like, with a blackish complexion and sunken eyes. At the end of seven days the man came back and asked the ugly girl before him where the beautiful girl was. She asserted her identity as that girl, but he could not recognize her. Finally, she told him she had separated her “beauty” and stored it in foul-smelling pots which she directed him to. So by the grace of this saintly girl, the man of bad character was able to distinguish between the shadow and substance and thus came to his senses.*

*I was profoundly moved by this story because it spoke to my own personal relationships in life. I had never heard such a clear and graphic description of the difference between lust and love and between shadow and substance. Swamiji spoke in heavily-accented English, some of which I couldn’t understand, yet his use of metaphor and simile to define and expand upon the philosophy of Krishna Consciousness was brilliant and captivating. I was determined that for the short time of my stay in New York, I would come to as many kirtans and lectures as possible.*

*One morning Swamiji brought me into his sitting room where a trunk covered with a cloth served as his desk. On top of the metal trunk were a few of his personal possessions, all very meticulously placed. I remember it looking very neat, but very spartan. On the right corner of his trunk was a stack of cards. In those days, the younger generation didn’t really think of using business cards; it was a bit unusual. Then Swamiji picked up a card and with great pleasure handed it to me. It said: Founder-Acharya “The International Society for Krishna Consciousness” on one side and had the mahamantra and temple schedule on the other. And he said, “I would like to give you one of my cards.” I said, “Thank you very much; I really appreciate it.” And he said, “Would you like some more?” “Okay.” “Do you have some friends you can give them to?” “Yes,” I replied. “I could do that when I return to Oregon.” I was thinking, “Who in Oregon will want these business cards with ‘The International Society for Krishna Consciousness’ on them?” But I took the cards. He was so genuinely enthusiastic to use each person and every opportunity to spread his mission of Krishna Consciousness that it was virtually impossible not to be swept up by his enthusiasm.*

When Yamuna returned to the West Coast, she in fact did distribute Srila Prabhupada’s business cards. Yamuna’s open-minded Aunt Edna Howell, her childhood dance teacher, attended many of the early San Francisco programs with Srila Prabhupada. In her last days, she sent a collection of Prabhupada memorabilia from those years to Yamuna and Janaki, and among them was one of those business cards. Yamuna later remembered this event in a prayer:

**Yamuna**: *I remember my third visit to your New York quarters the following day. At that time, you showed me a newly printed business card with your particulars on it along with the schedule of programs for the New York temple. You designed the card and seemed quite pleased with it. You asked me to take several and distribute them to my friends. As I lived on the West Coast, I did so reluctantly. In this connection, I pray to unreservedly distribute all that you have spoken or written, regardless of friend or otherwise (Vyasa puja homage 2002)*

**Yamuna**: *One morning Swamiji asked where my sister was and why she was not coming to the classes. I lied and said she did not feel well. He said, “Every morning she does not feel well?” I tried to hedge by saying I did not know. He said, “Try to get her to come with you,” but I was unable to do so. Still, she would visit at other times, bringing gifts or cooking something he had taught her to make, and those shared moments increased her attachment for him. He seemed to sense her vulnerability and was always unwavering in his kindness and tolerance with her.*

Although Janaki’s natural affection for Srila Prabhupada was resolute, she was dismayed by the compulsory rules and regulations for new initiates, as well as the wearing of robes and tilak, which she found strange. As virtually the only woman, she also felt little kinship with the men, something Yamuna also felt and empathized with. Yamuna found some of the men dismissive and somewhat condescending, and this in itself dissuaded her from any thought of becoming a student and remaining in New York. The men of her acquaintance in both Portland and San Francisco were friendly, open and supportive, treating women as equals, and the disparity and lack of amity at the storefront temple was discouraging, even as her appreciation for Srila Prabhupada and his teachings grew.

**Yamuna**: *Before I came to New York, my views on spirituality were simply not formulated. I had a quasi-utopian ideal—the “if it works for you, it’s good” school of religious thought. In that sense I was an innocent, if not ignorant. And although desirous of hearing, there had been no real authority to hear from. So my early exposure to Swamiji’s lectures in New York engendered two opposite reactions. When I heard, I liked it. And sometimes I was so moved that I cried out of appreciation. But it seemed to go in one ear and out the other, because I was not able to apply this Krishna Consciousness philosophy to my life at the time. Another reaction was to fall asleep. So the philosophy, while making tremendous sense to me and awakening an appreciation of religiosity I had never felt before, did not noticeably change the heart. It would not be until six months later that I realized that I was in fact forever changed—that Swamiji’s personal example, kirtan and philosophy had irrevocably impacted the fertile heart of one small soul, Yamuna, and that I would take up this process of Krishna bhakti as a lifelong dedication.*

Yamuna’s visit to New York lasted about three weeks, something she would describe to me later on as both life-changing and mind-boggling. Although her days centered around the morning and evening classes and kirtans with Srila Prabhupada, she would also often explore the neighborhood on her own, taking long walks to clear her mind and try to process what she was experiencing. One blistering hot September day, she returned to Mukunda and Janaki’s loft to find her sister frantic with worry.

**Yamuna**: *I lost account of the time that day, having spent much of it sipping herb tea at the Paradox, a Zen macrobiotic restaurant on East Street. We went there every day for a bowl of brown rice. A temple man I called Siddhartha sometimes camped out there for hours speaking about Swamiji’s philosophy. It was that kind of place. With swarthy skin and an ascetic demeanor, he looked like the main character from the Herman Hesse novel. A lot of different types frequented the Paradox—hippies, poets, artists, weird people and neighborhood people. On that day, an artist called Yoko Ono displayed a black bag contraption in the center of the room; the cook called it “cool art.”*

*When I returned to the loft, Jan was sitting in the sweltering heat in a bathing suit, an anemic fan blowing hot air nearby, and a look of relief combined with anger on her face. She asked me with some sarcasm if I had gotten lost, and when I mentioned my conversation at the Paradox with someone named Rabeen-soup, she laughed and said he was in fact a disciple of Swamiji’s named Ravindra Svarupa. This, combined with the watermelon I put on the kitchen counter, eased the tensions my tardiness had caused.*

Before Yamuna’s coming to New York, Janaki and Mukunda had already made plans to travel to India. In addition to his enthusiasm for Srila Prabhupada’s philosophy of Krishna Consciousness, Mukunda was interested in Indian music and Janaki in Indian dance. Yamuna had already cultivated an appreciation for Kathakali and Oriyan dance, and she also had long harbored a desire to go to India and Tibet. Now with the seed of bhakti planted firmly but imperceptibly in her heart, she was easily swept up into their plan to go to India. They would leave the first week of October; Yamuna would get her passport in San Francisco, and they would travel from there by ship to Madras. Unbeknownst to them, Krishna and Srila Prabhupada had other plans.

## “Try to Open a Temple in San Francisco” and India Interrupted

Mukunda had earlier spoken to Srila Prabhupada of their plans to travel to India via San Francisco. Harvey Cohen, an early student of Srila Prabhupada’s who had moved to the San Francisco area, had been writing enthusiastic letters about its potential for preaching and had already begun looking for possible storefront rentals.

**In January, a “Gathering of the Tribes” is scheduled, and a hundred thousand are expected. Hordes of young people are flocking to San Francisco with flowers in their hair, and the word is out that a new generation is blossoming, the “Flower Children,” nurtured on LSD, supposedly attuned to expanded consciousness, and waiting, we hope, to extend this consciousness beyond drugs. Harvey asks for help. He is already looking for a storefront in the Haight-Ashbury district near Golden Gate Park, an area where “it’s all happening.” Swamiji is eager. “Yes, we must go,” he says. “We will go as soon as he has found a place.”**

**— SRILA PRABHUPADA-LILAMRTA**

Srila Prabhupada, in his characteristic encouraging manner, suggested to Mukunda that they try to help open a temple in San Francisco before going to India. Thinking that their trip would only be postponed until March at the latest, Mukunda, Janaki and Yamuna all agreed.

Now enthusiastic about the San Francisco temple idea, Mukunda arranged a drive-delivery car (a contract to drive an owner’s car to a destination). Yamuna suggested stopping to visit their friends Sam and Melanie in the Cascade Mountains of Oregon to tell them about Srila Prabhupada and encourage them to come with them to San Francisco. Sam and Melanie worked at a seasonal job for the Forest Service, and Yamuna knew that the job typically lasted until the first snowfall of the year. Fortuitously that snowfall occurred the very day after their arrival.

**Yamuna**: *Four of us—Mukunda and Janaki, their gypsy friend Maurice, and I—shared a ride to San Francisco in a drive-delivery car that Mukunda had arranged. We had four days to get the car from New York to San Francisco, so in order to make a northern detour pit-stop in central Oregon, someone drove virtually around the clock; no motels. We drove coast-to-coast in three days to a remote Cascade Mountain Forest Service fire lookout tower near Three Sisters, Oregon, where Sam and Melanie worked*

Also along on the cross-country drive was Janaki’s cat, Skutzelbrunzer, whose later antics with Srila Prabhupada in San Francisco would not only delight the devotees but also increase Yamuna’s attraction and dedication by observing how he interacted so endearingly and personally with all of the temple residents—even one intractable cat.

**Yamuna**: *We arrived early in the afternoon, and were warmly greeted by our mutual friends, Sam and Melanie. The tower was on top of a mountain which overlooked three Cascade Mountain peaks. It was a cold and blustery day, the woodstove cranked up and warm inside their cabin. Janaki and I were eager to expose them to two things: cooking prasadam and kirtan. That night we showed Melanie how to make flame-toasted chapati flat breads and a simple vegetable curry. We then ate our simple meal, which was much appreciated by all.*

*Sam informed us that a big snowstorm was coming, one that would end their summer job, and it would be cool to climb the tower and watch the storm come our way. Sure, we all agreed, and started up to the top of the lookout tower. The higher we climbed, the stronger the winds became. Finally, as we arrived at the top, several hundred feet up, the panorama of the storm was visible. A tsunami wave of roiling black clouds was rolling over each major mountain peak in the Cascades, slowly coming south towards us. Sam encouraged us to get down to the safety of the cabin, as the winds before the storm would make a descent difficult.*

*Bundled in all the clothes we brought, warmed by the fire, lamps replacing daylight, we told Sam and Melanie about Swamiji and his philosophy of Krishna Consciousness, about Mukunda and Janaki’s initiation, and about Swamiji’s desire to open a temple in San Francisco. Mukunda then explained what chanting is and began a kirtan. Our voices melded together, offset by the crackling wood fire inside and the howling winds rattling the windows outside. Kirtan went on for an hour or more, merging into various tempos, and continued until we all fell asleep on the floor. The next morning we woke to a white wonderland, the snow already several inches deep and still falling.*

*Janaki is a good cook and had already learned to make some delicious dishes from Swamiji. She announced that she would treat us to a “Krishna prasadam” breakfast. Unpacking the groceries she had bought the day before—butter, milk, cheddar, whole wheat flour, potatoes, apples, raisins and some spices, she then announced the menu—Swamiji-style hash browns, cheddar-stuffed paratha flat breads, apple-raisin chutney and hot turmeric milk. Of course, she recruited me to help her, and we worked mostly in silence, my eyes taking in everything she did. At the same time we waited to hear what Melanie had to say about the painting on the cover of the Srimad-Bhagavatam Mukunda had placed on the table. She did not disappoint.*

In putting Yamuna’s words to paper here about cooking with Janaki at the lookout cabin, it occurred to me that had anyone not known Yamuna, it might be assumed that she had used artistic license in describing a meal prepared over 42 years ago; yet they would be mistaken. With regard to the art of cooking—the how, why and where, the colors, textures, ingredients and setting, Yamuna had almost perfect recall. Countless times over the years, someone would bring up a visit to a temple or program and immediately she would describe not only the meal, but how each preparation was prepared and what spices were used.

**Yamuna**: *Breaking the silence, Melanie remarked that the cover picture showing a blue person with four arms and a bunch of other smaller blue persons with four arms floating around on lotus flowers was totally bewildering to her. More bewildering was the big person with four arms and four heads, also blue, who had a lotus flower coming out of His navel. Melanie, a self-proclaimed hippy, was sharp-witted and plain-speaking, and had experimented with mind-altering drugs. She commented that she had seen a lot of strange things, but never anything as strange as this. Mukunda then explained that the picture represented forms of the “Supreme Personality of Godhead” that are described in the book. He said that it contained mindboggling spiritual information about God in His many forms. I doubted that Melanie would cotton to his reply, but she surprised me and instead questioned whether one of the blue figures described was the one called the Supreme Personality of Godhead. Mukunda then told her that the book not only contained information about the Supreme Personality of Godhead, but so much more as well. Melanie was intrigued, especially about the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and eagerly took the book to read.*

*The cabin now quiet, I focused my attention back on Janaki and her cooking. By the time the food was ready, the room was filled with fragrant scents from the mix of savory Indian and sweet Western spices. Janaki then called everyone together and said that before we ate anything, it had to be turned into “Krishna prasadam." She had us circle the stove, hold hands, and offer the food to Radha and Krishna by chanting the mahamantra out loud—Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. She explained that it was kind of like saying grace together, but better, because it changed ordinary food into sanctified food. She said that Swamiji said that this sanctified food or “prasadam" jump starts our spiritual consciousness. Though they had never done this before, Sam and Melanie joined in without complaint. The prasadam was ambrosial.*

*Sam then hustled us all out the door, casually commenting that if we didn’t leave right then, we’d be under several feet of snow and would have to be helicoptered out. He said that he and Melanie had discussed it and they wanted to come to San Francisco to help open the temple. Quickly packing up their cabin by throwing all their belongings into a large American flag, then dragging it to their car as the snow continued to fall fast and hard, they followed us down the mountain as we started toward our San Francisco adventure.*

Yamuna and I sometimes visited Aunt Edna Howell over the years in Longview, Washington, where she spent her last days. Even into her nineties she fondly recalled the infectious enthusiasm Yamuna and Janaki had for Srila Prabhupada and their desire to bring him to San Francisco all those years ago. For Yamuna, this enthusiasm was a reflection of her incipient love for Srila Prabhupada, and this, rather than any philosophical rationale, fueled her desire to help further his mission. She saw it as an exciting adventure, one that would also help others, and she welcomed the change in direction her life was taking.

## Chapter 3

**Opening the Heart to Bhakti (San Francisco 1966-1968)**

WHEN SRILA PRABHUPADA started chanting the Hare Krishna mahamantra in Tompkins Square Park in New York, the East Village Other, a popular underground newspaper, ran a front page picture and article parodying LSD guru Timothy Leary’s call to “Turn on, Tune in, and Drop out” by declaring: “In only three months, Swami A. C. Bhaktivedanta succeeded in convincing the world’s toughest audiencebohemians, acid heads, pot heads and hippies—that he knew the way to God: ‘Turn Off, Sing Out, and Fall In’.”

**“What are these hippies?” Swamiji asks. We try to explain as best we can. “I’m afraid that many people would consider us hippies,” I say. “No, we’re happies,” Swamiji laughs. “But whatever you once were, Krishna will change you. Right?”**

**We also have to explain ‘acid heads,’ ‘pot’ and ‘fuzz,’ and when Swamiji understands, he smiles and says, “Yes, that is right. Krishna Consciousness may seem like poison in the beginning, but it is nectar in the end. So it is sweeter.”**

**— HARE KRISHNA EXPLOSION**

When Yamuna returned to San Francisco, the early 6o’s beatnik subculture had now evolved into the hippie subculture. The word “hippy” was derived from “hipster,” a name initially used to describe the beatniks who had relocated to San Francisco’s low-rent Haight-Ashbury district. These people inherited the countercultural values of the Beat Generation, created their own communities, listened to psychedelic rock, embraced the sexual revolution and used drugs like cannabis and LSD to explore higher consciousness. The efforts of the pioneers in Haight-Ashbury to create an enlightened and utopian community reached its apex by the end of 1966, attracting tens of thousands of disenfranchised young people to the first “Human Be-In” on January 14,1967, in Golden Gate Park. This pivotal event broadcast the fundamental ideals of the hippie movement, i.e., personal empowerment, political change, ecological awareness and enlightened spiritual consciousness, throughout the country, and paved the way for what was to become known as the “Summer of Love”—the zenith of hippie idealism, as well as the prelude to its corruption and subsequent downfall.

Srila Prabhupada came into this culture of nonconformity on January 16, 1967, a mere two days after the “Human Be-In.” Just as with his fortuitous arrival in New York’s Lower East Side in 1965, the Supreme Lord, in His infinite kindness, arranged the perfect timing for Srila Prabhupada to come to San Francisco. He arrived during the pinnacle of the hippie movement, when his message of Krishna Consciousness would be eagerly received by thousands of sincere seekers. Through his preaching and by his personal example, Srila Prabhupada evoked the “Summer of Love” theme to show to whom that love should be directed—to God.

## A Temple on Frederick Street

When Sam and Melanie arrived in San Francisco, they rented an apartment with Yamuna in Lucky Alley in the Mission District, while Mukunda and Janaki temporarily stayed with friends in Berkeley.

**Yamuna**: *Mukunda was undoubtedly the most convinced, determined and eager to rent a storefront for Swamiji to come to San Francisco. Swamiji had already promised to come as soon as a temple could be arranged, and Mukunda was anxious to make it happen as soon as possible. Sam, Melanie and I agreed to help. Harvey Cohen and his girlfriend Hope came down from Mendocino County and joined us. Harvey had met Swamiji in New York, but moved to California for a job in graphic design. A bearded, compact man who was quiet but laughed easily, his signature wear was a herringbone tweed jacket with patches at the elbows. Hope was a flower child with a delicate demeanor and a soft, breathy voice.*

A storefront rental similar to the temple in New York was found at 518 Frederick Street near the Haight-Ashbury district. Not only were the rents cheaper there, but it was the nucleus of the burgeoning hippie movement, and young people from all over the country were flocking to the area in droves. Situated between the Diggers’ Free Store and a Chinese laundry, the storefront seemed ideally suited to becoming ISKCON’s first West Coast temple.

**Yamuna**: *In December, Janaki and Mukunda shifted from Berkeley to San Francisco and rented a third floor apartment at 512 Frederick Street, just on the edge of Haight-Ashbury. At the same time they rented a second apartment a few doors down from theirs for Swamiji to stay in. Their living room bay window was just above the larger bay window in the storefront below. I started spending most of my time at their apartment instead of my own in Lucky Alley.*

*The lease on the 518 Frederick Street storefront was signed in early January. The main space—about 16 by 30 feet with a large bay window at the front—would serve as the temple room. At the right back end of that room, three stairs led up to an elevated second room and a back door that opened onto an alley. This back area was roughly 16 by 16 feet, and our tentative plan was to divide it into two rooms—a kitchen and storeroom. At the left back end of the room, a door opened onto stairs that led down to a full basement. This San Francisco storefront was larger than the one in New York, with more possibilities for its use.*

*Before the lease was even signed, our small group met to decide what to do and who would do it. We were determined to make a beautiful temple out of the little storefront. Everyone was delegated various tasks. Harvey volunteered to begin a large oil painting of Radha and Krishna for the temple wall. Janaki and Hope cleaned and spackled the walls before giving them a new coat of paint. I sewed Prussian blue muslin curtains for the front window, framed Brijbasi prints for the temple walls and decorated a raised platform for Swamiji to sit on. Sam tackled the biggest jobs—constructing an altar, back-room kitchen, and the storeroom. Melanie ferreted out donations and goods for the project and set up the kitchen. Mukunda became the project coordinator and public liaison man. He had already sent tickets for Swamiji and a servant to come on January 16, so time was of the essence. A few newcomers also volunteered to help. Everyone worked as a team to ready the space for Swamiji’s arrival, and the next days passed in a frenzy of work.*

*Once people realized that the storefront was being turned into a temple, they started coming. While we worked all day, we played the album Swamiji recorded in the fall of 1966, and the chanting of Hare Krishna soon fanned out, becoming a “hip” thing to do and the temple a “hip” place to be. There was a popular donut shop on the corner, and the crowd, hearing our chanting, came by out of curiosity to check us out, and many ended up staying to help and chant with us. Most of us had memorized the short discourse Swamiji made on the album about the meaning and potency of chanting: “This chanting is a spiritual call for the Lord and His energy to give protection to the conditioned soul.” For me, chanting became an amazing form of meditation. You could still work, still perform what were “mundane” duties, but because you chanted, everything became different— spiritualized. How could three little words carry such potency? The one meaning that stayed with me was the most simple—chanting the Hare Krishna mahamantra is an exchange of love between God and the reciter. I found my enthusiasm for Swamiji’s arrival growing by leaps and bounds. The realization that the connection I had made with him in New York continued to grow in San Francisco, even without his physical presence, would become immensely important to me in the coming years. This was my first experience of the difference between vapu, the power of being in his personal presence, and vani, the power of being with him through his instructions.*

## “Bring Krishna Consciousness West”— Swamiji Invites the Hippies

The storefront temple, with the help of many newly-chanting souls, was now ready to receive Srila Prabhupada. The young family of devotees were greatly encouraged by the reception and help they had received from others, even before Srila Prabhupada arrived. One of the new volunteers was Roger Siegel:

**Yamuna***: In early January, shortly before Swamiji’s arrival, many of us stood every day on street corners in the Haight handing out a teaser flyer announcing Swamiji’s upcoming arrival. The flyer was a mimeographed black-and-white photo of Swamiji with my calligraphed words “Bring Krishna Consciousness West” on it. One person I handed a flyer to was Roger Siegel. Tall and lanky, he appeared out-doorsy, with curly fair hair, and dressed in jeans, shirt and well-worn cowboy boots. He had a friendly and outgoing personality, and we struck up a conversation and ended up spending the afternoon together walking in Golden Gate Park. I learned that he was a native New Yorker, a photographer recently back from residing in Mexico, and very interested in spiritual growth. Roger wanted to extensively photograph Swamiji’s stay, and we discussed collaborating on a photo essay book about it—I would do the text, layout and calligraphy, and Roger would supply the photos.*

Mukunda had wisely suggested that Srila Prabhupada’s activities in San Francisco be hlmed, photographed and recorded, just as the men in the New York temple had been doing. This began with the arrival of Srila Prabhupada at the San Francisco airport, and the short 8mm film of that event vividly captures not only the wildly enthusiastic welcome of Srila Prabhupada by about fifty ecstatic devotees and his loving reciprocation with them, but also the prevailing eccentricity of the times.

**Yamuna**: *There were nearly fifty of us in the airport entourage. Waiting for the plane, my eyes sought out the dozen or so friends and family who had prepared for Swamiji’s arrival. The group was respectfully dressed for the occasion. Mukunda, Janaki and Allen Ginsberg stood together and chatted. Mukunda, his short black beard and mustache neatly trimmed, wore white pants, a white shirt and a dark blazer, a double strand of large red japa beads around his neck and a red carnation in his lapel. Janaki looked well turned-out in my red wool Lanz dress and a single strand of pearls with the kanti mala around her neck. Allen, his bushy black beard and hair sticking out like a halo, wore a white shirt and tie, dark pants and jacket which sported a big yellow mum in its lapel. Sam, Melanie, Roger and I stood nearby. Sam’s dog Ralph and Roger’s dog Quetal sat quietly at our feet, taking it all in. Sam, rocking back and forth on the balls of his feet, wore black jeans, a patterned pullover sweater, and carried a small camera hanging off his wrist. Melanie, eyes ever dancing, wore a long skirt, a striped serape over a turtleneck tee, and tinkling gypsy-like jewelry. Roger was a study in earth tones, wearing khaki corduroys and a khaki turtleneck, a ubiquitous Nikon hanging from his neck. I wore a black, long-sleeved silk blouse and wool skirt with Taos silver filigree jewelry.*

*Our first glimpse of Swamiji was through the airport windows when he stepped onto the platform at the top of the plane’s stairs. He paused briefly while Ranchor, a New York initiate acting as Swamiji’s servant, opened a black umbrella and held it over his head. With measured steps, Swamiji glided down the stairs, his saffron robes fluttering in the breeze. By the time he reached the tarmac, we had headed en mass to the area just outside the baggage claim. When Swamiji stepped through the door, he was engulfed by eager devotees. Some shouted “Hare Krishna, Hare Rama!” Some cried out “Swamiji, Swamiji!” Some rushed forward to offer him a flower; the dogs weaved in and out of the crowd and barked; the airline staff looked stunned and momentarily speechless; and I simply froze in place, just staring at him in awe.*

*As Swamiji moved forward, a group surrounded him and he stopped. He had an oceanic smile on his face, and a slight scent of sandalwood oil emanated from him. Allen stepped forward and placed a garland around his neck; Swamiji folded his palms together and murmured, “Hare Krishna. Thank you. Hare Krishna.” One after another, different individuals presented him with either a single flower or flower bouquets, and Swamiji in turn gave most of them to others. When he briskly began to stride down the halls to the exit, the group flanked him on both sides and in back. Even the dogs picked up on who was the focus there, for they deftly weaved in and out of the crowd, all the while staying close to Swamiji’s feet.*

**Srila Prabhupada arrived at 518 Frederick Street and entered the storefront. Taking his seat on a cushion, he led a kirtan and then spoke, inviting everyone to take up Krishna Consciousness. After his lecture he left the storefront and walked next door and up the two flights of stairs to his apartment. As he entered his apartment... he was followed not only by his devotees and admirers, but also by reporters from San Francisco’s main newspapers, the Chronicle and the Examiner. While some devotees cooked his lunch, and Ranchor unpacked his suitcase, Swamiji talked with the reporters, who sat on the floor taking notes on their pads.**

**— SRILA PRABHUPADA-LILAMRTA**

Yamuna remembered remaining in a state of stunned amazement, and simply followed him, studying his movements, his words and his interactions with the devotees, the curiosity seekers and the press. The next day’s San Francisco Examiner wrote of their interview with Srila Prabhupada:

**In the middle of San Francisco’s hippieland, a holy man from India today began establishing a new temple devoted to the Science of God and the pursuit of world peace. “I invite everyone in any condition of life to come with us along the path of learning Krishna Consciousness,” declared Swami A. C. Bhaktivedanta. “Everyone, including the Haight-Ashbury bohemians and beatniks?” “Everyone, including you or anybody else, be he or she what is called an ‘acid head’ or a hippie or something else,” replied the 7I year-old Swami, who hastened to explain: “Once he is accepted for training, he becomes something else from what he had been before.”**

Yamuna was often nostalgic in reflecting on Srila Prabhupada’s San Francisco arrival and how it had impacted her. Seeing him again, she realized that during her short New York interlude, he had awakened her partially submerged spirituality, and it was rising to the forefront of her consciousness like cream rising in milk. This was mysterious; this was unexpected. She did not understand anything on a philosophical level yet, but she saw saintliness in him through his qualities of compassion, kindness, mercifulness, tolerance of their weaknesses, and his enthusiasm to share his love of Krishna with others. Yamuna later wrote:

**Yamuna**: *I remember your January 1967 arrival in San Francisco: how you seemed to glide down corridors, your cane stepping out before you, dog Ralphie sliding adeptly in front of your feet, and group members positioning themselves to get a first glimpse of you. Your smiling eyes drank it all in as you acknowledged those who were familiar to you and charmed the newcomers. In this connection, I pray that the compassion I saw in you when you delivered Krishna Consciousness grows in my heart and manifests by your mercy in my own attempts to give Krishna bhakti to others*

## First Initiations and Wedding

**Yamuna**: *Swamiji’s behavior from the very beginning was a most glorious thing to behold. He slept very little, and his entire being was dedicated to instructing us and encouraging us. From the onset he allowed us entrance into his personal practice by teaching us how to clean, how to cook, how to chant, how to dance; and slowly he was transforming us into devotees of Lord Chaitanya’s wondrous Sankirtan Movement. He very carefully studied each of our mentalities and thus was able to somehow dovetail our propensities in Krishna’s service. He would find the smallest talent or ability in us and fan it, all the while making us believe we were doing something wonderful for Krishna.*

On January 22, less than a week after Srila Prabhupada’s arrival, the first initiations were held at the Frederick Street temple. Here Sam became Shyamasundara das, Melanie became Malati devi dasi, Harvey became Hari das, and Hope became Harsharani devi dasi. The following day, Shyamasundara and Malati were married, and on January 25, Srila Prabhupada wrote to Brahmananda in New York about the events:

**Here everything is going well. Four devotees have been initiated and two devotees have been married. On the marriage ceremony day there was extraordinary gatherings (150 at least) and all of them were distributed prasadam. Sriman Ranchor assisted by some girls prepared kachoris, samosa, ISKCON balls, puri, chatni, etc., and there were many fruits also, and all the guests enjoyed the prasadam very nicely.**

**— LETTER TO BRAHMANANDA, JAN. 25, 1967**

**Yamuna**: *Swamiji had explained to us that men and women could not become initiated while living together unmarried, so Sam and Melanie decided to become initiated and married. Melanie borrowed Janaki’s red and gold silk sari that she had worn for her own wedding. Separating Swamiji and the couple was a large Chinese wok lined with tinfoil, which held the sacrificial fire. And just in front of Sam and Melanie were two bananas and three oranges on disposable paper plates. As neither of them had ever seen a fire sacrifice, they found it difficult to understand what Swamiji was saying. So at one point Swamiji told them to bow down to pay obeisances, and both Sam and Melanie thought that Swamiji said, “Blow, blow, blow out.” So they began trying to blow out the sacrificial fire— they got down on their hands and knees and started blowing very forcefully on the fire. So it created some disturbance, and Swamiji corrected them saying, “No, no, bow down, bow down—obeisances!” So they finally understood and got up. A while later, when the bananas were to be placed onto the fire, again Sam and Melanie, now initiated as Shyamasundara and Malati, thought that Swamiji wanted them to eat the bananas. So they began peeling and eating the bananas, and Swamiji said, “No, no, put on the fire.” So we were all so new, so neophyte, but Swamiji just saw the sincerity. Despite whatever our deficiencies were, he was invariably compassionate and patient with us, and this in turn increased our desire to please him.*

## The Frederick Street Temple is Open

Srila Prabhupada quickly instituted a regulated program of classes, kirtan, prasadam distribution and preaching.

**Yamuna**: *In the mornings our program began at 7 am, and Swamiji first chanted the Gurvastakam prayer. We had many instruments in the temple at the time, and in consideration of our neighbors, Swamiji trained us to try to have kirtan a little softly in the mornings. It was one of the few instructions he gave us on performing kirtan in those very early days. And when Swamiji chanted the Gurvastakam prayers, we would all play our instruments very softly. Swamiji told us it was a prayer to offer respect to the Spiritual Master, and he chanted it very, very slowly. Of course, we had no words, no song books, or any written prayers at this time, but we listened with rapt attention. Most often he played kartals, and he had a specific way of playing them that was very beautiful. It was the one, two, three rhythm with the kartals sizzling nicely on the third one. We also had handmade instruments such as Coke bottle lids with holes in the center that were strung on little wire rings, and up to thirty people played pairs of those. Then there were small kartals and a large set of orchestra-sized timpani drums we had rented. We also had an upright piano with the back taken off, and the strings on it were played like a harp. We had three kelp horns from the Pacific Ocean that were up to fifteen feet long. There was a fox horn, an old bow that twanged, a mridanga drum and a pair of tabla drums. And this was all in our small storefront temple room. Imagine that! Still, all these instruments were played very softly in the morning. When Swamiji sang the Gurvastakam prayer, it lasted about twenty minutes. Sometimes you could look around the room and actually see people crying, just listening to this great soul sing. Even though we didn’t know what he was singing at the time, he sang with such a depth of feeling that you couldn’t take your eyes off of him—and you couldn’t help but feel his sincerity and be deeply touched by it. Then after the Gurvastakam prayer, we all chanted Hare Krishna together, as we hadn’t started responsive chanting yet. After kirtan, he would have one of his students read from the Srimad-Bhagavatam or sometimes from Professor Sanyal’s book on Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. Then we would have another kirtan, and then Swamiji would go up to his room. So this became our first morning program schedule in San Francisco with Swamiji.*

*The evening programs began every Monday, Wednesday and Friday at 7 pm. Swamiji would first sing the Vande ham prayers for 17 to 20 minutes, and then we would all chant Hare Krishna together for about 25 minutes. Swamiji would then give a lecture, and after that we would have a second kirtan which was frequently “Govinda jaya jaya, gopala jaya jaya, radha ra-mana hari, govinda jaya jaya," again sung together. Sometimes we chanted “Sri rama, jaya rama, jaya jaya rama." Another popular chant in the early days was “Gopala gopala, yasodanandan gopala; Gopala gopala, devakinandan gopala.” So after the chanting, Swamiji would distribute fruit prasadam; there would be a question and answer period, and then the devotees would again begin kirtan. And these kirtans would sometimes go on until 10 or 1I pm, and they were absolutely rip-roaring, rocking kirtans, with all the instruments blaring, and long periods of dancing because there simply wasn’t room for anyone to sit on the floor. Sometimes the kirtans would also become responsive between the male and female members. The men would chant a chorus and then the women would chant a chorus. That was the beginning of responsive chanting in San Francisco.*

In a short film taken during kirtan at the Frederick Street temple, the diminutive size of the temple room is clearly visible. It is hard to imagine it fitting so many enthusiastic chanters along with the eclectic and variegated instruments. Yet, if anything, the tight quarters seemed to enhance the familial closeness of the devotees. Remembering those magical early days of Prabhupada’s presence in San Francisco, Yamuna wrote in a prayer:

**I remember in 1967, in the beginning, how you instructed us how to do almost everything—to chant, play instruments, cook, scrub pots, wash clothes, clean floors, wrap robes, make a recording, manufacture kartals, decorate, write letters, keep accounts, pronounce Sanskrit, be committed, responsible, and so on. You even taught us how to be diplomatic with our annoying hooligan neighbors, the Hells Angels Biker Club. In this connection, I pray to become expert in the many services you taught me, but more importantly, to become expert in trying to serve you.**

## The Mahamantra Rocks Haight-Ashbury

While preparations for the temple opening were progressing, Mukunda, Sam, Harvey and other volunteers had also been arranging for a program they coined the “Mantra Rock Dance” at the Avalon Ballroom to introduce Srila Prabhupada to San Francisco and raise money for the temple. Allen Ginsberg would introduce Srila Prabhupada and sit on the stage with him, and some of the most popular and “happening” musicians of the day agreed to appear either for free or a token gratuity. Much has previously been written about this pivotal event in the history of Krishna Consciousness in the West, but it cannot be emphasized enough how this one gathering popularized the Hare Krishna Movement among the entire hippie subculture and made the chanting of Hare Krishna a trendy and “hip” thing to do.

**Yamuna**: *In the early 60 s, before the popularization of psychedelic music, those of us living in the North Beach area of San Francisco knew many of the people who would go on to become famous icons of the genre. I knew Janis Joplin through our mutual friends Linda and Malcolm, and somehow they had persuaded her to sing at the Avalon event. In fact, she was performing just before Swamiji came onto the stage. To me it looked like he glided rather than walked. Here was this diminutive, refined, older gentleman in saffron among a group of rocked-out and drugged-out hippies, and yet he completely charmed and captivated everyone. How can the magnitude of his presence be described? It was simply unprecedented.*

One of the most vivid descriptions of the Avalon Ballroom event was told by Hayagriva das in his Hare Krishna Explosion:

**Suddenly Janis \[Joplin\] ends her song, and the slide show changes. Pictures of Krishna and the demigods are flashed onto the wall. Krishna and Arjuna in the chariot; Krishna eating butter; Krishna subduing the whirlwind demon; Krishna playing the flute. There’s a spontaneous roar of approval, and as Swamiji sits beside Ginsberg on the front center stage, the roar turns into an ovation. The bands also come on stage. Swamiji is garlanded again and again. Allen begins his introduction, commanding attention with the expertise of a Pied Piper. Swamiji sits quietly, his head held high, appearing like a golden Buddha—regal, transcendental, saintly—a strange contrast to poet Ginsberg. Allen tells how his own interest in**

**Hare Krishna started in India five years ago. Then he recounts how Swamiji opened his storefront on Second Avenue and chanted Hare Krishna in Tompkins Square Park. “Now, Krishna Consciousness has come West, to the Haight-Ashbury,” he says, inviting everyone to the Frederick Street temple. “I especially recommend the early morning kirtans,” he adds, “for those who want to stabilize their consciousness on LSD re-entry.”**

**— HARE KRISHNA EXPLOSION**

## The Peace Formula — Chanting, Dancing and Feasting

While the Avalon Ballroom program introduced Srila Prabhupada to San Francisco and allowed the temple to expand its activities through, among other things, a daily prasadam distribution program, it was Srila Prabhupada himself who spread the glories of Krishna Consciousness. He taught by example—by being the living personification of what it meant to be God conscious, and he gave of himself freely and impartially to others. In later years, if someone approached Yamuna to give a brief characterization of Srila Prabhupada, she would often say, “He lived Krishna Consciousness, and he gave it to others.” He directly instructed her that this was the duty of every disciple and asked her to do this throughout her life. “You must teach others what I have given you,” was an instruction Yamuna not only took to heart but felt duty bound to try to follow. Any project she initiated, whether it be her cookbooks, kirtans, festivals, Deity programs, classes or simply encouraging anyone who sought her out, derived instruction from Srila Prabhupada. She used to say, “What can I do? I am so unqualified, but Srila Prabhupada has asked this of me.”

**Yamuna**: *From the onset, Swamiji became the living emblem of the Krishna Consciousness philosophy. Just as a great thief is expert in stealing by practicing his pick-pocketing, so this extraordinary person stole the hearts of his young followers through his vibrant distribution of love of Godhead. He taught us the philosophy and made us eager to practice it. Our immediate program was to have kirtans in the temple on Monday, Wednesday and Friday nights, and on Tuesday and Thursday to go to a shop or gathering of people and chant Hare Krishna there. On the weekends we would go to Golden Gate Park and chant wherever there was a large gathering. Our small temple was soon filled to overflowing with ecstatic dancing and chanting. The responsive chanting of Swamiji and all of the students, accompanied by our eclectic collection of instruments, was transcendentally ecstatic. Swamiji observed everything while sitting on his humble vyasasana decorated with whatever anyone had brought for his pleasure—from tapestries to milk cans, a flower or a leaf. He encouraged everyone to simply bring whatever you have and offer it to Krishna. In this way our piecemeal temple was developing a wonderful family-like atmosphere. Everyone was accepted, encouraged and nourished— physically, emotionally and spiritually.*

*How Swamiji accepted each of us without judgment or rejection was beautifully illustrated by an eccentric person we called “Rabbit.” Dressed like a clown, with bald head and puffs coming out the sides, Rabbit had damaged his brain by taking so many drugs. Yet, every day without fail, he would bring an offering of some kind and place it on the altar. Just as Swamiji had accepted the meager offerings of the Bowery bums, he similarly accepted those of Haight-Ashbury’s mentally challenged, seeing the service rendered rather than the limitations of the server.*

Yamuna felt this compassionate, all-encompassing nature of Srila Prabhupada as unprecedented and almost otherworldly. This was before any of them knew anything about the conservative and proscribed society he had emerged from in India. He could never have imagined what a “hippie” was before coming to the West, nor could he have prepared for the relaxed morals and careless personal hygiene that epitomized their cultural ethos. As the years passed and more of Srila Prabhupada’s personal history became known, it only increased Yamuna’s gratitude and appreciation of him. Who else among the Gaudiya Vaishnavas would have associated with people who were considered so low in character? Who among them would have taken such a risk?

**Yamuna**: *At this time there were absolutely no disagreements among our small family. It was literally astonishing to see how our group of odd characters were becoming swept up by this sankirtan process, and actually tasting the nectar of chanting the Holy Names. Swamiji gave one example in his book Krsna about how these students were likened to jubilant peacocks who are dancing in ecstasy. But it was all through the spiritual potency of Swamiji himself, by his personal example of limitless compassion and sincerity, that thousands of people were getting little tastes of love of God through chanting the Holy Names of the Lord.*

For Yamuna, who had been working enthusiastically to bring Srila Prabhupada to San Francisco ever since her arrival there, the reality of the Frederick Street temple with its new legions of eager chanters increased her conviction in the power of chanting Hare Krishna, yet she was more profoundly convinced by the power of Srila Prabhupada himself. For her, he personified true saintliness in all of his qualities and interactions. At Yamuna at far right studying Srila Prabhupada every opportunity she studied him— how he spoke, how he instructed, how he selflessly gave his time and counsel to anyone who came to him. He became the cynosure of her life, and the evergrowing congregation became her family.

**“You Simply Make What Krishna Likes”— The Love Feasts Begin**

In New York, Kirtanananda had been Srila Prabhupada’s principal cook, but in the beginning in San Francisco, Srila Prabhupada himself trained anyone who wanted to learn, especially the women, in both the philosophical and practical aspects of cooking for Krishna. He taught them how to prepare the simple foods they were eating daily: rice, dal, chapatis and vegetables, as well as the special feast preparations such as kachoris, samosas, khir (sweet rice) and halava. And he taught them how to offer the food to the Supreme Lord so it would become sanctified and become prasadam.

**Yamuna**: *Swamiji began training us in cooking during the spring. His expertise in the kitchen always remained a great source of wonder to me. He would cook so quickly, while keeping four or five chapatis on the tawa at one time. From the beginning in 1966 to the end of his presence with us in late 1977, he was still emphasizing, “You simply make what Krishna likes, not what you like.”*

Intuitively, Srila Prabhupada seemed to understand that the combination of kirtan and prasadam distribution would draw an immediate and enthusiastic response, and so in addition to the daily temple kirtan and prasadam distribution programs, he wanted to inaugurate the Sunday Love Feasts right away.

**Yamuna**: *Swamiji soon established the Sunday Love Feast, which became instantly and immensely popular. We would go for our regular schedule of park kirtans or wherever there was a large gathering and invite people to come to the Sunday Love Feast. And in those days there were always nice people who were very eager to try chanting Hare Krishna, and the kirtans reflected that spirit and were open, free and very lively. So we would collect a large following of people and bring them to the temple. All of the lady members would cook something, and madras cloths were laid down all over the temple floor. Often the crowds were so large that we couldn’t all fit into the temple and would have to put madras cloths on the sidewalk as well. The line-up of people for the feast program began at the front door of the storefront and \[would\] snake past the Chinese laundry, past the entrance to the apartment building, and continue on for up to a hundred feet—all waiting to crowd into the temple to take prasadam. Prasadam became the medicine for the hippie era. What attracted people the most to come to the temple were the amazing kirtans and the amazing prasadam. The feasts were often so opulent that our pots would be spread from the very front to the very back of the temple—maybe sixty pots full of prasadam. All of us would make at least one huge dish. Some of the visitors would also make something, and we would share this at the Sunday Feast. So Swamiji, through instituting the Sunday Feast program of kirtan and prasadam distribution, had an immediate and tremendous impact on the hippie culture in San Francisco. That time-honored formula has been maintained in much the same way throughout the world to the present day.*

## Contemplating Initiation — “Just See! Just See!”

For months Yamuna had been agonizing over whether to become initiated. She had increasingly developed faith in Srila Prabhupada, pleasure in serving his mission, a deep attraction for the Holy Names and an abiding love for her devotee “family.” Yet she worried that she might not be able to follow the vows Srila Prabhupada asked of initiated disciples. Neither could she abide the hypocrisy of taking such vows knowing they would not be honored. This was so important to Yamuna that for the rest of her life she carried a copy of the “Notice” of requirements for initiated devotees that Srila Prabhupada had written in November 25,1966, and wherever we lived, she would place it prominently on the wall in the temple room.

**Yamuna**: *I had been coming since the fall of 1966, associating with Swamiji and the devotees and engaging in devotional service. And I would vacillate between moments of great feeling with tears pouring down my face, or I would be falling asleep. So I was wavering. “How can I apply this philosophy to my life?” I had developed a deep regard for Swamiji’s personal demeanor, his teachings, his genuineness, and slowly, slowly, I began to perceive that his unique character emanated from his purity and was like nothing I had ever experienced before. In full, he was learned and spiritually mature, compas sionate and encouraging, patient and loving. Undoubtedly he was the most powerful teacher I had ever come across—he consistently instructed both by example and precept, and he treated everyone with genuine respect, be they charlatan or ruffian, beggar or aristocrat, intelligent or foolish. He lis tened attentively, and his responses often included metaphors or allegories to make a philosophical truth easily understood. In short, his association fascinated and impacted me at every turn. And yet, whenever I yearned to take the next step, to become his initiated disciple, something inside held me back.*

*Swamiji asked all of his initiated students to daily chant japa, have kirtan, read Srimad-Bhagavatam, and most importantly, follow the four regulative principles: no gambling, no intoxicants, no meat eating, and no illicit sex life. I had no idea how this would sit with me, but I knew I had to try it first before vowing to do so in front of Swamiji. From his apartment window, Swamiji would watch the activities going on just outside the temple entrance, and occasionally he would notice a new disciple smoking, and this saddened him. He knew that for many hippies giving up intoxication and illicit sex life were the most difficult of the regulations to follow, and Swamiji said that he prayed that we would give up all such bad habits so that the peace and happiness of Krishna Conscious life could become firmly established in our hearts. “When will they stop? When will they stop?” he would question. I knew one thing for sure: I didn’t want to be a deceptive disciple. I wanted to be open and transparent with Swamiji.*

*I remember entering Swamiji’s room one day, and he immediately asked: “When you are going to become initiated?” I replied that I was still uncertain, but it was possible that I was going to take a trip to India and Tibet, because I respected high mountains and elevated spiritual consciousness, and I wanted to go to the highest place. He looked at me intently for a long time and with great feeling replied, “I can take you to a higher place than Tibet. Just see! Just see!” and when he said those words, “Just see! Just see!” I began to completely understand. “Oh, I have to see through his eyes what the highest place is—what this Krishna Consciousness philosophy is.” So I decided then and there to create an experiment to ascertain the level of my commitment.*

In retrospect, whenever Yamuna looked back at those years—at her initial reluctance to commit to initiation in Krishna Consciousness—she would often become emotional when recalling Srila Prabhupada’s patience, tolerance and limitless compassion for herself and for all who approached him. He endured her inconstancy with equanimity, waiting for what she referred to as the “Krishna Magic” to take effect on her heart. Yamuna’s opportunity to test her level of commitment came in an unusual way—through an invitation from her friend Roger to a remote cabin on the Northern California Coast.

## The Rockport Experiment

Srila Prabhupada had been in San Francisco for over a month when Yamuna was invited by Roger to Rockport. It was a defining moment in Yamuna’s life, both spiritually and personally. Yamuna and Roger had become firm friends since she handed him a flyer announcing “Bring Krishna Consciousness West,” and she saw Rockport as the perfect place to test her commitment to Swamiji, as well as to see if there was a possible future with Roger in marriage.

**Yamuna:** *At age 24,I did not seek out marriage, but quickly noted that life as an unmarried woman in ISKCON would be difficult—possibly ruinous. My idealized vision of living as ayogini or single female all but dissipated upon observing how some of the male devotees in New York seemed dismissive of my sister Janaki, Swamiji’s first female disciple. Janaki, always frank and plainspoken, quipped one day that the men were capable of pleasantness, but only in small doses. Able to look ahead into my own future challenges, I could not see myself remaining single in the long term. Fortunately, the early chemistry between the men and women in the Frederick Street temple was quite different from New York. Most were already paired off as couples, while the single men were almost, without exception, kind and nonjudg-mental. Men and women associated with each other comfortably, acting not only as good friends, but more like affectionate brothers and sisters— our common ground, Swamiji. I had never forgotten Swamiji’s lecture on “Liquid Beauty” in New York, and how it made me realize that what I had taken for love in this world was in fact only lust. So in deliberating on my own marriage, I was not looking to find love, but rather to find someone who would be a helpmate on the journey back home, Back to Godhead.*

*So on Saturday morning, February 18, Mukunda and Janaki drove Roger, his dog Quetal and me to Rockport, California, ft had taken six months, but I was finally at the point of considering initiation, and it was time to make a test of my seriousness and sincerity. Was I ready to commit without duplicity to the vows of initiation? So I saw this trip to Rockport as a two-fold opportunity: first, to practice the vows of an initiated devotee, and second, to see how things progressed with Roger. Many couples visiting the temple were hurriedly becoming initiated and getting married, but neither of us had felt ready to commit to either; both were to be taken very seriously. Neither was I willing to settle for a Haight-style, free-love relationship with Roger. I figured that if we spent some time alone together, away from the peer pressure of friends and family, it would all become clear to us.*

*For the first few days, while I cooked and cleaned, Roger chopped firewood and hauled water. We took afternoon walks to the cliffs above the sea with Quetal. We adjusted to the solitude, the rhythms of nature, and lack of city stimulus. I had begun my “experiment” routine on day one of our stay. It consisted of all three aspects of Swamiji’s program: kirtan, Srimad-Bhagavatam study, and following the four rules and regulations. A few days passed before Roger mentioned my obvious activities. I explained the gist of what I was doing, adding that it was my own “experiment,” and I would not impose any of it on him.*

*As far as my own feelings went, I was absolutely loving it—all of it. I felt happy, peaceful and balanced and noticed a silly grin on my face while doing everyday things—picking wild roses, chanting japa or kneading bread. As for kirtan, I pretty much chanted quietly all day. Mostly I sang Swamiji’s Hare Krishna melody, but sometimes other tunes came out spontaneously. No instruments. When I was not working, I liked to chant kirtan on the porch rocking chair looking towards the sea or sitting against an old-growth Redwood tree next to a creek. How different my consciousness was now! Two or three years ago I turned to nature for a meaningful psychedelic experience. Now I found that the chanting of Hare Krishna opened my heart to the most majestic beauty and awareness. It was deeply humbling and filled me with gratitude.*

*The study of the Srimad-Bhagavatam was a simultaneous revelation and epiphany. It was the first sacred book I had ever completely resonated with. Sometimes before reading it, I would hold the volume in my hands and pray with reverence to understand its contents. But I instinctively knew that the key to understanding the true meaning of the Bhagavatam rested with Swamiji. I quickly filled pages in my study notebook with questions, and ended each day with many pages having to do with personalities I’d never heard of, mystical activities, and histories not taught in any university.*

*Perhaps the biggest surprise of all was the sense of freedom I felt by following the discipline of the four regulative principles. Rather than feeling constrained by them, I felt empowered. My senses— hearing, seeing, tasting, smelling and feeling—were heightened to new levels of awareness. I could not understand why I had spent so long in Swamiji’s company before giving this process a serious try.*

*By the end of the tenth day, Roger honestly admitted that he was not in the same space at all. Our biggest tension was my following of the four regulative principles, and perhaps because of this, we were often at odds with each other. Our differences culminated one afternoon on a walk to the cliffs above the sea. While we quarreled, Roger’s dog Quetal charged towards a herd of sheep near the cliff’s edge. They panicked and ran blindly, their pitiful cries and Quetal’s furious barking filling the air, and within seconds some sheep had leapt off the cliffs to their deaths below. Almost immediately Quetal returned to Roger’s feet and sat there quietly. In one sense I saw the incident for what it was: animals with conflicting natures. Yet I also took the incident as a sign that it was definitely time for me to return to San Francisco. I knew the outcome of my “experiment,” and realized that I didn’t want to spend another day away from Swamiji.*

*The next morning I phoned Janaki from the corner store, asked her to pick me up, and requested Mukunda to make an appointment for me to speak with Swamiji. I was ready to discuss my initiation. They were elated. When I returned to the cabin, Roger and I had a blameless and productive conversation and we both expressed our differing points of view. We decided to give ourselves time apart to reflect on our relationship.*

During this time Srila Prabhupada had been tirelessly spreading the chanting of the Holy Names and his mission of Krishna Consciousness at every opportunity. His exuberance, conviction and tireless energy were infectious, and large numbers of people were attending his lectures and kirtans. In a letter to Brahmananda in New York on February io, he wrote:

**I think everything is going well here by the Grace of Lord Krishna. I have invitations from other organizations to lecture on nth, 12th and 14th at Self Realization Organization, Himalayan Academy Administration and San Francisco University College. Some of them write as follows: “Your Holiness: You have brought great beauty and harmony to our community through your love and devotion. Many souls have found their inner peace in your teachings of Krishna Consciousness.”**

**— LETTER TO BRAHMANANDA, FEB. 10, 1967**

On February 27 he went to Stanford University for a lecture and kirtan program which the Palo Ako Times facetiously reported on the following day:

**Hold on there a minute, all you “with it” people. There’s a new dance about to sweep the country. It’s called “the swami.” It’s going to replace the frug, watusi, swim and even the good old barn stomp. Why? Because you can do any old step to it and at the same time find “real happiness.” You can rid yourself of the illusion that you and your body are inseparable.... Before the night was over, 150 of the audience were stomping, swinging and chanting to the beat of Indian instruments and the words of the Holy Sanskrit Vedas—Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. They chanted without interruption for 70 minutes.**

Despite the reporter’s irreverent take on the program, Srila Prabhupada’s magnetism invariably impressed audiences wherever he went, often causing them to enthusiastically chant and dance for long stretches of time. Even with his satirical slant, the reporter clearly conveys this mood in his article.

## Yamuna Dedicates Herself to Guru and Krishna

Yamuna had now chosen to dedicate herself to the practice of Krishna Consciousness and was ready to become initiated as Srila Prabhupada’s disciple. Roger had also had a change of heart, and they decided that they would marry after becoming initiated. On March 7,1967, \]oan became Yamuna devi dasi and Roger became Guru das. The following day, March 8, they were married by Srila Prabhupada.

**Yamuna: I was married on March 8. Swamiji sat majestically wearing a garland of rhododendron flowers and leaves. Next to him sat none other than my Aunt Edna Howell, who had come for the wedding and gamely participated in the fire sacrifice, taking on the role of giving me away in marriage. And because we were thinking that butter was too costly for the fire sacrifice, we used melted margarine instead. So I remember we had an orange crate that was torn into little shreds for starting the fire sacrifice, and as Swamiji was sitting in front of the fire, he picked up one little toothpick-like shred with his long, delicate fingers, dipped it into the melted margarine, held it to the candle, and it went svit, svit, svit and then fizzled out. He picked up another one—svit, svit, svit—it went out. So he repeated this process using little and large pieces, at least four or five times. Finally he looked up with his beautiful and impish smile and said: “This marriage will have a very slow start.” So although he meant it in a lighthearted manner, I already had a premonition that marriage in this Krishna Consciousness Movement might not be the “happily ever after” scenario I had imagined in my childhood.**

Yamuna did not often revisit either her initiation or marriage ceremonies. She once remarked that she felt in an out-of-body state going through them—dazed and disoriented—and the few pictures of her marriage ceremony speak volumes about her state of mind. She had deliberated so long over the initiation issue and approached it with such gravity that perhaps the marriage coming the next day did not allow her to emotionally distinguish them.
