**I am pleased to learn that you are singing the Cintamani prayers of Brahma Samhita. This Brahma Samhita contains the highest of all spiritual knowledge. In lecturing too if we sing a verse from Brahma Samhita and then nicely explain the meaning it will be very much appreciated. Just as Krishna is the All-Attractive principle so, similarly, these Krishna kathas of the Brahma Samhita are All-Attractive and will gain favorable attention from listeners.**

**Also your description of progress in kirtan performance with Guru das playing sitar and Mukunda playing khole is encouraging. Practically we see that as we sincerely try to improve our chanting for the pleasure of Krishna, Krishna reciprocates and we feel our greatest pleasure which is devotional service to the Lord. So, you may continue with this method; it is very nice and approved by me.**

**— LETTER TO SHYAMASUNDARA, NOV. 24, 1968**

Although they had an immediate impact and were encouraged by the response, they all faced major challenges in finding living arrangements. After Herne Hill, they were forced to live separately in what Yamuna called “ghettos.” Each couple struggled in separate accommodation until they were temporarily brought together again in a rent-free four-story warehouse on Betterton Street. On the positive side, they were all in the same location and had free accommodation. On the negative side, there were no showers, only cold water, and no heat except space heaters. Still they soldiered on, and Srila Prabhupada wrote often, encouraging and nurturing them. Each of his letters was eagerly shared among them all—a perpetual reservoir of hope and strength. Of them all, Janaki was feeling especially lonely and disaffected. She wrote of this to Srila Prabhupada, and typically he encouraged each of them in his reply:

**I think also that it is a good sign that Krishna is delaying to give us a nice London temple because when it finally will come, it may be the most ideal temple for our purposes. So none of you be discouraged, but go on with your engagements and everything will come automatically—very nice. I have noted that you describe yourself as being just a “lump of ignorance.” Actually the devotee should always think like that. That the devotee should feel himself so lowly is the teaching of Lord Chaitanya. Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu also represented Himself as a very foolish disciple even though He proved Himself as the greatest scholar and was actually Krishna Himself. So one who feels humble and meek has the door for the Kingdom of God opened for him or her. So I thank you again for your nice letter and please continue to inform me of your well-being.**

**— LETTER TO JANAKI, DEC. 9, 1968**

**Yamuna**: *He was the supreme encourager. If I think of myself in relation to cooking, or if you see yourself in relationship to those that you value the most in devotional service, there are people that generously encourage you and see whatever strengths you have. So Srila Prabhupada was so brilliant at this—at understanding our minds and our needs. And when you just look at his letters and see how he wrote so much encouragement—to give us some very big, challenging thing to do and then more or less say, “You can do this.” So in that way I think that the spirit of creativity came that we had no idea what we were doing but, “Let’s do something. Right?” And just come up with it. And that was all because of Srila Prabhupada’s encourage-ment.(LONDON 40TH ANNIV.)*

Mukunda Goswami later wrote about Yamuna’s determination to keep the three couples focused on Krishna Consciousness during their difficult early months in England.

**Mukunda Goswami:** *In England when we first went over there, one of the few times that everyone would be assembled together would be at prasadam. And at that time she would always read. I mean every time the devotees got together she would read, usually from Caitanya-caritamrta. Because she knew it was just going to be prajalpa time if she didn’t read. But for whatever reason, it was a sign of her deep dedication to Krishna Consciousness philosophy that she would read constantly out loud to all of us.*

Thirty-five years before, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati encouraged his London-based disciples in much the same manner by, among other things, requesting them to be neither affected by praise nor neglect from others:

**We should call at the door of each and every seeker of the Truth, bearing on our heads the baggage of the Real Truth to be offered to them. It is no business of ours to be elated or discouraged by the praise or neglect of any person. We must be constantly alive to the duty of enhancing the pleasure of our Master by serving Him with perfect sincerity.**

**— SARASWATI THAKUR, ADDRESS TO LONDON-BOUND DISCIPLES, 1933**

It was important to Srila Prabhupada that his young disciples in London understood something of the origins of Krishna Consciousness in the West, as well as the honor and privilege they held in representing not only Srila Prabhupada, but the previous great Acharyas who began the mission of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu there. Srila Prabhupada asked that the society be formally registered as soon as possible. He also wanted a beautiful and elaborate Certificate of Membership to be awarded to all initiated disciples. On October 3,1968, Srila Prabhupada sent Yamuna a series of drawings by Muralidhara das of Lord Chaitanya, Radha and Krishna, Their Lordships Jagannatha, Subhadra and Balarama, and Srila Prabhupada himself, and he inscribed a small drawing of his design concept at the top of the letter. He first wrote words of praise, telling Yamuna that he was encouraged by all their activities:

**I am in due receipt of your nice letter of 9/27/68, from London Yatra, and it is so much encouraging to me. Your appreciation is so nice of Srimad Bhagavad-gita and Teachings of Lord Caitanya, and please continue to study and preach in this way to all you meet. I am very happy to learn that you are going to various homes and lecture halls, and holding kirtan and delivering lectures from these transcendental literatures. This is very nice. And if you continue in this way, gradually so many people will be attracted, and our London center will be very soon successful. I have received also your handbills, and they are also very nice. All this good news is very much encouraging to me, and I thank you all six sincere souls for carrying on this mission so enthusiastically.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, ОСТ. 3, 1968**

Srila Prabhupada then very specihcally instructed Yamuna on how to prepare the certificate.

**The drawings for the certificate are enclosed herewith, and you can place them in proper position, as they look best. These recommendations may also help you: Best use a 15 x 20 or similar proportion paper.... Be sure that after pasting in each corner, that the edges are kept clean, so that they do not show when photographed. For printing they can be reduced some, to about an inch or two larger than a piece of typewriting paper (with whatever exact proportions are convenient to use in the reduction). Muralidhara das has drawn these pictures, and they are very nicely done.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, ОСТ. 3, 1968**

Even though Yamuna was expert in the arts of calligraphy and graphic design, this letter illustrates how Srila Prabhupada wanted everything done to his exacting specifications. Yamuna learned this very early on in her relationship with him, and endeavored with determination to perfect each service or task, whether in the fields of calligraphy, kirtan, cooking, cleaning, preaching or anything else. On December 5, Yamuna sent the finished Certificate of Membership form to Srila Prabhupada, and in reply, he expressed his appreciation of her “glorious sentiments,” encouraged all of the London devotees in their progress in devotional service, and pronounced the completed certificates “very beautiful and nicely done.”

**I thank you so much for your letter of November 30, 1968, and the glorious sentiments you have expressed therein. I am so glad to read that you are doing very well and keeping always engaged. This is the key to elevating in Krishna Consciousness, that we always keep our thoughts, our words and our actions centered around our life and soul, this being Krishna. If we remember to practice this process then automatically all distresses and botherations will become nil. So I am very encouraged that all of you are progressing in learning this technique. So far as the certificates are concerned, they are very beautiful and nicely done.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, DEC. 9, 1968**

## Kirtan is the Universal Principle — Yamuna Devi and George Harrison

**Yamuna**: *Each one of us remembers the interlude with the Beatles, George Harrison and Apple Records differently, because we each experienced it differently. My remembrances by necessity differ from those of the others because the impact of each event, or each circumstance, affected each of us uniquely according to our individual consciousness. Over the years, I have been asked numerous times to describe George: my perception of him and my relationship with him.*

*If asked to describe him in a word, I would say that he was a gentleman in the truest sense of the word. He was genuinely nice, caring, with a funny—some would say zany—sense of humor. Of course, because he was enormously famous, the lens of his vision was inevitably colored by that. A private man, he could not escape the trappings of fame. I respected his privacy and never trammeled over him, seeking the magic touch of a connection with him. My relationship with him was based on our shared love of kirtan, and it was deep because of that—not anything else.*

*I would observe him in various situations over those years, both in England, in India, and later again in England. It was always kirtan, not conversation, which remained the glue in our friendship. At the Sydenham press conference for the “Hare Krishna Mantra” single release, I led kirtan. When it was over, I turned around and glanced at George, who sat slightly behind me. He smiled and then, teary-eyed, silently mouthed, “Hare Krishna, Yamuna.” It was practically our only exchange that day, but it meant more than words could say.*

*A memorable aspect of knowing George was observing him with Prabhupada. On several occasions— in England and later in India—I was present at their meetings. Their conversations were friendly, stimulating and frank. Both smiled frequently and genuinely. George exhibited an honest humility in Prabhupada’s presence, and Prabhupada treated George with no more nor less respect than he did with everyone he met. I think George perceived that and appreciated it.*

*After Lord Krishna’s Cuisine was published, we spoke as much about the spiritual aspects of Krishna prasadam—mA how to cook it—as we had about kirtan. George loved gardening, and he loved cooking, both activities dear to my heart as well. In retrospect, it is interesting seeing the interconnecting circles of that connection—always heartfelt, always respectful, always spiritual.*

## "Come Chant with Us”—An Apple a Day

The six members of the sankirtan party arrived in England with the notion fully developed that they would somehow meet the Beatles, who were already interested in yoga—specifically the teachings of Maharishi Mahesh Yogi. From their humble quarters, the women started making distinctive apple dishes—a different one each day—and delivering them to Apple Records in the hopes of attracting their attention. On top would be different eye-catching things—a smiling picture of them all, a Yamuna-calligraphed mahamantra with an invitation to “Come Chant with Us,” and other clever adaptations. They also sent a demo of the Govindam recordings they had been practicing. It worked.

**Yamuna**: *So we sent the apple prasadam, and it went from the lower floors of the Apple Studios to the upper floors, so that ultimately everyone tasted some apple prasadam, and they became a little addicted to that. When we stopped sending it, thinking it was having no effect, we were notified, “Where are those Hare Krishna people with the apples?”*

*Shyamasundara was the first to meet George, and they established an immediate rapport. A tall and thin man, Shyamasundara used to rock back and forth, and I remember that George also rocked back and forth like that. After they met, George invited him to lunch at his home, and later Shyamasundara invited George to our Betterton Street place for prasadam and kirtan. When he arrived, George initially chatted with the three men while we women finished frying samosas and puris and making an offering. After we were introduced, we had kirtan. As fate would have it, I led a short, but exuberant kirtan. Then we served prasadam.*

*The first time George spoke to me that night, he brought up kirtan. As I offered him kofta seconds, he casually mentioned that he liked my voice and my kirtan mood. He also said that he had heard me chant before. Stunned, I said I thought that quite impossible, but when I asked how and when, he chuckled and said that “out on a lark one night” in disguise and incognito, he had slipped into the dark room at the Arts Lab. I was leading kirtan in the room, and he stayed and chanted for about a half-hour before making a sneak departure. He again mentioned my voice, saying it was “mesmerizing.” I laughed and said I thought I sounded like a croaking frog, but that I loved chanting. He said he too loved to chant. I remember thinking that this was just Krishna’s magic-only Krishna’s magic.*

*Shortly after that dinner and kirtan at Betterton Street, George first invited Shyamasundara and then all of us to visit his house in Esher. There kirtan was the main event. For hours we chanted—long, deep kirtans. Billy Preston played organ. George played his upright white harmonium and guitar. Mukunda played mridanga. Shyamasundara played esraj. Guru das, Malati, Janaki and I played kartals. We chanted, then switched instruments and chanted some more. Then we had prasadam. When you chant with someone for hours, a connection is established. It happened with George that day.*

As the group continued their kirtans at every opportunity, Srila Prabhupada continued reinforcing their efforts by mail, calling kirtan the “universal principle”:

**It is very much encouraging to me to hear of so many activities of performing kirtan there. Kirtan is the universal principle; therefore, if you chant Hare Krishna offenselessly, that is to say, avoiding the io kinds of offenses, the vibration is sure to act. And anywhere this vibration is made, it will be liked because it is done on the spiritual platform. And on the spiritual platform, there will be certainly agreement. So long as one is on the material platform, there is no agreement. So our Movement is directly taken to the spiritual platform. So do it nicely, offenselessly, and it will be successful anywhere.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, DEC. 14, 1968**

**Yamuna**: *Musically, we were becoming a tight little group. Mukunda was our main arranger, but with so much practice and the mercy of the maha-mantra itself, we were becoming more and more confident that at least in that way, the way of kirtan, we were serving Srila Prabhupada to the best of our ability. Sometimes we would have kirtans at George’s house, and they were magical—several hours long and very intense—followed by prasadam feasts.*

In the meantime, the society had finally become legally registered in England, and a program was arranged at the Betterton Street address just after the New Year to formally launch the Hare Krishna Movement in London. Invitations were sent out, elaborate prasadam was prepared and served, and Srila Prabhupada sent a recorded greeting in which he spoke about Krishna and Lord Chaitanya, and then concluded with a charming message:

**Hear the message of Krishna as it is in the Bhagavad-gita.... The consciousness is there in you. Cleanse it of all dirty things. Make it clear Krishna Consciousness in \[this\] pleasant method by chanting the glorified names of God—Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama, Rama, Hare Hare.**

The first major countrywide exposure of the devotees in England occurred through an article in the Sunday Times, written by Atticus, a popular columnist of the day. Accompanied by a picture of the smiling group of devotees along with baby Saraswati, the largely favorable article introduced the shaven-headed Hare Krishna devotees by referring to them as “very gentle people, a bit unworldly, but not at all ingenuous.... What’s likely to earn them a public is their chanting.” His prediction could not have been more accurate.

Yamuna sent the article and picture to Srila Prabhupada, who was undoubtedly pleased by it. Seen in the light of the somewhat nebulous outcome of his Godbrothers’ attempts to establish a footing in England, the sincere efforts of his own young disciples and the results they produced must have given him great happiness:

**This picture is undoubtedly very unique because perhaps in the history of the world it is the first time that Western boys and girls in the dress of pure Vaishnavas are chanting on the streets of a very important quarter of the greatest city in the world, London. So by the Grace of Krishna you are all six together doing very nice Krishna Consciousness activities, and I am so much pleased.... I have received a report from Mr. Parikh and others that they are enamored by your behavior, your character, and your devotion. In the newspaper cuttings also they gave such hints. In other words, everyone is appreciating your presentation. Please keep up this standard of behavior. Do not make any artificial discrepancies amongst yourselves because you are acting on a very responsible business.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS AND YAMUNA, JAN. 21, 1969**

Srila Prabhupada also alluded in the letter to some of the differences that had arisen among the London devotees, and reminded them in his gentle way to keep focused on the goal and not let anything disturb that. It would be natural to assume that within the tumult of their lives, with little money and no real housing, differences would ensue, so these letters of encouragement, along with promises of his imminent arrival there, enlivened and surcharged them. They were also enthused by the obvious impact they were having with their kirtans, as well as their new relationship with George Harrison and the Beatles, and the exposure that recording with them would bring to the Sankirtan Movement.

**I thank you very much for your assurance that I will find London a most flourishing center for our world Sankirtan Movement. That is my ideal of life, to form a nice group of devotees to perform sankirtan and to distribute our books in wider circles. Here, Tamai Krishna’s group has proved a very nice sankirtan party, and we can combine with your group which is also a very nice sankirtan party. Then we could immediately take the responsibility of a round the world trip, and I am sure it will be successful. You can let me know by return mail if my services in London are immediately required. I am prepared to go.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, FEB. 5, 1969**

Janaki had again written to Srila Prabhupada in January expressing her discouragement due to their financial hardships and what she perceived as inequities among themselves. She felt it was making her “unstable.” Srila Prabhupada wrote an extraordinary reply, again reminding them of the great mission they were on and the responsibility it entailed. In their sisterly relationship, Yamuna often tried to encourage Janaki by making her laugh at their impossible situation. Once she said, “Janaki, you know how the Beatles made that song ‘Magical Mystery Tour’? Well, that’s us. We are on a magical mystery tour.” And Janaki would again find humor amid their difficulties:

**Regarding your unstable condition of mind, I beg to request you to always remember that you have all gone to London with a great mission and responsibility. I am so much pleased with you all six boys and girls who are doing so much for my missionary work. My Guru Maharaja, Bhaktisiddhanta Thakur, Lord Chaitanya, and at the end Lord Krishna Himself, all are surely very much pleased for your noble activities. You have already made the city of London feel something about the Hare Krishna Movement. This is a great credit for you all and I appreciate it very much. Please do your duty combinedly without any disruption of peaceful attitudes amongst yourselves. We are pushing our Movement on the background of a peaceful atmosphere in the world, and if we show a little disturbance in our own camp that will not be a very good example. Therefore, everyone should be forbearing, tolerant and cooperative. That is my special request to you all.**

**— LETTER TO JANAKI, JAN. l8, 1969**

**‘You are Doing Very Nicely — More than Having a Temple”**

Over the next months, despite the highs of periodic kirtans with George Harrison and others, new members joining their ranks, continued recognition and harinam sankirtan, Yamuna’s health had begun to deteriorate under the austere living conditions. After four months they were asked to leave Betterton Street and were again forced to find separate living accommodations. Despite Mukunda and the men diligently working to arrange a permanent temple, it had not yet transpired, despite the willingness of George Harrison to guarantee a loan to buy or rent a building. This was especially disheartening because Mukunda and Guru das had written Srila Prabhupada in January that “Mr. George Harrison is arranging for a first-class temple, better than the one to be had on Baker Street.” In the midst of this, Srila Prabhupada wrote requesting the devotees to distribute Back to Godhead magazines for fifty cents each and contribute a sum to his Book Trust, a seeming impossibility for the cash-starved devotees. Yet, by asking as an affectionate father asks his child, Srila Prabhupada nonetheless charmed and motivated them:

**I am just claiming this contribution as your pet child. My father was very much affectionate, and in my childhood, whatever I wanted from my father he would at once give me. One time he purchased for me one rifle, and so after taking it I demanded that he must give me another. My father denied: “You already have one. Why do you ask me for another?” So my argument was that I must have two rifles, one for each hand. Due to my obstinacy my father finally agreed. Later on when I was young and lost my father, I was very sorry to have lost such an affectionate father, but by Krishna’s Grace, I have now many American fathers and mothers. So I am appealing to all of my American fathers and mothers to help me by this contribution. Please let me know if you will do this. I am awaiting your early reply.**

**— LETTER TO MUKUNDA, FEB. 20, I969**

When Srila Prabhupada found out about Yamuna’s health problems, he wrote to her:

**I am in due receipt of your very nice letter, and I am both happy and unhappy on reading it. I am happy to hear from you, but I am unhappy because I hear that for the last three months you are not keeping your good health. I do not know why you should reduce in your health, but after all, this body is external—we should not be very much disturbed with it. It is advised in the Bhagavad-gita that this bodily happiness and unhappiness are temporary, like seasonal changes, so as we are not very much disturbed even in severe cold or scorching heat—we have to execute our daily duties—we \[should\] not be very much disturbed with our bodily pains. But because we are long associated with this material body, sometimes we are afflicted, but by higher knowledge we have to tolerate the pains, wisely thinking that these bodily pains are not mine. But I am very much happy for your nice spiritual sentiments. In London there may be a temple or not, it does not matter; you are doing very nicely, more than having a temple. If Krishna gives us a better temple, that is all right, otherwise, your engagement in kirtan is very, very nice. So continue this program in cooperation with your other godbrothers and sisters, and Krishna will make you very happy. You six together are doing so nicely that I am very much proud of you. Be blessed by Lord Sri Chaitanya and go on like this.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, MAR. 13, I969**

Another hopeful avenue during this time for securing a London temple came through the Gujarati woman guru, Shyama Mataji. She was introduced to the devotees sometime near the New Year, and Malati wrote about her to Srila Prabhupada. Yamuna eventually had many interactions with Shyama Ma, who was very taken with Yamuna’s presence and her kirtan. Those interactions and Srila Prabhupada’s revealing commentary concisely illustrate how he carefully nourished the inner creeper of bhakti in his disciples while teaching them to be aware of ulterior motivations in others. As Shyama Ma showed increasing interest in and affection for Yamuna, Srila Prabhupada realized that she was trying to entice her into becoming her own disciple. The following quotations describe in Srila Prabhupada’s own words the introductions, promises, expectations and ultimate disillusionment in relationship to Shyama Ma.

**Regarding this Shyama Mataji dasi from Vrindavan, does she sing Hare Krishna mantra or not? If she chants Hare Krishna it is all right, and if she does not chant the Hare Krishna mantra, you should ask her why she does not do so. I am not familiar with her Spiritual Master, Gaurangidas, but if he has taught her to sing this Radha-Shyama song, then he also is not authorized.**

**— LETTER TO MALATI, JAN. 28, 1969**

Sometime before the end of February, Shyama Mataji came to Los Angeles to meet Srila Prabhupada. He found her sympathetic and respectful of his efforts. She assured him of her intention to help in securing a temple, as well as in their overall preaching efforts, but this turned out to be a fruitless promise:

**Another news is that Mother Shyamadasi came to L.A. with some of her Gujarati devotees. She appeared to be nice Vaishnavi. And she wants to work in cooperation with me. I have told her that I have no objection but how we shall cooperate, that is to be formulated when we meet next. In the meantime, she has said that she has collected some money from the Indian community in London, perhaps 10,000 pounds, and she is anxious to start a temple there. So you can think over this matter, how we can cooperate with her.... She offered her respect unto me just like her Spiritual Master, several times she touched my feet.... She has got Sri Sri Radha-Krishna murti with her always, and she chants Hare Krishna, so if there is any possibility of cooperating, then we shall welcome it.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, MAR. 13 , 1969**

**I understand that Mataji Shyamadevi is back there in London, so she will also help in your efforts. I hope you will contact me soon by post to inform me of the position of the new address and how you are. I hope you are well.**

**— LETTER TO SHYAMASUNDARA, APR. 5, I969**

**And what about \[Shyama\] Mataji? When she was here she assured me so many things hopeful that she wants to work conjointly. I understand that Shyamasundara has gone to Mataji to build an altar. This means that she has already started the temple. She wanted me also to go to London, and I told her that as soon as the opening of a temple is assured, I shall go to London, leaving aside all other engagements here. But since she has departed she has not written me anything, although I have written her one letter forwarded through Malati, acknowledging receipt of her book, Mataji Charitavali.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, APR. 27, 1969**

**Regarding Mataji, she must have some trouble because she has done something which is nescience. How could she marry a young girl to Krishna? Is Krishna so play thing that He can be handled in such a way? This means she has no knowledge of Krishna. She is simply a sentimental devotee. When a sentimental devotee takes the part of becoming representative of Krishna, there is simply havoc.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, MAY 15, I969**

Srila Prabhupada wrote to Yamuna on May 27 in answer to questions about the upcoming Rathayatra festival. In it he again raised the topic of Shyama Ma, and in so doing gave a most profound and inviolable definition of Krishna Consciousness:

**I am writing Mataji Shyamadasi in Hindi.... Of course there are many Indians who may be delighted to have a Hindu temple there, but we are especially interested in something else. Our plan is not to sponsor the Hindus or any other individual group. Our real purpose is to spread Krishna Consciousness. This means that there is one God, Krishna; there is one scripture, Bhagavad-gita As It Is; there is one mantra, Hare Krishna; and there is one work, service of Lord Krishna. We want to preach this all over the world, and I am sure people from all groups of religion will join us. If we establish a temple on the principles of Mataji, it is also very nice, we may draw the attention of a section of Hindus, but we cannot really execute our ideals. So we cannot be very much enthusiastic in this connection. She is undoubtedly a good devotee of Krishna, but she has to learn the science of Krishna Consciousness.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, MAY 27, I969**

**Regarding \[Shyama\] Mataji, I have noted your remarks, and actually we do not want to create a group of prakrta sahajiya, or devotees who do not know the science of Krishna and do not know the science of devotion, but simply worship the Deity with no depth of knowledge. That is called materialistic devotee, but it is also not rejected. It is a beginning, but a preacher must be above this. Anyway, keep friendship with her. She is trying to love Krishna and that is good. Why not ask her to help you perform the Rathayatra?**

**— LETTER TO SHYAMASUNDARA, JUNE 3, 1969**

**I am pleased to learn that you now have Radha-Krishna murtis given to you by Mataji Shyamadevi. For the time being you should keep Them covered, and when I go there I shall install Them and teach you how to do everything nicely. In the meantime you should not tend these Deities, but a nice throne should be constructed in the same fashion as the picture which was sent to you recently. In Los Angeles temple they have constructed a beautiful throne, just on the measurements and colors as depicted on the picture sent to you, and it has come very successful.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, AUG. 5, 1969**

Unfortunately, even those Deities were taken back by Shyama Mataji, so all in all, the entire alliance was another hopeful avenue which ultimately reached a dead end. However, in his usual fashion, Srila Prabhupada continued to enliven and inspire each devotee, in this case seeing Yamuna’s loss of Shyama Mataji’s Deities as Krishna’s kindness. The Deities she had hoped to worship were taken back, but in the end were replaced by the most exquisite manifestation of Their Lordships in the forms of Sri Sri Radha- Londonisvara.

**You were very much anxious to worship Radha Krishna Deity and you took one pair from Mataji. At that time I advised you to wait. Now when the pair of Deities were taken by Mataji again and you were little bit sorry, but Krishna is so kind upon you that He has come to you again in a better position and now you can engage yourself in His service heart and soul.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA AND GURU DAS, APR. 16, 1970**

The relationship between ISKCON and Shyama Mataji did not end there, however. As Srila Prabhupada hinted in his letters and later elaborated on to Yamuna, she increasingly became inimical to the Krishna Consciousness Movement, something Srila Prabhupada understood long before the devotees.

## A Temple Grows in London—7 Bury Place

There is a famous opening line in Charles Dickens’s classic book Tale of Two Cities which best summarizes Yamuna’s later reflections on those early months in London—“It was the best of times; it was the worst of times.” Some discord still existed among the devotees, as they were still scattered about in what Yamuna felt were substandard living conditions. Although the men were busily engaged and Malati had a small child to care for, Yamuna and Janaki struggled under the weight of their lack of devotee association, lack of funds and lack of acceptable housing. Srila Prabhupada’s individual letters to them are astonishing in his insightful understanding of their dilemma. In every letter to one of them, he encouraged them all, figuratively holding them up by the strength of his love, encouragement and spiritual stamina.

**So far as I am concerned, I always wish only to expedite my mission of life to spread Krishna Consciousness in the Western part of the world. I am still firmly convinced that if I can establish this Movement through the help of all the boys and girls who have now joined with me, then it will be a great achievement. I am old man, and there has already been warning, but before I leave this body, I wish to see some of you very strong in Krishna Consciousness understanding. I am very glad and proud also that you six boys and girls, although you have not been able to establish a nice center in London, still you have done your best.... So there is no need to be disappointed. You go on with your work as best as Krishna gives you the opportunity, and there is no cause of your anxiety. Everything is going smoothly. But since you are now separated, the strength of your activities appears to be a little disturbed. Now you try to assemble together in the same spirit as you were doing, and in that case, temple or no temple, your Movement will go on progressively. We are not much concerned about the temple because temple worship is not the primary factor in this age. The primary factor is sankirtan. But sometimes we want a center where people may gather and see, so a temple is required secondarily. So try your best immediately to live together. I am very much eager to see that you are again living together.**

**— LETTER TO MUKUNDA, MAY 27, I969**

Srila Prabhupada again reassured the devotees that the sankirtan party mission was the most important, and encouraged them not to be disillusioned by the disturbances in their lives or their inability to secure a temple. Yamuna would often say that the depth of love and compassion in his encouragement to them in those days sustained her more than her words could ever express:

**I also understand from Malati’s letter that you have been feeling some disturbance. Perhaps this is because there is difficulty there in finding a temple that you feel that you are not doing nicely, but this is not a fact. Your efforts there are especially nice and pleasing to me. Actually, sankirtan party is our main business, and even you do not find a temple there for some time it is not cause for any disturbance. Continue to propagate Krishna Consciousness through sankirtan party, and surely you will come out fully successful.**

**— LETTER TO SHYAMASUNDARA, APR. 5, I969**

In the midst of these disturbances, Yamuna had a vivid dream unlike anything she had experienced since becoming a devotee:

**Yamuna**: *In this dream, I was standing on the shore of the ocean. First it was calm, but then large waves came and pulled me out to sea. I immediately thought of Srila Prabhupada and called out, “Srila Prabhupada! Srila Prabhupada!” Then I saw a boat come. Somehow I knew that it was him, and that he would lift me up, so there was no fear. But when the boat came, it was not Srila Prabhupada alone, but rather Lord Nrsimhadeva behind him in His loving rather than fierce mood. Then I became afraid. What had I done to incur the wrath of Lord Nrsimhadeva. The next moment, I was again on the shore, and the Lord was still there standing behind Srila Prabhupada. It was so vivid. I could recall every feature—the expressions, the jeweled helmet, so many things, but mainly the loving expression and the obvious fact that He was protecting Srila Prabhupada. It was an extraordinary dream that I never forgot, and I wrote to Srila Prabhupada about it, not quite sure how to understand it or process it.*

**Please accept my blessings. I am replying to your nice letter dated April io, 1969. The description of your dream is very fascinating. It appears that you are constantly thinking of me and Lord Nrsimha has given you the chance to see Him because of your constant devotion. It is very encouraging.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, APR. l6, 1969**

Then, backed by loan assurances from both Srila Prabhupada and Apple Records, a temple was finally secured on June 25,1969, at 7 Bury Place, an ideal central location literally a stone’s throw from the esteemed British Museum. The devotees were ecstatic. Now they would be able to elaborately worship Deities, have wonderful kirtans and festivals and serve prasadam feasts. Unfortunately, due to planning permissions and other difficulties, they were not allowed to live there until all the legal requirements were met, so the householders remained in their “substandard” housing. Shyamasundara, with the help of the new brahmacharis and others, began work immediately, eventually creating a temple room which Yamuna described as looking something like the inside of an ark. Srila Prabhupada also requested that an altar be made which allowed space for large Radha and Krishna Deities underneath the Jagannatha Deities.

For the most part, the upcoming recording sessions with George Harrison at Apple Studios, as well as the inevitability of their moving into the new temple, alleviated many of the “disturbances” alluded to in the devotees’ letters to Srila Prabhupada, and especially gave renewed strength to Yamuna. In a letter to her on July 3,1969, Srila Prabhupada wrote:

**So now we have got a very great responsibility to spread this message all over the world, and in London you have got now a good chance to preach in the most important city of the world. Decorate the place very nicely, as far as possible.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, JULY 3, I969**

## Recording the Mahamantra with George Harrison—“He Knew How to Get the Best from Us”

The group felt ready to record whenever the opportunity arose. Srila Prabhupada offered all encouragement to them and again thanked them for their efforts. He reminded them that he still held dear the idea of a World Sankirtan Party to travel around the world carrying the message of the Krishna Consciousness Movement.

**I am very glad to know that George is interested in recording some Krishna Consciousness album, and it is very happy news.... Try to make this Hare Krishna Movement popular through any source that is possible. That is our business. I thank you very much for your gorgeous, hopeful words that when I go to London, the London center will be the pivot for our Krishna Consciousness Movement. I still maintain the idea of a World Sankirtan Party, so we have got men now in Los Angeles, in Montreal, in Boston, in New York, in New Vrindavan and in London, who can form a nice group of sankirtan, at least with 25 heads. If we travel, beginning from London, around the world and again back to London, surely your foretelling will be a factual event. So try your best, and Krishna will help us as He is helping us. Krishna can help us immediately with all of His resources, but first of all He wants to see how much we can work seriously. So the more we become steady and serious, the more help we will have from Him—rest assured.**

**— LETTER TO SHYAMASUNDARA, JUNE 29, 1969**

Then on July 7, 1969, the window of opportunity opened, and the mahamantra was recorded. It was a monumental day in the history of the Hare Krishna Movement—now the Holy Names would be heard around the world.

**Yamuna**: *One day George Harrison called Shyamasundara and asked us to come to the Abbey Road Studios to record. He was there recording “Here Comes the Sun” and had slotted in some time to record the mahamantra as a single. In his role as record producer, George was soft-spoken, but no-nonsense. As an expert musician, he knew how to get the best from us, tapping into each of our strengths and making them better. He knew where to place us to take the best advantage of what he saw we had. He was a genuine, likeable person and, in spite of his fame, a gentleman and a terrific record producer. This manifested in many ways, particularly with how he worked with our group of nonprofessional musicians*

**On the day of the recording, about a dozen devotees, including some newly-recruited Britishers, assembled at the recording studios on Abbey Road. When the first group of devotees arrived in George’s Mercedes, a crowd of teenagers began singing Hare Krishna to the tune popularized by the rock musical Hair. While Yamuna applied Vaishnava tilak to the foreheads of the recording technicians, Malati unpacked picnic baskets of prasadam, and some of the other devotees put up pictures of Krishna and lit incense. The studio was duly Krishnized. With Paul McCartney and his wife, Linda, operating the control console, the recording session began. Everyone worked quickly, making Side One of the 45 rpm record in about an hour. George played organ and Mukunda played mridanga. Yamuna sang the lead with Shyamasundara backing her, and the other voices blended in a chorus. And to make it come out exactly right, everyone concentrated on Prabhupada and prayed for spiritual strength.**

**— SRILA PRABHUPADA-LILAMRTA**

## Londons First Rathayatra — “Sometimes Failure is Considered a Pillar of Success"

In the midst of finally securing the new temple and recording the maha-mantra at Apple Records, preparations were also going on for the first London Rathayatra. Srila Prabhupada had previously made his desire for it and its importance to him known to the devotees. The London devotees, now including several new brahmacharis, had hoped that Srila Prabhupada would come for the Rathayatra festival, but unable to come, he wrote an inspiring letter to Yamuna:

**If you decorate your face, you do not see directly how your face has become beautiful, but when you see the reflection of your face in the mirror, then indirectly you can see the beauty. Therefore, by serving Krishna directly the result of the service indirectly comes to us. Just like we offer very nice prasadam directly to Krishna, but indirectly we enjoy the nice taste of the prasadam. So we should always remember this—that Krishna is always full in Himself; He does not want a pinch of our help for His satisfaction, but if we try to satisfy Him in so many ways as directed by Acharyas and scriptures, indirectly we become benefited by such activities. So try to nicely observe this Rathayatra Festival in London.... So some way or other, if you can introduce this Car Festival in London, by all means London center will be successful. It doesn’t matter if you can or cannot establish a temple there, but if you can introduce the Rathayatra Festival, surely it will be a great success. So try to execute this as far as possible.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, MAY 27, 1969**

Yamuna had written to Srila Prabhupada with specific questions about how to decorate the Jagannatha Deities, and he wrote back illuminating both the importance of the decoration and the benefit it would give all who had the good fortune to view the Deities during the Rathayatra ceremonies:

**Please decorate Jagannatha with very attractive nice clothing and ornaments, helmets, as brightly and magnificently as possible.... There shall be sufficient flower garlands for them daily also. The decoration should be so attractive that people when seeing Jagannatha will forget all attractiveness of maya. Then it will be successful, and actually this is the process of decorating Jagannatha. Our eyes are attracted by the beauty of maya, but if our eyes are attracted by the beauty of Krishna, Jagannatha, then there is no more chance of our being attracted by maya. In other words, when seeing Jagannatha nicely decorated, we become freed from the clutches of maya.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, JUNE 7, 1968**

**Yamuna**: *Although Prabhupada wanted us to perform an elaborate and gorgeous Rathayatra, there were only the six of us and three new brahmacharis. So Shyamasundara, with one or two assistants, was trying to build a cart like the Rathayatra cart in Puri.*

*Meanwhile, in Los Angeles and San Francisco, there were about twenty men building the carts, many ladies were sewing, and massive amounts of prasadam were being prepared for distribution—so right until the end, there were these letters going back and forth, “Where will Prabhupada go for Rathayatra—to San Francisco or to London?” So by Krishna’s arrangement, he went to San Francisco. Telegrams were sent to him, “You must come; there are so many people.” So he went.*

*So when the London cart was finished, the wheels could not hold the massive weight of the new design. Shyamasundara towed it with the red truck to Hyde Park Corner in the middle of the night, and it took six hours to get there from Battersea where it was built. At this point mostly the Indian population was there. The Deities were placed on the cart, it went about sixty feet and then, all of a sudden, Ka boom!—the wheels just fell apart. It was obviously a tremendous tragedy for us; we were all completely crestfallen, thinking that it was somehow a mystical experience, that Lord Jagannatha didn’t like us; that our preaching was finished in Great Britain; that we should all go somewhere else.*

*Each of us wrote heartbroken letters to Srila Prabhupada. And their experience in San Francisco had been just the opposite, because that was the year that Rathayatra really took off. I don’t think there has ever been such an ecstatic Rathayatra in San Francisco as in 1969. Srila Prabhupada got right off the cart and danced, and he wrote letters to us with pictures and newspaper accounts of the great success it had been. So, in contrast, we had this very terrible experience where our cart fell apart in Trafalgar Square, and the contrast with the San Francisco success made it even more painful for us.*

*And yet, Prabhupada was wonderfully kind and merciful to us. He was able to see the guiding and loving hand of the Supreme Lord behind every action, and in that way, he taught us to try to see our “failure” in an entirely different light, not as a failure, but a success of sorts—something to be learned from—to expand our vision to see the higher principle at work.*

**But I could understand that you are immersed in great confusion on account of the wheels giving way just after starting. So there is no question of being disappointed. I have not received any detailed information either from you or from the others, but even if the Festival was not properly performed, you should not be discouraged. As in the material world sometimes failure is considered as a pillar of success, similarly in the spiritual order also the same principle can be applied. So don’t be disappointed. Maybe Krishna’s desire is something higher in this connection.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, JULY 11, 1969**

**When I first heard that the wheels of the car collapsed it was so great a shock to me that the whole day I was sick and morose, and now after receiving this letter and your pictures I am very much enlivened. The car was on the road and the photo is taken with a multitude of people. That is your success and as a result of this collapse you have got now the sympathy of the Indian community as well as all the people of London—so much so that next year you can timely and conveniently erect three cars like that.**

**— LETTER TO SHYAMASUNDARA, AUG. 13, 1969**

## Srila Prabhupada Comes to England — The John and Yoko Interlude

On August 28, 1969, the “Hare Krishna Mantra” single was launched at a press conference in Sydenham Hill. George Harrison and the devotees held a wonderful kirtan. Apple Records was already in the process of arranging various programs to promote the record. After the release of the single, George visited John and Yoko at their new estate, Tittenhurst Manor, the former Cadbury Chocolate family estate in Ascot, Berkshire, and told them how the devotees were living scattered all over. John and Yoko offered housing on their estate in exchange for the brahmacharis’ work on renovations, and this allowed the devotees to finally invite Srila Prabhupada to come. He arrived on September it, 1969.

**Yamuna**: *So it was at that time that Srila Prabhupada finally decided to come. He had been ceaselessly instructing us how to broadcast the sublime and spotless glories of the Supreme Personality of Godhead in London. I remember from the very moment that Srila Prabhupada stepped on the airport tarmac, each and every one of his students felt him embracing them within their hearts. Afterward, he spoke to each of us so intimately, so feelingly, and each one of us thought, “Oh, Srila Prabhupada is so kind. He is encouraging me so much. Did you see how he looked at me? How he spoke with me? Or how he walked with me?”*

*So many people were there to greet him, and that was the time of his famous answer to the reporter’s question, “What have you come to teach?” And Srila Prabhupada answered, “I have come to teach what you have forgotten—that is God.” So then he was taken in John Lennon’s white Rolls-Royce to Tittenhurst Manor in Ascot.*

*The Tittenhurst estate had over 60 acres of formal gardens, with many large structures on it. John and Yoko lived in the main house and gave us a block of empty servants’ quarters to live in—four separate two-up and two-down units in a row constructed in red brick and situated near the stables. In front was a walkway, next to which was a patch of lawn about 25 feet across, and next to that a 20-foot high yew hedge. Yoko let all the grass areas grow long, but in this hidden area, the servants’ quarters, they kept the grass cut.*

*Srila Prabhupada and his secretary-servant Purushottama lived in one unit. Prabhupada was upstairs, with a greeting-office-temple room space, a bedroom and a bathroom. It was a cozy square room with high ceilings, one transom window, and a closet that served as a small temple for the Radha-Krishna Deities he had brought with him. Aside from some shelves for his books and a low table that served as his desk, the room was bare. Prabhupada never used any of the downstairs facilities. Downstairs his servant, Purushottama, had the front sitting room, and there was a bathroom, and we cooks—Malati or me— used the kitchen. So around the world, anywhere Prabhupada stayed, we knew what he wanted for his living quarters—the bare minimum.*

*It was with these little six-inch Deities that Srila Prabhupada taught me Deity worship. I had seen Them first in New York, and here he kept Them in a little converted closet. He told me I would serve as head pujari in our new London temple. Prabhupada taught by example as well as precept. He said that chanting Hare Krishna was the essence of Deity worship, and we should try to chant without offense. We should be clean, prompt and present in all of our services. He taught us the rudiments of performing arati (archanam), bathing the Deity (abhishekham), and decorating the Deity (sringar). One day Malati and I collected a wide assortment of dahlias from the nearby formal gardens. I arranged them as artfully as I could behind the Deities, making an elaborate wall tapestry of patterned flowers. Prabhupada came back from his morning walk, and before sitting down he spoke: “Oh, you have done this? It is very nice. But,” he paused, opening his eyes a little wider, “it could be even better.” “How?” I asked, excitement spilling over. So he sat down in front of the Deities, dismantled the flower tapestry and put up another one. Without explanation, it was clear why this was better. Using perspective, he had showcased the Deities’ forms. He allowed the flower tapestry to play a supporting role to the beautiful forms of the Deities Themselves, explaining that the same principle should be observed in dressing the Deity. The sringar, or dresses, should not cover the form of the Lord, but rather showcase the form of the Lord.*

*In later years while I was in his service, Prabhupada revealed layer upon layer of information to me regarding Deity worship and cooking. In whatever location or circumstance we found ourselves, he continued to train me, and I have continued following that training throughout my life. The essence of his instruction was threefold—quality, cleanliness and purity. These principles are timeless—as important today and tomorrow as they were decades ago.*

*One day Srila Prabhupada asked me to paint a set of Radha-Krishna Deities that he was sending to Hamburg to have installed. When I informed him I was not an artist and didn’t feel I could do it, he said that he would show me what to do. So he told me to find a special black, white and red paint, and that evening we sat Them on his small desk and Srila Prabhupada personally painted the Deities and instructed me at the same time. I sat in front of him, and as time seemed to disappear, the lovely forms of the Lords slowly became manifest through the painting. After we were finished, I immediately went to my room and wrote what he had explained. He said that the painting of Radha and Krishna Deities is called Anga-Raga. Anga means “body,” and Raga means “painting of.” So Radharani holds her fingers in a mudra. Mudras can also be used by the Spiritual Master when he is preaching, and different mudras have special meanings. And Srila Prabhupada held up his fingers just as Srimati Radharani’s were—with forefinger and thumb together. Srila Prabhupada often used that “mudra" when he made a specific point. I remember many instances where Srila Prabhupada was extremely expressive with his hands. He said that these mudras have special meanings and are used to emphasize a specific point. He added that the gopis also expressed so many things though mudras.*

*Srila Prabhupada’s big reel-to-reel tape recorder sat under a low desk. We had no furniture—we slept in sleeping bags on the floor. We also had very little in the way of clothes. I had only two saris, one black with dark blue and one gray-pink. We shared the Wellingtons, high rubber boots necessary for the wet weather of England. Srila Prabhupada’s belongings were also very sparse. If devotees gave him things, he would often give them away. He traveled lightly and did not keep separate wardrobes in different temples around the world.*

*The adjoining apartments each had one front window. The wall in my room in the next apartment adjoined Srila Prabhupada’s, and I put my bed tightly against the wall to be as close to him as possible. His bed was just on the other side of the wall. Whenever I slept I was completely aware of his schedule.*

*We stayed at Tittenhurst with Prabhupada just short of two months. Not far from the main house was an Elizabethan structure, the “Orangery,” which John had given us for our temple. This had been a classical harpsichord recital hall, with ceilings thirty to forty feet high, and acoustics that were especially transcendentally suited for sankirtan. We constructed a small altar at one end of this hall next to Srila Prabhupada’s vyasasana, and even with twenty-five persons the sound was magnified twenty-five times, so the kirtans sounded like hundreds of voices. With the resonant and transcendental sound qualities, there was no need for microphones or amplification systems—the acoustics were just magnificent.*

*Every morning we met there with Prabhupada for arati, Srimad-Bhagavatam class and kirtan. On special Vaishnava holidays, George and his wife Pattie, and John and Yoko would come and join in. So it was just wonderful, and Srila Prabhupada’s strong and powerful voice didn’t need a sound system. It just rang out with such powerful energy that when we sang we were just lifted up like there were many, many voices. It was so glorious. Srila Prabhupada was also lecturing at that time on the Srimad-Bhagavatam account of Rsabhadeva’s instructions to His sons, and they were all such very moving and relevant instructions; it was very exciting for all of the devotees there.*

*Prabhupada had a fixed but slightly different schedule at Tittenhurst than anywhere else. Here, he had more time to rest; he didn’t have many outside guests, and could devote at least one hour to solitary kirtan in his room. He most often chanted the prayers of Bhaktivinoda Thakur or Narottama das Thakur, but also chanted the Brahma Samhita and other Vaishnava prayers. Every morning after the morning walk and after breakfast, I would be downstairs in the kitchen, when I would hear this most sublime singing and harmonium coming out of his window. Just like in nature when you hear the birds singing and the rustle of the leaves in the trees, it was a symphony of transcendental sound.*

## An Epoch-Making Incident

In 1980, at the Bhaktivedanta Manor, Yamuna spoke of her remembrances of Srila Prabhupada’s chanting at Tittenhurst. Her deep realizations and how she understood Srila Prabhupada’s sometimes recondite meanings can be felt in her reflections:

**Yamuna**: *So I remember he was on the second floor, and I used to sit at the base of the stairs in tears every morning. It was autumn, and as this sound would come out, the fog would burn off—it was like the sound burned the fog away. And it would pour out the windows and just fill this little garden and the sky, the servants’ quarters, everywhere. Prabhupada chanting to Krishna was like nothing of this world. It had nothing to do with this world. And I would sit at the bottom of the stairs and cry. I never made a sound. Never. But one day Prabhupada said, “Yamuna, come here.” So I came up the stairs, and I had started to pay my obeisances when he said, “Do you like the chanting?” That really made the tears pour out. I replied, “Oh, Prabhupada!” He said, “Would you like to stay here?” Then I asked if we could record the bhajans, as we heard that they had recorded some in Los Angeles. He said, “Yes.” So for several days we made recordings, some of which you can hear today. I can’t describe them all. One was Cintamani, where Srila Prabhupada was playing harmonium in such an extraordinary way that afterwards, when we heard the playback, he said, “Anyone who hears this will be forced to get up and dance.” So then all of us would play; I would thump away at mridanga—one beat. Finally, after several days of this, he began chanting Bhagavad-gita. So for eighteen mornings, a chapter every morning, he chanted Bhagavad-gita. He said that this sound vibration is so powerful that wherever we chant Bhagavad-gita, that place becomes a tirtha. So powerful. So chant Bhagavad-gita. It is just a tiny little opening of the door; but now you can jump into the room and find an eternity in there. You can close the door at any particular time again, and it is always a treasure house. But the key for this treasure house is the Guru Maharaja’s instructions. So it is all of our responsibility, whether Srila Prabhupada is directly our Spiritual Master or whether he is our grand-Spiritual Master. I don’t know if the younger disciples have been told, but Srila Prabhupada told us that sometimes the grandfather Guru is a little bit more lenient than your own Guru, just like with the grandchild, the grandfather is very kind and affectionate. So you can have a very close relationship with Srila Prabhupada that certainly would not affect your relationship with your own Guru Maharaja. In fact it would intensify your feelings of appreciation for your own Guru Maharaja, knowing that what your Guru Maharaja has learned is from him, and what his Guru Maharaja learned is from his Guru Maharaja, and it is all a glorious chain, from Srila Prabhupada, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta, Gaura Kishora das Babaji, Bhaktivinoda Thakur and this wonderful chain of dis-ciplic succession that is carrying to us the vibrant fruit of transcendental knowledge. So your relationship with Srila Prabhupada can be very sweet and have great spiritual significance.*

*His harmonium playing was very unique. It had so much life to it, like a babbling brook, the water falling and hitting the rocks, and as it falls each rock makes a different sound. He would go all over and embellish in a way that wasn’t Indian or Western or any kind of style—it was his own style— especially when he chanted alone. If he recorded or played in a kirtan, it was different. When he chanted alone, praying to Krishna, it was very special. So on this one morning Srila Prabhupada was alone, so when he started singing the few of us there gravitated to the stairs to listen to him. So right after he finished, he rang his bell and I came up. He said, “How did you get here so fast?” I said, “Well, we were down the stairs listening to you.” And I asked him what he was singing. He said, “The prayers of Bhaktivinoda Thakur.” And then he continued to explain. “The prayers of Bhaktivinoda Thakur and Narottama das Thakur are so very powerful that they act on the heart just like lightning in a storm.” Then he said, “Have you ever been in a lightning storm, where the lightning came and hit very close by?”*

*So I immediately thought of once when I was in a boat in the middle of a lake and lightning hit very close to me. So then he clapped his hands together and said, “Just like lightning, these prayers will act upon the heart.” Then he clapped his hands together again and repeated, “It will act upon the heart.” “So,” he continued, “even if you don’t understand the language, it is that strong. The vibration alone carries the potency and the depth of purity of the composer of these prayers.”*

*On another occasion he knew I was there—he had a very close rapport with his servants. He knew not only where you were, but also where your consciousness was. It was uncanny. So when the chanting was over, he called, “Yamuna!” I went in. “What do you think?” he said. “It was beautiful, Srila Prabhupada, so beautiful. Can I record you?” So this was around the time of the beginning of Golden Avatar—we had just received tapes of some Bhagavada-gita lectures. But there was very little yet on tape.*

*“Yes, we can record,” he replied. “What is your favorite prayer?” “Lord Chaitanya’s Siksastakam,” I answered. I had seen the translation in the original Srimad-Bhagavatam. “What’s yours?” I asked. “Hari Hari Biphale," he replied. I then requested him to sing Hari Hari Biphale. It was the first of four times I had the great fortune to be in his presence when he sang that prayer. It is difficult to express, but he went so deeply into the prayer that I could see his body changing shape. His face changed. He was physically altered. Sometimes he would sing the first line ten times, over and over and over—just diving into it. And successive verses were also repeated. I recorded it.*

It is interesting to note that later Srila Prabhupada recommended that George Harrison record this prayer in English. In a letter to Shyamasundara on February 25,1970, he provided an English translation of Hari Hari Biphale and suggested that George’s recording it would be “epoch making”:

**“My Dear Lord, I have simply wasted my privileges of the human form of life. This life was meant for understanding Krishna Consciousness and the pastimes of Lord Krishna with Radharani, but I did not take care of this important business of life. Therefore I have not only wasted my valuable time, but also I have willingly drunk poison for committing suicide. My heart is always in blazing fire because of my association with material sense enjoyment, and I did not fix up my mind in the Krishna Consciousness Movement which is imported directly from the Kingdom of God. This Krishna Consciousness Movement is inaugurated by Lord Chaitanya and Lord Nityananda Who are Krishna and Balarama respectively. They have descended very kindly to reclaim all fallen souls of this age of whom the typical examples are the two brothers \]agai and Madhai. Now, forgetting all mistakes that I have committed in my past life, I humbly surrender unto You, my Lord Krishna, the Son of Nanda Maharaja, and also to Srimati Radharani, the daughter of King Vrsabhanu. So both of You are present together, and I fully surrender unto You. Please do not reject me as I have no other shelter except Yourselves.”**

**Perhaps you have heard, and George has also heard, my song on this theme, “Hari hari bifale janama gonainu” ... So if George can compose a nice song in his own words, and sings, I am sure it will be an epoch-making incident.**

**— LETTER TO SHYAMASUNDARA, FEB. 25, 1970**

**Yamuna**: *After he finished, I asked if he could he chant the verses of Bhagavad-gita. “I can chant,” he replied. And for the next 18 mornings he chanted a chapter in Sanskrit. I don’t recall any other time like it. I kept those tapes—there were two reels—and sent them to Los Angeles. The first reel was lost in the mail, but the other survived.*

*He chanted all day long. If he wasn’t talking, he had his hand in his bead bag. He virtually only took his bead bag off to eat and sleep. He trained us to chant japa out loud, but in his own chanting, there were times when his lips barely moved, and no sound came out.*

*When I was with him I was always in awe of Srila Prabhupada. I hadn’t known previously what a saint was, but I knew I was now in the presence of one. Everything he did was real and powerful and genuine and very deep. Even his humor was deep. All of the 26 qualities of a devotee found in the scripture were found in him.*

*His schedule ran close to this:*

- *1:00 am: Rises; chants japa and translates;*
- *3:30 am: Attends arati in his room, performed by either Purushottama or me;*
- *4:30 am: Attends arati, Srimad-Bhagavatam class, and kirtan in the main temple;*
- *6:30 am: Goes on a morning walk for about one hour; takes Ayurvedic medicine and then a light breakfast (either Purushottama or I would go on the morning walk);*
- *9:oo am: Chants kirtan or sings prayers alone in his room; sometimes he requests Purushottama and me to play instruments;*
- *10:00 am: Dictates letters; instructs devotees, or has guests;*
- *12:00 pm: Takes massage, bathes, then chants Gayatri mantra;*
- *1:00 pm: Respects lunch prasadam, chants more rounds of japa and then rests;*
- *4:30 pm: Takes a little fresh juice; frequently sits with devotees for informal talks;*
- *6:30 pm: Attends evening arati in his room—on occasion he respects a light meal; alternately goes to London or elsewhere for an engagement or has open visiting hours; and*
- *10:30 to 11:00 pm: Retires.*

*Most of the devotee men living at Titten-hurst spent the day renovating what we called the Big House—where John and Yoko lived. Shyamasundara and Tirthapad lived and worked in Bury Place. Mukunda and Guru das were often dispatched to London on some special assignment. Malati cooked for the devotees, took care of baby Saraswati and did Prabhupada’s laundry; Janaki cleaned Prabhupada’s quarters; and I did most of his cooking— though in some ways, the three of us were interchangeable. Newly-arrived Trivikrama and Ishan switched off giving Prabhupada a daily massage. Guru das and Mukunda would sometimes visit Srila Prabhupada after his morning walk, before going into London. Then he would have breakfast, write letters, take a massage, then lunch. After lunch Srila Prabhupada sometimes rested, then when visiting hours commenced, he would speak so many things informally. Sometimes he would have guests, but not often. He was pushing us to get the temple open, and he wanted a report every evening.*

*Srila Prabhupada had a personal relationship with every one of his disciples, and each was a wonder to behold. My sister Janaki’s was special. She was his first female disciple and behaved like the youngest daughter in a family. She always spoke her mind to him, and he often called her his “naughty daughter” or his “little mother.” She loved to surprise him by giving gifts she found or had been given, whether it be a gold ring or something inexpensive. Once she decorated his plate with little Chinese paper umbrellas, and Srila Prabhupada, encouraging her, told how Radharani and the gopis always decorated everything very nicely for Krishna. He knew how to draw out the best in each of us—to make each of us feel as though our service was necessary to him and to his mission*

Srila Prabhupada also wanted the devotees to become knowledgeable on the fundamental philosophy of Krishna Consciousness, and he created a test which all the devotees had to pass. Those who passed the test would be given a calligraphed certificate created by Yamuna devi.

**Mukunda Goswami**: *Yamuna was very expert at calligraphy. One of the things she did (among many) was to calligraph \[certificates for\] the first Bhakti Shastri examinations. The exams were given in London, in 1969, by Prabhupada, and there were certificates. And ... all of us had to take an examination. It consisted of something like ten questions at that time—the Bhakti Shastri course. Things like, Who is Krishna? Kind of essay answers. Everyone pretty much passed and got this certificate. But she calligraphed very ornate certificates. Each certificate had a golden seal, maybe three centimeters in diameter, and with two silver ribbons hanging down from it. So everyone got one of those certificates on passing the Bhakti Shastri exam—everyone, meaning about the seven or eight devotees who were at John Lennon’s house at the time.*

**Yamuna**: *Once, during the month of October, I became very ill with an extremely high fever and was forced to leave Srila Prabhupada’s service. As I said before, I was living in the apartment just next to his, and even though I was constantly praying to him, thinking about him and meditating on his presence, the fever went on for three days like this. Finally, at the end of the third day, I more or less woke up from a delirious condition, and I decided that this morning when Srila Prabhupada came back from his morning walk, I’d just hide behind the door at the bottom of the stairway and glance at him as he walked past.*

*So I wrapped a huge blanket around myself, still in my nightwear but hiding behind the door, and Srila Prabhupada walked past and, just as he got to the door, he opened it and hollered up the stairway in a loud voice, “Yamuna!” and here I was standing just behind the door watching him. Embarrassed, I fell to the ground all wrapped up in this blanket, paid my obeisances and said, “Oh, Srila Prabhupada, I’m so very sorry to be appearing this way, but I had to catch a glimpse of you. I was thinking about you so very much.” And he said, “I have also been thinking about you very much. How are you feeling?” I replied that I was feeling much better, and that I should be back in his service in about two days or so. And he said, “Yes. The fever will last three days, and two days to recover. Five days and you will be back.” He knew, exactly, the condition. Srila Prabhupada always had an uncanny way of saying something—even something like a comment on my fever—and it became like a prophecy. This happened so many times in my years with Srila Prabhupada, I almost came to expect and rely on it*.

In a talk given by Yamuna many years ago, she poignantly equated Srila Prabhupada’s relationship and accessibility to his young devotees with a verse in the Caitanya-caritamrta:

**Although the members of the Pancha Tattva \[Lord Chaitanya’s close associates\] plundered the storehouse of love of Godhead and ate and distributed its contents, there was no scarcity, for this wonderful storehouse is so complete that as the love is distributed, the supply increases hundreds of times.**

**— ADI LILA 7:24**

**Yamuna**: *Prabhupada’s spiritual potency inundated the whole atmosphere with his transcendental presence. From morning to night he was a great source of inspiration to all of us. And all of us felt as if he were personally guiding us in our activities at every moment. He made little distinction between the young men and women in those days, and trained us each to become preachers of Krishna Consciousness. He encouraged us to strictly follow the rules and regulations, rise early in the morning, chant our rounds, chant our Gayatri mantras and keep very clean; and he was instilling a sense of responsibility in each one of us to be reliable and steady in our service. He made arrangements on an individual level to make each student strive to do everything to the best of his ability. He had an intuitive way to enthuse you to work harder and harder and longer and longer, and become more and more enthusiastic to do your service, never mind what the service was.*

## The Lie

**Yamuna**: *I was in the middle of preparing his breakfast plate one morning when Srila Prabhupada rang his bell, indicating I should come to his room. I climbed the stairs and paid obeisances at his doorway. Before I got up, he asked, “Yamuna, where are my clean socks?” pointing his fingers toward an empty space by his sitting cushion. “Which socks ... would that be ... Prabhupada?” I replied. “The socks I took off yesterday after my morning walk.” His voice dipped with gravity. Why, I cannot fathom now, but bad judgment took hold of me, and I began telling a useless lie with four horrible words, “I don’t know, Prabhupada.” I knew where the socks were; I had put them in the wash. But I did not want to risk Srila Prabhupada’s chastisement, so I lied. Of course, this was a horrible offense, because he knew anyway, and with a slight raise in tone, he said firmly, “You don’t know? You must know. I put them right here by my cushion. The new beige socks. I only wore them for one hour yesterday on my morning walk.” He looked at me with dismay. Again I repeated the unfortunate words, “I don’t know, Prabhupada,” this time with even greater discomfort. I now felt physically ill. Why did I lie to Prabhupada? To avoid chastisement I had perpetuated a deception, and Prabhupada knew that I had lied, for I felt all the color leave my face. He was silent for a minute, then looked at me straight in the eye and said, “I am sure you can find them. This should not happen again—never again.” “No, Prabhupada. It will not,” I confessed, my voice barely audible. I paid obeisances, and by the time I reached the bottom of the staircase, tears spilled over my cheeks. I felt so awful and fasted for the rest of the day. I have never forgotten that experience. Even repeating it now actually makes me feel ill. Out of fear of chastisement, I tried to lay blame elsewhere. I could just as easily have spoken the truth: “Srila Prabhupada, I put the socks in the laundry. If that was a mistake, please correct me so I can avoid it in the future.” I know that now. And I also understood that these tests were of the nature of trying to graphically remind me of my faults and weaknesses—those things that must be corrected to reach the spiritual goal.*

During this period Srila Prabhupada gave many instructions on how one should view the Spiritual Master. The graphic example of lying about the socks taught so much to Yamuna. As painful as the experience was, she placed the episode deep within the repository of her experience—never to be forgotten; never to be repeated. On another occasion, Srila Prabhupada clarified and elaborated on how the disciple should view the instructions of the Spiritual Master:

**The Spiritual Master’s instructions should be taken as the Spiritual Master himself, not his physical presence. How are we living? Not for a single moment am I out of touch with my Guru Maharaja because I’m trying to follow his instructions. One should take the words of his Spiritual Master as his life and soul. I don’t care for my salvation, his words are my life. Everything else is secondary. To them who have full faith in the Spiritual Master, all knowledge will be revealed. This is the disciplic succession, and the Spiritual Master is one who is in touch with his Spiritual Master like electricity crossing thousands of miles. They are all connected.**

**— LETTER TO PURUSHOTTAMA, OCT. 14, 1969**

## The Seer and the Seen—Morning Walks

In 1996, Yamuna and I went back to the Tittenhurst estate, which was then owned by one of the oil-rich Middle Eastern potentates. Twelve-foot-high walls surrounded the estate, and guard houses with armed guards awaited anyone intrepid enough to try to gain entry. Fortunately, Yamuna did meet a gardener who had worked there before John and Yoko, during their ownership, and afterward. He remembered Srila Prabhupada and the devotees, but not Yamuna specifically. In her interview with him, he chronicled the changes since the “glory” days of the Cadbury gardens. Work on those gardens had begun in earnest in the early 1800’s, with many plants and specimens having been brought in from all over the world. When John and Yoko bought Tittenhurst, Yoko was in her “black and white” phase, and informed the gardeners that she only wanted to see white or black. So to create her “vision,” all of the decades-old roses were dug up to make room for a helicopter pad and other things, and the lawns and specific environments were allowed to grow uncut. Although the gardener was very reserved and laconic in both his speech and remembrances, it must have been extremely difficult for him to bear witness to how such a magnificent landscape which took centuries to construct could have been demolished in such a way.

**Yamuna**: *The grounds at Tittenhurst were unique and wonderful, almost like an Alice in Wonderland fantasy. At one end of the land was a large orchard bearing all kinds of fruit trees, a very large vegetable garden and immense greenhouses. There were nearly a hundred acres of cultivated land, with over two thousand varieties of trees on it. Every kind of foliage was planted in this area, interspersed with swimming pool, tennis courts and sectioned-off areas filled with fountains and rose gardens. Walks around the grounds with Srila Prabhupada were especially cherished memories for me. Sometimes, when it was just the two of us walking, Guru das would take pictures from the bushes or trees. So Srila Prabhupada initially asked that the pictures showing the two of us not be circulated, as he would be criticized by his Godbrothers. In fact, although it was obvious that at least three people were there, as pictures were being taken, he was still careful about the etiquette.*

*There were immense old trees, and as this was late in the fall, they were becoming golden. After the fog burned off at about 9:30 am, the leaves and grass were laden with dew. One day we were walking towards the camera, me wearing my blue-black sari, black cape and Wellingtons, and Srila Prabhupada wearing his black coat, his black Russian hat and his black Wellingtons. In the dew-laden, long grass that Yoko Ono had allowed to grow, we walked down a little hillock. “I have been called many names in my life.” he said, without breaking stride. “At birth I was called ‘Nandu,’ as I was born on Nandotsava, the festival of Nanda Maharaja, which falls on the day after Lord Krishna’s birth. Later I got my formal given name, Abhay Charan. A nickname, coined by my maternal aunt, was the ‘Little Lion,’ because in her eyes I was raucous and fearless, like a male lion cub. Another childhood name was ‘Kachori Mukhi,’ for I had the habit of keeping a store of kachoris in my vest pockets. These were some of my many names.
