Perhaps the episode of the “Govindam” recording reveals more than anything the level of commitment and Krishna Conscious dedication of Yamuna devi. It is an extraordinary story—one which she eloquently expressed in an interview a few years before passing on:

**Yamuna**: *As an aspiring devotee for almost forty years now, I have never identified with any occupation. Though I sang on three released records with Apple in the late 1960s—the “Hare Krishna Mantra” single, the “Govindam” single and the LP that came after it—and although I penned three cookbooks in the late 80 s and early 90’s, I feel I am neither a singer nor an author. These were merely activities I fell into in the course of exploring the culture and practice of Gaudiya Vaishnavism, which is what my life is really all about.*

The devotees in London recognized her focus and dedication. She herself reflected on those days as ones in which her feet never touched the ground. She loved serving the gorgeous Sri Sri Radha-Londonisvara Deities, and she loved her other variegated services in the temple. To her they were all equally important as long as they propelled her forward in her Krishna Consciousness—and especially in her service to Srila Prabhupada.

**Yogesvara das**: There was no down time with Yamuna—no taking time off. She was on 24/7—that’s a fact. When she gave class, she would start by chanting, and she had a way of chanting with her eyes closed. You’d listen to her chant the prayers before class and you would just say to yourself, “Where is she?” She was in some very far away place. That was actually encouraging.... It was always memorable being with her when she gave class.... And every class she gave was a Prabhupada class.

**Shyamasundara das**: We started wearing dhotis and shaved our heads to become a “band” under Yamuna’s direction. As a formal band, all dressed alike, Yamuna taught us the words. She made us memorize all these prayers: “Govindam adi purusham ...” And she made up ... all these melodies. \[For\] the Hare Krishna mantra, she had melodies—the Govindam prayers, all the prayers we did on those records, Yamuna composed the melodies, sometimes with Mukunda. ^

**Dhananjaya das**: “Govindam” must have been \[recorded\] in the beginning of 1970—as far as I recall, January 1970.I went along to that. I was in the chorus. In fact, I recall that George told me to sing a little more quietly, because I was too enthusiastic and drowned everybody else out.

**Yamuna**: *From the success of the first “Hare Krishna Mantra” single, George Harrison and Apple wanted to record the Govindam prayers, which we had been practicing for the past several months. The essential melody was conceived of by Mukunda, and although it felt compelling in and of itself, the addition of the instrumentation catapulted it into another realm—one of transcendence. At the time, I was reluctant to sing on the single because I was fully engaged with so many services at the temple. But I also realized the immense preaching potential, and so we recorded it sometime in late January or early February.*

It is interesting to note here that when I first read Yamuna’s account of the “Govindam” recordings, she did not distinguish herself as the lead singer, nor mention herself at all except to say that she was “one of a chorus of singers.” Even in her earlier writings, she didn’t recognize how her not being present at the recording would have made any difference to the result. In reading her memoir notes, I realized that had someone not known Yamuna, they may have taken her mood or attitude as one of pretentiousness or false humility, but in fact, even as a devotee of a mere three years, she had a very real and visceral humility which characterized her throughout her life. In a later interview, Yamuna spoke of the actual recording:

**Yamuna**: *Shyamasundara was the second voice that came in after I sang the lead. There were the original six of us. And in those days the studio had eight tracks. So we recorded over and over, and over so it sounded like sixty-four voices. George wanted that number because he liked the sound of the Mormon Tabernacle Choir, and they had sixty-four voices. So he wanted to emulate that sound. And, of course, he was able to hire the London String Quartet. Billy Preston played organ, and George played his guitar. A new devotee had just come, who is now Harivilasa, and he played the oud. Guru das and Janaki played kartals, Tamai Krishna, Dhananjaya and others sang, and I played harmonium. Then actually it turned out that after they got all of our voices down, another group of devotees from France were added, including Yogesvara, Mondakini and others—I don’t know how many, but by the expert mixing and engineering talents of George Harrison and others, it turned into something magical.*

During the recording of the “Govindam” single, George Harrison again asked Yamuna to become a solo artist for Apple Records. The fact that she flatly refused illuminates more about her one-pointed spiritual focus than any words could characterize. In all of the years of our friendship, I never knew Yamuna to be impressed by someone’s fame, wealth or prestige, whether in the music, culinary or political spectrum. She had an uncanny ability to look at the underlying motivation within, and if the person had a guileless and genuine heart, Yamuna understood that and never forgot them. I wrote to some friends shortly after her passing away, reminding them that even though Yamuna saw them infrequently, she considered them very dear to her because she had seen the sincerity within.

Further elaborating on the offers from George Harrison and Apple Records to become a solo artist, Yamuna said:

**Yamuna**: *I would have never even considered it at the time. It was an unappealing notion to me, as it would have taken time away from my service as head pujari to Sri Sri Radha-Londonisvara. I was also concerned about the association aspect of it—how it might infect me with the desire for fame, profit or adoration—and I simply did not want to take such a risk.*

**Yogesvara das:** Sometimes George would come to the temple. I remember playing kartals at the back of the temple room one evening—maybe February of 1970. Shyamasundara had built the temple like an upside down Noah’s Ark—the door had this round window like a porthole. I turned around and there was George’s face in the window, smiling and waving at me. He would just show up like that sometimes and hang out with the devotees, have prasadam and just talk about things. It was all very warm and loving. He wanted to make Yamuna a star and told her he could make her a very popular singer, but she would always demur. She turned down fame. She turned down having George as her manager; it just wasn’t her thing. But I think she \[acted\] with him how she was with pretty much anybody.

**Mukunda Goswami**: Actually there is an interesting story that I wrote about. It took place when “Govindam” first came out, when the recording was first released. I was in England, and she \[Yamuna\] was in England, and we sent this recording to the devotees in Los Angeles to show how we were really preaching big time to the Beatles, and we did this record, and so on and so forth. But the devotees in Los Angeles didn’t want Prabhupada to hear this because they thought it was very strange that a woman’s voice would be leading the Hare Krishna mantra. And so they didn’t let Prabhupada hear it. So one morning, just before the greeting of the Deities, Prabhupada was sitting on his vyasasana. When the Deity doors open in Los Angeles, there is a big billow of incense smoke from the charcoals. The devotees use a lot of incense, and when they open the doors, it kind of pours out like a big cloud coming out. So right before this, Prabhupada said, “What about that record that the devotees sent from London?” He had heard about it. So they told him, “It is just Yamuna singing; we don’t want you to hear it.” And they said, “There is no place to play it.” So he said, “Just play it on the system—the speakers.”

So in \[the\] Los Angeles temple there are very large speakers where they play lectures. So when they told Prabhupada there was nothing to play it on, he said, “Just play it on the speakers.” So they said, “Okay,” and very reluctantly went and fetched the recording and played it. And it was just at the right time, and it is about six minutes long. As the Deity doors opened, Prabhupada was sitting on his vyasasana, and he didn’t say a word. He just listened with his eyes closed. And devotees got to see streams of tears coming down his cheeks. And that day Prabhupada ordered that the song be played in temples all over the world at the time of greeting the Deities.

So that was the end of that controversy. Except in December 12, 1975, when Prabhupada got a letter from a devotee who also had a recording. A gentleman, whose name I won’t mention, made a recording of “Govindam,” and he wrote this letter to Prabhupada saying that he thought it was improper for this Govindam led by a female voice to be played in temples all over the world. And he said that “I want to replace it now with my recording.” And he sent a copy of his recording to Prabhupada. Prabhupada was in India at the time—in Vrindavan no less—when he got it. So I have a copy of the letter that Prabhupada wrote back to this devotee.

**Please accept my blessings. I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter dated December 12,1975. No! You have made some discovery. All along you have been hearing the recording of Yamuna devi and now you want to change. It is not ordinary singing. It is concert. Many people are singing. So it is not bad. Just like sankirtan. Many voices are there, men and women. So it is the same thing, sankirtan. So I approve of it. Here in Hare Krishna Balarama temple, we are hearing the same recording every morning. So it is good here, why not there?**

**— LETTER TO JAYA SACINANDANA DAS, DEC. 12, 1975**

In an interview with Yamuna in 2008, Satyaraja das referred to her as a “lover of kirtan.” Her reply illustrates that nearly forty years after the initial London recordings, she still maintained the same single-minded focus and determination.

**Yamuna**: *“Lover of kirtan.” Mmm. Well, I can’t deny it. Kirtan is the easiest way to control the mind, and, ultimately, the only way into the higher realm of Radha and Krishna—the ultimate kirtan in the spiritual world. Such perfection is the cynosure of my life, and I know it can be obtained through attentive, pure Krishna kirtan.*

On February 16,1970, Shyamasundara sent Srila Prabhupada a copy of their recording of “Govindam.”

**Please find enclosed the first copy of “Govindam,” which you have taught us, and which we quite badly have rendered for the glorification of your Guru Maharaja and the world at large. Yamuna, myself, Mukunda and Janaki are singing, with everyone joining on the chorus. George plays guitar, Mukunda plays organ, a new boy, Hampar (an Armenian boy), plays oud, I play esraj, Guru das and I play kartals, and there is an orchestra of 6 violins, 6 violas, 2 double-bass, 2 tubas, 3 cellos, and one harp. Please accept this record as our humble offering unto your Divine Lotus Feet.**

**— SHYAMASUNDARA DAS**

When Srila Prabhupada wrote back to Shyamasundara on March 8, he could not have expressed in words more pleasure in the song and in their efforts. In later years he called it many things, but one of Yamuna’s favorites was “A symphony of Krishna Consciousness.”

**The record \[“Govindam”\] is so nice that I am playing it at least once in a day, and it is giving me transcendental pleasure with tears in my eyes. I am sure this record will be the first-class hit as already opined by the experts.**

**— LETTER TO SHYAMASUNDARA, MAR. 8, I970**

Srila Prabhupada also added an addendum to a letter to Guru das on March 15,1970, saying:

**My special thanks are due to your good wife, Srimati Yamuna devi. Her singing songs of Krishna consciousness will certainly bless her and you all.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, MAR. 15, I970**

## Promoting “Govindam”—A Remembrance

**Yogesvara das**: We \[once\] played in a place called, ironically, the Temple, near Trafalgar Square, and we went on at midnight or some hour like that. We went down the stairs, and looking inside this basement club, you could hardly see anything—there was so much cigarette smoke. There were only these red spotlights on, so it looked like something out of Dante’s Inferno. It was the Stones or some really heavy music on the speakers. One of the crew guides us to this tiny little green room at the back and we’re just sitting there on benches, holding our instruments and chanting on our japa beads, and this was pretty much what it was like. Then we hear an announcement saying, “AND NOW! GEORGE HARRISON’S LATEST FIND, THE RADHA-KRISHNA TEMPLLLLE!” Yamuna would go to the center of the stage. Dead silence. Deafening, deadly, dead silence. Everyone’s looking at us through their dark glasses—the place is pitch black and everyone has sunglasses on, with this look like “Who the hell are you?” Mukunda gets up and says, “Actually Hare Krishna is not a pop tune.” Yamuna already has her eyes closed, with her head going back and forth like Stevie Wonder. Then we start playing; she’s chanting away; I close my eyes. When it starts speeding up maybe twenty minutes later, I open my eyes \[and\] the smoke had cleared, the house lights were on, everybody had removed their glasses, and they were holding hands, dancing in circles! I’m looking over at Yamuna, and she looks at me with this huge Cheshire Cat grin on her face, and then Malati bangs her gong to signal the end. The place goes bananas. They’re yelling, whistling, applauding. We collect our stuff and over the loudspeaker, the guy says, “AND YOU CAN BE SURE WE’RE GOING TO HAVE THEM BACK, THE RADHA-KRISHNA TEMPLLLLE!” As we were walking out of the club, I was the last one leaving. I turned around and looked back inside, and bang! The smoke was back, the red lights were on; it was dark again, and Mick Jagger was wailing on the speaker. It was like for the last 45 minutes, this transcendental cloud, led by Yamuna, had just wafted in through this basement club and wafted out. That’s what she was like; she would waft in and waft out, and she set the pace and the mood for some of those club gigs. But she was not the one to talk with reporters; she didn’t want to interact. That was Mukunda, Shyamasundara and sometimes me. She was the transcendental voice. That was her role. She was not only aloof, she stayed in the background; even at the gigs that we did, she never put herself front and center—that was not her way. When she was called to do something, she did it with a full heart, but I cannot recall a time when she ever put herself in the spotlight—not once.

## Harinam. Sankirtan

Ever since the arrival of Tamai Krishna das in London, he had taken on the service of structuring the rather erratic assembly of chanting devotees into an attractive and choreographed group—one that would evolve into Srila Prabhupada’s much-desired World Sankirtan Party. In February, Srila Prabhupada had written a letter to Mukunda reaffirming the purpose and goals of the World Sankirtan Party:

**Therefore World Sankirtan Party means to establish a center everywhere we go. I do not mean a concert party or musical party that may go to a city, have some performances and collect some money without any permanent effect. For this purpose the World Sankirtan Party should consist of members who can impress spiritual ecstasy in the hearts of the people so that some of them may come forward and agree to establish a center where the sankirtan party may go on continually.**

**— LETTER TO MUKUNDA, FEB. 8, 1970**

A natural organizer, Tamai Krishna had soon configured the devotees into a uniform harinam party. Yamuna loved to go on these street harinam programs—she often spoke of them as celebrations of the Holy Name—and of course, her loud yet melodious voice carried without need of a microphone. Yet, due to her already overtaxed schedule, she was only able to attend sporadically.

**Aditi devi**: We would go out on harinam often—usually two or three times a day. Sometimes after breakfast, I remember going to the British Museum and distributing literature. Then after lunch we would all go on harinam, usually on Oxford Street.... Tuesday and Thursday nights Yamuna would lead us in evening bhajans—Vande ham sri guruh—very solemn and beautiful-then ending up with the Hare Krishna mantra. On Saturday everyone would go on harinam to a special outdoor shopping area. We would be in double file; Yamuna would be at the head of one file, and she would lead. We would all walk and dance together, from side to side. Sometimes Yamuna would take us women on a walk around Russell Square, which was just a few blocks from the temple. Srila Prabhupada used to walk in the mornings there when he was in London. That was always a special occasion, and we would walk quickly and quietly, chanting our japa. v

**Dhananjaya das**: And I remember also when we used to do harinam in different parts of London, like in Kings Road in Chelsea, Kensington, Knightsbridge—different areas like that. And one time we went to Chelsea, and there was a busload of Yugoslavian tourists; they got the driver to stop the bus and they ran over to us, and wanted to take all of our autographs, because our single was number one in their country.

## 1970 Rathayatra

**Yamuna**: *The London devotees were now ready to prepare for our second Rathayatra festival. This was a climactic event for us because in the previous year, we were a very small group of devotees who had diligently worked towards the Rathayatra, only to face a near catastrophic result. The Jagannatha cart that Shyamasundara had almost single-handedly built had its wheels collapse due to wood rot. So the cart never made it to its final destination. We were all crestfallen, and had to report the discouraging news to Srila Prabhupada. Yet, in his infinite kindness, he encouraged us: “Next year everything will be very wonderful. Don’t be discouraged; you simply try very hard.” So we were enthusiastic, determined, and ready to make the 1970 London Rathayatra a spectacular event.*

Interestingly, Srila Prabhupada’s mood of encouragement on their Rathayatra debacle was similar to his mood on the disappointments surrounding the Deity installation. As the date of the temple opening and Deity installation approached with no marble Radha and Krishna Deities having come, Srila Prabhupada told Yamuna not to be discouraged: “Krishna will surely come if you are sincere,” he said.

Yamuna wrote to Srila Prabhupada on June 1, 1970, detailing the plans currently in place for the upcoming Rathayatra, and asking him questions about the bathing ceremony. Srila Prabhupada replied:

**Regarding your first question, the bathing ceremony of Lord Jagannatha is observed by His Lordship standing in a bathing tank while each of the devotees in turn offers prayers and obeisances, then pours water to bathe the Lord, then offers obeisances, and the next devotee follows the same procedure. All the other devotees are holding kirtan throughout the bathing ceremony which takes place on June 19.**

**Regarding your second question, after being bathed, Lord Jagannatha catches fever and at that time you may carry Him along with Balaramaji and Subhadra to my room for recovering. During this time, up to Rathayatra, any repairs may be made.... Then Lord Jagannatha reappears on the day of the Rathayatra festival. During His convalescence bhoga is offered as usual, but no visitors are allowed to see the Lord.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, JUNE 1, 1970**

Yamuna was taking no chances on misunderstanding any procedure or service to Their Lordships before, during or after the Rathayatra. She again wrote to Srila Prabhupada on June 15, asking what Lord Jagannatha should be served on His Ratha cart. Srila Prabhupada answered that for the full duration of the festivities and for eight days following, Their Lordships should be served bunchi kitchari, along with other preparations. He then proceeded to give detailed instructions on its preparation.

**Yamuna**: *So we had prepared in advance for the 1970 Rathayatra, and devotees came from Germany and France to assist. By this time our ranks had swelled to enormous proportions. We had many supporters in London from the Indian community and the youth. Our kirtans were attracting massive numbers, and the records we had made with George Harrison through Apple had increased interest in our movement and activities on a phenomenal scale. By the time of the Rathayatra, we were all simply astounded at the numbers of people who came, what to speak of those lining the streets, who were pulled into the great caravan of dancing and chanting souls.*

*The sankirtan for Lord Jagannatha at the Rathayatra Festival was ecstatic. The Deities of Their Lordships Jagannatha, Subhadra and Balarama had come to us before Sri Sri Radha-Londonisvara, and all of us were very attached to Them. They wore a golden-red dress, inspired by one that Srila Prabhupada instructed me to make for his Radha-Krishna Deities at Tittenhurst Manor. Remembering an earlier instruction Srila Prabhupada had given me in 1968 about making the Deities appear so beautiful that anyone who saw Them would no longer be allured by mayas attractions, we tried to make the outfits gorgeous and opulent. I was assisted in all the sewing services by Aditi and the wonderful French devotees, Mondakini, Jyotirmayi, and llavati.*

**Aditi devi**: One time \[Yamuna\] wrote a letter and also sent some socks from all of us \[to Srila Prabhupada\], She also asked some questions about Rathayatra and taking care of Their Lordships Jagannatha, Balarama and Subhadra. Srila Prabhupada said that... They should have “gorgeous” outfits for the Rathayatra. Yamuna had asked me to help with the Rathayatra outfit. I don’t remember very much, but I do remember that I had an idea of helmets made with styrofoam. Yamuna liked the idea, and for several days she would heat a knife and then shape helmets for Lord Jagannatha and Lord Balarama out of large blocks of styrofoam. The helmets were then covered with shiny gold cloth, and decorations were added.

**Yamuna**: *We made banners—“Holy Jagannatha Car Procession” and “World Sankirtan Party.” I remember that Malati made the World Sankirtan Party banners we took to India as well. From the beginning, Srila Prabhupada had this idea for a traveling sankirtan party, and in fact it did manifest after this Rathayatra. Devotees from America, England and Europe gathered together and went to India. So his transcendental desire was fulfilled. Srila Prabhupada actually sent a description to me of how the sankirtan parties should be arranged during the Rathayatra procession, just as Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu had arranged His sankirtan procession for Rathayatra in Puri over 500 years before.*

*So as our procession reached Trafalgar Square, you could not see to the end of people—so many were there. Thinking of the many souls who got the special mercy of seeing Lord Jagannatha, I was reminded again of a letter Srila Prabhupada wrote to me saying, “When seeing Lord Jagannatha nicely decorated, we become freed from the clutches of maya.” How nice to think of Srila Prabhupada’s prophetic statement while watching this sea of people receiving the blessings of Lord Jagannatha.*

*So this was an incredible growth period in London. This was that magic portal which opened at just the right time and which allowed Srila Prabhupada and the Holy Names to inject their real potency into the hearts and souls of so many people. Just to see the change in two years—it was phenomenal; and it was all by the mercy of Srila Prabhupada. We were the seeds being planted, and he was the blossoming creeper of Lord Chaitanya’s love. And when he came, everything ignited like a firestorm. It was truly magical—the Krishna Magic!*

## The “Radha-Krishna Temple” Album

**Yamuna**: *I remember that I wasn’t initially very enthusiastic at the prospect of recording the Radha-Krishna Temple album. My thinking was that I didn’t have the time. I had to almost be pressured into becoming involved in the project, because when you record, there’s a lot of down time, like doing a movie. There’s playback time, discussion, adjustment, more playback, more discussion. Already we had toured to promote the singles, sometimes in very low, mode of ignorance places. I feared that we would become “contaminated” being in such environments, but on at least two occasions Srila Prabhupada encouraged me to remain detached and remember that we were giving the greatest gift—the gift of the Holy Names. Once, close to the time of his leaving London, he told the story of Jagai and Madhai, using it to illustrate how even the most sinful persons can be liberated by hearing the Holy Names. He told us that if we chanted our rounds and remained strong in the principles of Krishna Consciousness, then we would be able to lift up even the lowest among men through the potency of our sincere chanting.*

*The Radha-Krishna Temple album was finished just a few nights before we left for India. Late one night, after finishing our recording for the day, I sat by myself at the harmonium, my voice scratchy and a good octave lower because I was so exhausted. Pumping the harmonium with one hand and tapping it with the other, I began singing—Bhaja mana hure, bhaja mana hure, sri nandananda abhaya caranaravinda re. I did not know anyone was listening, nor did I know that the microphone was on and that George Harrison was recording it. When I finished, all of a sudden George said, “Excellent. That’s a take.” I was completely shocked. From that time on, many people asked me who the man was, singing the Bhaja hure mana song incorrectly.*

**Dhananjaya das**: When she made the mistake with Bhaja hure mana on the album, someone came to Prabhupada and said “How could you accept this; it’s wrong?” Prabhupada responded, “Anyone who listens to her voice will surely become Krishna Conscious, regardless of all their defects.”

**Yamuna**: *Once, in India, I was sitting behind Srila Prabhupada when he halfturned his head to me and said simply, “The words are wrong.” Confused, I asked, “What words, Srila Prabhupada?” “The words to the prayer you recorded. Bhaja mana hure means nothing. It should be Bhaja hure mana." I was so embarrassed. Of course, we had no songbooks in the 1960’s, and I had incorrectly heard Prabhupada when he chanted it. But then he said, “Never mind. If someone sincerely hears the chanting, they will be benefited because you chanted sincerely. That is the secret of Krishna Consciousness. It is a matter of sincerity.*

## Yamuna’s India Prayer Fulfilled — “Miracle Done, Your Divine Grace”

**Yamuna:** *When Sri Sri Radha-Londonisvara were installed, Srila Prabhupada told Guru das and me to remain in London for the rest of our lives and serve Them. We remained there only nine months before he changed his mind, and in September he requested us to prepare to go to India. He also asked Shyamasundara, Malati and Tamai Krishna—now married to Madri—to prepare to go as well, in a switch of roles, he requested Mukunda and Janaki to prepare to take up the service of managing Bury Place. Surely they were qualified—senior to us by a few devotional months—but I was unsure if Janaki had the necessary tolerance, patience and enthusiasm for it. One great relief was that three women—Mondakini, Aditi and Lilashakti— were trained up as cooks and pujaris and were absolutely dedicated to serving Sri Sri Radha-Londonisvara. Dhananjaya was expert in many services as well.*

Whatever Srila Prabhupada had planned had certainly come as a surprise to Yamuna. He had just written to her on September 16,1970:

**I am so glad to learn that our London temple is very, very well managed under your supervision. Kindly continue this standard of temple management—that will make me very happy.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA, SEPT. 16, I970**

It is clear from this letter that at least until this point, Srila Prabhupada was expecting Yamuna and Guru das to remain in London. Yet, by October 4, 1970, little more than two weeks later, they were already in Bombay. Looking back from our more circumscribed lives of today, this would seem impulsive, but devotees in those days were ready at a moment’s notice to drop everything to try to fulfill Srila Prabhupada’s wishes.

**Yamuna**: *ISKCON temples had now been established in major cities in Europe and America. Prabhupada felt it was time to establish ISKCON temples in India, the cradle of Krishna Consciousness. He wanted his World Sankirtan Party to ignite the fire of sankirtan in India by literally shocking them with previously unseen and unheard of mostly Caucasian young devotees who chanted Hare Krishna with great sincerity and musicality. In addition to the London and European devotees, Prabhupada also brought others from America: Revatinandana, Giriraja, Dinanatha, Cidananda, Hansadutta, Himavati, Kaushalya and more. We were his first World Sankirtan Party. What a statement we all made!*

*For my husband and me, it all came as a great surprise. We had almost no time to prepare, and left at the beginning of October 1970, just over two years after arriving in London in late August of 1968. I had mixed feelings at the time. Certainly a deep love and nostalgia had grown within me for everything we had shared and experienced in endeavoring to start the London Yatra. Also, the entire “Govindam” experience and the chanting opportunities it engendered were lifetime memories to be savored. Worshiping the glorious Sri Sri Radha-Londonisvara Deities was so monumentally life-changing that I cannot find words to describe it to this day. In summary, helping to establish the London Yatra was not only a high point in my life, but in the lives of many other devotees as well. Everything before London had been encouragement and preparation for the process of Krishna bhakti, but London Yatra was the first real training ground in the practice of Krishna Consciousness for me. And yet, I was ready for the next service—-the next adventure—and the desire to go to India had never left my heart. So, like the marionette Srila Prabhupada described in his prayer on the Jaladuta, I was ready for the next dance.*

## Janaki Devi—An Exhibition of Srila Prabhupada’s Unequalled Compassion

One of the difficulties facing Yamuna in going to India was her reluctance to leave her sister, Janaki. In the absence of Yamuna and Guru das, Srila Prabhupada wanted Mukunda and Janaki to take charge of the London temple, and the thought of Janaki in that position was dismaying to Yamuna. Janaki, always a sensitive and fragile soul, had become more intransigent and increasingly disengaged from Krishna Consciousness over the last year. In fact, Yamuna had seen little of her sister in the months prior to her departure for India, and she feared that management responsibilities would be too much for Janaki to endure.

When Janaki had last seen Srila Prabhupada at his Baker Street apartment, to Yamuna’s and everyone else’s surprise, she had appeared before him in non-devotee attire. At that time, she frankly expressed her desire to leave. Yamuna never forgot the overwhelming love and compassion Srila Prabhupada demonstrated to Janaki on that day.

**Yamuna**: *So my sister bluntly expressed to Srila Prabhupada that she wanted to leave. She told him that “When you are here, everything is fine; but when you leave, everything becomes harder to deal with, especially the men, and I don’t want to do it.” I looked at Srila Prabhupada, whose eyes glistened with tears of love. I was also crying—we all were. With a combination of deep love and gravity, he said:*

***Please do not leave. We have the best philosophy. You will not find a better philosophy in this world. There is nothing like the knowledge that we have in Krishna Consciousness. We have the best scriptures, like Bhagavad-gita, Srimad-Bhagavatam, The Nectar of Devotion and Caitanya-caritamrta. And there is nothing like our food—prasadam. Not only does it taste wonderful, but just by eating it, you become spiritually advanced. You won’t find any other kind of nourishment like this Krishna Consciousness. And best of all, we have the Holy Names—the mahamantra— which is the perfect and most blissful way to reach the highest goal. And we have the best association. Please don’t go.***

*And all this time tears were pouring from his eyes.*

Yamuna told this story to a group of young students at the Govardhan Academy in Saranagati in 2010. She used the example of Srila Prabhupada’s mercy toward her sister to show how false ego can make us lose our ability to appreciate even something as powerful as the Guru’s compassion and love for us.

**Yamuna**: *When the false ego comes in, we can quickly become covered over by not following the process. Forgetting Krishna can happen really quickly—we know it in a day. And if you look at yourself in a twenty-four-hour day, where your mind goes—it’s amazing; it can go all kinds of places. Can’t it? In twenty-four hours. What to speak of twenty-four hours; in five minutes it can go all kinds of places!*

*So when we don’t follow the process of Krishna Consciousness that Prabhupada gave us, then we become a little dull, and our ideas become very prominent, and our personal opinions become very prominent; and we become a little weak, and then we forget Krishna.*

*So Srila Prabhupada gave us this process, and he said, “It is glorious. Please take it. Make it your life.” This life goes by so quickly. I know if you are teenagers, it seems like forever between one year and the next. But those who are in your mid-thirties now; you see how fast the years go by. They really do. I am almost seventy years old. And all I can say is that this life went so fast. It seems like just a few days ago I was twenty-five. It just shoots by.*

*But we want to commit. We want to get to the big “commit” word. How do we get to the big “commit” word? Try to associate with people who are more advanced than you are. Put time into the process of self-realization. Look at how you are doing. Look at where you can improve—where you can be better. What do you need to make yourselves stronger? And you know if you do this, then just baby step by baby step you start to crawl, and then you walk, and then you run. It will happen, and you will feel the magic—the Krishna Magic.*

*It is the peace formula. It is the path of freedom. We are all looking for freedom, aren’t we? In the material world, they have a song that says, “Let freedom ring.” So we want that freedom, but actually we are bound up, almost in shackles—almost as if we are shackled down by material consciousness. There is no freedom better than the freedom of Krishna Consciousness.*

*And sometimes when a devotee so-called leaves, or they get weak, they are almost always looking for some kind of freedom separate from Krishna. But this is a very wonderful process. We have the most wonderful guides; we have support systems everywhere, if we just know where to look for them. And Krishna, our Gurus and the Vaishnavas are holding the rope out to us. We just need to grab onto it—and that means to commit.*

Yamuna was always able to convince the young devotees of the sweetness to be found in the process of Krishna Consciousness. When she spoke, when she connected with them, each of them thought Krishna Consciousness was accessible and not just something intangible. They would invariably leave enthused and “on fire” with the possibilities that lay before them through this wonderful process. It was one of Yamuna’s many gifts—deeply felt by many.

## A Call to India

So the first World Sankirtan Party was now gathering for the India preaching adventure. Yet, for the devotees in London, Yamuna’s absence would be deeply felt, and she would be sorely missed.

**Yogesvara das**: Yamuna kind of kept it all together with spiritual glue. She was the one you could go to for succor, for solace, for a spiritual injection of whatever it might be, and she would always engage us in service for the Deities.

What Yamuna offered me was the lesson of focus. Not just chanting; this pervaded everything she did. She was focused, undistracted by other things. The risk in devotional life, particularly in the beginning stages, is to fall into a routine, to think “now this is what we do,” rather than diving deep into the moment, and realizing, “Oh, my, I’m actually inviting Krishna to be here with me right now.” This is about as personal as it gets. With Yamuna it was always personal. There wasn’t a moment of doing something out of habit or mechanically. I would say that I never saw her do anything mechanically. Everything was intentional.

The whole India adventure was not only new for the devotees, but an excursion into the “unknown.” Yamuna said that although she was a hundred percent committed to whatever Srila Prabhupada wanted, she had some fear of how they would be received in India. How would people react to them? How would they remain safe? Would they depend on Krishna’s protection? And then Yamuna remembered a story Srila Prabhupada related about his early life during one of their talks at John Lennon’s estate in Ascot. First he said, “I am revealing a little of these things to you, and at a later date I will reveal much more.”

**Yamuna**: *But they were such amazing and nectarean pastimes that although we did not distribute them to the public, I very carefully wrote them down in my notebook. But later, that notebook was lost in Vrindavan, and I was only left with my memories of those sweet pastimes. On this particular day, Srila Prabhupada was explaining how the pure devotee is always protected by the Lord. He said that once when he was a very little baby, he was sitting on his elder sister’s lap in a tonga, which was a horse-drawn cart. He said that this sister, who was three or four years older than Prabhupada, was a great devotee of Krishna. There were many people in the cart, including his mother and others. Somehow the horse became startled, and the driver lost control and was thrown out. So the tonga was now driverless, and the wheel hit a rock, and everyone inside was hurled out. But when he was thrown out, he landed in a pile of soft grasses, and he didn’t even have a scratch on him. He said that this kind of thing happened a lot in his life, and Krishna had always protected him from all kinds of havoc. So I drew strength from this story. I was not a pure devotee, but because I was under Srila Prabhupada’s protection, I felt secure in the knowledge that Krishna would also protect me.*

During our pilgrimages to India over the years, I honestly lost count of how many people approached Yamuna and said something like, “You probably don’t remember me, but I was one of the young devotees you preached to in London in the early days.” They would go on to say that the experience, in whatever form it took, had changed their lives in a substantial way, making them want to become a devotee or “commit” more to the practice of devotional service. This was “Yamuna” exemplified. Whatever Prabhupada gave her, whatever the Vaishnavas gave her, she immediately distributed to others. That was the gift—the “miracle done” aspect of Srila Prabhupada’s blessings to her. She instinctively felt the desire to give his gift to others, and whether it took the form of her chanting, her cooking or her preaching, it was always given freely and with love.

## An Endnote on London

For me, as the chronicler of Yamuna’s devotional journey, one of the most interesting revelations about the London experience came through Srila Prabhupada’s numerous letters to her. It is clear from the letters that Yamuna wrote little to him about George Harrison, John Lennon or the “Govindam” or other recordings. In fact, virtually all of her letters were either updates on her own devotional progress or questions about her service to the Deities or to the devotees in the temple. Reading Srila Prabhupada’s letters to Yamuna in London is a revelation in itself, for in them you see what was truly important to her—you see into the heart of Yamuna devi.

**Bala Gopal devi**: I saw the influence Yamuna had left on all those devotees. Even for that time, it was an extremely organized temple. She was an amazing organizer and manager, and they really tried to implement all of the things that she had taught, so it was a very loving temple. We’d have mangal arati, then we’d have the Isopanisad class, then chant rounds, then harinam—there was never a time to space out, and that was all Yamuna. She had managed all of that.

## Chapter 6

**A Prayer Fulfilled - Yamuna Devi's India Sojourn (India, 1970-1972)**

BEFORE LEAVING FOR India, Yamuna wrote a short prayer on binding of her journal that she had remembered from her childhood. Although the journal was later lost, she pointed the prayer out to me years later when she came across it again. She expressed that this prayer perfectly reflected how she felt at the time of their journey to India—except that her full faith was placed at the lotus feet of both Guru and Krishna.

**Dear Lord, You have called on us, Your servants, to ventures of which we cannot see the ending, by paths as yet untrodden, through perils unknown. Give us faith to go out with good courage, not knowing where we go, but only that Your hand is leading us and Your love supporting us.**

## India via Egypt Through Perils Unknown

Now that the London devotees had been called to India, the next necessity was finding the cheapest means of travel to get there. As they had been engaged cent percent in the service of guru and Krishna in London, they were likely unaware of or unconcerned by the recent political unrest in the Arab world. So Guru das found surprisingly cheap tickets to Bombay on an airline called “Brothers Air Services.” Delighted by the cheap prices, the devotees would most likely have not felt the need to research either the Brothers’ operation or the political volatility of the Arab world they were flying through. Just as Srila Prabhupada had told Yamuna about Krishna protecting him in the tonga as an infant, so Krishna protected the India-bound devotees in two significant ways. First, Brothers Air Services consisted of one DC3 propeller plane. Gordon Rayney, the Director of Civil Aviation at the time, made a short but succinct comment on the Brothers’ operation: “They had no idea what they were doing!” Another frequent Mideast flyer during the late 6o’s and early 70’s wrote about the Brothers’ plane:

**The Baharoons, calling themselves Brothers Air Services, with a single DC3, didn’t last long, and I never risked a trip (and I’ve flown on some pretty chancy operators).**

**— D. TOMLINSON, SHELL OIL DIRECTOR FOR ARABIA AND YEMEN**

The airplane itself brings to mind comic parodies we’ve all seen of airline travel. Malati devi described some of the salient aspects of the plane:

**Malati devi**: Everything was being done by hand. They had burlap sacks over the doors in the “bathrooms.” And there was a big tank in the middle of the plane with a water dipper, and that was our water supply. It wasn’t even a jet. When we got off at one point, I saw this string going from the cockpit to the tail and the rudders, and I said, “What’s that?” And they said, “Oh, when you make a turn, you pull the string.” This was the plane we took to India! v

**Yamuna**: *The plane was actually not fit for flying. In addition to its questionable airworthiness—and the political volatility unknown to us at the time—there was absolutely nothing on the plane to make the long flight comfortable. I could have borne that reasonably peacefully, but at one point I actually caught a glimpse of a mechanic kicking one of the engines from his forklift. It was simply Krishna’s mercy—nothing else—that allowed us to reach Bombay on that plane.*

In fact, the flight to Bombay was the last flight of the fledgling company, which then quickly disbanded. Giriraja das, who had just joined their traveling party from America, summed up his own disposition as well as the general mood of the devotees at the time:

**Giriraja Swami**: Guru das had arranged a cheap flight on a small airline, and so that evening we boarded an old converted dual-propeller cargo plane bound for Bombay with a stop in Cairo. In my mood of Krishna Consciousness then, I was quite oblivious to things around me. I wanted to avoid maya—anything that could distract me from Krishna—and didn’t pay much heed to anything that didn’t relate directly to my service. I was focused on the idea of chanting and hearing every word of the Hare Krishna mantra distinctly, on always thinking about Krishna and never forgetting Him. And I had heard that Srila Prabhupada had said that if you have trouble hearing, you should chant loudly. And sometimes, to really get into the Holy Names—and to break out of any possible lethargy—I would jump up and down. One or two of the devotees told me that they were anxious about how people in Egypt might react to my chanting, but I was determined

What the devotees were unaware of was the fact that at this time King Hussein was at war with several Palestinian militant groups in an attempt to expel them from Jordan. The month of September 1970 was given the name “Black September,” or “the era of regrettable events” in Arabic, due to the many thousands of people killed in the uprisings. In that month alone, five jumbo jets were hijacked by a terrorist organization called the Popular Front for the Liberation of Palestine. One of them, a Pan Am flight, was forced to land in Cairo on September 6, and was then blown up as soon as it was evacuated. The situation became so volatile that Egypt’s president, Gamal Abdel Nasser, held an Arab League Summit on September 27 in an effort to alleviate tensions and avert an all-out war. Unfortunately, the day after the summit, on September 28, he had a heart attack and died. When the devotees landed in Egypt a few days later, tensions could not have been more explosive. Riots had broken out in the streets, and the other Arab leaders who surrounded Nasser’s coffin had to be whisked to safety. So it is no wonder the Egyptian guards at the airport thought the devotees’ behavior suspicious. To add fuel to the fire, Giriraja had a habit of jumping while he chanted—not a little jump—but very high jumps—Hare Krishna (jump) Hare Krishna (jump). Yamuna loved to tell the story of walking along the tarmac and all of a sudden seeing the guards’ machine guns moving up and down in a rhythmic pattern. She turned and saw to her amazement that they were following the jumping movements of Giriraja—Hare Krishna (jump—gun up), Hare Krishna (jump—gun down). In the midst of the obvious chaos, she found his detachment very amusing and revealing, and over the years if anyone spoke about Giriraja Swami, she would invariably tell that story.

**Giriraja Swami**: *There was unrest there at that time, and when we landed in Cairo there were blown-up jumbo jets and tanks in and around the airport. We were met on the tarmac by soldiers and armed security guards with bandoliers of bullets around their chests and machine guns over their shoulders, and as we deplaned, walking down the steps, the men were pointing machine guns in direction. Then Yamuna, as I was later told, saw the guards suddenly move their guns up and down, shifting their aim. And when she turned around to see why, she saw me behind her, walking down the stairs chanting japa, jumping up and down*

Whenever the devotees traveled anywhere, it was their habit to set up a little altar and immediately begin harinam sankirtan. If you look at the civil unrest in countries like Egypt today, you can just imagine the risks they took in an Islamic country at that most volatile time, but they were simply depending on Krishna and Srila Prabhupada to protect them in all circumstances.

**Yamuna**: *Our London contingent of devotees— Shyamasundara, Malati (with baby Saraswati), Guru das, myself and Madri, flew with all the devotees from the United States and Europe, and the stop in the Cairo airport was the first time we got together for sankirtan in public. It became our habit from then on that the minute we arrived somewhere, we would jump out and have kirtan. There is a film of us in the Cairo airport—all jumping out and doing the same thing. We set up a little altar with pictures of Srila Prabhupada and Back to Godheads, and stood there in the middle of this Muslim country performing sankirtan— completely oblivious to the imminent danger surrounding us.*

*Most people had their faces skewed, staring and wondering, “What are they doing?” We even tried to preach to them in English. As soon as the kirtan party would stop, we would all either chant japa with serious intention or go out and preach to whoever was standing and staring at us. If we were saved by anything that day (aside from the mercy of the Lord), it was by how our child member, Saraswati, captured peoples’ hearts with her chanting and dancing. Everyone was captivated by her dancing and her kirtan, even though they didn’t know what kirtan was. She was just so endearing.*

## The World Sankirtan Party in Bombay—“Welcome to India”

Some things in India have changed dramatically over the years; bandhs, or strikes, are one thing that hasn’t. Regardless of what kind of work one does, to take a day off to protest some inequity seems to be the accepted method of displaying angst. For some reason, the airport workers seem to display this angst more than many others. Of the six times I flew internationally into Bombay, three of them were on such bandh days. The last one happened to Yamuna and me in 2008. Try to imagine it being the middle of the night, and you have spent an hour flying in circles around Mumbai in a jumbo jet because they have no gate assignment for you to arrive at. As there is no gate, you land and taxi around the airport for another hour, and then finally a bus comes and takes you to a variety of entrances, where you are perfunctorily turned away because there are no customs officials available. Yamuna joked about the experience, which was so similar to their original Bombay landing in 1970. “Welcome to India,” she joked. “This is just like forty years ago.” Yamuna spoke of the 1970 experience as being remarkably similar except for the open cockpit, the unveiled anger of the pilots, who shouted in Hindi at the air traffic controllers, and the fact that they were not in a jumbo jet, but rather a comical excuse for an airplane. And again, just as in 1970, some wonderful devotees waited patiently to pick us up. We asked how long they had been waiting. “Oh, not so long,” they said. Yamuna pressed again. “How long have you waited?” “Oh, only five or six hours—not so long.”

**Yamuna**: *After a continual shouting match between the pilots, the ground crew, bus drivers and anyone else in the vicinity, we were told to collect our gear and depart the plane. The plane hatch was opened and a rickety staircase attached. We climbed down to the hot, sticky tarmac almost in total darkness. Within a few minutes, a bus that looked about fifty years old belched to a stop before us. We climbed on, headed to the arrival terminal, and began the arduous process of trying to find a functioning building entrance to get inside the terminal. The bus driver said that because airport workers were on strike, the entrances were closed. Finally we were dropped off at a baggage entrance, and the driver pointed us through the door. We entered a barely lit, unmarked hallway. Now what? Gear in hand, we arbitrarily walked on.*

*Even in the middle of the night the airport was chaotically loud and stiflingly hot. Its concrete walls were institution-green and floors ironoxide red—both stained with paan and scuffed with wear. After repeated inquiries to English-speaking locals, we at last reached the Customs hall, identified by a large sign in English that read “CUSTOMS HERE”.*

*It took a full hour for our party to get through customs. When we went to the arrivals area, literally hundreds were waiting in the chaos to pick up travelers. Now what do we do? We were officially in India and let out enthusiastic whoops of “Haribol” and “Prabhupada Ki jaya”. But we were in a quandary about how to get to our destination. Then Revatinandana spotted a raised sign that read “ISKCON Sankirtan Party Here.” He led us to a refined and cultured-looking man holding the sign. Cordially welcoming us all, he introduced himself as Mr. Kailash Seksaria. We had heard that Mr. Seksaria was one of Bombay’s wealthiest industrialists, and were surprised to find that he had fought this chaos and stayed up so late to personally welcome us to Bombay. Despite the heat, humidity and unclean conditions around us, he was impeccably attired in a voile-thin, starched white kurta, with not a hair of his thick black hair out of place. He waved a telegram and asked for Guru das, the “in-charge,” to introduce himself, which he did in his typically gregarious and friendly manner.*

*I was surrounded by old friends and new friends. We were an odd assortment of about eighteen souls. My husband Guru das, my Godsister Malati with her toddler Saraswati—a can-do woman if ever there was one. Years later, whenever I thought of Malati, I saw her as inexorable—if there was something impossible to do, she would work on it until it was done, no matter how difficult or how long it took. There was also a new, young friend in our party, Kaushalya devi, with a round, laughing face and a deep love for kirtan. Another female member of our party was Madri, recently married to Tamai Krishna—she was quiet and sweet, yet reserved. We all saw ourselves as a family—a family of Godbrothers and -sisters under the banner of Srila Prabhupada’s World Sankirtan Party. The later divisions and misunderstandings that would provide persistent challenges for women had not yet taken root. I remember looking forward with great happiness to the coming adventures in India. There was not a note of apprehension in the sweet song of India for me.*

## Srila Prabhupada — “Startling India with Kirtan”

**Yamuna**: *My possessions were really few and sparse: a red, bulky sleeping bag; three black writing notebooks; good writing pens; calligraphy pens; and even ink. I brought the few saris that I’d had for three years. My husband was also traveling lightly, but one in our party, Malati’s husband, Shyamasundara, who was a carpenter, had actually come with a chain saw and skill saw. In India! We were incredulous. He also brought a set of carving tools and wanted to bring a load of redwood, but that didn’t happen.*

*Mr. Seksaria was the nephew of Mr. Dandharia, who knew Srila Prabhupada before he left for the United States and had given money for the original Srimad-Bhagavatams to be written. He made wonderful living arrangements for Srila Prabhupada’s disciples on the first floor of his multi-story home on Marine Drive; and then, to our great happiness, Srila Prabhupada himself came from Calcutta on October 8.*

**Giriraja Swami**: So after we had been in Bombay for a couple of days, we received a telegram that Srila Prabhupada was coming, and we were all very ecstatic that we would be seeing our Guru Maharaja again. So our host, Mr. Kailash Seksaria, who had a big house on Marine Drive, arranged a procession of cars to receive Srila Prabhupada at the airport. Prabhupada’s car was completely covered with flowers, which we had never seen before, but Mr. Seksaria knew how to do it. So we greeted Srila Prabhupada with a large kirtan at the airport, and then we brought him to Mr. Seksaria’s house.

**Yamuna**: *Marine Drive winds around Back Bay. Coconut palms line the side facing the water. There is a median of small bushes down the center. As we drove up to Kailash Seksaria’s residence, the building was a creamy beige color—seven floors. There were two bushes on either side of the driveway as we arrived at the marble front entrance, green marble on the sides, a darker green marble facing the front, and white marble steps. A lone plumeria plant stood facing the sea.*

*When Srila Prabhupada came, there was a tumultuous reception waiting in anticipation in a small enclave about twelve feet square, filled with around thirty devotees. As you entered into the foyer through two carved wooden doors, there was a small marble entryway where the stairway stood, next to two lifts. On the top of one lift, a two-foot-square clock ticked away the time. Our quarters were on the first floor, through a double entry door. Srila Prabhupada was whisked into the lift and brought up to the fourth floor, where his bedroom was located.*

*The first room we were brought into was on the ground floor—an empty room. I looked up, and the white bars on the windows were disguised in a pattern that resembled a key to me—the top of the key round and coming down to a half moon at the bottom. I envisioned it to be a key that Srila Prabhupada would unlock India for me with, as this is what he promised years ago in San Francisco. This pattern of bars did not appear anywhere on the upper floors.*

## Seeing Harinam Sankirtan Act on the Hearts of Others

**Yamuna**: *From the very beginning of our programs in Bombay, Srila Prabhupada became known as one “who is startling India with kirtan.” Our kirtans were full of so much excitement— they were so thrilling—that we were like one throbbing heartbeat, the heartbeat of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s mission of Krishna Consciousness, ft is difficult to describe how much potency we felt in the kirtans—not just in the chanting itself, but how the chanting was being received by others. It was amazing how clearly we could see the chanting changing the hearts and psyches of so many people, and this simply spurred us on even more. Like a holistic circle—the dynamic circle of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu’s Sankirtan Movement— we took the process our Guru Maharaja gave us to heart, practiced it, gave it to others through harinam sankirtan, and then saw it act on their hearts. It was truly a magical, wonderful thing, and I felt so privileged to be part of it.*

*Srila Prabhupada’s interplay with us at this time was truly wondrous. I can only describe him as being like a conductor with many devotee “instruments,” watching each of us carefully and directing the rhythms and tenors of our individual services. He knew our strengths and weaknesses, tried to bring out the best in each of us, and protected us. We felt that we couldn’t have figured out anything regarding the day-to-day adjustments to being in India without his constant guidance. He set the example of how to live, how to behave, and he allowed us access to him nearly twenty-four hours a day.*

*Srila Prabhupada’s energy level at this time was also beyond description. Here he was in his seventies, while we were all in our twenties or less, and yet he worked circles around us. He was present, alert, and up each night until after midnight translating. Then he had a full-on day of activities, including instructions to us, letters to write and send around the world, meetings with important men and aspiring devotees, preaching programs, and of course, his daily personal sadhana. It was simply inconceivable, and yet he did this every day, regardless of where he was.*

**One of the first formal programs that Srila Prabhupada and the devotees were invited to was on Chowpatty Beach—the annual pandal of the Bharat Sadhu Samaj, an interfaith organization of holy men in India formed in 1956. Essentially a social and cultural organization, it provided a large audience to hear Srila Prabhupada speak on Krishna Consciousness and his Western disciples chant the mahamantra for the first time.**

**There had already been two lectures expounding the Mayavada philosophy, and now it was time for Prabhupada to speak—the last scheduled speaker of the evening. The audience was eager to hear him; his accomplishments in the West had caused great curiosity, especially now that he had arrived in Bombay and his devotees were chanting daily in public. Prabhupada’s disciples, bored and exasperated by the preceding two hours of Hindi oratory, could scarcely wait any longer for Prabhupada to speak. But Prabhupada, instead of addressing the audience, turned to his disciples and said, “Begin chanting.”**

**As soon as the devotees began the kirtan, little Saraswati stoodand began to dance. Following her, the other devotees rose and began to dance. As the kirtan came alive with mridangas and kartals, the dancing and chanting of the devotees seemed to disturb some of the sadhus onstage, who rose one by one and left. The audience, however, responded enthusiastically, many of them standing and clapping. After five minutes of ecstatic kirtan, the devotees spontaneously jumped down onto the Yamuna far left Yamuna in center between mridanga players sand and headed toward the audience. Thousands in the crowd rose to their feet and began to move along with the devotees in a dance, backward and forward.**

**Indians began crying in uncontrolled happiness, overwhelmed by the genuine Krishna bhakti of these foreigners. Never before had such a thing happened. Policemen and press reporters joined in the chanting and dancing. Chowpatty Beach was in an uproar of Hare Krishna kirtan, as Prabhupada and his disciples showed the potency of Lord Chaitanya’s sankirtan movement.**

**— SRILA PRABHUPADA-LILAMRTA**

In beginning his presentation by directing his Western students to chant, Srila Prabhupada brilliantly illuminated to the thousands of attendees that the message of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu—the message of harinam sankirtan—is not limited to India, or to time and place, but rather it is universal and appealing to everyone who opens their hearts to it. He gave a short discourse, and in summation simply said:

**I do not feel that I have to say very much. You can see what is the result of this Krishna Consciousness. It is not something artificial. It is there in everyone. I have not done anything magical. But this Krishna Consciousness is present in all of us. We simply have to revive it.**

**— Yamuna’s journal**

One night after they returned from the pandal, Yamuna wrote in her notebook:

Yamuna: *October 20, 1970—Srila Prabhupada said:*

**Let them go on talking on Vedanta. We will reach Krishna by taking prasadam, having arati and dancing. Let them labor on, but this is so easy.**

**— Yamuna’s journal**

*Srila Prabhupada’s Western disciples quickly became the “talk” of Bombay, and, with the help of Kailash Seksaria, we were introduced to many of Bombay’s elite at his functions. He would arrange very grand and elegant programs in the evenings on the rooftop of his house on Marine Drive and invite prominent members of society. Srila Prabhupada would speak at these programs, and then we would have wonderful kirtans. He would simply direct us to begin kirtan by picking up a pair of kartals and playing them—ching, ching, sizzle. He would play very definitively, with straight back, eyes closed, head raised, and side-to-side movement, his garland gently swaying as he played. Then, with a sober face and half-closed eyes, he would often direct me to lead, and I would pick up the microphone and begin chanting. Srila Prabhupada had taught us a new melody for chanting the Gurvastakam, and I would generally start with this. There is an interesting instruction in his teaching of this prayer. One morning, soon after our arrival at Kailash Seksaria’s home, Srila Prabhupada called on a male devotee to chant the new melody of Gurvastakam. After two lines of the prayer, he asked him to stop and then requested another devotee to continue. The same thing happened, and he asked another devotee to chant, with the same result. Then he asked me to lead the prayer, and he did not stop me. So later, I asked him why he had done that, and he replied:*

**Learn to listen. You cannot follow nicely unless you hear nicely, and you cannot lead nicely unless you have learned to follow nicely.**

**— Yamuna’s journal**

*Of course, we did not know the guests at the rooftop programs; we had only just arrived. But I reflected much later on how much difficulty Srila Prabhupada must have previously endured to meet them and try to persuade them to support his preaching and writing programs. Now, with the help of his Western disciples, he drew their immediate interest because we were such an anomaly at that time in India. So I’ve spoken and written before about the “Krishna portal”— that unique opening where Krishna brought Srila Prabhupada to a place at exactly the right time, under the most auspicious circumstances. So India was another portal in that sense, with us arriving there with no land, no temples, and having to learn how to “speak” the language of diplomacy as representatives of Prabhupada. It was imperative that we try to learn this, and in my own case, it was a great blessing for my future spiritual life.*

*After chanting the Gurvastakam, Sri Krishna Chaitanya and Hare Krishna, we would often make a circle in front of Srila Prabhupada and begin swaying back and forth in our coordinated “Swami step.” Some of the guests would join us. Srila Prabhupada always became deeply immersed in the sound of the Holy Names, and I noticed that many of the guests were profoundly moved both by his presence and the dynamic and sincere chanting of his Western students.*

Also during this time, Srila Prabhupada’s patron, Sumati Morarji, who had provided him with free passage to the West on the \]aladuta, a ship from her Scindia Steamship Company, arranged a well-attended program to welcome him back to Bombay. This was especially significant, because she had vigorously discouraged him from traveling to the West out of fear for his age and health, and her enthusiastic welcome was a tribute and validation of his successful preaching endeavors.

**Giriraja Swami**: When Srila Prabhupada returned to Bombay from America, his first patron, Sumati Morarji, wanted to arrange a grand function to welcome him back. She staged a spectacular event on top of the Scindia office building in prestigious Ballard Estate, downtown Bombay, and she invited all the elite of Bombay. The press also came. Srila Prabhupada spoke, and the devotees performed kirtan.... Prabhupada sang three verses from the Brahma Samhita and invited the audi- ence to join in the chorus: govindam adi-purusam tarn aham bhajami. After speaking for half an hour, he accepted prasadam with Sumati Morarji and the honored guests and dignitaries.... The function was reported in the newspapers. One carried a full-page article on the back page. After describing Srila Prabhupada’s accomplishments in the West, the reporter asked Srila Prabhupada, “To what do you attribute your great success?” “It is all the mercy of my Guru Maharaja,” Srila Prabhupada replied. V

## Srila Prabhupadas Sankirtan Mission Rocks Bombay

Srila Prabhupada had long envisioned having a World Sankirtan Party, and he knew well in advance the effect his dedicated Western students would produce in India.

**Yamuna**: *The center of our activities each day was nagar (processional) sankirtan. That was our main engagement. We had a morning program, chanted our rounds, honored prasadam, and then went out on sankirtan, sometimes twice a day. The effect of the enthusiastic and powerful chanters of the sankirtan party was immediate and extraordinary. We were all like a tight family, with each person playing a specific role. Malati’s “Prabhupada’s*

*World Sankirtan” banners, along with one bearing the mahamantra, announced us to the thousands who heard us in the streets. In addition to our London group, some of the members of that first transcendental World Sankirtan Party included Dinanatha das, who had a wonderful voice and magical drumming abilities, Rsi Kumara das, Nanda Kumara das, Tamai Krishna das, Cidananda das, Giriraja das, Aravinda das, Durlaba das, Revatinandana das, Devananda Swami, Kaushalya dasi and Madri dasi. The mridangas were the heartbeat of the sankirtan and kept the rhythms going. Each of us played either other drums, kartals or tambourines, and we chanted and danced shoulder to shoulder, with so much affection and respect for each other. Each of us felt as if Srila Prabhupada was our spiritual father, and we his spiritual children.*

*I never forgot that mood during this early sankirtan leg of Srila Prabhupada’s mission in India. We chanted in the streets, and Bombay was just burning hot for us, especially those of us just coming from England, but we chanted until we almost couldn’t chant anymore, and then our host, Kailash Seksaria, would come with big urns of cold nimbu pani \[lemonade\] served in silver cups on silver platters, and we would become rejuvenated and then go back out onto the streets. And we continued this nagar sankirtan all over India for the next year and a half. Sometimes Srila Prabhupada would send some of us off to perform a different service, but our main engagement was nagar sankirtan in the lanes, streets, byways, villages and cities of India.*

**The impact of the Western devotees on Bombay was immediate and dynamic. They were noticed and appreciated by everyone from beggars in the streets to the highest rungs of the Bombay aristocracy. The Times of India succinctly wrote about their impact in an article only six days after their arrival:**

**A group of Americans, including women with babes in arms, belonging to the International Society for Krishna Consciousness (1SKCON) has been moving around Bombay during the past few days chanting Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare, to the accompaniment of cymbals, castanets and drums \[mridangas\].**

**Can the materialistic West, or at any rate, a microscopic part of it, have turned at last to embrace the spiritualism of the East? I met several of the kirtan-chanting Americans (who have come here to attend the seventh All-lndia Conference at the Bharat Sadhu Samaj which begins here today) and was at once struck by their sincerity and utter surrender to the cult they have adopted. The Vaishnavas of Mathura could not be so guileless, I thought, as this band of bhakti enthusiasts.**

**— TIMES OF INDIA, OCT. 10, I970**

**Yamuna**: *Wherever we performed sankirtan, Srila Prabhupada wanted his books displayed. And if he was there, he would inevitably speak something about his books or have a disciple speak. I can think of nowhere this did not take place. It was simply understood by all that his books were to be displayed and sold. And he would invariably give a gift copy to whoever hosted us.*

## “Every Town and Village”— The World Sankirtan Party in India

Srila Prabhupada and the devotees stayed in Bombay as guests of Kailash Seksaria for about two weeks and then moved for a few days to another residence. Srila Prabhupada was concerned about not overly imposing on the hospitality of his hosts with such a large party of students. Then Srila Prabhupada’s friend, Hari Krishna das Agarwal, arranged for him to be invited to the All India Vedanta Sammelan \[Conference\] in Amritsar, Punjab. Before coming to America, Srila Prabhupada had stayed at Mr. Agarwal’s dharmshala \[hostel\] in Bombay, called Prem Kutir. It is interesting to note that the World Sankirtan Party was so much on Srila Prabhupada’s consciousness that in 1968 he wrote to Mr. Agarwal asking him to form such a party. Srila Prabhupada promised that once the Party was formed, he would then send trained-up Western boys and girls to join it. This was astonishing, because it again reaffirmed that the formation of a World Sankirtan Party was an imperative for Srila Prabhupada from the very beginning of his preaching mission.

**Here the boys and girls, they are very serious about chanting, but they are not trained singers, or singers in the tune we chant in India. Therefore, I wish that if you organize a sankirtan party there, completely trained in spiritual ways, and the American students combine with them, I think a very nice sankirtan party can be organized to travel all over the world. I have tested it definitely that melodious vibration of sankirtan, if they are performed by serious devotees, can attract people from the very spiritual platform, and it at once makes the spiritual background very smooth, then a spiritual instruction from the Bhagavad-gita can be implemented very nicely. So my first concrete program is that if you agree to organize such a sankirtan party, a batch of American students may join, and I can combine these American and Indian devotees together under discipline.**

**— LETTER TO MR. AGARWAL, MAR. 3, 1968**

**Yamuna**: *It was arranged that some of Srila Prabhupada’s students would also go to Amritsar with him. So a party of ten—eight men and two women, Kaushalya and 1—went with Srila Prabhupada by train from Bombay to Amritsar. In the car on the drive to the railway station, our host, Kailash Seksaria, spoke volubly about the glories of the train we would ride—the Frontier Mail, now called the Golden Temple Mail. Considered the height of luxury in its day, it would be the first of many Indian trains I would take—mostly in third class, the antithesis of luxury. I wrote in my notebook in a kind of shorthand as Mr. Seksaria spoke about the virtues of the train. He said its inaugural voyage from Bombay to Amritsar was in 1928. It took 72 hours; today it will take a mere 36 hours, with 37 stops. He mentioned that the train would pass through Mathura on the way. This would be my first sight of Krishna’s holy land.*

*When our cars pulled up at the Kolaba train station, I noted Kailash Seksaria and Srila Prabhupada as they walked into the faded and soot-smudged Victorian-style building. Earlier that morning, Mr. Seksaria had given us pointers on train travel: keep together or in pairs in the stations; keep an eye on your luggage at all times, or it will likely disappear; keep documents and money on your person, hidden in a money belt; and know for certain that Westerners are automatic targets for pickpockets. This was all new to us and a bit overwhelming. Once inside the station, we were immediately surrounded by a scrimmage of wiry porters, official-looking in gray dhotis and frayed crimson jackets with numbered brass badges. In assertive, clipped Hindi, our driver took charge and negotiated a luggage deal for our whole entourage. I had no idea if you were supposed to tip the driver, but I thanked him and handed over a small photo of Sri Sri Radha-Londonisvara. He smiled broadly, touched the photo to his forehead and said, “Very good. I will keep the change.” The porters loaded mountains of luggage on their heads, and we followed them to our bogie \[train car\].*

*At first glance I saw that the Frontier Mail was definitely not the Orient Express; in fact, it probably looked much as it had on its maiden voyage in 1928—sturdy, gray and formidable. Also, we were most certainly not staying in the kind of accommodations described by our host. Guru das had the tickets for the party and brought them to the attention of a conductor. “Yes, the porters have brought you to the right bogie”—three-tiered third class. It was a rusty, red metal cage with barred windows. Along with other pushing, shoving passengers, we embarked and struggled to find the hard benches we would spend the next 36 hours on. Third class meant that as many people as could fit in the car got in the car. There was no question of a reserved seat of any kind. So everyone was accustomed to bringing their biscuit tins, and therefore making at least 80 or 90 extra seats within the car. So after the hard seats were taken, the biscuit tins were taken; then people sat on their suitcases. All in all, traveling third class on an Indian train was an unforgettable experience—unforgettable in the sense that you may have wanted to forget, but the experience was so encroaching, such an assault on the senses, that you could not.*

As Yamuna left Bombay for the first time with Srila Prabhupada for Amritsar, she realized from observing his interactions with others that she needed to develop more discernment and insight in her own interactions with India’s people during the coming months and years. She understood that in the arena of etiquette in particular, there was so much to learn. The ordinary routines of daily life in India, such as washing the hands and feet before entering a sacred space, were simply unknown to Yamuna and the others, even though Srila Prabhupada had trained them in the fundamentals of cleanliness and behavioral etiquette.

**Yamuna**: *What Srila Prabhupada did that first year was to preach himself and allow us to assist in his preaching. As far as possible, he would directly engage the people we were staying with. He was the head of our party; he set the pace, the atmosphere—everything. And usually we were at the mercy of our hosts, dependent on their ability to organize. And therefore some of our programs were well organized and some weren’t. But we were not in a position where we could just go out and organize. We didn’t have the facilities for that. So a core component of how we did arrange things was by trying to make the best of whatever situation Krishna put us in, even though we were in a completely foreign place, and then somehow reach out to others with what Srila Prabhupada had given us—the gift of Krishna Consciousness*

## First Sight of the Holy Dhama - With Srila Prabhupada on the Frontier Mail

There is a short film of an ecstatic kirtan held by the devotees at the Mathura Junction station on the way to Amritsar. Yamuna described it as like feeling “out of body.” This was her first vision of the holy dhama—on a railway platform, no less—yet she felt encompassed by the mercy of the dhama and completely ecstatic. Although the train stopped for only a few minutes, the short film is quite telling, especially in contrasting the ecstatic, bright faces of the devotees with the often expressionless and somber faces of others just going about their business. Some of them simply stared in awe—stunned by these foreigners who played mridangas and kartals and danced back and forth on the platform. They say that one picture is worth a thousand words, and in this case, the film is priceless in its portraiture of that unique moment in time.

**Yamuna:** *After the stop at Mathura Junction, we looked for any opportunity to jump out of the train and chant. Once, Srila Prabhupada called us up from our third-class “cattle car” and held his beautiful hand out towards the window as though he were offering a flower or other offering—palm up, hand extended. He said that this was near where the actual battle of Kurukshetra took place. And Srila Prabhupada said, “How can they say that Kurukshetra is not a real place? It is just here, before us.” Even though it appeared to us as mile after mile of mostly flat land, we felt privileged to have seen this sacred place, albeit whizzing by, and fell flat on the floor of the train offering obeisances. This was our general mood in those days. Each of us felt varying degrees of gratitude for being called to come to the seat of Krishna Consciousness, and each of us felt privileged. It was such an adventure, yet a humbling one at that.*

## Srila Prabhupadas Tireless Preaching in Amritsar
