**When the train arrived at Amritsar station, members of the Vedanta Sammelan committee received Prabhupada and escorted him and his disciples to a park on the outskirts of the city. They showed him the large pandal the Niketan Ashram had erected for the Vedanta Sammelan and assigned him and his disciples their quarters—three small rooms.... Available bedding was meager, and none of the devotees had brought warm clothing.**

**At four the next morning the devotees congregated in Srila Prabhupada’s room for mangal arati and kirtan before the Deities of Radha and Krishna—the same Deities who had been traveling with Prabhupada for the past one and a half years. Despite the austere conditions, the devotees felt fortunate to have such intimate contact with Prabhupada and Radha-Krishna. Prabhupada played mridanga, leading the chanting of prayers to the Spiritual Master. It was still before sunrise, and the room was chilly. As the devotees sat huddled beneath a naked bulb, Prabhupada had them read aloud from Srimad-Bhagavatam.**

**That same morning Prabhupada attended the Vedanta Sammelan. There were thousands of people in the audience, and since most of them did not understand English, Prabhupada spoke in Hindi. His presentation pleased everyone, and the committee members honored him by making him president of the Vedanta Sammelan. Although the program was scheduled only for several hours in the morning and evening, Prabhupada did not limit his preaching to these times; he preached every hour of the day. While he sat in his room, a constant stream of guests came to him, hundreds of pious Hindus seeking his blessings. Recognizing this vestige of Vedic culture, he pointed it out to his disciples. “Just see,” he said, “how they treat a saintly person.”**

**Prabhupada al so began receiving the usual flood of invitations to visit the homes of Hindu families. He accepted as many invitations as possible—more than possible, it seemed to his disciples. Prabhupada moved quickly. When the cars were ready, he would come out of his room and go, leaving behind anyone who wasn’t ready. After each engagement, he would get into his car and go directly to the next. Latecomers would sometimes find he had already left. They would then jump into bicycle rickshaw and try to catch him. A wrong direction or a missed turn might make them miss the next engagement. And when at last they would catch up, they would find Prabhupada coolly, gravely in the midst of a lecture on Bhagavad-gita, or laughing and taking prasadam with his host.**

**— SRILA PRABHUPADA-LILAMRTA**

This description clearly illustrates the energy, dynamism and charisma of Srila Prabhupada. Yamuna later elaborated on how they were virtually left “in the dust” by his intense desire to accept every preaching opportunity.

**Yamuna**: *It was unique and indescribable. Throughout our short stay in Amritsar, Srila Prabhupada exhibited superhuman energy—as though the mercy of Lord Nityananda became personified in him. Just imagine that his age was over seventy, yet he went through his own morning program, then we had a group morning program, then there was the pandal program which Prabhupada attended, and then we would attend up to five engagements a day, often lasting until midnight or later. Sometimes Srila Prabhupada did not even sleep. And we would all have to run to keep up with him. Not only was he elected president of the Sammelan, but a large segment of the city of Amritsar also honored Srila Prabhupada. He was invited to many, many places, and he accepted almost all of them. So this preaching would just go on nonstop, and the energy that he had for preaching Lord Chaitanya’s message of Krishna Consciousness was just inconceivable. I can honestly say that even at the age of 28 and at the zenith of my health, I struggled to keep up with him—not only me, but all of us, men and women.*

**Giriraja Swami**: Srila Prabhupada was very protective of the women, and he would have them ride to programs with him in his car (while the men took rickshaws). He did programs in the morning and evening—and often in between. Kaushalya told me that while driving to one engagement, he had mentioned that he needed new shoes. “Stop at the next Bata shoe store,” he had said. In the store, he told Yamuna and Kaushalya, “You choose the shoes for me,” and sat down. So they looked all around the store and found some white crisscross plastic sandals that they thought would be just right. Each of them carried one shoe up to Srila Prabhupada, and they slipped them on his feet. He smiled and asked, “Do you like them?” They responded, “Yes.” “Then we will buy them.” And so he did.

In the afternoons when there was some free time, Yamuna devi would chant in the courtyard. It was very cold in Amritsar in November, but it would be a little warmer when the sun came out in the afternoon, and she would sit cross-legged, with her back erect, and chant the Hare Krishna mahamantra japa continuously with her eyes closed—nonstop. She told me that when she chanted, her ears and mind and heart opened up to the Holy Names, and that the names would enter in this way, and she would just hear the sound. She would be fully absorbed in the sound, not even thinking that she was chanting the Holy Names or that these were names she was hearing—she was just absorbed in the sound.

On the Mahadvadasi, October 26, 1970, Srila Prabhupada gave an encouraging class after mangal arati on how one should approach God. Yamuna would faithfully take notes whenever Srila Prabhupada spoke, and on this day she wrote in her journal:

**God should not be approached for any material profit, but only to enhance our spiritual consciousness. Then as we surrender in our devotional service, He reciprocates with us ten times more than we do with Him.**

**— Yamuna’s journal**

## A Reluctant Yamuna Devi Gives Srimad-Bhagavatam Class in Amritsar

**Yamuna**: *I clearly remember the first time Srila Prabhupada asked me to give a class in India—October 24—because although I didn’t mind leading kirtans and was used to dealing with crowds in that way, I have always felt inadequate when speaking the philosophy of Krishna Consciousness and being able to support it with scripture. My ability to memorize shlokas was never strong, and I simply felt unqualified. So not only was this the first time he had asked me to lecture, but it was also in front of a gathering of lawyers, barristers and around 200 other professionals. Of course, he had not given me any warning at all. Instead of directing me to lead kirtan, he said, “And this morning my disciple, Yamuna devi, will give a lecture on Srimad-Bhagavatam." Incredulous, I looked up at him with a pleading expression which could not be misinterpreted. But he just glanced down at me and said, “Begin.”*

*I wanted to try to speak of something I had studied, so I began by misquoting the Sanskrit from one of my favorite verses: “I bum sum baro namah” \[sa vai pumsam paro dharmo\] instead of the proper pronunciation, and then continued on with the text and almost verbatim purport of Srila Prabhupada’s from the First Canto, Second Chapter, sixth shloka of Srimad-Bhagavatam, which I had previously memorized (without the Sanskrit). And when I was finished, all the barristers and professionals clapped enthusiastically, and Srila Prabhupada just beamed. He was so proud! And I hadn’t strayed from anything he said in his purport at all. So that was the beginning. And actually, although I’m embarrassed to admit it, I actually went up to him afterward and said something to the effect that I didn’t mind leading the kirtans, but please don’t ask me to give class anymore. Such boldness!*

*Srila Prabhupada’s programs invariably began with a Hare Krishna kirtan, which either he would lead or have a male member of the sankirtan party lead. Then he would give a discourse, and then he would usually ask me to lead the second kirtan. Sometimes it would be Govinda jaya jaya and sometimes Hare Krishna. He structured the programs in this way from the beginning in India. From the time of Amritsar on, Srila Prabhupada also began calling on his female students as well as the male students to give discourses. My feeling was that he was very proud of his Western disciples and wanted to show others how we were taking to the process of Krishna Consciousness and to the chanting of the Holy Names. Whenever a disciple spoke or led kirtan, Srila Prabhupada would close his eyes and become immersed in it, as though it was the greatest thing. In this way, he was teaching us, nurturing us, encouraging us, and training us how to spread Krishna Consciousness in India.*

The Vedanta Sammelan was essentially an impersonalist gathering, and Srila Prabhupada was under no illusion that the organizers wanted to showcase his Western followers to further encourage attendance.

**Giriraja Swami**: One day a devotee said to Srila Prabhupada that he noticed that there were different signs posted around the ashram. One of the signs said, “Tat tvam asi.’’ So the devotee said, “What is this?” So Srila Prabhupada explained that actually these people here are impersonalists— that their idea of Vedanta is impersonal. I think even on the sign itself there was a translation—“You are it,” or “You are God,” or something. So Srila Prabhupada said, “Actually they know that I disagree with them, but still they have invited me because they want to see the white elephants \[his disciples\] dance.”

The attendees were especially captivated by Yamuna who, with her charming demeanor, open and heartfelt presentation of Krishna Consciousness and wonderful chanting, was always able to stimulate the bhakti in the hearts of people wherever they held gatherings.

**Giriraja Swami**: Yamuna had become quite famous and popular because she led wonderful kirtan, she could speak, she could play mridanga— she could do so many things. So every morning and every afternoon practically hundreds of people used to come to the back of the ashram premises where we had our rooms, and they would come asking for Yamuna, and they would come and look in all the windows. Finally Yamuna got very agitated. She was starting to feel like an animal on exhibit in the zoo. And then they would always ask the questions, “What is your name? Where are you coming from?” She would complain that “Why don’t they ask questions about Krishna?”

## The Golden Temple — “This is How to Distribute Prasadam”

One day Srila Prabhupada went with his disciples to the Harmandir, the Golden Temple of the Sikhs. This temple is the main gurdwara, or place of worship, for all Sikhs in the world, and Srila Prabhupada was very impressed with their organizational structure. Their guide informed them that there were four entrances to the temple, to show that any person of any class is allowed entrance. He said that the Sikhs particularly pride themselves on langar, a free kitchen where a sanctified meal is prepared daily and offered at the temple. This meal is served to the tens of thousands of pilgrims who visit daily. All cooking of food and maintenance is carried out by worshipers who volunteer their services, and all costs are provided by donations. This particularly interested Prabhupada, and he carefully observed their massive cooking operation. He watched as one group rolled chapatis, then deftly flipped them through the air onto a giant tawa, while others turned the chapatis with long wooden paddles, then held them briefly over hot coals and put them into stacks. Srila Prabhupada, very impressed, said, “This is how to distribute prasadam”

**Yamuna**: *There’s an interesting extension to the story of the chapatis in Amritsar. In 1976, Dinatarini and I visited Srila Prabhupada in Los Angeles, and one day he called me to his rooms and said, “Yamuna, do you remember when we went to Amritsar and saw the giant tawa and all the chapatis being made and served?” I replied, “Yes, Srila Prabhupada, I remember.” He then said, “Can you go down to the kitchen here and show them how to do it?” I coughed to hide my shock and said, “But Prabhupada, that tawa was twenty feet in diameter! How can I teach them to make them on our stoves?” He then dismissively said, “No, they cannot make them.” This showed how impressed he remained with the procedures in Amritsar.*

*Much of what we learned from Srila Prabhupada was through observing his behavior. We can hear what a perfect devotee is—what the twenty-six qualifications of a devotee are. But to live with Srila Prabhupada and watch him day in and day out was an eye-opening experience for all of us, because how Prabhupada saw India and how he allowed us to see India was like being in a living academy of bhakti-yoga. The example of the chapati-making in the Golden Temple in Amritsar demonstrated this. Not only in Los Angeles, but on at least two other occasions, Srila Prabhupada brought this up to me by again reiterating how expertly it was done. Srila Prabhupada taught us to observe things that were done well and learn from them. He expected us to be mindful whenever there was great expertise shown in an activity related to devotional service. Wherever I traveled with Srila Prabhupada, when he saw something made well or done well, he would direct me, “Now you go learn how to do it.” And, of course, I had no idea how to do whatever “it” was—whether in the realm of cooking, managerial or any number of things. Still, I would try because for me, as well for each of us, to see him pleased when we did something well was a highlight of our lives.*

## Visit to Maharaja Baladeva Indra Singh

One afternoon, Srila Prabhupada and his disciples were invited to a dinner with Maharaja Baladeva Indra Singh, scion of one of the most ancient ksatriya ruling families of the Punjab. Yamuna, always observant of quality in art and architecture, was very impressed with both his family and his home.

**Yamuna**: *We traveled by cars and stopped in front of a beautiful singlestory Lutyens building. Composed of thick walls, lead-framed windows, and rooms with fourteen-foot-high ceilings, it was beautifully detailed in every way. Hanging high on the walls in ornate frames were five- to eightfoot paintings of ancestral family members. Corpulent warriors in ancient armor sat on top of caparisoned horses, or bejeweled men stared with proud visages in kingly costumes and magnificent crowns—all wearing their ceremonial swords encrusted with gems, along with silk sashes, feathers and peacock fans.*

*Maharaja Singh himself was a compact man of small stature, but he carried himself confidently. His skin was smooth, his eyes dark and recessed, his face bearded and mustached, and his head elegantly turbaned. We were invited to eat in their large dining room—no pictures here,—just animal heads on the walls: wildebeests, lions, tigers, antelope, deer and other unidentifiable heads. Srila Prabhupada immediately tried to diffuse our discomfort by saying that ksatriyas must hunt animals to practice how to kill in battle. It is their dharma to fight, and this is described in the Vedas. Srila Prabhupada then began eating, and I relaxed, not daring to look upward during the meal.*

Srila Prabhupada and the devotees found Maharaja Singh to be a memorable host who honestly admitted that he was sceptical of them at first. At one point he told Prabhupada that he was worried because an astrologer had previously related to him that he had fought in the Battle of Kurukshetra, but on the side of the Kurus. Srila Prabhupada immediately defeated that view by stating that all of the fighters in the battle received liberation, and he would not be here now had he fought then. This greatly relieved the Maharaja.

## Rama Tirtha and Yamuna’s Reflections on Prabhupada in Amritsar

**Yamuna**: *On October 24, 1970, the devotees and Srila Prabhupada were taken by our host to Rama Tirtha near Amritsar. The terrain was dry and rocky—something like Vrindavan—and because it was in the fall, there wasn’t much vegetation. Neem trees were dotted across the land. As we were standing around this beautiful holy place, terraced down on four sides with stairs that went down to the bathing ghat, Srila Prabhupada spoke:*

**This is the place of residence of Valmiki, called Valmiki ashram. Sita was kidnapped by Ravana.... Even though Sita is Laksmi devi, the supreme pleasure potency of Lord Ramachandra, when one washerman criticized Lord Ramachandra for living with Sita devi after she had been kidnapped, since He was living as the ideal king, He left the company of Sita devi. He asked Laksmana to accompany Sita devi to Valmiki’s ashram, and there she raised her sons Lava and Kush under the guidance and protection of Valmiki.**

**— Yamuna’s journal**

There is one revealing history in the Caitanya-caritamrta where a South Indian brahmana cried constantly because he could not understand how Lord Rama could seemingly cast off Sita devi, the Goddess of Fortune. But Lord Chaitanya explained the recondite meaning of the history which illuminated both the glories of Sita devi and the mercy of Lord Rama. It was also at this ashram that Valmiki Muni wrote the Ramayana.

When Yamuna and I first moved to Oregon in 1975, Srila Prabhupada wrote to us referencing Sita devi’s life at the ashram of Valmiki Muni. He told us that Sita devi should be our exemplar on how to live as renounced women.

**Sita devi, Mother Laksmi, wife of Lord Ramachandra, went to live with Valmiki Muni in a cottage. Although she was a king’s daughter and a king’s wife, she preferred to live very humbly in the cottage of Valmiki Muni with two sons in the absence of Ramachandra. That should be the ideal example.**

**— LETTER TO YAMUNA AND DINATAR1N 1, JAN. 13, 1976**

The Amritsar visit lasted only about ten days, and then Srila Prabhupada and the devotees again boarded a train bound for Bombay, via Delhi. This time, Guru das rode in first class with Srila Prabhupada. Yamuna wrote a short prayer reflecting on the experience with Srila Prabhupada in Amritsar:

**The energy you displayed, the enthusiasm to preach you exhibited, the love and compassion to all fallen souls you freely gave—I pray to keep all of what I witnessed close to my heart so that one day they may well up in me like the eternal spring of your love for Guru and Krishna.**

**— Yamuna’s journal**

## The Punjab Mail to Delhi

The Punjab Mail, the oldest broad-gauge train in India, holds the distinction of being in service for over a century. In the days of the English occupation, it was the preferred method of travel for the English sahibs who Punjab Mail completes Century of runs came by sea from Southampton to Bombay, and then traveled in incomparable luxury to Delhi, the Punjab or Peshawar. After Indian Independence, train service became more utilitarian, and during the early 70’s, first class meant that although you had more room and cushioned seats, you were closest to the engine and therefore exposed to even more choking soot than those sitting on hard benches and biscuit tins in third class.

## My Guru Has Asked for Rice — “No” Is Not an Option

Srila Prabhupada and the small group of devotees left Amritsar for Bombay, via Delhi, on October 27,1970. Guru das rode in First Class with Srila Prabhupada, and Yamuna shared an unforgettable experience with Kaushalya in Srila Prabhupada’s service on the day-long trip to Delhi.

**Yamuna**: *The Punjab Mail was an old train by this time, and the First Class compartments were closest to the engine. Srila Prabhupada’s compartment had no air conditioning, of course, and the heat was unbearable—just unimaginably hot. And the closer you were to the front of the train, the more soot you were enshrouded in from the coal-burning engine. So everyone was covered from head to toe with this black soot, even Srila Prabhupada.*

*Before we left Amritsar, some Indian ladies had prepared lunch for Srila Prabhupada—parathas, a dry sabji, sweets, kachoris and puris. At one point in the journey I decided to see if there was anything he wanted, because sometimes when the train stopped, he would request something from the men selling their wares at the train stations. So Kaushalya and I made our way to Prabhupada’s First Class compartment, and there we found him laying back just like a monarch—like a king, with one knee up, several pillows behind him, and a beautiful transcendental smile on his face. We offered our obeisances and asked if we could bring anything. Srila Prabhupada looked up with an almost childlike smile on his face and said, “Is there anything hot to eat?” “Would you like more of your lunch?” I answered. He replied, “No. Not that. I would like some hot rice.”*

*I didn’t know how to speak Hindi or anything close to it, but Srila Prabhupada had asked for rice, and it was our mood in those days to move heaven and earth in order to try to please him. It is difficult to express in words, but just to see a glance of approval from him meant so much to each of us. So I took on the responsibility that somehow or other I would get him hot rice.*

*Having no idea how I was going to bring this hot rice to Srila Prabhupada, Kaushalya and I made our way to the kitchen, only to find two small, filthy men standing over a gigantic coal stove and smoking bidis. Not only did they have soot and cooking oil smudged all over them, but also wore black, turmeric-stained shorts. With my lack of language skills, I substituted gestures to make the point that my Guru Maharaja wanted some “garan-chavo,” my mispronunciation of hot rice. They immediately laughed at my feeble attempt at Hindi, and we quickly realized that we had better find a conductor who spoke English. Finally we found the restaurant manager, repeated our request, and he simply said, “No.” I calmly replied, “I’m sorry, but this is for my Guru Maharaja. There is no question of choice. I have told him I would do this, so I have to honor my word.” Again he simply said, “No. It is not possible.” So then we went to find the conductor and again explained the situation. This time I added that if I was unable to fulfill this simple request of my Guru Maharaja, I might as well jump off the train. That got his attention, and I am sure he thought he’d better find someplace for these crazy ladies to make some hot rice, or she just might do it.*

*So the conductor took me seriously and brought us back to the kitchen. So here we were in this train kitchen in front of a massive coal stove, amid all these ugly aluminum pots interspersed with various kinds of fish hanging from the kitchen roof. I had already seen in India how some people cleaned their pots by rubbing them with coal; so we cleaned out one of the pots as best we could, boiled the water, made the rice and then added ghee \[clarified butter\] at the end. We offered a huge platter of very hot rice, with ghee, fresh lemon, salt and pepper, and carried it all the way through the train to Srila Prabhupada’s compartment. I knocked on the door, and he said “Yesss” in that way he had of making it sound like a question, or crescendo. So we came in, set down the hot platter, and said, “Here’s your rice, Srila Prabhupada.” And his eyes lit up just like big saucers, followed by a huge grin from ear to ear, and he said, “Oh, my goddesses of fortune have come, and they have brought my rice. Thank you. Thank you very much.” And Srila Prabhupada ate so much of the rice on that huge platter. “This is just what I wanted,” he said. Along with the rice, he ate a small amount of kachoris, puris and pickle. And he was very pleased. For us, this was like climbing Mount Meru. We could not have felt happier—that Srila Prabhupada had given us an impossible task, and somehow we had accomplished it—and this gave him great pleasure, which in turn gave us great pleasure. It was simply a sublime experience.*

*Later, I reflected that perhaps Srila Prabhupada did not even want the rice, but rather wanted to test our determination to serve. By his mercy he allowed women close proximity to him on the World Sankirtan Party in those days. There was little separation. In our Vaishnava history this was revolutionary, and the effect it had in India was profound. In fact, it shocked India. I felt at that time that whether male or female, we never took for granted what fortune we had been given in the form of Srila Prabhupada’s personal association. In looking back on the experience, I felt a combination of deep gratitude and a determination to somehow make myself more worthy of the personal association he gave me.*

## An Unexpected Detour in Delhi

When speaking about how a disciple should always be ready to serve the Spiritual Master with mind, words and actions Yamuna often alluded to the unexpected detour in Delhi in late October with Guru das and three brahmacharis. As far as they knew, they were on their way back to Bombay with Srila Prabhupada for the next leg of the World Sankirtan Party tour. However, a surprising instruction from Srila Prabhupada given with little notice changed all that. Giriraja Swami gave his account of the ensuing events:

**Giriraja Swami**: After Amritsar, Srila Prabhupada and his party traveled by train back to Bombay. On the way, the train stopped at the New Delhi station, and a gentleman, a lawyer named D. D. Gupta, who had been corresponding with Prabhupada and had been informed of his stopover, came to meet him. He requested Srila Prabhupada to leave some disciples in Delhi to start the activities there. Prabhupada turned to Guru das, who was riding in the same compartment, and said, “This man is inviting us. Get down and see what you can do.” Guru das asked for some devotees, and then he and Srila Prabhupada agreed on a team: Yamuna devi, Gopala, Bhakta Bruce (now Bhanu Swami) and me. Mr. Gupta arranged for us to stay in two rooms in Old Delhi, near Delhi Gate. The rooms were very basic—just plain concrete with whitewash on the walls—and they abutted the courtyard at the center of the building. We would have to walk around the courtyard to use the simple latrine (though, in urgent cases, we would often have to run!). Mr. Gupta, it turned out, was a peculiar man. He was an advocate, but not a very big one. And he was miserly. He would keep his used, dead batteries in a drawer, in the hope that they would come back to life. Carefully, he would take them out, show them to us, and ask if we could revive, or “recharge,” them. The whole situation was very austere, but it was wonderful being with Guru das and Yamuna. We were like a family, with Guru das and Yamuna like our older brother and sister, taking care of us in the absence of our father, Srila Prabhupada.

For Yamuna, being the only woman in the party had its own unique difficulties as far as living conditions and hygiene were concerned. Ultimately, she again saw it all as a test—a challenge as to her commitment and perseverance.

**Yamuna**: *Srila Prabhupada wanted us to start something in the major cities of India, especially through making Life Members and performing harinam sankirtan. So when we arrived at New Delhi station, a Mr. Gupta, who had corresponded with Srila Prabhupada, came onto the train to greet him. Waving a piece of paper in front of Srila Prabhupada, he said that quarters had been found for Srila Prabhupada and his disciples at the Delhi Dharmshala. We had just been passing through Delhi, and with no prior notice, Srila Prabhupada told Guru das and me to get down in Delhi and see what we could do in terms of preaching and Life Membership. He asked Guru das to pick three brahmacharis, so there were five of us altogether.*

*It was such an adventure for us. Whatever Srila Prabhupada said to do, we did, and to me it really was no different than going on to Bombay. When you were with Srila Prabhupada, it was all such a new and exciting experience, and the core of it was chanting. So whether we were at a big program with tens of thousands of people, or whether we were on a street corner with only five people—whether we were at a home, or in a palace or in a river bed—what we were there for was chanting, for bringing harinam sankirtan. So being left in Delhi was really just another facet of that. We were going to do the same thing we did with Prabhupada, only he was now sending us off on our own. Ultimately we knew that Prabhupada was going to send each of us out over the next two years to preach in this way, so we accepted Srila Prabhupada’s surprise instruction readily.*

*At the time it didn’t seem like such a massive challenge; however, it turned out to be a bigger test than we all anticipated for several reasons. First, in those days there was no question of a bank account. None of us had any money of our own, and we wouldn’t even think of spending a paisa to buy contaminated water in dirty glasses from the vendors. From the time of our arrival in India, all of our needs had been beautifully taken care of by our hosts, but this was the first time we were completely on our own and fully dependent on the mercy of Krishna.*

*Mr. Gupta, who had promised all facilities for us in Delhi, took the five of us in a taxi to Old Delhi. This area, next to Delhi Gate, was the beginning of a predominantly Muslim area of Delhi. Mr. Gupta’s promised dharmshala was just at Delhi Gate. The final lane had to be traversed on foot, so we passed what seemed to me a sea of Muslim ladies in their burqas. And then to get to the front door of his residence, we had to climb a kind of ladder from the main street up to the top veranda. It was the most unusual entrance I had ever seen. When we got to the veranda, there was a little concrete room with bars on it—bars on the windows and bars for doors. So Mr. Gupta brought us in and sat us down. So far he had not spoken very much, but then, with great care, he pulled out a big ring of keys hooked onto his dhoti. He picked a little key from the ring, pulled out a wooden box, and opened it to reveal that it was filled with used batteries. Then, with all seriousness, he looked at us and said, “Can you make these batteries work again for me?” and all of us were just kind of frozen at this point, thinking, “We are really in trouble now. What are we going to do? This is our host?” And that was his opening salvo as to how he would assist us in opening a temple in Delhi. So we tactfully explained to him that the batteries had lost their life, and they now had to be discarded. Somehow he thought that because we were from America, we could magically recharge his batteries.*

*Then Mr. Gupta showed us the dharmshala he had arranged for us to stay in. Suffice it to say that on an accommodation level, it equaled the battery experience. It was on a rooftop near Delhi Gate, again with two concrete rooms and bars for windows. There was no toilet, no running water, and no beds. I immediately noticed that we were not alone on the veranda and pointed to what looked like a lumbering white possum. I asked what it was. Mr. Gupta casually answered, “Oh, that is just a white rat. Never mind.” And this rat was enormous, with pink eyes. I had never seen anything like it. So everyone was undoubtedly disquieted and thinking, “We have to sleep on the floor with these rats?” And I believe it was Giriraja das who kindly proposed that we should have at least one bed so the lady of the group didn’t have to sleep on the floor. So Mr. Gupta got one charpoy for me. We all had sleeping bags, and I slept on the charpoy. But all night long the brahmacharis in their little room had to tolerate having these enormous rats meandering over their bodies.*

*Not only was the facility austere, but we had no money and no connections in New Delhi. This made our attempts to establish Life Membership difficult without Srila Prabhupada’s charismatic presence. He had given us the instruction to make Life Members, and he had even given us a quota—I believe one a day—which we felt to be an impossibility at the time. He also sent by letter some names to contact first, and this was really the motivation we needed to begin Life Membership in Delhi.*

## Making New Friends and Life Members

Srila Prabhupada had previously written that he would like the Bombay devotees to make a quota of three Life Memberships a day, Calcutta would make two Life Memberships a day and Delhi would make one. As the devotees in Delhi had not made any as yet, they were feeling despondent. Then Srila Prabhupada wrote requesting them to go see Mr. Jaya Dayal Dalmia, and something very encouraging happened.

**You should certainly see J. Dalmia of Scindia House, New Delhi. He will become a Life Member and he can suggest others who may also become Life Members. He is a relative and very close to Ram Das Dandharia. Also you can see his big brother Ram Krishna Dalmia and make him a Life Member. His daughter came to London, Ascot, to see me. If there is any difficulty in staying where you are, you can ask \]. Dalmia to provide accommodation in Birla’s dharmshala. That dharmshala is a very good place with lecture hall. You can speak in the lecture hall in English, and you can advertise for members, and they will appreciate it very much.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, NOV. 7, I970**

**Giriraja Swami**: \[Guru das and I\] were chanting very intently in the auto rickshaw. And when we met him, in a very grave and cooperative spirit, \[we\] both did our best to present Krishna Consciousness to Mr. Dalmia, and he immediately agreed to become a Life Member and pay the money. And not only that, but he had a friend \[Dr. Lokesh Chandra\] who had been visiting him at his office, and he immediately became a member. \[Dr. Chandra\] was going to visit the mayor. So Mr. Dalmia said to \[him\], “Why don’t you take them with you to meet the mayor?” So he took us, and we met the mayor, and he was very pleased to meet us. Then at the mayor’s house, I think Dr. Chandra met another friend of his who also agreed to become a Life Member. So in one day we were able to make three Life Members, and we felt that our stay had a little credit, because just after that we were to meet Srila Prabhupada in Indore, and we wanted to have something to report after so many weeks in Delhi

**Yamuna**: *As Srila Prabhupada had assured us, Mr. J. Dalmia became our first Life Member in Delhi, and he kindly introduced us to other important people, among them an honorary Member of Parliament who would become a helpful friend to us in the coming months and years, Dr. Lokesh Chandra.*

## A Cordial First Meeting with Prime Minister Indira Gandhi

**Yamuna**: *Unfortunately, the austerity of our living conditions made all of us extremely ill, as there was only contaminated water and no facilities with which to stay clean. The toilet facilities were nonexistent, and everyone had dysentery, fevers and other illnesses. The challenges we had to surmount were herculean. Yet, even with the sickness, we went out each day onto the street corners to perform harinam sankirtan. Even by India standards, it was unbearably hot, crowded and unclean. In those days people would not give rupee donations, but rather paisa donations. Sometimes we’d collect only enough for one meal of prasadam daily. And, of course, when we were invited to a home, they would always provide nice meals, and that would enliven us immensely—just to get a clean and full meal.*

When the Delhi devotees reported to Srila Prabhupada on their almost daily street harinam sankirtan program, he redirected their efforts to focus on making Life Members and trying to cultivate prominent citizens and government leaders. In fact, he wanted them to go to the very top—Prime Minister Indira Gandhi herself. On November 7, Srila Prabhupada wrote to Guru das:

**Instead of engaging in sankirtan, if you, husband and wife, try to see so many government members and ministers and other important men, that will be nice. You may try and see Indira Gandhi. And perhaps you can meet with this President Giri shown in the enclosed news clipping. I think because your pictures are shown together with his, he will meet you.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, NOV. 7, 1970**

Because Dr. Chandra was present during the meeting of Guru das and Giri-raja das with Mr. J. Dalmia, and because of his suggestion that Dr. Chandra take them to his meeting with the mayor of Delhi, doors began to open very quickly for the devotees in Delhi. Dr. Chandra, a pious and prominent man, was very enthusiastic to help. Srila Prabhupada was becoming very concerned about propaganda being circulated that the Western ISKCON devotees were really CIA members in disguise sent by the U.S. Government to spy, and he wanted the propaganda stopped. So his strategy was that if the devotees could somehow have a picture taken with Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, it would give more credibility to our movement and quash the rumors. Dr. Chandra spoke to many prominent people about the sincerity and bona fide credentials of the Hare Krishna Movement, and somehow through him an appointment was made with the Prime Minister.

**Yamuna**: *It was Dr. Chandra who first went to the Prime Minister, Indira Gandhi, and asked if she would meet with some of Srila Prabhupada’s disciples. So the first meeting was arranged with Guru das, Bhanu das, Giriraja das, Gopal das and me. We met her at her home after breakfast and brought her little gifts, and we ended up having a longer meeting with her than expected. She was quite fascinated, and asked rather provocative questions about why we were embracing Krishna Consciousness. She was very fascinated that Westerners were trying to go deeply into the practice of Vaishnavism, not just externally, but internally. So she asked philosophical questions—not just superficial ones like “What are you doing?” or “What is your program?”—but she seemed interested in our spiritual endeavors, and especially in me, because I was a woman and she was a woman, and so she connected with me in some way. So we had a very nice, long discussion with her and then met her again on two other occasions to invite her to programs. Ultimately she didn’t accept the invitations, but she assisted us behind the scenes by speaking up on our behalf when people wanted to hamper our programs due to political agitation. So in the end she was very positive towards our movement and very helpful in significant ways. And I remember feeling at the time that she was going far beyond the call of an obligatory audience with people—she was actually interested.*

Feeling the interview nearing its end, the devotees worried about how to ask for a picture, as this was what Srila Prabhupada had asked of them, but Mrs. Gandhi suggested it herself. That now well known picture not only pleased Srila Prabhupada, but boosted their preaching efforts all over India.

Later in Indore, during a visit with Maharaja Tukoji Rao Holkar and Maharani Sarmistha Bhai Holkar at the Lal Bhag Palace, Srila Prabhupada showed them the picture of the Delhi devotees with Mrs. Gandhi, and they asked Yamuna how the meeting with her went. Yamuna replied:

**Yamuna**: *She took a courteous interest. As I say, there was no doubt that at the time she saw us she was pressed with other matters. A very personal friend of hers who Guru das is now staying with told us that she was very impressed and her personal secretary was very impressed, and that she said—we have it on tape—that she would like to see us again. She added that she was sorry that she hadn’t realized that we had been waiting for so long. Otherwise we could have come earlier, and she would have spent more time with us. In that way, it was arranged that we would again meet her sometime in the near future.*

*Another very helpful connection were the Joshi’s, a lovely family who assisted Srila Prabhupada when he came to Delhi on his frequent trips from Vrindavan to oversee the publishing of his original Srimad-Bhagavatams and Back to Godhead magazines. One of the most memorable for me was Mrs. Joshi, a devotee with connections to Vrindavan’s famous Sri Radha-Raman Temple. This kind and intelligent woman not only became a good friend and nursed me back to health after my first serious bout with dysentery, but more importantly, she was a veritable treasure trove of stories about Srila Prabhupada during his many visits to her home. Mrs. Joshi was also an inspiring example of spiritual standards in the kitchen. She had deep devotion to Lord Krishna, and her intuition, skill and experience merged with the subtle compositions of her dishes. In Mrs. Joshi’s capable hands, I learned some of the preparation techniques and dishes that Srila Prabhupada would later commend as “superexcellent.”*

## Problems at Bury Place — "Be Prepared to Return to London”

Meanwhile, as Yamuna had feared, there were already cracks appearing in the management of the all-important Bury Place temple. Srila Prabhupada’s concern is clearly visible in the letter written on November 7, a mere ten days after the devotees left Amritsar.

**Also I’ve received some other letters that things in London are not as they should be. It seems that Murari has now become president of London temple. This is all right for a while, but you will have to go back to the London temple. London temple is one of the most important centers in our society and it should not suffer for lack of good management. Under you and your wife’s good care, things have gone very nicely there. So I want you and Yamuna to both be prepared to go back to London in the near future. You have come all the way to India, so for the time being you should remain here and see what can be done in Delhi.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, NOV. 7, I970**

This letter, requesting Guru das and Yamuna to “be prepared to go back to London in the near future” again illustrated to Yamuna that a sincere disciple must always carry the mentality of relinquishing one’s own desires for service in order to fulfill the desires of the Spiritual Master—in other words, the service attitude must be unconditional, as difficult a concept to understand and apply then as it is today.

**P.S. My dear Yamuna, please accept my blessings. Practically you are the leader of the party. Please let me know how things are going. Hope you are all well. ACB**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, NOV. 7, I970**

This poignant little postscript to Yamuna at the end of the November 7 letter saying, “Practically you are the leader of the party” was extremely important to Yamuna, not for the words themselves, but because they reminded her that Srila Prabhupada was thinking of her, was aware of the unique challenges she faced, and was acknowledging her sacrifices and service to him. This was more meaningful to Yamuna than volumes of accolades. I personally witnessed Srila Prabhupada express this same sentiment towards Yamuna in India and America at other times.

**Yamuna**: *In spite of the illness, uncleanliness and a host of other challenges, I was actually enthused on one level because I got my first taste of what Srila Prabhupada had to confront when he came from Vrindavan to Delhi for his books—he was just fully dependent on Krishna for even the most basic means of survival. We were also in that position, even though we came from the West. So whenever something came to us, we were just incredibly aware that it was Krishna’s gift because we were trying to do this little service for Srila Prabhupada. We would all get together and have philosophical discussions to try and understand, to put into perspective what we were to do and how we were to do it in Krishna Consciousness and for Srila Prabhupada. Despite the enormous challenges, we all were imbued with the consciousness that we were like marionettes, and Srila Prabhupada was pulling the strings. For me, that core concept or understanding in bhakti—that service to the Guru and Krishna is not only pleasing, but enhances one’s identity instead of diminishing it—was gradually becoming more and more clear as the months and years went by. How could we be in such unappealing conditions and yet feel growth from them? This was the Krishna Magic at work in Delhi. Knowing how important the Life Membership program was to Srila Prabhupada gave us constant motivation in our service. We ended up staying in Delhi this first time for just over a month, and then Srila Prabhupada called us to Indore for the Gita Jayanti celebrations.*

Yamuna would later cite this inaugural Delhi experience with those young and committed devotees as foundational to her understanding of how one becomes dependent on Krishna and the Spiritual Master. She felt that the sanga of sharing their experiences and philosophical understanding, however rudimentary, was central to their actually achieving a positive and encouraging devotional outcome despite the enormous challenges. They saw it as their training ground, and were ready to take what they had learned to the next outpost.

## The Key to the Spiritual Universe — Yamuna Devi in Vrindavan Dhama

Not long into their stay in Delhi, Srila Prabhupada sent them another missive, this time a package containing a large iron key. Yamuna used to well up with tears when describing this experience. It is hard to imagine that in the midst of all the austerities, sickness and penury they had been enduring, this key represented the unlocking of something wonderful—something long desired by Yamuna—her first visit to the holy land of Vrindavan and entrance into what Srila Prabhupada described as the “hub of the spiritual universe,” Sri Radha-Damodara Mandir and his rooms there. For the five Delhi devotees, it was quite literally the key to unlocking the spiritual world. Fortunately, Yamuna’s journal recording her incisive and deeply penetrating account of the two-day journey was carefully kept by her over the years:

**Yamuna’s Journal**: *November 1970 —The large iron key, sent by registered post, fell heavily onto the sandstone roof of the Delhi dharmshala. Ten hands darted to retrieve it. We passed it around respectfully, knowing that it was our passport into Vrindavan, Lord Krishna’s eternal abode, whose counterpart in this world lay only ninety miles to our south. Srila Prabhupada’s handwritten note that came with it told our small group to travel there and clean his quarters in the Radha-Damodara Temple compound. The rooms had been vacant for over two years. He described them as two rooms—a kitchen and a bedroom-study separated by a veranda—and referred to these rooms as his eternal quarters in Vrindavan, where he had resided prior to coming to the West to introduce Krishna Consciousness. With great eagerness we made arrangements for our first visit to Vrindavan.*

*The next day we followed our morning program: rise at 3:30 am, chant to Prabhupada; 4:00 am—heat water; 4:30 am—bathe, cook for morning train to Mathura; 5:30 am—tilak, chant Gurvastakam, Sri Krishna Chaitanya and mahamantra-, 6:00 am—offer bhoga and puja—Vande ham; 6:20 am—Gayatri mantra; 7:00 am—catch Agra Special to Mathura Junction; chant 16 rounds japa; 9:00 am—arrive at Mathura; 9:15 am—take tonga through lands touched by the lotus feet of Krishna and His associates; 9:50 am—enter Vrindavan—fall on sacred ground and offer obeisances; 11:00 am—visit Mandir Shyama ashram and respect prasadam-, 12:00 pm— chant; 2:30 pm—walk down cobbled streets in Raman Reti sheathed in shimmering white sands with silver slate where Krishna and Balarama play. There are peacocks and tamal trees; there are pastures of cows. The ground is fertile and green, and there is a haze over the sugar fields. Swans, herons, peacocks, cows, bulls and calves are all going to Vrindavan. The ground has changed hue. Everywhere there are temples and sugarcane fields. Go means land; go means senses; and go means cows. All of the inhabitants of Vrindavan sing of Radha and Krishna’s glories; the constant sounds of “Jaya Radhe” and Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare are going on twenty-four hours a day.*

*4:00 pm—We reach the holy temple of Radha-Damodara. This was where Srila Prabhupada compiled the first three volumes of Srimad-Bhagavatam, and it is the temple housing the Deities of Jiva Goswami (Sri Radha-Damodara), Krishnadas Kaviraja and Bugarbha Goswami. It also houses the glorious Govardhan shila that Krishna gave to Sanatana Goswami and which bears His footprint, a print of a calf hoof, and His staff. The transcendental grounds also house the samadhi and bhajan kutir of Rupa Goswami, the samadhis of Jiva Goswami and Krishnadas Kaviraja Goswami, Bugarbha Goswami and many pushpa samadhis of great Vaishnavas of earlier times. We entered the temple gate into another dimension—one where we could feel the bliss and mercy of our entire lineage of Vaishnava Acharyas, beginning with Srila Prabhupada, our beloved Guru Maharaja. How had we been able to enter the realm of the Goswamis who, in the perfectional stage of bhakti-yoga, had mercifully spread love of Godhead through their writings and by their living example? I instinctively knew that I was here because of their kindness and because of Srila Prabhupada’s kindness. It was as simple as that.*

*In the samadhi of Krishnadas Kaviraja are his old clothes, bed and beads, and a red-saffron scarf. In the bhajan kutir of Rupa Goswami are his immense japa beads and his neck beads. The Deities are all dressed in white. The room was very dark and the Deities had just awakened from Their afternoon naps. Beholding the exquisite forms of these Deities causes me to literally collapse onto the marbled floor offering my humble obeisances. How can these places exist to worldly men? It is impossible, but in my case there was some terrible error, and I was allowed to enter. I collapsed in sobbing appreciation that in their abundant mercy the Goswamis and Srila Prabhupada had allowed my sinful eyes to behold Their Lordships.*

*We took out the enormous key and opened Srila Prabhupada’s kitchen door. The wooden door swung open slowly, its iron hinges groaning from disuse and its weight. Shafts of sunlight shone through carved window shutters and fell onto shades of silvery gray. The scene was like a still life from a previous century. Every surface was coated with at least two inches of powdery Vrindavan sand that obliterated corners and angles and made all forms look ethereal. The niches all had little items in them, and there was a round wooden chair on which Srila Prabhupada would honor prasadam while looking out over Rupa Goswami’s samadhi and bhajan kutir. Krishna and his Guru Maharaja had situated him in the most auspicious place on the planet in preparation for writing his books and preaching in the West. It was just so evident to see.*

*The equipment was sparse—spoons, metal plates, two clay jugs for water, an iron griddle for chapatis, a bowl-shaped karai frying pan, and a Bengali knife—the kind that’s held between one’s feet for cutting vegetables. A pair of reading glasses and a paper notebook rested in a niche in the wall.*

*So if you could close your eyes and imagine—it was about roo degrees Fahrenheit. And, of course, there was no electricity. You open the door to find a steamer trunk in the corner, and there is a round wooden platform with a round back. And all the surfaces are covered with Vrindavan sand. When the windy season comes to Vrindavan, it stirs up the sand, which then enters any opening. The shutter that overlooked the samadhi was split, so there was even more dust in there. It reminded me of what I thought of as a moonscape. It was very surreal-looking. And Vrindavan sand is flaky and has little flecks of mica and other glistening things in it. But what was in this room was the very, very, fine dusty sand of Seva Kunj. In fact, except for the samadhis of Jiva Goswami and Krishnadas Kaviraja Goswami, the entire compound of Radha-Damodara was covered in this fine sand.*

*So our first job was to clean and remove the dust. We went to the market and got some metal buckets. Wrapping our cloth around our heads so that just our eyes were showing, we started removing cup after cup of dust, placing it in the buckets and then emptying them in an open area outside the compound. The dust was so thick in the air that we almost couldn’t see each other. So we painstakingly did that in both of the rooms. After we removed all of the dust, we drew up buckets of water from the well outside and threw water all over the walls and floors, and then we cleaned them nicely with brooms. Guru das took a picture of the room that day when it had just been cleaned and the floor still wet. Afterward, we sat in those rooms and chanted a round, just as we had done in the morning before we began. We had kirtan, and then each of us entered into our own prayerful reflections.*

*Srila Prabhupada had given instructions that his papers were to be cleaned out and burned. This was a very difficult instruction for us to follow, because everything relating to Srila Prabhupada was sacred to us, even the seemingly ordinary receipts for small purchases or papers having to do with his business or householder life. Yet he had given the instruction, so we tried to follow it, although we did not burn everything. Srila Prabhupada’s trunks were not locked. When we opened one, we found some of his clothes inside—a quilted saffron jacket \[bandhi\], which the mice had eaten holes in, and a heavy woolen chaddar, which had disintegrated to the extent that when we picked it up, it almost completely fell apart. There were also the personal papers which we later took to the Yamuna, where we made a bonfire and burned them.*

## Yamuna’s Later Reflections on the Radha-Damodara Temple

**Yamuna**: *The atmosphere at the Radha-Damodara Mandir was very peaceful. It was very unique and difficult to describe in retrospect, especially in contrast to the Vrindavan of today. When you came into the main gate, virtually all you saw was dirt. Where there is now a little shop of paraphernalia and books, there used to be a tiny cave-like room with a very short door, and that was where the widow Sarajini lived. I came to know Sarajini well during my time in Vrindavan and appreciated her Vaishnava qualities. She was dedicated and very devotional, and even though I spoke no Hindi and she spoke no English, she later became a friend to me. Her heart belonged to Radha-Damodara, and she had a great attachment for Srila Prabhupada. When Srila Prabhupada lived there, he would sometimes allow her to cook, shop, wash his dishes or make his fires—his chula, or mud stove. She would go every morning without fail with a bucket to the Yamuna River, fill it with water and bring it to the pujaris for the Deities’ service. Srila Prabhupada once told me that she would go back to Godhead just for performing that service with so much devotion and constancy.*

*During the cleaning of Srila Prabhupada’s kitchen that first day, I came across a jar with what looked like little rock-hard golden dollops the size and shape of Hershey’s chocolate kisses. Curious to know what they were, I set the jar aside for later. As we left the temple compound, I found Sarajini, showed her the jar and asked about its contents. With a toothy grin, she indicated, “Mung badi, mung badi—Swami’s favorite—especially with aloo.” Delighted with the information, I was eager to learn how it was made and everything else about badis.*

*At that time the temple was divided among three sevaite families. It was a complicated and litigious structure. There was Sri Gaurachand Goswami and Sri Nivendranath Bannerjee, and the third was Madan Mohan Goswami. Srila Prabhupada said that they had been i n litigation in the courts for forty years over the standards of worship of Sri Radha-Damodara. So when we came, Gaurachand Goswami was assisted by his young son, Nirmal Chandra, who he called Panchu. At that time, young Nirmal Chandra was already performing much of the seva, including cooking, offerings and ara-tis. One of the commonly heard sounds in those days at Radha-Damodara Mandir was the loud keening sound of “PAAAAANCHU!” And he would then just run to assist his father. Madan Mohan Goswami lived mostly in Jaipur. Srila Prabhupada later told us that he had never had any dealings with Madan Mohan Goswami, except when he tried to evict Srila Prabhupada from his rooms. So in general it was very quiet and peaceful in the Radha-Damodara compound. The widow Sarajini was there, and maybe one or two dogs. In those days, almost no one came to Vrindavan, except during Kartikatime.*

## Vrindavan—“Everything Is Simple and Uncomplicated”

**Yamuna**: *Bearing a letter of introduction, the next day we called on Dr. O. B. L. Kapoor, one of Srila Prabhupada’s Godbrothers and friends. During our pleasant visit, I asked about mung badi and showed him the jar. He explained that badi was made from wet-ground legume pastes, seasoned, shaped, and dried until brittle. He then ushered us into his kitchen and showed us three homemade varieties: mung badi with green chilies; spicy urad badi, Punjabi style; and mung badi with tomato mixed with urad badi with peppercorns. On the spot I got a detailed lesson on how they are made and stored and several ideas for usage. Dr. Kapoor insisted we stay for lunch, which featured a badi dish. The meal included fresh wheat chapati flatbreads, a yogurt salad, and a dish called “Vrindavan badi sabji.”*

It is worth mentioning here that a fundamental aspect of Yamuna devi’s nature was that although she would sometimes not be able to remember someone’s name even after a period of time, she could often recall in exacting detail what was prepared and offered at an engagement, temple offering, festival or simple dinner thirty or forty years earlier. This, of course, greatly helped in developing the recipes for her first cookbook, Lord Krishna’s Cuisine, and her remembrance of the menu and procedures for making badi at this meeting with Dr. Kapoor is a wonderful example of that unique talent of hers.

Yamuna continued her reflections on that first visit to Vrindavan in her journal, and her depth of feeling and absorption in Krishna Consciousness are readily apparent in her words. It is clear that she was seeing through eyes tinged with love.

**Yamuna**: *We walked back to our ashram in the evening and watched the sunset from the rooftop. I thought about the residents of Vrindavan looking out in the same way for their beloved Krishna and Balarama as They returned with the cows 5,000 years ago. The nights in Vrindavan are strangely reticent, the stars all-encompassing and appearing almost touchable. There are no loud sounds in Vrindavan at night—only kirtans from temples and houses, bicycle bells, temple bells, birds singing, peacocks keening and dogs barking. Vrindavan is like a dense forest of longing—great longing and urgency for Krishna captured in every vision.*

*In Vrindavan everything is simple and uncomplicated. The water is either salty or very sweet. The salty water cleans everything. There is no soap, only Vrindavan dust—and the salty water. And the flowers are so sweet and plentiful—whites, reds, maroons, pinks and greens. Monkeys, pigs, elephants, horses, dogs, camels and hundreds of cows, bulls and calves all reside on Vrindavan’s streets. The market bazaars sell sweet pera, gulab jamuns, laddu, rasgulla and ras malai, as well as devotional accessories. I was so excited, it was hard to rest. With early morning came the shouts of “Radhe-Shyam!” from every direction and the softer sounds of japa.*

*At 5:30 am, we walked around Raman Reti on the parikrama path circumambulating Vrindavan. The beautiful sands were white and cold, the trees filled with peacocks; black and white birds flew in schools, and then the rising sun revealed the emerging outline of buildings, creepers, trees and the gorgeous red brick outline of the ancient Madana Mohana Temple, the oldest in Vrindavan. We climbed the red brick stairs to the temple, our feet traversing the same paths touched by the lotus feet of the Goswamis and our predecessor Acharyas. Around the side of the temple an old man sat chanting the morning melody of the Hare Krishna mantra, while bringing up buckets of water from the famous well Krishna brought water up for Sanatana Goswami. He knows Srila Prabhupada and our Vaishnava sampradaya. There by that very well lived Srila Sanatana Goswami. As the dawn poured the golden light of warmth onto my icy cold and brittle heart, I fell to the ground that had touched his lotus feet, offering obeisances and remembering with deep gratitude the talks between Lord Chaitanya Mahaprabhu and Sanatana Goswami. I chanted my Gayatri mantra there in the temple, as well as Sri Krishna Chaitanya, Hare Krishna and Vande Rupa Sanatana, and then we received maha prasadam—laddus made of coconut and gur. It was a magical moment when all time and space ceased, and I was left with the most important thing—the resonating sounds of the Holy Names sung by an old man as he chanted to his beloved Lord.*

*Srila Prabhupada told us that we should consider all of the inhabitants of Vraja as devotees. In this first visit, that was easy to do because everything was mystical and colored with the dyes of its newness and its spirituality. We saw all Vaishnavas as honoring other Vaishnavas. We saw everyone as servants of Krishna, always chanting and serving and glorifying Radha and Krishna. That was the special mystique of this place—the spiritual dimension of Vrindavan dhama.*

## Intrigues with the Maharaja of Bharatpur and the Palace at Keshi Ghat

**I just received one letter from Radha Madhava Sharan and he has informed me that a big temple and compound belonging to the Maharaja of Bharatpur on the bank of the Yamuna at Keshi Ghat is for sale. Therefore I would like you to go immediately to see Radha Madhava Sharan in Vrindavan.... You can go and see the site and find out exactly from him the terms of negotiation of purchasing the temple and property.... I will come myself and complete the purchase. We would like to get this temple and land at all costs, as it is very nicely situated on the Yamuna River. I know of this temple. I used to live next to it before living in the Radha-Damodara Temple. It is a very palatial building.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, NOV. 7, 1970**

This letter appears to be the first mention of the purported offer for sale by the Maharaja of Bharatpur of the Laxmi Rani Kunj temple at Keshi Ghat. In a letter to Srila Prabhupada on May 28,1970, Radha Madhava Sharan, although a seventy-year-old man himself, offered his services from Vrindavan, and Srila Prabhupada again mentioned to him the World Sankirtan Party idea:

**Besides that, next year I am contemplating to send a World Sankirtan Party, therefore I wish to have a nice place in India either in Vrindavan or at Prayag Sangam. So I shall be glad to know if you can help us in this connection.**

**— LETTER TO RADHA MADHAVA SHARAN, JUNE 6, 1970**

In answer to this, Mr. Sharan wrote of the possible availability of the Keshi Ghat palace, and although there is no record of Srila Prabhupada’s answer to him, it is obvious from his letter to Guru das of November 7,1970, that he very much wanted the property for ISKCON.

**Yamuna**: *We arrived at Keshi Ghat, where Krishna killed the Keshi demon, to see the old palace of the Maharaja of Bharatpur, Laxmi Rani Kunj. Srila Prabhupada, knowing that Bharatpur Maharaja wanted to sell the temple, very much wanted to pursue the matter. The temple was in a disused and dilapidated condition, but the original structure was very beautiful and unique, and the location could not have been better for our purposes.*

**Guru das**: I was in ecstasy because I was waiting to go to Vrindavan. We knocked on the door... a sleepy-eyed pujari opened up.... There were three floors, which were seemingly run down, full of bats and bat guano. There was a garden where the ling used to walk, but it also was not taken care of. The sandstone windows opened up onto the Yamuna River though, and that was glorious. Prabhupada wanted this palace....

I returned to Delhi, and Yamuna and I went to meet this Maharaja of Bharatpur. So we went to a very nice big, sprawling house on Malta Marg.... So this Maharaja of Bharatpur saw that we were Westerners, and we might have a lot of money. So his idea was that we would pay for the Laxmi Rani Kunj Palace. Well at that time we had our first pilgrimage, devotees from the West were coming to Vrindavan, and this is where we stayed, in Laxmi Rani Kunj, even though it was run down. At that time Maharaja had sent a julana, a swing made of silver and gold, which he was giving for only sixty thousand rupees. Acutyananda Maharaja got angry and said we will not accept it and sent it back....

So I wrote Prabhupada about that, and he wrote back to try to cultivate this king, because this palace is a place for us to stay, but we don’t want to pay for it. Then \[the Maharaja\] said that there are 33 hectares of land in Govardhan, another palace, some Deities, plus this Laxmi Rani Kunj that we could have for three lakhs of rupees, which was really a pretty good deal.... I wrote Prabhupada. Prabhupada’s idea was, he is a king; we are brahmanas; he should give it to us.

Yamuna loved the palace of Laxmi Rani Kunj and felt that it would be a perfect Vrindavan temple for 1SKCON, but Sri Sri Radha-Shyamasundara had other plans. The painstaking negotiations and melodrama surrounding the attempts of her and Guru das to secure the property spanned a period of almost two years, and Yamuna was extremely distressed by its ultimate failure. Especially discouraging to her was the offer of the palace and land by the Maharaja for a very reasonable sum, only to have Srila Prabhupada then say that the Maharaja should donate it. This was especially confusing in light of his original instruction to them that they would buy the Laxmi Rani Kunj palace. (See November 7, 1970 letter to Guru das). Ultimately, Yamuna said that this was another example of accepting the Spiritual Master’s direction without equivocation—a rope is a snake.

**Yamuna**: *I always want to remember the sounds of Vrindavan—its quiet, punctuated by the song of flying green parrots and strutting peacocks, monkey shrieks and cow lowing; the call of “Jaya Radhe” or “Hare Krishna” proffered as greetings exchanged by strangers on the street; the hoofs of cows and wooden clogs of sadhus on cobblestone lanes; the recitation of shastra, temple kirtans and widow bhajans. These are the sounds that give Vrindavan a spiritual vitality—a wonderful persona.*

*When I return to Delhi from quiet Vrindavan, the first impression is continuous, oppressive, meaningless noise. Traffic noise—the snarl of lorries and buses shifting on pneumatic gears; the rattle of small engine auto-rickshaws, scooters and automobile traffic; choking diesel brays, street babble and chatter from sidewalk hawkers; food vendors, tea stalls, brash snatches of Bollywood cinema music songs from open windows; the rackety clatter of machines, horn blares and brake squeals. Vrindavan is a different world a mere ninety miles away.*

## Srila Prabhupada Takes the World Sankirtan Party to Indore

In 1970, Indore was the largest city and commercial capital of Madhya Pradesh in central India, and it remains so today. Located only 35 miles from its well-known neighbor Ujjain, Indore’s landscape still showcases some of the many Hindu temples and other architectural masterpieces built in the 18th century by the great philosopher Queen Ahilyabai Holkar. Often referred to as the female Akbar for her fearless leadership qualities, she ruled the Malwa kingdom for 30 years, rode into battle herself, and brought peace and prosperity to her citizens.

In the two short months since their arrival in India, Srila Prabhupada and his World Sankirtan Party had already become known among satsang and sammelan organizers, and invitations were being received to festivals and programs throughout the country. From Indore, Srila Prabhupada was invited to their annual Gita Jayanti, held each year in December at the Gita Bhavan Mandir. The intention of the event was ostensibly to glorify the Bhagavad-gita, and among the guests were many impersonalists who either accepted the Gita as allegorical or repudiated Krishna as the Supreme Personality of Godhead. When he first entered the Gita Bhavan Mandir, Srila Prabhupada was immediately disturbed by the fact that no picture either from the Gita or of Krishna Himself appeared in the temple—a single lamp appeared on the altar instead. Later, he decisively spoke out about how the Gita was being misrepresented.

**Guest: What is wrongly preached about Gita?**

**Srila Prabhupada: Here is an example: Yesterday I went to that Gita Samiti. There is a lamp. Why is there a lamp instead of Krishna? Krishna is a lamp? Therefore I say it is being wrongly preached. Why is there a lamp? Bhagavad-gita is spoken by Krishna. So why is there no picture of Krishna? That means you have not understood Krishna. Therefore your so-called Gita Society is not bona fide. Even in ordinary affairs, if there is some political meeting, you keep Gandhi’s photo, Nehru’s photo, because they are the political leaders. Gita Samiti is preaching Bhagavad-gita, and there is not a single picture of Krishna. This is misguided. Gita Bhavan has invited me because we are teaching Bhagavadgita. But they celebrate Gita’s Jayanti and yet the speaker of Gita is not present? Therefore I say there are so many places, even here, which are wrongly representing Bhagavad-gita. So our position is to rectify that wrong propaganda.**

**— CONVERSATION, DEC. 1970**

Srila Prabhupada called for Yamuna and the Delhi devotees to come because he wanted his World Sankirtan Party to be featured at the event. All of them came except for Yamuna’s husband, Guru das, who stayed behind to work on getting customs’ clearance for Srila Prabhupada’s books. On arriving at Indore, Yamuna was astounded to find Srila Prabhupada himself waiting to receive them and to personally take her to her quarters:

**Yamuna**: *How he dealt with us each individually was the greatest gift. I’m astounded when I reflect on it— he treated everyone on a personal basis and encouraged us in our practice of Krishna Consciousness. I felt that he genuinely loved each of us, and he exhibited that love through how he took care of us—with great concern, compassion, and correction when required.*

*It was extremely hot and dusty when our train pulled into Indore the afternoon of December 8. Yet when we arrived at the venue, there was Srila Prabhupada standing majestically, with his hand in his bead bag, waiting to greet us. Of course, I paid my obeisances, and then with concern and kindness, he asked specific questions about how our trip went and how the Delhi program was progressing. Then he said to me, “Come, I will show you to your quarters.” He personally took me to my room, which contained a small bed and a metal armoire. Then he took out a small key, opened the armoire and said, “Here is space for your belongings. Is this all right?” I was thinking, “Here I am, an insignificant person in his party, yet he is showing so much concern for my welfare.” This so clearly characterized Srila Prabhupada. He was such an extraordinary personality. Prior to meeting him I did not know that anyone could so wholly represent qualities such as compassion or mercy. But in Srila Prabhupada, I learned that he in fact was the living embodiment of those qualities.*

*Srila Prabhupada had been given a small apartment to stay in, and attached to it was a rather large hall, where he would chant his morning japa sometime around 2:00 am. I had the habit in those days of rising early and trying to keep to Srila Prabhupada’s schedule because I was always a little greedy to be in his presence during the early morning hours. The hosts had provided a big iron kettle in the courtyard, perhaps five feet in diameter with a fire underneath keeping it hot. I would wait until I heard Prabhupada finishing his bath, and then I would head over to the corner and get my bath water. After bathing, I would sit very quietly in the back corner of this hall. There was one little light bulb at one end, and Srila Prabhupada would sit underneath that light bulb chanting japa. I thought he couldn’t see me because it was dark, and I was chanting silently—just watching Srila Prabhupada. After maybe an hour had passed, he came back to where I was sitting because he knew I had been there all along. Looking down at me, he simply said, “Thank you for chanting like this. Thank you for getting up in the morning and chanting.” So I took it as a requisite—that the Spiritual Master is pleased when he sees our activities and our achievements, but he is especially pleased when we embrace sadhana bhakti by trying to rise early in the morning and chanting japa.*

*It is important to reiterate here that although I am using myself as an example, Srila Prabhupada acted with each of us on an individual basis. That same concern and kindness he showed to me, he also showed to everyone in the party by taking into account our natures, our characters and our individuality. We were his World Sankirtan Party—his preachers—and at every moment we were reminded how important this was to Srila Prabhupada, this traveling sankirtan.*

*I was always a little hungry to experience Srila Prabhupada’s company and, in those days—perhaps because of my youth—I was a little bold. So I found that Srila Prabhupada would chant and perform his translation work in the hall in the morning. And one morning I got up at i am, took my bead bag and Teachings of Lord Caitanya, which I was reading at the time, and quiet like a mouse, I slunk in through the back entrance and huddled in a little corner, praying that Srila Prabhupada wouldn’t see me—that I would be able to stay in that space (there was nobody else in the room).*

*I generally chant with my eyes closed, and every once in a while I would just take a little peek to see if Srila Prabhupada was disturbed or looking at me. And like that, I got to chant all my rounds there. Then I picked up my book and thought, “Well, I have gotten this far; why don’t I do my studying now?” So I picked up Teachings of Lord Caitanya and started to read, and right then Srila Prabhupada got up and came to where I was sitting in the back of the room. Looking down at me, he said, “So what are you studying?” I replied, “Teachings of Lord Caitanya,” and he smiled and said, “This is very nice.” He continued, “Please study my books. I write my books so that you will read them and study them.” So even though we didn’t have many books in those days, this was a firm injunction of Srila Prabhupada’s. Whatever was written, we were to read—not just read, but study*

**On the first night of the festival, Prabhupada was scheduled as the last speaker. His disciples, who sat with him onstage, grew bored and restless from the ordeal of so many hours of Hindi speeches. And knowing that these speakers were presenting Mayavada misconceptions made the evening especially painful. Srila Prabhupada sat sternly and waited, his hand in his bead bag, his head held high, his lips murmuring the Hare Krishna mantra.**

**When Prabhupada finally spoke, he began by explaining that in the West he was spreading the teachings of the Gita as it is. Bhagavad-gita, he said, could be properly understood only in a disciplic succession, just as Arjuna, the original student of the Bhagavad-gita, had understood it. The Gita was for the devotee of Krishna, and should not be misinterpreted by nondevotees. To misinterpret the Gita, he said, was to cheat in the name of religion. He also spoke strongly against pseudo incarnations.**

**Prabhupada concluded his talk and asked his disciples to begin kirtan. It was an ecstatic, spontaneous event, and Prabhupada began dancing onstage along with his disciples. The crowd came to life and began clapping rhythmically. Hansadutta jumped down from the stage, still playing mridanga, and began inducing members of the audience to join in chanting and dancing. Several other devotees also jumped down, and soon hundreds of people had risen to their feet, swaying, clapping, and singing: Hare Krishna, Hare Krishna, Krishna Krishna, Hare Hare, Hare Rama, Hare Rama, Rama Rama, Hare Hare. This was the real Gita Jayanti Mahotsava. The Holy Name of Krishna was being sung, and everyone was happily united in the kirtan.**

**— SRILA PRАВHUPADA - LILAMRTA**

The organizers appreciated how Srila Prabhupada’s sankirtan party had so spontaneously and meaningfully impacted the attendees and asked for a similar performance the next day. But Srila Prabhupada demurred, saying that his disciples should not have to sit through so many Hindi lectures, and further, he continued, the speeches were not properly presenting Bhagavad-gita as it is. The next day the director of the Gita Jayanti, along with at least six representatives, came to Srila Prabhupada’s bungalow to try to reason with him and soften his philosophical stance. They said, “We do not subscribe wholly that Krishna is God, but rather there is a higher power above Him.” Srila Prabhupada then embarked on a remarkable and revealing exchange with them about the supremacy of Krishna—that He is the highest truth, and that the Bhagavad-gita represents His direct and personal teachings. Srila Prabhupada was uncompromising in his defense of Krishna’s supremacy as the Supreme Personality of Godhead, and later told Yamuna, “If I don’t speak up when they are trying to present a Gita without Krishna, then who will speak?”

**Guest: If each person has an individual identity of soul above the body, you must treat everyone as equal.**  
**Srila Prabhupada: They are not equal. There are three gunas, or modes of material nature, and Bhagavad-gita analyzes: These persons are in sattva-guna \[goodness\], these persons are in rajo-guna \[passion\], these persons are in tamo-guna \[ignorance\]. Guest: That is not the personality of the atma. The atma is everyone’s soul. You have the potency to rise and go higher and higher. Srila Prabhupada: You are not in the atma stage; I am not in the atma stage. You are in the bodily stage. Still, if you see everyone equally, why do you find fault in me? If you are in the atma stage, you have no argument with me. Panditah sama-darsinah. This is stated in the Bhagavad-gita. That is the correct position. But if you find that “Swamiji is not on the standard,” that means you are not in the position of sama-darsinah, equal vision.**  
**Guest: I think they have made many mistakes in writing the shlokas \[verses\].**  
**Srila Prabhupada: Now you are finding faults in Vyasa. Who can talk with you? Please excuse me. Please go out. You are finding fault with Vyasa.**  
**Guest: We only want you to be understood here.**  
**Srila Prabhupada: \[shouting\] I am not sama-darsi. I don’t say I am sama-darsi. You say you are sama-darsi.**  
**Guest: You should be sama-darsi.**  
**Srila Prabhupada: But I’m not in that stage. I say that because you don’t surrender to Krishna, you are sinful. That is my darshan \[vision\], I am not in that position. I am simply repeating the words of Krishna. That is my point. I may be sama-darsi, I may not be sama-darsi. My position is simply to repeat. That’s all.**

**— CONVERSATION, DEC. I970**

From this point on Srila Prabhupada did not speak again at the Jayanti site, but he would ask individual devotees to speak. Hansadutta sometimes spoke, as well as his wife, Himavati.
