In an interview shortly after Yamuna devi’s samadhi and Immersion ceremonies in 2013, Jananivasa Prabhu reflected that the main quality that came to mind when he thought of Yamuna devi was “mature.” He said that he has never known a more mature person, male or female, but feels she particularly stands apart from other women in that regard. From his earliest days in ISKCON through the present, he has never met a more mature individual. The main reason he feels that way is because she exuded Srila Prabhupada’s mood and character. One immediately thought of Srila Prabhupada in her presence, and conversations with her inevitably ended up being about Srila Prabhupada.

**After the five-day festival, Prabhupada left Mayapur for Vrindavan, where he planned to hold another ground-breaking ceremony. The Mayapur land was still completely undeveloped, and Prabhupada urged his disciples in India to continue collecting the necessary funds.**

**— SRILA PRABHUPADA-LILAMRTA**

**We are making a very gorgeous plan at Mayapur, and if you all together can give shape to this plan it will be unique in the whole world. It will be a world center for teaching spiritual life. Students from all over the world will come and we shall revolutionize the atheistic and communistic tendencies of rascal philosophers. So we must be responsible for this great task. Not for a single moment shall we be without ISKCON thoughts. That is my request to you all.**

**— SRILA PRABHUPADA QUOTE, SRILA PRABHUPADA-LILAMRTA**

## A Pilgrimage with Prabhupada to Bhaktivinoda Thakur's Birthplace in Birnagar

On the return trip from the festival in Mayapur on March 2, Srila Prabhupada made a pilgrimage with some of his disciples to the birthplace of Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakur in Birnagar, known as Ulagram in the Thakur’s youth. Maintained by the last surviving son of the Thakur, Srila Lalita Prasad, it was known as the Bhaktivinoda Institute. As Srila Lalita Prasad was the son of Bhaktivinoda Thakur and the brother of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakur, Srila Prabhupada was careful to humbly extend all honor and respect to him. Yamuna, who was also present, attentively observed the etiquette, and the meeting and exchanges between Srila Prabhupada and Srila Lalita Prasad were very respectful and sweet.

**Yamuna**: *Here is the ideal simplicity of pure spiritual living. The land is untouched by the corruption of Kali Yuga and remains the same as it was 500 years ago when Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu appeared. There are orchards and forests lush with growth as far as the eye can see. Within the confines of Bhaktivinoda Thakur’s birth site are trees of bael, banyan, mango, guava, papaya, jackfruit, banana, coconut, sitaphal and pineapple, as well as jasmine, mogra and champa plants. Cows are abundant, and milk is plentiful. Many birds sing beautiful harmonies. It is a transcendental setting.*

Although Srila Prabhupada certainly knew of the philosophical differences between Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati and Srila Lalita Prasad during his manifest presence, he wanted to preserve the birthplace of Bhaktivinoda Thakur, recognizing his importance to the mission of Sri Chaitanya Mahaprabhu. To this end, Srila Lalita Prasad promised to lease property to Srila Prabhupada to develop an ISKCON temple, and Srila Prabhupada in turn would rehabilitate the surrounding grounds.

During the visit, Srila Lalita Prasad took a particular interest in preaching to and encouraging Yamuna devi, and there are wonderful pictures of an attentive Yamuna with him. Although she wrote his comments in her journal, they were so removed from what Srila Prabhupada had taught her that she was left in some confusion. She later approached Srila Prabhupada about this, and he pointed out that although there may be differences between great souls, such as between Srila Lalita Prasad and his Guru Maharaja, these differences should be seen in the nature of pastimes, and Srila Prabhupada’s disciples should be careful not to criticize. However, as the following letters of Srila Prabhupada indicate, the differences proved too much to overlook, especially when the land promised for an ISKCON temple was not forthcoming, and later, when Srila Prabhupada saw derogatory comments about Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakur in one of Lalit Prasad’s books.

On March 4, Srila Prabhupada wrote to Srila Lalita Prasad:

**Kindly accept my humble obeisances at your Lotus Feet. The whole day spent at your temple on Thursday was so pleasant and happy that all my disciples felt celestial blessings in your association. Personally, I am so much encouraged by you that I appreciate this as the blessings of Bhaktivinoda Thakur through his living representative. Now you can expedite the lease agreement immediately so that before returning to U.S. in about three weeks’ time, I may advise my assistants to take up the work seriously and begin construction and other things.**

**— LETTER TO SRILA LAL1TA PRASAD, MAR. 4, 1972**

On May 17 he wrote to Jayapataka regarding leasing land at Bhaktivinoda Thakur’s birthplace:

**Regarding Lalita Prasad Thakur’s proposal ... They can keep aside their portion independently, and the land which is given to us on lease, we keep ourselves independently. So far our relationship is concerned, even though we keep independent of one another, there will be no misunderstanding, because the central point is Bhaktivinoda Thakur. Our only ambition is that the birth site of Bhaktivinoda Thakur must be gorgeous and attractive so that people may come to see from all parts of the world. Bhaktivinoda Thakur is no longer localized. His holy name is being expanded along with Lord Chaitanya’s. So let them understand this point.**

**— LETTER TO JAYAPATAKA, MAY 17, 1972**

By the end of May, Srila Prabhupada realized that it would not be possible to lease the land at Bhaktivinoda Thakur’s birthplace for an ISKCON temple in Birnagar. He further requested that no devotees go there in the future except for Yadubara das, who Srila Prabhupada wanted to take photographs of the decaying, handwritten manuscripts of Bhaktivinoda Thakur and other great Acharyas. (See July 29,1972, letter to Acyutananda Swami)

## A Short Stop in Calcutta, Then on to Vrindavan

**Yamuna**: *When we returned to Calcutta with Srila Prabhupada, a cablegram had come from Srila Prabhupada’s disciple Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das in Vrindavan that ISKCON had been given the gift of a choice parcel of land in Raman Reti on Chattikara Road from Kashiram and Gitabhai Saraf.*

Srila Prabhupada had initially sent Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das to Vrindavan on December 26, 1971, to secure the land which Mr. Saraf had already promised him. (see Dec. 26, 1971, letter). Then on February 15, 1972, Srila Prabhupada wrote to Gargamuni that Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das had sent a cable confirming that the land had been gifted to 1SKCON. Knowing the land to have been highly coveted by other sadhus, including Shyama Ma, Srila Prabhupada was determined to have the Gift Deed formalized legally before anyone could change their minds. Therefore he immediately sent Guru das and Yamuna to Vrindavan to assist in obtaining the land.

**Yamuna**: *So Srila Prabhupada said that before they changed their minds, my husband and I should immediately try to secure the land in legal terms. So we left without delay for Vrindavan to work on this project.*

## Yamanas Letter to Srila Prabhupada on Leaving Calcutta

In her open notes, I found a letter Yamuna wrote to Srila Prabhupada just prior to leaving Calcutta for Vrindavan. It vividly portrays a constant theme in all of her written and verbal expressions—that of seeking more sincerity in her service to Srila Prabhupada:

*Dear Srila Prabhupada, As we leave on another service, I wanted to express to you that I will continue to try to understand and apply all that you have so mercifully given to me. To somehow please Your Grace is the only purpose and mission of my life. Whether we are traveling with you on sankirtan, assisting in Deity or cooking services or just sitting and hearing the ambrosial words emanating from your mouth, I pray that I may never leave your sublime service, and that somehow, someday, I may be able to freely share with an open heart what you have selflessly given us—the rare opportunity to go back home, back to Godhead.*

## Chapter 7

**A Confluence of Change (Vrindavan, 1972)**

YAMUNA DEVI SAW a compelling symbolism in the fact that securing the land in both Mayapur and Vrindavan occurred within weeks of one another. For her it was the fulfillment by Krishna of Srila Prabhupada’s desire to comfortably accommodate his disciples from the West, allow them to receive the mercy of the holy dhamas, and learn the etiquette of Vaishnava culture.

**Yamuna**: *It was massively significant to me that the groundwork for the Mayapur and Vrindavan projects was concluded so closely together. I felt strongly that this was because they were conceived for the same purpose.*

*Once, after we had moved into quarters at the Radha-Damodara temple, Srila Prabhupada called me into his room and said, “Yamuna, some of our men are coming from the West—five boys.” Unfortunately, our temple at that time was going through a state of flux. For various reasons, we weren’t very organized, and there was a lack of Vaishnava behavior in our party, especially in how we failed to properly respect and honor each other as Vaishnavas, and therefore the cohesive element of Krishna Consciousness was disturbed. So Srila Prabhupada called me in. I was surprised as to why he would often consult me on issues important to him, as this in itself sometimes caused disturbance among some of the men. So he continued, “There are five boys coming, and it is very important that they are given a very comfortable facility. I want you to personally take care that they have a nice place to sleep and that they have very tasty prasadam, because if our men come from the West and they don’t have comfortable arrangements, they will immediately get sick and leave.” Srila Prabhupada was so concerned about the care of his disciples that he also brought this matter up to me in London and also when we first arrived in India.*

*So actually, from the very beginning Srila Prabhupada endeavored to train us in Vaishnava etiquette. What the Indians would do for us, he wanted us to emulate; and he wanted us to care for each other civilly, because we could sometimes be terribly harsh with each other. So Prabhupada, of course, could see that, and so he brought this matter up very early in our India travels. So naturally, when Srila Prabhupada asked me to perform this service in the holy dhama, I was determined to try to please him by learning all I could about Vaishnava behavior and by trying to take care of devotees who came to the holy dhama.*

As many devotees would later reveal in their own memories of Yamuna, not only did she take this instruction of Srila Prabhupada very seriously, but throughout her years in India she often ended up cooking, making lodging arrangements and taking care of sick devotees herself. As she was also a good listener, she was often the devotee they went to with their problems and grievances as well.

**Yamuna**: *Towards the early part of March, as per Srila Prabhupada’s desire, my husband and I went to Vrindavan to assist in the Raman Reti project. As we had no living facilities yet, we stayed at Saraf Bhavan at the crossroads of Vrindavan (not the Saraf who later gave the land in Raman Reti). We were given the upper floor of the build ing for Srila Prabhupada to reside in.So my husband, Guru das, Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das, Shyamasundara and Nanda Kumara stayed there. Malati was also there and myself. When Srila Prabhupada arrived, he was quite excited and for us, just watching how he interacted with the various types of Brijbasis was illuminating. Srila Prabhupada at this time exhibited his consummate skill in every realm. Especially exciting for us was how he dealt with others in business—it was business, but for him it was Krishna’s business. He knew the mentality of the people and how to encourage, cajole and, when necessary, be firm.*

## Srimati Radharani Gives Her Sanction for the Land at Raman Reti

In 1994 in Vrindavan, Yamuna devi interviewed Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das regarding how the land was procured for the Krishna-Balarama Temple in Raman Reti. Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das, although a sincere devotee, was seen by Yamuna as “old-school” in that, as an older Indian gentleman, he was secure in his understanding of Vaishnavism and resistant to change. Therefore, he found it difficult to work cooperatively with devotees from the West and, more particularly, women devotees from the West.

Srila Prabhupada had sent him in December from Calcutta to work on acquiring the Raman Reti property already promised by Mr. Saraf. At the time, Mr. Saraf’s wife, Gitabhai, whose name the property was held in, was in Assam, so they had to wait for her return to finalize the acquisition of the land.

**Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das**: So he \[Mr. Saraf\] said, “The land belongs \[in\] the name of my wife, and she will come sometime on Gaura Purnima or Holi, and you come here then.”

In the interim, a Mr. Sharma had offered land from the municipality, and letters were exchanged between Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das and Srila Prabhupada. Srila Prabhupada ultimately decided that the municipality land would involve too much time and red tape, so he encouraged Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das to push for the Raman Reti land. When Mrs. Saraf returned, Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das came from Delhi to Vrindavan and met with them both.

**Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das**: Mr. Saraf said, “This place is especially reserved for a temple, and so many sadhus and saintly persons are coming there, but we are not sure if they will be able to make a temple or not. So how can we really be sure that your Guru Maharaja will build a temple?”

So I very humbly said that, “My Guru Maharaja has opened many temples all over the world, and he has got so many disciples all over the world. When he went to America, he had no money, and by Krishna’s mercy, he has been empowered, and I assure you that he will build a temple.”

So when the third day came, Mr. Saraf said that they had decided that the land would be given.... “\[But\] how will we be sure that somebody will maintain it?” So I said that, “If the temple is not built within two years, then you can put it in the conditions \[of the Gift Deed\] that you can take it back. I can assure you that Radharani and Prabhupada’s mercy will be bestowed, and if you are sincere to give the land, take it back if we do not make the temple in two years.” And they \[agreed it was\] all right, and that the land would be given the next day.

There must have been serious opposition to the gift of the Raman Reti land, because by the next day, another condition had been added.

**Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das**: So the next day, \[Mr. Saraf\] said, “Radharani is the Queen of Vraja, and without Her sanction, you cannot have the land.” So I said, “Well, I don’t know Radharani. You have been chanting Radha and Krishna’s names in your temple. You ask Her and ask Krishna if They want to give the land or not. All I know is that I am the servant of Prabhupada, and I am asking.”

So the next day, they said that Radharani had inspired them to give the land, but “The condition is that you must put ‘yes’ and ‘no’ on two \[pieces of\] paper. And before Them, if you take the paper out that says ‘yes,’ then the land is yours, and if it says ‘no,’ then at any cost, it is not yours.” So I said, “No, I am sorry, I cannot do gambling. Gambling is restricted by Prabhupada.” And I had no one to guide me.

So they asked me to think it over. So in the morning, they asked, “What is your decision? Do you want to do this or not?” So by Krishna and Radharani’s mercy, I thought, “All right, 1’1I do it.” So Mr. Saraf took two papers from his pujari and put “yes” and “no” on them. Then he said to pick one up. “If Krishna and Radharani want you to have the land, I can’t stop it,” he said. “And if Radharani doesn’t want to give it, then it will not be given.” So I just prayed to Srila Prabhupada, then chose, and the “yes” paper came up. Then Mr. Saraf said to the pujari, “This land is to go to the temple.” I immediately sent a telegram to Srila Prabhupada in Calcutta saying, “Saraf promised to donate the land, and everything is in our possession.” So Prabhupada then sent a return telegram, followed by a letter about the importance of getting the deed legally signed over.

**First, concerning the Saraf land, I want to sign the documents before going to Bombay within a few days from now, and if there is possibility to lay down the cornerstone there, I can also do that before leaving from India. This will please me very much and give me great relief to know that we have done something solid in Vrindavan before I leave, and the credit is yours. So I am entrusting that you can arrange everything very nicely about getting the deed prepared for the Saraf land, and you may also prepare one nice foundation stone and we shall hold a public ceremony and lay the foundation stone. Second thing is, it appears that Madan Mohan Goswami has changed his heart and become favorable to give us the downstairs veranda and some rooms upstairs above my rooms in the Radha-Damodara temple, so for that I expect to come to Vrindavan from Calcutta as soon as I am informed by Subala Maharaja and your good self, on my way to Bombay for our pandal program there in Juhu. So kindly go to Vrindavan immediately and make all arrangements for the legal documents and cornerstone laying-down, and if Subala needs assistance you may help him also, but one thing is I want to come there immediately, so go immediately to Vrindavan and send me cable when I shall come there.**

**— LETTER TO KSIRODAKASAYI VISHNU DAS, MAR. 4, 1972**

Srila Prabhupada arrived in Vrindavan on March 10 to personally oversee the transference of the Gift Deed for the Raman Reti land. He also wanted to legally finalize the one-year rental of the rooms above his own at Radha-Damodara Mandir with Madan Mohan Goswami. Although many things move at a snail’s pace in India, the courts hold the distinction of being notoriously slow; small disputes are summarily shifted from desk to desk for years. In order to avoid this, according to Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das, some favorable friends had the “court” brought to Srila Prabhupada. So on March 12,1972, a diverse group of Brijbasis gathered in Srila Prabhupada’s rooms at Saraf Bhavan.

## A Prophecy Foretold — “We Will Have Centers in Mayapur and Vrindavan for the Pleasure of Srila Bhaktivinoda Thakur”

**Yamuna**: This was one of the first times I observed Srila Prabhupada dealing with Brijbasis from all spiritual, social and political spectrums—from the babajis, Godbrothers, Court officials, caste goswamis and his own disciples. I did not know the personalities at the time, but I believe that Narayana Maharaja came from Mathura, another goswami came from Vrindavan’s Lala Babu temple, and a representative came from another Gaudiya Math in Vrindavan. Also present was the ever-transcendental Sri Akincana Krishna das Babaji, a resident of Radha Kunda at that time. Madan Mohan Goswami and Gaurachand Goswami represented the Radha-Damodara temple. Also present was Haridas Goswami, a sevaite from the Radha-Raman temple. And of course Mr. and Mrs. Saraf were present for the official signing of the Gift Deed to the property. It was Srila Prabhupada’s intention to have many witnesses to attest to the fact that Gitabhai Saraf was officially donating the land in Raman Reti for Srila Prabhupada to build a temple for Krishna and Balarama.

For me, to observe him in his dealings with each of those present was simply glorious. Srila Prabhupada was sitting at his desk in such an aristocratic fashion, and all these men were attentively gathered around him just waiting for him to make the next move. Srila Prabhupada had an air of authority and complete command of the situation, and even though they were all speaking in a very businesslike fashion, Srila Prabhupada brilliantly retained complete control of the proceedings. Even though much of the speaking was in Hindi, accompanied by a great deal of gesturing with the hands, we could understand something of what was happening, and were just awestruck because during that one meeting Srila Prabhupada was not only able to legally acquire the donated land in Raman Reti, but also to secure the agreement from Madan Mohan Goswami to lease the rooms above Srila Prabhupada’s rooms at Radha-Damodara for a year while we worked on the Krishna-Balarama Temple.

An interesting postscript occurred when the electricity went off near the end of the meeting. This is a still a regular occurrence in Vrindavan, but Srila Prabhupada knew that the spoken word can always be contested at a later point, even with the presence of so many witnesses, so he wanted them all to sign a written contract. Since Shyamasundara’s electric typewriter was not working, Srila Prabhupada called on me to calligraph the contract for them to sign on the spot. He drafted the wording for the final contract, and then I took it into another room and hand-calligraphed it, including gold embossing of all the capitals. It was a simple contract with the terms and with Srila Prabhupada’s name and the names of all the other members and goswamis present there. Within fifteen or twenty minutes, I presented the calligraphed contract to Srila Prabhupada. He had just concluded this great achievement by influencing the minds of these Brijbasis through the power of his Krishna Consciousness and business acumen. Then, much to my embarrassment, he held up the calligraphed contract, flourished it in the air with a beaming smile on his face and said, “\]ust see my disciples. They are expert in everything.” And he was so proud that one of his disciples could come up with such a beautiful handwritten document on a moment’s notice. He then added how Lord Chaitanya had one devotee who was very expert in handwriting manuscripts, and how the Six Goswamis were also expert in handwriting. So all the members signed the contract, and our Krishna-Balarama Temple land was finalized. Srila Prabhupada had foretold that in both Mayapur and Vrindavan we would have centers for the pleasure of Bhaktivinoda Thakur, and I saw this as another move toward the fulfillment of Srila Prabhupada’s prophetic statement. It was one of those moments when all sense of time and space seemed to stop, and I became submerged in the ocean of Srila Prabhupada’s greatness.

## The Cornerstone Ceremony for the Krishna-Balarama Temple

Immediately following the signing of the Gift Deed for the land in Raman Reti, Srila Prabhupada wanted to have a cornerstone ceremony to formally consecrate the land for ISKCON and ward off any challenges to its ownership. In Yamuna’s 1994 interview with Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das, he spoke at some length about how Shyama Ma immediately went to the courts to challenge the ownership of the land, claiming that the Sarafs were her disciples, that she had been promised the land, and that monies had even been given by her toward its purchase. This all proved unconvincing to the courts, but it did not deter her, a previous “friend” of ISKCON, from trying to desecrate the cornerstone ceremony.

**Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das**: I had to go to Agra to get the cornerstone, and within twenty four hours it was laid.  
**Yamuna**: What did the stone say, and what did it look like?  
**Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das**: It said Prabhupada’s name and the date.  
**Yamuna**: Is this the original stone that is in the gurukula now, with the names and date?  
**Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das**: Yes.  
— YAMUNA INTERVIEW, 1994

**Yamuna**: *On March 13, 1972, Srila Prabhupada laid the cornerstone for the Krishna-Balarama Temple and ashram, just within a fortnight of the Mayapur cornerstone ceremony and only a day after the legal signing. Again, according to scripture, a hole was dug at least 15 feet deep and included the following five kinds of each item offered to the Lord:*

- *Flowers: jasmine, lotus, tulasi, parijata, mogra-, Grains: rice, wheat, barley, mung, urad',*
- *Leaf: mango, peepal, neem, bael, banyan;*
- *Metal: gold, silver, copper, lead, nickel;*
- *Nectar: sugar, honey, ghee, yogurt, cream;*
- *Powder: yellow, blue, green, red, white;*
- *Fruit: mango, apple, grape, banana, chiku', Jewel: coral, diamond, sapphire, ruby, emerald.*

**Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das**: So I took all these ingredients for this and that and chanted Vedic mantras, the brahmanas chanted, and the devotees had kirtan. So when I was down in the hole, Srila Prabhupada said, “You should stay down there.” This was some sweet nectar of rasa with Srila Prabhupada, but at this time he wanted me to stay in Vrindavan, so he said “You stay there \[in the hole\].

## Anand Prabhu—“My Old Godbrother, A Sincere Vaishnava”

**Yamuna**: *Srila Prabhupada then immediately departed for Bombay from Vrindavan. He left three members in Vrindavan for preaching and beginning work on the Krishna-Balarama Temple: Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das was to be the president; Guru das was to be the treasurer; and I was to be the secretary. Our offices and headquarters were to be at the Radha-Damodara temple in the newly-rented rooms directly above Srila Prabhupada’s. Along with all of the preparations for constructing and opening the Krishna-Balarama Temple, we were instructed to worship his rooms there daily, cleanse them each morning with water, and in general keep them clean and orderly. We were also allowed to cook in his kitchen.*

*The fourth member of our party at that time was a great Vaishnava soul named Anand Prabhu, a Godbrother of Srila Prabhupada who had actually cooked for Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakur. We met him in Visakhapatnam, and at that time he asked Srila Prabhupada to come to Vrindavan and serve Srila Prabhupada’s mission there. So now, Anand Prabhu lived in the small adjoining courtyard on the main floor between Srila Prabhupada’s kitchen and study room, and the rest of us stayed upstairs.*

From the very beginning, Yamuna established a very warm and respectful relationship with Anand Prabhu even though he spoke no English, and she spoke no Hindi or other regional dialects. They shared, however, the universal language of cooking—the love of preparing, offering and serving prasadam to others. Theirs was akin to a father-daughter relationship from the beginning, which was interesting in itself because Srila Prabhupada later wrote to Guru das:

**I am very glad to know that Anand Prabhu is staying with you. Please offer him my dandavats. He is my old Godbrother, a sincere Vaishnava. Please treat him like your father.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, MAY 6, 1973**

I first met Anand Prabhu in Vrindavan in late 1973, and again when I stayed there during the summer of 1974. Even though I was told that he was Srila Prabhupada’s Godbrother and had cooked for Srila Saraswati Thakur, due to my neophyte position, I had no understanding of the profundity of those words, nor did I have the maturity to offer him proper respect. He was a sweet and simple Vaishnava, and each day he would cook and serve the midday prasadam, always with a smiling face, back straight, while squatting on his haunches, and a humble attitude. Each evening he would go for pravachan to hear Srimad-Bhagavatam in his own language; and every morning he would perform impossibly difficult yoga asanas, even though he was in his early seventies at the time. I once came into the kitchen area in the morning to find him in the horizontal mayurasana \[peacock posture\], using only one hand.

Although I did not have the devotional maturity to properly appreciate the service attitude of Anand Prabhu, Yamuna devi assuredly did. She learned from him dishes she thought Srila Prabhupada would like, and often questioned him in her “pidgin” Hindi on his cooking for Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati. Below are some of the notes from her journal dated in March and April 1972 regarding Anand Prabhu:

**Yamuna’s Journal:** *Informally during prasadam I asked what Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati liked to honor for breakfast. Anand Prabhu replied that Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati was very fond of ripened jackfruit with soaked cheera in sugar and served with yogurt for his breakfast in Mayapur. For lunch he had chapatis, rice, dal and yogurt. Sabjis (vegetables) were prepared with ginger chunks and powdered spices: coriander, cumin, salt and black pepper.*

*When his students honored prasadam, Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati would stand at the head of his seated students and tell them to eat more and more.*

*During Caturmasya, he would rarely speak with anyone and would mostly chant the Holy Name and study. He would chant three lakhs of the Holy Name daily.*

*He once spoke about the Yogapith temple in Mayapur. He said that Bhaktivinoda Thakur built the Yogapith temple for 10,000 rupees. At night each Deity takes three chapatis, two puris, sandesh, sabji and milk. He said that “Only my sons who are strict Vaishnavas can run this temple.” Then he gave Bhaktivinoda Thakur’s recipe for keeping chapatis moist for offering: make regular chapatis and put them in a covered dechi (pot) to keep them warm. Put some water in the tawa and dip each chapati in water on one side for two or three seconds and lay them out to dry. Spread with ghee. Keep warm.*

Yamuna considered Anand Prabhu as a mentor, especially in the art of cooking, and out of a deep and lasting respect for him, at Radha-Banabehari’s ashrams she always kept his picture along with Srila Prabhupada’s next to Srila Prabhupada’s personal three-tiered cooker.

**Yamuna Devi at Radha-Damodara Mandir — A Portrait of Change**

Later that March, Yamuna and Guru das arrived at their new quarters at Radha-Damodara Mandir. Initially Yamuna was ecstatic to be in the “hub of the wheel of the spiritual world.” Even though she was aware of resistance from some of the Brijbasis due to their presence there, she was deeply immersed in the spiritual potency of Radha-Damodara, the samadhis of Srila Rupa Goswami, Srila Jiva Goswami and Srila Kaviraja Goswami, and particularly the eternal rooms of Srila Prabhupada, and felt honored to be given the rare and unprecedented opportunity to live and serve there.

**Yamuna**: *Our bicycle rickshaws pulled up in front of the Radha-Damodara Mandir under a clear blue sky. I noticed that our exposed skin was sunburn pink, and our sweaty clothes coated with dust. Guru das paid the rickshaw drivers and placed our metal trunks on the cobblestone lane, while I looked around for a welcoming party—no one in sight. We lugged the trunks through a newly-installed door with access to Prabhupada’s two rooms and a stairway leading upstairs. His sitting room door was open.*

*After the blistering clarity of the noonday sun, the room was as dark as a cave. Its only light came from a window near the floor, latticed in carved stone. We fell down on the cool sandstone floor in full dandavats. When I sat up and saw the room, I noted that it had not changed since our visit the year before—slab stone floor, high ceiling, painted walls, a charpoy bed nestled in a corner, an aged writing seat near the window, a ceiling light and fan, a battered clothes chest, a heavy wood door at one end and a barred screen door at the other end. The paint was chipped and the chair warped, but the room evoked Prabhupada’s purity and his eternal physical presence.*

*A closed door creaked open and, adjusting my eyes to the light, I found that a slight Indian man had entered the room. A familiar figure, he’s our project president, Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das. Dressed in a white khadi kurta and dhoti, he holds two cups of water in his outstretched hands.*

*“Pranams. Dandavats,’’ he said with a heavy Hindi accent. “Veery good. Now you have come. We have much to do. First take some water, then we will go upstairs. There is good austerity up there—no electric, no fan, no light bulb—not like downstairs with electric fan and light. Upstairs we use kerosene lamps. The Bengali boy Satchidananda is already with me. Subala Swami arrives soon. Maybe Devananda Swami also. We will be four or five in number. When you...”*

*“Dandavats Ksirodakasayi Prabhu,” I interrupt. “Thank you for your kind welcome. Sorry to interrupt, but could you show us the bathroom please?”*

*We were shown to a cement toilet downstairs, just off the new entrance. There was no water in the taps. Water only runs an hour each morning and evening. As our arrival time was uncertain, no water had been saved for a bath. While I was trying to figure out how to deal with the water situation, we moved the trunks upstairs and dropped them in front of what looked like side-by-side brick ovens, a door on the front of each. Heat waves glimmered off the roof like a mirage. Our host extracted a key from the folds of his dhoti and unlocked a padlock the size of a tennis shoe. He swung the door inward to reveal a room perhaps fifteen by twenty-five feet, its cement floors painted oxide red, and with not a stick of furniture—only two lamps. Three windows, barred and without glass or screening, were shuttered on the outside. A thick wood door to the right of the entrance revealed a small square room which was designated as mine. My husband had its twin, accessed through the main room. Etiquette in Radha-Damodara, as in all established temples, required that husband and wife live in separate rooms.*

*After seeing our quarters, Ksirodakasayi resumed in a nasal voice, “Heat is veery strong this year. Too many days now with heat over 120 Fahrenheit. Heat will increase more in May and June.” “Oh, Lord,” I thought. “Did I hear that right?” The blazing heat indoors already felt like a sauna; the brick walls carry an ageless dusty aroma. I’m in a sauna and covered head to toe with a petticoat, blouse and sari. Could anyplace on earth be hotter? Where was that Vrindavan I had imagined—the one described in Srimad-Bhagavatam as neither too hot nor too cold? I had to stop the mind and remember Prabhupada’s example. He had endured similar heat during the summers he lived in this very spot.*

*Then Ksirodakasayi resumes, “The men are next door. We have use of Prabhupada’s two rooms downstairs. Yamuna, I think you will want to use his kitchen. We take prasadam on the veranda between his rooms. Mangai arati for Radha-Damodara is at 4:30 am. Prabhupada wants us to go on nagar sankirtan from here to Raman Reti every morning. When we return, a morning class is held downstairs in the sitting room. To sleep outside is best. Anything else? I think not.” With that, he gives Guru das the key, asks for permission to take his leave, and we are on our own.*

*Light-headed and reeling, I collapse on a trunk, and when my eyes meet my husband’s eyes, we break into laughter. “You look just a leetle undone Yamuna,” Guru das said. “All right if we take our first Vrindavan bath in your namesake?” “A good idea,” I said, applying sunburn cream to my pink skin. “An auspicious bath at Keshi Ghat in Krishna’s favorite river—the perfect antidote. On the way back, we can shop in Loi Bazaar.”*

*We took a change of clothes and went to Keshi Ghat. The Laxmi Rani Kunj palace (which we were still hoping to acquire for Srila Prabhupada) is intricately carved in red sandstone. We entered the palace compound through massive wooden doors. Originally constructed as a vacation retreat for the Bharatpur royals, in its heyday it was elegantly appointed in every detail. Now it stands neglected, its foundation slowly sinking in the river and empty except for a resident chokidar and an occasional sadhu sleeping on the bathing ghat steps. Though I had only visited Vrindavan three times, Keshi Ghat was our favored place to bathe in the Yamuna....Silent, I stood still on the steps going down to the river, mesmerized by Vrindavan’s sounds and its picturesque visage. First, partially clothed, we bathed by dunking ourselves in the Yamuna a customary three times to rid ourselves of unwanted karma. Then we each bathed in our own way: Guru das afloat with his eyes closed, and me submerged to the chest, chanting Sanskrit Isopanisad verses. Silty and silky, the water soothed to the core. We changed into fresh clothes, washed the dirty ones and spread them out to dry on the hot stone steps. Five minutes later, opulently clean, we chanted our Gayatri mantras overlooking watermelon fields across the river. A breeze blew in soft gusts. “Want to stay here the rest of your life?” Guru das said. “I want Vrindavan to help me become Krishna Conscious. I’ve always wanted to live here. But we shall see,” I answered. We folded our dry clothes and headed off to Loi Bazaar.*

Of course, readers will see a different Yamuna River today than the one eloquently described by Yamuna in the early 70’s. And yet, she often reminisced about Keshi Ghat and its importance to her, and therefore, by Krishna’s grace, there could not have been a more fitting place to hold her final immersion ceremony than in the Yamuna River at Keshi Ghat.

**Yamuna**: *In the summer, shopkeepers in Loi Bazaar take a siesta during the heat of the day. But by late afternoon shops are again alive with activity. Loi Bazaar is Vrindavan’s main mercantile market, and the shops offer goods and services from basic supplies to finely designed and crafted religious paraphernalia. News of our arrival spread quickly from shop to shop. We purchased heavy cotton bed sheets, four buckets, roasted peanuts and fresh orange juice, and then headed for the temple. On the way, the three brothers who manage Nanda Kishore Mukutwalla literally jumped into the road, grabbed our goods and dragged us into their shop. Smiles and warm greetings abounded, and flower garlands were placed around our necks. We thanked them and assured them that we would return, but now wished to settle into our rooms before dark. Then, while they stood with huge grins on their faces, the eldest proudly presented us with a large, cloth-wrapped gift basket to be opened later. They loaded everything into a rickshaw and sent us off to Radha-Damodara Mandir.*

*It was nearly twilight when we stepped onto the roof at Radha-Damodara. Guru das went next door and invited Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das and Satchidananda das to join us. I unwrapped the basket and spread the white cloth on the floor. Then I transferred a stack of leaf cups and plates onto the cloth, followed by a clay dish of fresh, thick yogurt. A three-tiered stainless steel tiffin included a container of fragrant methi paratha flat breads, a container filled with a dry-textured spinach and potato vegetable, and a third one filled with creamy cardamom-scented rice pudding studded with apricot nuggets. Small bunches of baby bananas, oranges, chikus and mangoes were also included, along with a knife. Finally, tiny clay cups of the trademark Radha-Raman temple kuliya sweet (clotted milk fudge) capped off this perfect meal. I lit the lamps and two sticks of incense and placed each before a window. This was our first day as residents of Radha-Damodara Mandir—“the hub of the wheel of the spiritual universe.”*

Although Yamuna and Guru das were enlivened by their first experience as residents of Radha-Damodara Mandir, Yamuna later wrote a short prayer summing up that day:

*Today, Lord Krishna, Srila Prabhupada and the Brijbasis welcomed us to the holy dhama. Now the work begins, and, О Prabhupada, I have the feeling it will greatly challenge us.*

**Yamuna**: *By the end of the first month, I had learned enough Hindi to haggle-shop in nearby Loi Bazaar. Only a four-minute stroll from Radha-Damodara, it still remains the commercial main street for Vrindavan locals and pilgrims. Shops of every variety line the street, and I quickly learned to navigate through the masses of people while speaking in pidgin Hindi and negotiating for necessities like dry pantry items, fruits and vegetables, yogurt and milk, cloth, coal and kerosene, stainless steel pots and dishes, incense and flower garlands.*

During those early days at Radha-Damodara Mandir, Yamuna was determined to undergo any austerity to serve Srila Prabhupada’s mission in the dhama. Unfortunately, Srila Prabhupada’s desire to have an Indian man as president in Vrindavan, chosen from the limited number of Indian disciples, would prove to have devastating consequences for Yamuna. Of course, she had clearly understood the necessity of such a decision. In everything from purchasing vegetables to riding a rickshaw, the foreign devotees were routinely cheated. What would happen if they were charged with building a large temple and guesthouse? As Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das was a businessman, Srila Prabhupada thought that ISKCON had a better chance of not being cheated if he was in charge. He also felt that an Indian president would elicit more respect toward the devotees from the Vrindavan community.

**Yamuna**: *Shortly thereafter, another devotee from the Punjab, Chaitya-guru das, joined us, as did Devananda Swami, who came from Bombay. Srila Prabhupada did not have many Indian students at this time, and he felt that the townspeople might be more respectful if some of the students were of Indian ethnicity. So having Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das as president and then having a Bengali boy, Satchidananda das, and another Indian man, Chaityaguru das, made our group more integrated. Srila Prabhupada was always fully conversant with the importance of time and place. This party was to be the nucleus of Srila Prabhupada’s initial Vrindavan program from April until the fall. Sometimes other devotees would come for short periods, but essentially that first summer consisted of just myself and six or seven men.*

*We knew that Srila Prabhupada had promised to reside in his rooms at Radha-Damodara during Kartika and speak to on The Nectar of Devotion at the samadhi of Srila Rupa Goswami. So for me, renovating his rooms was my first priority.*

## Yamuna on the Renovation of Srila Prabhupada's Rooms at Radha-Damodara Mandir

One of the first services given by Srila Prabhupada to Yamuna in Vrindavan was the renovating of his rooms at Radha-Damodara Mandir, a service she undertook with her usual meticulous planning and determination. (See April 26 letter to Gargamuni das)

**Yamuna**: *We immediately began to \[refurbish\] Srila Prabhupada’s rooms so \[when\] he came during Kartika 1972 for The Nectar of Devotion series of lectures, \[he\] would have renovated rooms to stay in. Just try to imagine. There was nothing—no support systems. I do not speak the language; I am a stranger in a strange transcendental land which my Spiritual Master has given me some access to. Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das was \[from\] a business class, and he had what he felt was a clear understanding of how to behave here, but none of the rest of us did.*

*When the sun sets, we gravitate to the outdoors to welcome the oncoming dusk air on the veranda roof overlooking Rupa Goswami’s samadhi. We sit directly on the slowly cooling cement or on coarse woven rugs called durries, their thick fibers scratching our legs. Along the rooftop ridges of the buildings around us is a silvery fog, at first fading from pale blue to mauve, and then slowly flushing to the color of ripe mango flesh. The two trees standing guard in the samadhi courtyard of Rupa Goswami are first brilliant green orbs, then fade to purple, mauve, and finally soft black, illuminated only by the waxing moon.*

*When I first came to Radha-Damodara Mandir, I was very much immersed in trying to study The Nectar of Devotion because we were in the place of Rupa Goswami’s samadhi. From our roof upstairs, we could look down and see the samadhi and bhajan kutir of Rupa Goswami. So, I had read in The Nectar of Devotion a description of stayi bhava, twelve kinds of transcendental humors which are controlled by different incarnations of God—Kapila, Madhava, Upendra, Nrsimha, Nanda-nandana, Kurma, Kalki, Raghava, Balarama, Varaha, Bhargava and Matysa. So Jiva Goswami informs us that in this stayi bhava there are different colors which represent these various incarnations.*

**Devotional service can therefore be divided into twelve types, each of which has a different color. The colors are white, multicolored, orange, red, light green, gray, yellow, off-whitish, smoky, pink, black and cloudy. The twelve different kinds of transcendental humors are controlled by different incarnations of God, such as Kapila, Madhava, Upendra, Nrsimha, Nanda-nandana, Balarama, Kurma, Kalki, Raghava, Bhargava, Varaha and Matsya.**

**— NECTAR OF DEVOTION, CHAPTER 34, DIRECT AND INDIRECT ATTRACTION FOR KRISHNA**

**Yamuna**: *So I found out the colors. I asked \[Dr.\] О. B. L. Kapoor what the colors were that matched these incarnations, and that is how I came up with the color scheme for Prabhupada’s rooms in Radha-Damodara. So the lower portion of the room (the floor is redder now than I remember) was a nice, reddish sandstone color.... This yellowish-white or ecru color, I believe that’s pandara.... That is represented by Balarama. So the bottom here was the reddish floor, then this lovely ecru color, and then about 18 inches down from the ceiling I painted the color of friendship, which was a reddish-brown color that kind of echoed the color of the sandstone, and that is represented by Upendra. So just at the time when I came to paint this, one lady came from England, and her name was Gangamayi devi dasi. She was a lovely, cheerful person, so anxious to help me, and I was grateful that Krishna had sent her to help me. So the two of us did all the painting.*

*Then above that, in the mood of parenthood, sona was a rather deep red color, and that was the Sanskrit mahamantra—not in English—and with bold letters. So I was a calligrapher, and we did a stencil of the mahamantra going around \[the room\] a little bit down from the ceiling. Then there was a repeated line of this reddish-brown color. So that is what was here in this room, and the same theme was repeated in the kitchen. We had a new wooden seat made ... and a new bed brought in, with cotton webbing.*

*Srila Prabhupada’s asana was cotton saffron and had cotton saffron bedcovers. We had someone bring a lightweight duvet from the West, covered that in saffron cloth and added pillows. We also had a mosquito net for him, with a bamboo frame. Then we built a little shelf, and \[placed there\] a picture of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakur. There were also two jars. Srila Prabhupada was very famous for distributing prasadam. At any given time when someone came to visit, he insisted prasadam be taken. So I had two jars. I filled one with Vrindavan pera from the market, and the other had a Bengali salty snack in it, so one was salty and one sweet.*

*He also had a spittoon, which was kept right next to his chair. Next to that was a shelf where he kept his pen case. He was very particular about his pens and pencils and his tilak. That was also kept right next to his chair. And a little lamp was also there. The lamp was a bona fide electric lamp for reading, because he said \[otherwise\] the light was not bright enough.*

*It would be so nice if it was just as if Prabhupada could come and go, get his clothes out of the trunk and spend the night here any time he wants, because these rooms are his eternal residence. I’ve heard different accounts over the years. But I was personally present in this room when Prabhupada said that these rooms are the hub of the wheel of the spiritual world. Those were the exact words he used. He may have used different words to others, but to me he said, “They are my eternal residence, and they are the hub of the wheel of the spiritual world.” So we can’t even imagine the potency of these rooms.*

## “Making this Vrindavan Project a Heaven on Earth”

It quickly became clear that working with Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das as president was both bewildering and distressing for Yamuna. As he himself later admitted, he was very fixed in the certainty of his philosophical positions, particularly with regard to the position of women. His prior experiences were with Indian ladies of his own cultural orbit, and suffice it to say, Yamuna did not conform to his expectations. Further, he was already causing distress to Srila Prabhupada in managing the Raman Reti construction due to what Srila Prabhupada called his “overspending,” while demanding severe restrictions from the devotees working under him. Devotees would come and not be able to stay, due to a lack of “devotee care” so important to Srila Prabhupada, and this cut to the heart of Yamuna. It is clear from Srila Prabhupada’s letter of April 2,1972, that Yamuna and Guru das had written to him about this. Srila Prabhupada’s reply for them to work cooperatively with others and to “take charge mostly of supervising the building work,” combined with his direction that Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das spend more time laying out the Hindi Back to Godheads and engaging in printing and translating work, indicated a change in direction on that front.

Yamuna strongly retained the desire to fulfill Srila Prabhupada’s instruction to create an atmosphere in the holy dhamas where devotees from all over the world could come and taste the “special atmosphere of spiritual life.” She was particularly touched by his calling his American and European students “angels by coming to Krishna Consciousness more and more.”

**Now in India you must develop things also very nicely, especially for attracting overseas visitors to come there and enjoy \[the\] Indian special atmosphere of spiritual life. Our Indian boys and girls are not very much interested to become devotees, but I am seeing that these fair-skinned Americans and Europeans are like angels by coming to Krishna Consciousness increasingly more and more, and that very soon the whole world will become filled with such angels, and so I am very optimistic that if we continue in this way by sticking very tightly to our pure standards that the Lord Chaitanya’s prediction will very soon be realized all over the world....**

**I am very much thankful for the letter of Yamuna. Now you two work cooperatively for making our Vrindavan a dazzling success, along with others you work nicely, and I think Ksirodakasayi may spend more time on laying out the Hindi BTG and doing that printing and translating work and you take mostly charge of supervising building work. I have requested Saurabha, our new Holland devotee in Bombay, who is an excellent designer, to send you plans for the Vrindavan scheme, but meanwhile you should concentrate on collecting as much cement, sand, stone chips and steel as possible and stockpile them, along with bricks, etc. Meanwhile Gargamuni is collecting very nicely in Bombay for Vrindavan scheme, so you have not to worry about money as he will be in charge of that department, so you may correspond with him frequently and work together all of you for making this Vrindavan project a heaven on earth.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS AND YAMUNA, APR. 2, 1972**

One such young “angel” who came to visit Yamuna and Guru das in those early Radha-Damodara days was a very renounced young Western man who would become His Holiness Radhanath Swami. Yamuna remembered him in those days as being very quiet and shy and looking very much like a Brijbasi babaji. His natural humility, gravity and kindness were a wonderful relief from the sometimes harsh and forceful personalities in their devotional community, and Yamuna very much appreciated his visits:

**Radhanath Swami**: And then \[Yamuna\] was called to India. And she traveled at Prabhupada’s side throughout this country, and was eventually assigned to come to Vrindavan, Srila Prabhupada’s eternal home. Srila Prabhupada gave her and Guru das the task of establishing a temple here, something that was not only a sacred vision of Srila Prabhupada, imagine, he lived in Radha-Damodara temple for about six years. And it was his dream to bring people from all over the world here. He entrusted that service to Yamuna devi and Guru das prabhu. And in those days, it was so difficult; so many obstacles. I remember one of the most transforming experiences in my own personal life. In 1972,I already had to leave Vrindavan, because of my visa. But from Nepal I came just for a week. And when I came back to Vrindavan, Yamuna devi and Guru das prabhu were staying then at Radha-Damodara temple. And I would sit with them for hours and hours and hours, and help them with some seva. When they would talk to each other, the only thing they ever said, hour after hour, day after day, is, “What will please Srila Prabhupada? This will please Srila Prabhupada. This is what Srila Prabhupada wants.” I had never, ever experienced anything like this. Such total devotion, total absorption in pleasing the guru. It was from Yamuna devi that I first got a glimpse of understanding what is guru nistha, what is faith in guru, what is guru seva, what is that total absorption, where every word, every act, every thought is an offering of love to one’s spiritual master. And I remember thinking at that time—because I had met Srila Prabhupada, and accepted him as my Spiritual Master—this is the standard I must strive for; this is pure devotional service.

## A Snapshot of Yamuna’s First Summer at Radha-Damodara Mandir

**Yamuna**: If possible, Brijbasis prefer sleeping under the night sky, not under a ceiling. Buildings are constructed with flat roofs with this purpose in mind. Whether a two-room single family home, large joint-family dwelling or thirty-room ashram surrounding a central courtyard—all residential buildings are designed with flat roofs. Mendicant sadhus and yogis without a permanent roof are content to blanket down on the ground—under trees, on the banks of the Yamuna River, even by the roadside. Night lamps twinkle on Vrindavan rooftops like stars in the firmament, or like giant fire flies.

We gravitated to the roof to relish the short light show and discuss the progress of our work. Street smells and sounds drifted upward: bicycle horns cut through the foot traffic; cow hooves echoed off brick lanes; thick smoke rose from coal and dung fires, mingled with the spicy fragrance of vegetable curries and buttery flat breads sold by street vendors. Before joining the others, I usually made a chilled lassi of yogurt, water, shaved ice, crushed mint leaves, a little salt and freshly-crushed roasted cumin, placed in a jug and whisked into a lacy froth with a wooden whisk.

The lassis helped us to relax as we discussed the status of our work— what had been done, what was pending, what to do next. Everything was a struggle, even the current simple task of buying materials for a temporary fence and the foundation—cement, steel rebar and bricks. After this, we talked about something on all of our minds. At dawn each morning, we walked, chanting kirtan, from Radha-Damodara to our construction site in Raman Reti. For the last three mornings we arrived at the site to find an immense, fiery-tempered bull under our tamal tree. Whether he was sitting or standing, his menace and breathy snorts terrified us all. Today we heard he was called “The Sadhu Killer” by the Brijbasis. Of course, we must somehow encourage him to go, because our workers and deliveries will soon arrive. But after three days, he still kept us at bay. We try everything—gongs, kartals, bull handlers—but nothing seems to work. We hear rumors that the bull has killed three, four, five or ten sadhus, depending on who was speaking. Finally, by Krishna’s mercy, the bull appeared to lumber off on his own—another casualty averted.

## Yamuna Becomes Fireproof and Waterproof

**Yamuna**: My husband sleeps outside with the other men. It is not the first time since arriving in India I have regretted being in a woman’s body, and certainly not the last. Vrindavan etiquette requires that unrelated men and women sleep separately. As the only woman, I have no choice but to sleep inside. I retire early and get up early, so having my own space is not all bad. When I step in my room it feels as hot as an oven. The exterior wall has begun to creak and moan, audibly cooling down. Today marks two weeks of blistering temperatures over 125 Fahrenheit. The window frame in my room is barred, without glass, and draped with a cloth for privacy. No night air. No cross ventilation.

By candlelight, I settle into a two-bucket ritual to deal with my predicament. Indian rooms are typically built with a drain hole at one corner of a barely sloping floor. It is there to facilitate washing the floor. First the floor is doused with water and swished around with a short-handled broom; then the excess water is shooed out the drain hole. With the door bolted, I remove my lengths of cloth and take a bucket-bath using silky gray Yamuna River mud in lieu of soap; then I rinse off with ladles of sandal-infused scented water from the first bucket. When the bathing water is swished out the hole, I place an inflated air mattress on the cement floor. The Radha-Damodara temple priest saves me the rose garlands offered daily and these are soaked in the second bucket of water now at my side. When on the mattress, I wet a length of gauzy cotton, wring it out, cover myself head to toe and then lay down at last. Mmm. Hmm. Sweet relief—for about ten minutes.

If I’m not asleep in minutes, I begin to pray, “Please dear Radha-Damodara, help me to conquer this heat—become impervious to it and deal with it, as Prabhupada before me, and as goswamis do. Let me tolerate it better tomorrow than I have today.” Or I reflect on an instruction Prabhupada gave me some months earlier in Calcutta. He must have foreseen me in this situation, for he chuckled as he said, “Yamuna, in Vrindavan you must become fireproof. Sometimes the heat is unbearable there. You have already lived in London and become waterproof; so much rain is there. You must become both fireproof and waterproof. Then you can live anywhere and not be bothered.”

Until I learn to deal with the heat more effectively, my sleep habits will remain scattered. Because my cloth tent dries in ten minutes, I wake to repeat the process several times a night. Or I wake up and chant japa and again take rest. Late afternoon is another rest period, and I repeat the process yet again. In this way I sleep about five or six hours a day. Sometimes I just take the opportunity to reflect on the fact that I have been allowed to live in the same temple that Prabhupada lived in before he came to America. I want to learn more about the lives of other great saints who have lived here before then. I want to research the lives of the Six Goswamis of Vrindavan, the history of this temple, the Deities in the temple, and the life of its founder, Srila \]iva Goswami.

Srila Prabhupada’s study has one of the few ceiling fans in the Radha-Damodara complex. Few homes are equipped with ceiling fans, and if they are, they are usually saved for the intense afternoon heat or when company calls. Locals tolerate heat without complaining, without fans - many even without lights. Prabhupada’s first two years in Radha-Damodara were spent upstairs without electricity. In the early 60 s, when electric lines were stretched to Seva Kunj, he agreed to put 1,000 rupees into the renovation of his two rented rooms downstairs, and installed a ceiling fan in one of them. Now, in the 70’s, there is still no electricity upstairs, but we have rigged it with an extension cord from downstairs to provide us with one bulb and one plug. Electricity plunged Vrindavan into the modern world, its nighttime bazaar now illuminated by ubiquitous single bulbs dangling over saleable wares. The taste of summer refreshment also changed dramatically, for now stalls offer ice and cold or iced items—sodas, ice cream lollies, shaved ice and chilled, frothy lassi yogurt drinks. Every night at dusk, my husband and 1, sometimes with others, walk to Loi Bazaar and purchase thick fresh yogurt and ice to make a lassi refreshment. Maybe we add freshly roasted peanuts, fresh water chestnuts or cape gooseberries, if they are available. We find it too hot to eat anything more than that.

## Yamuna’s Struggles with Calligraphy in the Heat

**Yamuna**: *The walls in our quarters are made with a single thickness of small red bricks, originally mortared in place with an adobe mixture of river mud and broken straw. Most of the mortar is now gone, so the sunlight peeks through junctures in the brick in several places. The elements have rounded off the corners of the bricks, enabling a mother swallow to nest in one of the larger crevices. Now her family lives in a wall of the room that serves as our office at Radha-Damodara temple. As elsewhere, the office is the coolest during the brahma muharta hours, the two hours before dawn, when it is still dark outside. I prefer to do office work just after mangal arati, which is held at 4:30 am in the summer. When it is dark outside, the mother and chicks remain quiet, but with the first morning sun, bits of straw and mud rain down on the floor, and hungry mouths chirp. This bird family and a female monkey named Harsharani are pets of a sort, for I feed them on a regular basis, and they are entertaining company.*

*We have one electric typewriter, but it is used infrequently because even with our one electric cord, city electricity is off as much as on. It is rarely on during the hours I like to work. At these times, I resort to writing correspondence as it has been done for the last several centuries—by hand. This is a way to keep my calligraphy skills alive. The heat plays a role even in letter writing. It is hard to find a moment in the day when my arm is not damp with sweat. The moisture wrinkles my writing paper and blurs the ink. So in the early morning, I place a fold of cotton cloth under my forearm and write correspondence.*

*I wonder during what hours Krishnadas Kaviraja Goswami and )iva Goswami calligraphed their manuscripts in this very place. How did they treat palm leaves so they did not absorb moisture as paper does in damp conditions? Four hundred years ago, Radha-Damodara temple held the largest library of Vaishnava literature in Vrindavan. How was it stored? In previous centuries, did these great Vaishnava authors write in the cool dark hours of night instead of during the day? Perhaps, as Bhaktivinoda Thakur and Srila Prabhupada did, they wrote the bulk of their manuscripts between midnight and dawn. Prabhupada began this writing routine during his residence at Radha-Damodara in the early 60 s, and when he left Vrindavan, he continued this system no matter where he was in the world. During his residence here, he either handwrote and then typed, or directly typed all his manuscripts on a small portable machine. In 1966 in the United States, he began using a Dictaphone, speaking text or purports only once, which was later transcribed, copy- and Sanskrit-edited, proofed and put into production. All prolific writers follow a writing schedule, and his was so fixed that he was able to complete 75 full-length volumes in 11 years using this system.*

It is so illuminating all these years later to read Yamuna’s abstract on Vrindavan in the summer of 1972. Although it is almost impossible to make comparisons to the Vrindavan of today, it takes us back into another era, one where cars were scarce, Vrindavan was still a village, and the hunger for Western materialism had not yet infected the hearts of some of its populace. Yamuna’s colorful portrait of Vrindavan is all the more enduring and timeless because of her honest accounting of her personal struggles as a woman, something that would continue in injurious and even sinister ways.

## Srila Prabhupada’s Displeasure with the Progress at Raman Reti

**Yamuna**: *Srila Prabhupada wanted a design for our Raman Reti temple similar to that of the Radha-Govinda temple in Vrindavan. There seemed to be a continual confusion that summer over design, construction progress and many other aspects of the construction. Saurabha das, the current architect, was then in Bombay. So during that summer a tone of displeasure appeared in many of Srila Prabhupada’s letters at the endless delays in the construction work, one after another, from the first fence building, to getting the foundation built, to finalizing the architecture, to obtaining the materials, to finding laborers, and to our not being cheated a great deal. There were just so many things that seemed to meet with Srila Prabhupada’s displeasure. There was also a bypassing of mails, where we would send him a letter, and he would have already sent us another letter, and they would be crossing in the mails, so he would not get the report that he wanted. That mood was there. It was both an exciting time and also very challenging time, because displeasure of the Spiritual Master is an intense experience.*

Another complication during this time was the ongoing attempts to obtain the glorious Keshi Ghat palace of Bharatpur Maharaja, Laxmi Rani Kunj. Yamuna and Guru das had worked diligently to have the palace either donated or sold for a modest amount to ISKCON. The negotiations began in 1971, and by late August of 1972 the Maharaja had agreed to donate the palace with the proviso that ISKCON pay for the surrounding land and guest quarters. Yamuna very much wanted this palace for the glory of Srila Prabhupada, but unfortunately it was not meant to be. The Trust, however, did allow the visiting devotees coming for Kartika to reside in rooms there.

**Please accept my blessings. I am in due receipt of your telegram as follows: “Bharatpur Trust will donate Kesi Ghat temple will sell surrounding rooms and garden we must offer price wire immediately.” So I have received this telegram and have replied by telegram as follows: “Why not donate the whole thing and we spend money to make super gorgeous.”**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, SEPT. I, 1972**

## Yamuna’s Crucible—An Accusation of Impropriety and its Outcome

In writing of Yamuna’s devotional odyssey, I have been careful to avoid rehashing ISKCON’s political mistakes on a personal or collective level where those mistakes do not directly impact the progression of Yamuna’s devotional life. Where it is necessary to touch on these incidences or name a person involved, I humbly apologize in advance for any unintentional offenses to others, because Yamuna’s journey was one of trying to see each event or occurrence, whether instructional or challenging, as an opportunity to advance in her own devotional life. However, the particular episode chronicled in this section changed Yamuna’s spiritual perspective for the remainder of her life, and is essential to understanding how she was able to draw on hidden strengths and continually rededicate herself heart and soul to Srila Prabhupada and to devotional service. Much of the information is in the public domain, but the threads of its impact have not before been woven into the tapestry of Yamuna’s life history.

**Yamuna**: *Our early Radha-Damodara team is a family of sorts, held together by the easy bond between my husband and me. Because our relationship is warm, relaxed, comfortable and kind, so are our extended family relationships, whether at meals, in classes or at work. In some ways, every male in the party finds a way to extend some type of special kindness to me. They rotate doing jobs traditionally considered women’s work—fetching pails of cooking and bathing water, shopping, or washing up the dishes after a meal. I spend the little down time I have with my husband, and when he is out of station, I am content being alone. If there is any vacuum in my life at Radha-Damodara, it is the lack of female companionship. My closest English-speaking friend, Madira, the wife of the ISKCON Delhi president, resides 90 miles away. A talented young woman who sings like a nightingale and plays a mridanga drum like a Bengali professional, she shares my love for kirtan and chanting together, and when she comes we ferret out a quiet nook and begin chanting. Those moments are especially memorable to me. Unfortunately, Madira does not come often. Were it not for Sarajini, the wizened Bengali widow living in the cranny outside the main temple gate, I would be entirely devoid of the company of a woman.*

*Jaya Sarajini — the woman Srila Prabhupada said would go Back to Godhead by her service of bringing Yamuna water every day for Radha-Damodara. Her rheumy gray eyes are set in a face etched with deep lines; her leathery, loose skin hangs on a bony frame. I suspect she is in her late sixties. Like many longtime Vrindavan widows, she wears a single length of once white cotton cloth, now gray with age, tied into a sari Bengali-style. Her sticklike body is bent almost in half from the waist, pitching her forward to a near 45 degree angle, her head tilted upright to see. The only comfortable way for Sarajini to work, relax or converse is to drop on her haunches, hips to heel, and balance on the balls of her feet. When I do the same, we are eye to eye. Though our pidgin language is incomplete, we still manage to communicate using hand gestures, crude illustrations made in sand, and the few Hindi words and phrases I have picked up. Our first shared company is at mangal arati, where she invariably plays a brass gong—Boing boing-boing being—like a metronome. Often we are the only ones present, so I sing and play kartals, following along with her beat. The mood is serene yet exciting, timeless and connected.*

*Slowly we begin conversing, mostly about practical things. One day when I am struggling with a coal fire that smokes instead of burns, she shows me how to get it going. Or she shows me how to design and construct a free-standing stove out of mud and brick. Another time she comes with me to the market and shows me the best places to purchase different grades of hard and soft coal used in cooking fires. Sometimes we worship tulasi together or chant japa at the samadhi of Rupa Goswami.*

*Dr. Kapoor informs us that Vrindavan residents are eyeing the behavior of our group, especially mine. Not only am I the first Western woman Vaishnava to live in Vrindavan, I’m the first Caucasian woman to reside in the Radha-Damodara temple compound—the only woman in an ever-fluctuating number of men. It is obvious that the village residents deem me a curiosity: my every public gesture is met with a smile or nod, along with eyebrowraising scrutiny. This makes me all the more dependent on following the etiquette I have been taught by Prabhupada.*

However, this familial mood was soon to change. It was clear that by May, even though Srila Prabhupada had instructed Yamuna to assist in the building project along with her other services (see letter of April 2, 1972), Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das was uncomfortable with her role due to her gender. From the beginning of her devotional life, Srila Prabhupada routinely requested Yamuna to oversee important projects and often relied on her opinion, but despite this, Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das was unable to accept her participation. Even though Yamuna’s husband, Guru das, tried to intervene on her behalf, Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das remained intransigent, and Guru das was compelled to write Srila Prabhupada requesting his clarification on the matter:

**So far your question regarding women, I have always accepted the service of women without any discrimination, so I have no objection if Yamuna devi contributes her ideas on this construction project. Nothing should be done without group consultation. Our work in Vrindavan and elsewhere should be encouraged by good consultation.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, MAY 26, 1972**

In June, Ksirodakasayi Vishnu das informed Srila Prabhupada that he was leaving India for London for some time. Perhaps because he was so immovably wedded to his understanding of Vedic culture, his short stint as president had proved challenging not only to Yamuna, but to other devotees as well. With his departure, Yamuna hoped to have more freedom and flexibility in her service.

**Now I understand that Ksirodakasayi is going to London soon, so in his absence you shall be the president and I think if Tejiyas is there, that he can be treasurer, or I have heard that Vaikunthanatha is there, so if it is better arrangement, then he can be treasurer and your wife Yamuna devi may act as secretary.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, JUNE 12, 1972**

Unfortunately, before leaving Vrindavan, the president and three brahma-charis wrote letters to Srila Prabhupada asserting that inappropriate relations were going on between a young sannyasi and Yamuna devi. The troubled young sannyasi had come to Vrindavan and found in Yamuna someone who would listen to his problems in a nonjudgmental way. By nature, Yamuna was compassionate, caring and motherly. She was also a good listener and had taken seriously Srila Prabhupada’s instruction to try to encourage devotees coming from the West. It is not necessary to disparage the sannyasi here, as he left long ago, but he was a troubled soul, and Yamuna tried to help him. That was the extent of the relationship. To those who truly knew Yamuna and the sannyasi, it was a ridiculous slander to both, but it devastated Yamuna to the core of her being, not just because of the slander itself and the subsequent damage to her reputation it temporarily caused, but how Srila Prabhupada originally addressed it. Instead of writing her for clarification as he had always previously done, he instead wrote to her husband:

**Please accept my blessings. I have recently received several letters from the others there in Vrindavan, wherein they have mentioned there may be some illicit relationship between Devananda Swami and your wife, Yamuna devi. I want to know if there is any substance to this claim, you may be frank and honest with me as much as possible because I am very much in anxiety on this account. Therefore I have asked Devananda to leave India for working as pujari in Nairobi.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS, JULY 22, 1972**

Yamuna once described the above letter as like a dagger to her heart. She could not comprehend how Srila Prabhupada, knowing her total dedication and complete surrender as he did, would consider that she would insult him and his mission by behaving inappropriately in the holy dhama. She was deeply wounded by that much more than the accusation itself. Srila Prabhupada later wrote to Guru das and Yamuna the following letter on August 3,1972, and, in an addendum to a letter to Acyutananda Swami on August 5, reaffirmed that he had never doubted her “impeccable character.”

**Please accept my blessings. I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letters dated July 30,1972, along with letters from Satchidananda and Acyutananda, and I have noted the contents carefully. Do not be disturbed, now I understand everything. You and your husband live in Vrindavan permanently. I never took the accusations seriously because I did not believe it, therefore I enquired from you what is the situation. Now the matter is clear, so do not be disturbed.**

**Now you, husband and wife, develop the Vrindavan scheme. Long ago you wanted to go to Vrindavan, so I think you are perfectly meant to remain there and look after the things. But live carefully, it is India, we must live according to the time, place and circumstances, that is intelligence. On the whole, except with your husband, you should not mix with anyone very intimately, just like Indian ladies do.**

**So you may not be disturbed that Ksirodakasayi is coming back there, I shall ask him to remain here for developing London center.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS AND YAMUNA, AUG. 3, 1972**

**So far Yamuna is concerned, I never doubted once her impeccable character, simply I wanted to find out the actual position. There is a saying in Bengali, that whenever there is scandalous talk, there is something to it, so we must be careful always to avoid even what may be mistaken by others for scandalous situation. You know how the things are taken in India so be yourself very careful to always avoid these things and instruct others how to do it also.**

**— LETTER TO ACYUTANANDA SWAMI, AUG. 5, 1972**

Yamuna’s despair was not completely allayed by the letters, but ultimately they caused her to internally reevaluate the depth of her faith and commitment to the process of Krishna Consciousness as well as to Srila Prabhupada himself. She became certain that there was an underlying reason that Srila Prabhupada and Krishna had challenged her in this way, and although it took a great deal of introspection, chanting and prayer, she gradually understood it as a gift—the gift of Srila Prabhupada teaching her to internalize his teachings, instructions and love so that she could draw strength from them for the rest of her life.

Srila Prabhupada’s ISKCON Movement had been gradually experiencing a conversion in the behavior of some of its men towards women, particularly now that many men were taking sannyasa. Being the only woman on the Krishna-Balarama Temple project alongside an ever-changing influx of men gave Yamuna a unique perspective on the difficulties to come. This created within her an increased urgency and impetus to somehow protect her fledgling devotional creeper by full immersion in her service to Srila Prabhupada and the Vaishnavas. In the end, she saw this experience as her first massive test—one which would take time to process, understand and, ultimately, to benefit by. Years later, Yamuna would draw parallels between her experience and the banishment of Jiva Goswami by his Guru, Rupa Goswami—not by comparing herself to Jiva Goswami, but in seeing how he had humbly and unquestionably accepted the severe chastisement of Rupa Goswami. He had merely been defending the reputation of his Guru, something all disciples must do, yet Rupa Goswami banished him for having false pride. Yamuna realized from this challenge, as she would from others in the ensuing years, that in order to protect her devotional creeper and ultimately advance in Krishna Consciousness, she would have to dive deeply into the practice of determination, tolerance and humility—taking strength from the vivid examples in the scriptures and the experiences of our predecessor Acharyas.

**Certainly it was right for Jiva Goswami to stop such a dishonest scholar from advertising that he had defeated Srila Rupa Goswami and Sanatana Goswami, but due to their illiteracy the sahajiya class refer to this incident to accuse Srila Jiva Goswami of deviating from the principle of humility. They do not know, however, that humility and meekness are appropriate when one’s own honor is insulted but not when Lord Vishnu or the Acharyas are blasphemed.**

**— CAITANYA-CARITAMRTA 2.10.85 PURPORT**

As with the experience in Allahabad when she was asked to sit in the back after having had free access to Srila Prabhupada from the beginning of her spiritual life, Yamuna realized that Srila Prabhupada was training her to take more shelter of his vani—his instructions and training—and not depend on his physical presence.
