She came to understand that Srila Prabhupada, knowing her dependence on him, was preparing her for his departure by forcing her to stand on her own devotional “feet.” The events of the next few years would clarify this, as he continued to teach her to understand that her relationship with him was eternal, and that he would always be present with her through her faith, her dependence on him and her adherence to the practice of devotional service. Yamuna felt the presence of Srila Prabhupada’s mercy for the rest of her life, fully understanding what Srila Prabhupada meant when he said about his own Spiritual Master, “I have never been apart from him—not for one second.” Whenever a challenge would later present itself, she would immediately say, “What does Srila Prabhupada want me to learn from this? What is Krishna trying to teach me in this situation?”

Yamuna expanded on this principle in a talk to a group of young devotees in 201I in Melbourne Beach, Florida, shortly before she passed on. Commenting on a statement of Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati Thakur:

**Yamuna**: **Cancala jivana**—*“The precarious current of your life is relentlessly flowing into the ocean of time.”*

*So this is one of these kinds of statements that takes you out of your frog-in-the-well hole to a different world, out of the sphere of “1, Me, and Mine.” It opens the door into a whole other dimension. Krishna Consciousness is not in this dimension. Sometimes in my youth, when I first lived in Vraja, I would see people come from the West for the first time or even look at myself for the first time that day, and I would realize how much I was caught up in my own “1, Me, Mine” world. And the Krishna Consciousness that the sadhus, saints and great advanced devotees who live in the dhama and know what the dhama really is, they don’t live this life, this “1, Me, Mine” life. So this is one of those statements, “The precarious current of your life is relentlessly pouring into the ocean of time,” that changes how you evaluate your internal life and your relationships.*

*So the purport, I believe, to his statement says, “When a person has attained this wisdom, his tendency to serve Sri Hari will manifest at every step.” Therefore it is our duty ... to accept with a satisfied heart whatever pleases Lord Sri Krishna. Now that is not so easy to do, because in this world of opposites, we are always evaluating, “What is to be done; what is not to be done.” That is one of the principles of Rupa Goswami. But actually, the more we get established in the \[nine-fold\] processes of bhakti... the more we are just tasting these processes, it will become self-evident, so that we actually know what pleases Krishna. If Sri Krishna feels happy by keeping me in a state of aversion to Him, even then I shall respectfully accept any suffering I must consequently endure. And that \[wisdom\] comes when you have big challenges.*

Srila Prabhupada also wrote to Guru das and Yamuna again, reiterating to Yamuna the importance of observing the etiquette of ladies in India. This principle was extremely difficult for Yamuna, not just because of the unfamiliar etiquette itself, but because she had been given so many services to perform. How would she be able to “not mix with anyone”?

Yamuna had already been given important services to perform, such as preparing Srila Prabhupada’s rooms at Radha-Damodara, something she took very seriously, as seen before. But especially important was arranging for the Deities and seva for the Krishna-Balarama Mandir. She also wanted to ensure that the facilities for the arriving devotees were clean and the prasadam healthful and filling. When Srila Prabhupada finally arrived on October 15,1972, Yamuna was often so engaged in serving Srila Prabhupada and the devotees that she was frequently not present for his discourses.

## Srila Prabhupada Arrives for the Month of Damodara

**Yamuna**: As the time came for Srila Prabhupada’s arrival, more and more devotees began filtering in. An arrangement had been made through the Bharatpur Trust that the devotees would reside at the palace known as Laxmi Rani Kunj, at Keshi Ghat, on the Yamuna River. The devotees would then come morning and evening to the Radha-Damodara temple and attend the programs at sunrise and sunset. Srila Prabhupada had come to Vrindavan with a new servant, Srutakirti das, and from the very beginning, he informed me that Srutakirti was never to leave him alone. Srila Prabhupada would often ask me, “Where is Srutakirti? Where is Srutakirti?” and he told me that he never wanted a moment when he was not protected by his servant or guarded by one or more of his men. Although he had never stressed it, some of his servants may not have been as strict about this as they could have been. As the years progressed, his close servants became more attentive to his protection without his having to speak to them. But in those days he was so humble he used to have to ask for such things. He said, “I always want my men surrounding me,” and he likened it to being on the battlefield, where there are so many difficulties. He said that we are on the battlefield, preaching against the demons and the onslaughts of maya, and a close-knit community is required. The general may direct, but the soldiers go out and do the fighting. So Srila Prabhupada was the general, and his soldiers were to be present at any time. He added that there are many envious people in Vrindavan, and we had to deal very carefully with them, especially those of us who lived here on a regular basis. Srila Prabhupada had left his humble rooms in Radha-Damodara alone, and now he came back to Vrindavan with a large following of devotees. So it was natural that enviousness would increase in some residents, and we should be on our guard for that.

## Sweet Exchanges Between Yamuna and Srila Prabhupada

Perhaps because of the earlier debacle with the accusations of impropriety and its obvious impact on Yamuna, other devotees noted during this time that Srila Prabhupada was especially solicitous of Yamuna and often wanted her close by. Yamuna also felt that Srila Prabhupada, although holding her to his usual rigorous standards, was especially kind in engaging her and allowing her ample access to him.

**Gangamayi devi**: I remember once taking prasadam to Srila Prabhupada’s room. This was downstairs, and because Prabhupada was so used to Yamuna taking in the plate, she said, “Why don’t you take it in today?” And I thought, “This is such a wonderful thing, having the chance to serve Srila Prabhupada by taking in his prasadam.” I was feeling very blissful. And so I went in, and Prabhupada said, “Where is Yamuna?” And I thought, “Oh, I can’t have this relationship, no matter how hard I try.” So I said, “1’1I go get her, Srila Prabhupada.” At least I can do that; I can fly across the courtyard to get Yamuna. I think after that I was reluctant to do anything, to take things in, because Prabhupada was very concerned even where Yamuna was, because she was with him so much. Even at the darshans at night, if she was doing some service, he would look around and say, “Where is Yamuna?” And someone would say, “She is working here” or there or wherever. But he wanted to know immediately where she was and was concerned.

**Yamuna**: *Except during the months of Kartika or Damodara, generally speaking there is little devotional activity in the Radha-Damodara temple from outside. During the entire time we stayed there, we were usually among the only devotees who attended the aratis. Of course, there was Sarajini, the Bengali widow who brought water for the Deities, and there was another Bengali baba who played the gong, and the pujari, and that was it. But during the month of Damodara, the temple priest would dress himself nicely and decorate his body with tilak in twelve places, then go on parikrama and speak to the guests who came. At 1:30 am many pilgrims began to filter into the temple, and all of them would have already taken bath in the Yamuna River and then come to the Radha-Damodara temple. We would hear all kinds of devotional bhajans,japa and sankirtan before the Deities had Their mangal arati at about 4:15 am. So by 2:45 am, there was a transcendental roar of different transcendental sound vibrations going on. And of course, Srila Prabhupada wanted our party to participate as well.*

*So it was my habit when Srila Prabhupada allowed me to serve him that I rose quite early and always presented myself as cleanly as possible, externally and internally. In fact, throughout my Krishna Conscious life, much of my association with Srila Prabhupada was during those morning hours. Whether we were in Bombay, Surat, Indore, Jaipur, Madras, Visakha-patnam, Calcutta, Mayapur, Delhi or Vrindavan, I always tried to be near Srila Prabhupada during that time. Usually I would just sit very quietly at some distant place within the area Srila Prabhupada was residing, to draw in the incredible strength of his Krishna Consciousness at this time of morning.*

*Srila Prabhupada rose at about i:oo am, so this one morning at about 2:30 am, I was in the courtyard along with many other pilgrims, and somehow Srila Prabhupada knew I was there. I heard a resounding, “Yamuna, come here.” Then he asked, “Where is our kirtan party?” as if I knew where they were. Of course, I had no idea. He repeated, “Why are they not here?” I said, “I can’t say, Srila Prabhupada.” So he was very anxious for the kirtan party to come, but they didn’t come. And when it came time for mangal arati, our party had not come, and then after mangal arati, as all the pilgrims took parikrama around the Deities, they had still not arrived. By then it was about 5:30 am, and Srila Prabhupada was continually asking, “Where is our party? Where is our party?” Then we heard this resounding roar, “HARE KRISHNA, HARE KRISHNA, KRISHNA KRISHNA, HARE HARE.” I was sitting just outside Srila Prabhupada’s door, and our party members danced in as if to say, “Where are all the pilgrims? How come they are not here?” And everyone had already come and gone, and Srila Prabhupada was extremely displeased. He said if someone can’t get up before four in the morning and have the sankirtan party here for mangal arati, they are useless. So he was displeased at that. He wanted sankirtan, and especially during the month of Damodara he expected that our devotees would be here along with all the other pilgrims. Sometimes this was done and sometimes it wasn’t done, but it was one of those requests that Srila Prabhupada seemed to emphasize to me, as if I should somehow make this clear to others. He would say to me “Why are they sleeping so late?” He was always very pleased when he saw the devotees rising early in the mangal hours of the morning and practicing Krishna Consciousness.*

*Srila Prabhupada generally stayed inside his room with his shutters closed and listened to the early morning kirtans like that. When mangal arati started, his doors opened, and he attended by sitting in his room and watching the Deities from his seat. He told me that many years earlier, he had observed the Deities from the same position as he now sat—worshiping Sri Sri Radha-Damodara from his room.*

A prominent feature of the exchanges between Srila Prabhupada and Yamuna was this “expectation” element of their relationship, where he would expect her to know why something was not being done, even though it was not related to her service. She understood this as another way that Srila Prabhupada was training her to learn from the mistakes of others and apply them in the future of her Krishna Conscious life. The uncovered mridangas were an example of this.

**Yamuna**: *Another thing I observed repeatedly was Srila Prabhupada’s displeasure whenever our mridanga drums were not covered. As early as San Francisco, I saw Srila Prabhupada take off his own outer cloth and cover the drum with it. He said then that drums must be covered. So during this time, on several occasions Srila Prabhupada asked me why the drums were not covered, as if I were somehow responsible. Once, after the sankirtan party came to the Radha-Damodara temple, we had our program, and then Srila Prabhupada stored the drums in his kitchen and wouldn’t even eat his breakfast—he was so angry. Another time he personally took off his covering before his breakfast and covered the drum with it—wrapped it up. And another time when the drum came back uncovered, after he had covered it with his own cloth, he chastised me and said, “I don’t want to see these drums in my rooms anymore.” And so I was the recipient of his anger, even though I had nothing to do with the sankirtan party then or the persons who were playing the drums. There were some things that he asked of us over and over again, and somehow when they weren’t done he could be consummately patient on one hand, but on the other hand, he would become a little disgusted. He expected us to learn from his instructions and from our mistakes.*

*One morning I was making Srila Prabhupada’s bed, and under his pillow he had left a molar tooth which had fallen out. He knew I would be cleaning his room, so he left his tooth for me to find. I cherished that tooth as I did all gifts from Srila Prabhupada. It was later taken from me, but I never forgot the sweetness of that gesture.*

*Srila Prabhupada had an extraordinary tolerance for pain. During this month he had cut his toe, and it had become infected. Even as early as 1972, Srila Prabhupada was sometimes bothered by edema in the lower legs and feet. But his foot was definitely becoming infected, and his leg had swollen considerably up to the mid-calf. It appeared to be extremely painful. Even the swelling must have been extremely painful, what to speak of the infection. And what did Srila Prabhupada want as a medicine? He said to grind neem leaves on a stone, mix it with turmeric and mustard oil and make a poultice. He then spread the poultice over the wound and over his lower leg, and then he bound it all with fresh banana leaves. When he sat, he held that leg out, so he couldn’t sit in a cross-legged fashion. But never once did he complain of pain, nor did he want any Western medicines. This lasted for four or five days, and then it began to subside. Unless one observed the raw and swollen foot, one might not have known that Srila Prabhupada had to have been in pain. He did not limp when he walked, and his preaching never stopped or slowed down in any way. It was painful for me to even look at his foot, but he just continued on with his preaching and other services*

## Yamuna Cooks for Srila Prabhupada at Radha-Damodara

**Yamuna**: *Before Prabhupada arrived in October, we had refurbished his rooms, including his kitchen. As far as possible, we tried to preserve the existing design of the room, and divided it into a cooking area and an eating area with a neat row of bricks. Two coats of white paint brightened the ceiling and walls. Wanting to please Srila Prabhupada by learning as much as I could about the Vrindavan style of cooking, I found that a cook was judged on how well they could prepare a specific type of chapati known as a Vraja phulka. I studied this art from the locals, finding out the nuances of everything, from its preparation to the best type of wheat to use.*

*So when Srila Prabhupada came, I prepared and served this Vraja phulka with his first lunch. I obtained a preferred strain of wheat known as Pisi Lahore—a soft, plump wheat with an amber-gold hue. Ground at the local flour mill, it was fine and light, nearly bran-free, and ideal for use within twenty-four hours. I rolled the dough evenly into a paper-thin disk ten-to-twelve inches across, cooked it on a griddle until nearly done, and then rested it directly on neem wood embers to puff up into a balloon. When Srila Prabhupada entered his kitchen, its sparseness was filled with his presence, and he smiled in appreciation. He commented on everything, from the clay water jugs to the newly stenciled mahamantra that circled the room near the ceiling. Before taking his seat on the small chair overlooking the samadhi of Srila Rupa Goswami, he gazed out the window toward the samadhi and folded his hands in respect.*

*Then I served him the meal, along with a hot Vraja phulka. With the first bite of the chapati he noted, “You have done everything right. It is Pisi Lahore wheat, milled yesterday, and the neem wood gives it a special, distinctive flavor. One thing though—it should cook for one or two seconds more on the griddle; then it will be perfect.” I was stunned by his perceptive critique. As in all things, Srila Prabhupada was truly a connoisseur of foods, wanting us to learn how to prepare and offer the best of everything for Krishna. For me, these chapatis always remained one of my favorite things to make for Srila Prabhupada.*

**Visakha devi**: During Kartika of 1972, Srila Prabhupada spoke in the mornings and evenings next to the bhajan kutir of Rupa Goswami at the Radha-Damodara temple, but Yamuna didn’t attend. Her time was fully devoted to her seva: cooking for Srila Prabhupada. Cooking was her constant meditation. She would shop for, clean and cut the bhoga; pick out foreign particles from the dais, rice and spices; soak and marinate; make chaunces and fresh pastes; and consistently clean the utensils, kitchen and eating areas. The loving intensity of her absorption was a wonder to behold and, sampling the preparations she made, one could only think they’d descended directly from Goloka. I sensed Srila Prabhupada’s pleasure in her service, dedication and expertise. Yamuna was attentive and sensitive to Srila Prabhupada’s needs, deferential to him, and keenly appreciative of his presence and the gift of bhakti he selflessly and continuously offered.

There is an unforgettable picture of Srila Prabhupada honoring prasadam in his newly-decorated kitchen at Radha-Damodara which came about through the collaboration of Yamuna and Visakha devi. For many devotees, this iconic photograph remains transcendent.

**Visakha devi:** Yamuna devi was cooking for Srila Prabhupada at this time, expertly making traditional dishes. One day, after Yamuna served Prabhupada his luncheon repast, she asked him if I could photograph him honoring prasadam, and he kindly agreed. I silently entered his dining area, a small, simple space that adjoined the kitchen, and made photographs of Srila Prabhupada meditatively honoring this luncheon that had been so lovingly and exquisitely prepared by his beloved disciple.

It’s an historic scene, as this is one of Srila Prabhupada’s two original rooms at the Radha-Damodara temple. It was at this same spot where, in the years before he’d come to America, Srila Prabhupada had looked out the same latticed window at the meeting place of the Six Goswamis of Vrindavan. Deeply contemplating the Goswamis’ profound realizations and his own Spiritual Master’s directive to him to bring Krishna Consciousness to the English-speaking people of the world, Prabhupada had prepared to come West.

## Pishima Cooks for Srila Prabhupada and Yamuna Learns from Her

Yamuna had already established a meaningful relationship with Srila Prabhupada’s sister, Pishima, in Mayapur, and that relationship continued to grow whenever Yamuna had the good fortune of her company. She cherished the memories of their association throughout her life, and especially enjoyed the sweet sisterly relationship she had with Srila Prabhupada:

**Yamuna**: *Srila Prabhupada called me into his room early into his Vrindavan stay and informed me that his sister, Pishima, had arrived in Vrindavan and would be coming for lunch prasadam. So on that day I made Bengali dishes and served them in Bengali fashion, arranged on the thali in the order that Bengalis preferred. Srila Prabhupada respected lunch in his sitting/sleeping room, so he sat behind his desk, and we set a small chonki (eating table) directly opposite him for Pishima. So as soon as I brought in the thalis and set them down, Srila Prabhupada started making these little comical asides in English about his sister. Addressing her weight, he said, “You know, she says it is water; I say it is fat.” Then he would chuckle and she would smile in her sweet and charming way. I had never seen Srila Prabhupada quite like this before, and felt almost out-of-body in elation. Then Prabhupada continued while laughing, “All this,” and he held up his arm and was flapping it back and forth, “this is fat,” he said. “But she calls it water. It is not so.” Now seeing Srila Prabhupada’s obvious movements, Pishima started chuckling and then laughing herself. And then Prabhupada began telling about their childhood when they used to fly kites, and he said, “I always used to beat her at kites. I prayed to Krishna to please let my kite fly higher.” And then he would laugh very heartily. So in this way he was teasing her in a brotherly/ sisterly manner, and she was laughing along with him, just happy to be in his association again.*

*During of all of this jesting, I was bringing relays of chapatis in. And when Srila Prabhupada finished his meal, I noticed that every katori (the little round bowls that moist preparations are served in on a thali) was now piled, one on top of the other, from the largest to the smallest, nearly twelve inches high in total. And when I walked into the room, he flicked his little finger, knocked down the whole stack and said, “Yamunamayi ki jayal" And I said, “Srila Prabhupada ki jayal” and Pishima said, “Gaura Nitai ki jayal” It was indescribably sweet. I said, “Oh, Srila Prabhupada, you ate everything.” And he then waved his hand above his head. Since I cooked frequently for him, Srila Prabhupada had devised a signal system for what the quality of the prasadam was. If he patted his stomach, that meant it was third class. If he patted his chest area, it was second class. If he made a cutting motion at his neck, it was first class. And if he waved his hand above his head, it meant excellent—above first class.*

*So in this way, I always remember that very light, sweet, jovial, humorous first meeting with Pishima in Vrindavan, where she didn’t understand a word of what was being said, but she reveled in its sweetness. She was so very devoted to Srila Prabhupada. From the first day I met her until the very last time I saw her in 1976, she worshipped him, and he obviously was very fond of her.*

*One day I brought a lunch in to Srila Prabhupada, and he said, “This prasadam is so nice, but I have no appetite. When I come to Vrindavan, I lose my appetite. In a holy place one should cut down on his eating and sleeping.” During this time Pishima stayed with her Bengali friend Bhavatarini, near the sacred site of Imli Tala, where Lord Chaitanya sat when He visited Vrindavan. So as Srila Prabhupada requested, Pishima sometimes cooked his luncheon prasadam for him, and during those times, I was Pishima’s official helper. She loved to cook for Srila Prabhupada, and she put her whole heart into it. She was glorious to watch in the kitchen. Sitting in one place, hunched on a low stool and rotating back and forth while managing to do several things at once, she cooked in the strict Bengali style of their childhood. She was miraculous. Her little hands would flash very artistically and quickly from container to spoon to bowl to pitcher. Bengali cuisine is typically characterized by cooking over a high flame, so everything cooks very quickly. To cook in the Bengali fashion, and to do it properly, requires a masterful command of timing, as well as a proficient knowledge of ingredients. So it was classic Bengali prasadam, and of course, even if Srila Prabhupada had a small appetite, he would always respect her shukta. She would fix a different kind of shukta every day. That is the special art in this style of cooking—the wonderful preparation of foods in the Vedic tradition. Once one becomes conversant in the methods, the procedures, the timing and the ingredients, one can always cook something fresh and new depending on the likes and taste preferences of the person one is cooking for. So Pishima knew very well Srila Prabhupada’s preferences, and she would fix many new and different things every time she cooked for his pleasure.*

*Another day Srila Prabhupada called me in and said, “Her \[Pishima’s\] cooking is killing me. She can’t cook.” But I knew that on the one hand he was relishing her cooking very much, yet, at the same time, he was no longer able to digest the spicy and fried Bengali cuisine of his youth. Sometimes he would say, “Please learn to cook from her. She cooks so nicely.” So he had many brother-sister pastimes with Pishima, and they were endlessly variable. To her he was very affectionate and kind, but sometimes to us he would make little jokes about her cooking.*

**“Pishima is teaching Yamuna to cook,” Prabhupada says. “She knows many first-class preparations. When Yamuna learns the art, she can compile one cookbook of pure Vaishnava recipes. It should sell many copies in America, no? Some people were requesting such a cookbook when I was in Hamburg. Once they try these Vaishnava recipes, they will give up cooking all those nasty things. What do you think, Hayagriva?”**

**— HAYAGRIVA DAS, VRINDAVAN DAYS**

**Yamuna**: *Addressing the digestion problem, one morning Srila Prabhupada instructed me to make a special preparation. He said, “My mother used to fix me this when I was a small boy, and I would like you to prepare it for my breakfast.” It was simply a steamed apple made in his cooker. I added water to the bottom part of the cooker and placed one steaming chamber onto it. I then added the apple, covered the cooker and steamed it. He said it was very healthful, easy to digest and good for him. I would also make some idli with some fresh pulverized coconut, and sometimes I put some thickened clotted cream (malai) over the steamed apple. He liked that very much. He also insisted on sliced fresh ginger root and some soaked dal with a spice called chat masala. He commented that this was also good for his digestion and gave him a little appetite in the morning.*

## Srila Prabhupada's Radha-Damodara Schedule

**Yamuna**: *After the morning program Srila Prabhupada would often meet with groups of disciples or visitors, then take his massage on the roof above his rooms in the full sunlight. He then bathed and took his lunch, often in his sitting room—breakfasts were always taken in his kitchen. After the midday meal, he frequently took some rest in the afternoons. I think this was one of the only times Srila Prabhupada might have had some quiet time because in the afternoons the temple gate is closed. Otherwise there were always people milling about, sometimes in large numbers, and always a trickle or stream of them coursing through the temple. Of course they were hollering “Jaya Radhe!” “\]aya Damodara!” and so many other things. So there was never any quiet. Often people would congregate just outside Srila Prabhupada’s shuttered windows and try to peer inside at the great personality. Much had now changed because of Srila Prabhupada’s glorious preaching work. He had become Vrindavan’s own national treasure of sorts, and therefore the Radha-Damodara compound, already the center of activity because of Damodara month, held a heightened interest due to his presence.*

*On rising in the afternoon, Srila Prabhupada would take a little fruit or fruit juice. Then he would often have visiting hours with his students. Sometimes one or two members of the Vrindavan town would also come, and these were very warm and wonderful meetings with Srila Prabhupada. He would inevitably enquire about the preaching activities going on all over the world, as the assembled group of devotees had come from America, Europe, Australia and Japan. It was awe inspiring to see how eagerly Srila Prabhupada would hear their reports, and particularly moving was how he would commend each of them for their achievements. It was different than when he would praise an outstanding member like Giriraja brahmachari for giving up so much for the service of the Lord or coming from such a high family. Now he was commending each devotee who had rendered some service, and whenever a guest would come, he would speak, “Oh, this is my student, and he is so nice. He has done such and such to serve Krishna.” So he was very anxious to show the residents of Vrindavan, especially the caste-conscious brahmanas and temple sevaites, just how fixed in devotional service his Western students were; how they weren’t interested in a pinch of sense gratification and had given up so much to serve the Lord. So these visiting hours were very relishable and special to all, much like they had been in Mayapur during the Gaura Purnima festival.*

Unfortunately, there had already been serious reports of exactly the opposite behavior by a few of Srila Prabhupada’s disciples, and this disturbed him very much. A revered elder statesman of Vrindavan, Vishvambhara Goswami of the Radha-Raman temple, had informed Srila Prabhupada that some disciples were riding through Loi Bazaar in rickshaws and stealing sweets and other items from the shopkeepers. When Srila Prabhupada confronted them, their feeble reply was that Krishna had stolen sweets too. Needless to say, Srila Prabhupada strongly lectured them, again reiterating that they were not being judged by their behavior, but rather, Srila Prabhupada himself was being judged. After this, relations between the townspeople and devotees gradually improved.

**Yamuna**: *One’s mind becomes clean by honoring prasadam prepared in a neat and clean kitchen and offered to Krishna with devotion. One day in Vrindavan, while I was pouring Srila Prabhupada a glass of water from a clay jug, he said that his disciples must learn to act in a brahminical way, carefully cultivating clean habits. If the disciple fails to do things properly, he said, it is not the disciple but the Spiritual Master who is criticized. He asked us to act in such a way as to bring him credit, not dishonor.*

*One day when I was in his kitchen, Srila Prabhupada called, “Yamuna, come here,” so I entered his rooms. In one single gesture he unfolded his arms, beautifully stretched out his fingertips and pointed to a heavily-bearded man sitting in front of him. “Yamuna,” he said, “a very distinguished guest has come to stay with us while we are in Vrindavan, Mr. Howard Wheeler, your Godbrother Hayagriva das.” I was a little taken back by his dramatic introduction and, of course, I had already met Hayagriva before. But it illuminated the special relationship Srila Prabhupada had with Hayagriva—one of love and appreciation for the services already rendered by him. He continued, “He will stay for prasadam. Please make him a plate of very nice prasadam." So Srila Prabhupada would sometimes single out one or two devotees and give them so much personal encouragement, both privately and openly, and Hayagriva das was one of the recipients of the benedicting rays of Srila Prabhupada’s mercy and affection.*

Yamuna used to say that Srila Prabhupada distinctly treated devotees differently according to the degree of their surrender or commitment. He was very strict with some devotees, often chastising them for minor infringements to correct and train them. Yamuna herself experienced this relationship with Srila Prabhupada. Others would be given what she termed “long leashes”—their behavior or commitment sometimes lacking, but their sincerity very real and deep. Hayagriva das had been one of the first disciples of Srila Prabhupada from New York in 1966, and Srila Prabhupada always encouraged and honored him, whether he was strictly following or not.

**The lecture concludes, and we offer obeisances. Even before we have a chance to rise, a loud voice suddenly says, “Question!” “Yes?” “What is the relationship between the disciple and the spiritual master?” There’s a silence. The person who asked the question is a newly arrived devotee. I haven’t even learned his name yet. He’s a short boy with thick glasses, a shaved head and a fiery red sikha so long that he must have been a hippy before shaving up. Now Srila Prabhupada turns to me and says, “How do you answer him, Hayagriva?” “The disciple does whatever the Spiritual Master asks,” I say. “His relationship is that of servant to master.”**

**“It’s said that the Spiritual Master is the well-wisher,” the boy continues. “What does this mean?”**

**“Krishna is the friend of everyone,” Prabhupada says. “If I deliver the message to you that Krishna is your friend, I also become your friend. This is friendship: preaching Krishna Consciousness. When you are in danger, no one can give you protection but Krishna. Therefore He is your only friend. Our business is only to deliver the message of Krishna and point out that Krishna is your friend. He’s also the proprietor. Whatever you claim as your property will be taken by Krishna when you die. To educate people that Krishna is the proprietor is real friendship. Just spread this message of Krishna, and you become the friend and well-wisher of all people. To become a Spiritual Master is not very difficult: we simply have to carry the message of Krishna with no adulteration. I’m just a peon delivering the message of Krishna to you. Although I personally may be the greatest fool, since the message I am delivering is from your dearmost friend, I also become your dearmost friend. Is that clear?” “Yes, thank you,” the boy says loudly.**

**— HAYAGRIVA DAS, VRINDAVAN DAYS**

## Srila Prabhupadas Dealings with Vrindavahs Monkeys

**Yamuna**: Even in those early days there were many monkeys in Vrindavan, especially in the Seva Kunj area the Radha-Damodara temple is situated in. They lived on the many rooftops, in all the trees, on the telephone lines, on the porches—everywhere one saw and heard the scattering and scurrying of the monkeys. So in order to survive in Seva Kunj one had to learn to deal with monkeys, because they are an integral part of daily life. At any moment they may be lurking behind some hidden portico, just waiting to grab something to eat or disturb the peaceful nature of some temple activity. The Brijbasis all knew how to avoid them as far as possible, but the new devotees from the West often found themselves in trouble. So as I had been living upstairs at Radha-Damodara for some time now, I was quite familiar with the local monkeys who actually lived in the compound. There were perhaps twenty or twenty-five regulars, but four or five were prominent.

One female monkey was not too mischievous as far as monkeys in Vrindavan go, and I had established a kind of relationship with her, feeding her on a regulated basis and even giving her a name—Harsharani. So she knew me and I knew her, and I noticed that when Srila Prabhupada was giving his lectures in the courtyard, this one monkey would sometimes come very quietly and sit on a branch of the tamal tree—very quietly, with, practically speaking, her hands folded—and listen to Srila Prabhupada speak. I never saw this monkey sit still at any other time during the year and three months I lived at the Radha-Damodara temple. She was always racing about or getting into something, but during these lectures, she would come, sit in the tree, listen with folded hands and then leave after the lecture was completed. Knowing this monkey as I did, I found this extraordinary.

Then, at some point during his stay, Srila Prabhupada asked to move upstairs to stay in the same rooftop area where his servants were residing. There were two entrances into two separate apartments upstairs, surrounded by a large terrace which overlooked the samadhi of Srila Rupa Goswami. So on climbing the stairwell there was a door to a small room about twelve by eighteen feet, and in that room there were two sets of windows and a wooden bolted door. This had been my room before Srila Prabhupada came for Kartika, and now I slept either at Saraf Bhavan or at Laxmi Rani Kunj with the other devotees, even though Srila Prabhupada had kindly offered me his kitchen. Another separate entrance led to two rooms that housed his servant Srutakirti, Shyamasundara, Pradyumna and Guru das.

So Srila Prabhupada stayed upstairs and came down in the mornings and evenings for the lectures and darshans in his room. It was hoped that Srila Prabhupada would be able to get more rest upstairs because, in addition to its being more quiet, in the early morning hours and in the evening hours there was a cool breeze, enhanced by the nearby neem, eucalyptus and other trees, which added to the cooling effect.

So as these had previously been my rooms, my monkey “friend” Harsha-rani would come at the same time each day for a prasadam handout. She was one of two female monkeys I had been feeding. They, of course, had many baby monkeys and would come to one window in the early afternoon and wait for their prasadam, each with its own unique way of talking to let me know they were there. So I would feed them some little prasadam. One learns that feeding the animals must be done on a regular basis. You don’t just feed them one day and then decide the next day not to feed them, because they become dependent on you. Srila Prabhupada told us that Srila Bhaktisiddhanta Saraswati said that unless you can feed an animal on a regular basis, it is better not to feed it at all, because the animals are actually very regulated—even animals in the modes of ignorance like the monkeys. So these girl monkeys used to come like clockwork, and even when I was not staying there, I tried to arrange prasadam for them. So when Srila Prabhupada first moved up there, I was present one day when the two monkeys came to the window. Srila Prabhupada was sitting in his bed, leaning back with one knee up, his hand on his knee. He was cleaning his teeth with a toothpick. So the monkey who had come to the classes (Harsharani) began speaking, and Srila Prabhupada responded in monkey language, actually sounding just like the monkeys. Much to my amazement, he carried on a conversation with her for a few minutes. I was astonished, to say the least, and asked him what he had said to her. He replied that he simply told her to leave and return at another time. Then later, of course, in order to pacify them both, I gave them prasadam, because if you don’t, then they begin to cause trouble. They may scream, rip up things and become a little hostile. Srila Prabhupada never ceased to amaze me. It is said that the greatest devotees naturally have mystic abilities, but do not like to use them. Yet in my time with Srila Prabhupada, I had seen him visually see ghosts, see and acknowledge demigods and departed saints like Narada Muni and the Six Goswamis, and now speak in monkey language.

## Srila Prabhupada’s Lectures from the Courtyard at Radha-Damodara

**Visakha devi**: We lived in Keshi Ghat by the banks of the Yamuna, and every morning we would attend mangal arati in Keshi Ghat. And after that, Acyutananda Swami would take a sankirtan party, and we’d go all the way to Raman Reti, where the Krishna-Balarama Temple was under construction. And then we’d walk back along the parikrama path that followed the Yamuna River and go to the Radha-Damodara temple in time to meet Srila Prabhupada there. Prabhupada would lead us in the Jaya Radha-Madhava prayers, and then he would speak on Srimad-Bhagavatam, First Canto, Chapter 2, “Divinity and Divine Service.” And although we had heard what he was saying before—it was the basic Krishna conscious philosophyin that atmosphere it had tremendous impact. I can’t imagine how fortunate we were, that small group of us, to be in the most auspicious place, Vrindavan, and then within Vrindavan in such an auspicious place where the Goswamis used to sit together—and to be there at such an auspicious time, Kartika, with Krishna’s pure representative, Srila Prabhupada. It was simply Srila Prabhupada’s kindness upon us that he made this arrangement to impress upon us this incredible philosophy of Krishna Consciousness—so powerful, so important, so profound. So it was an incredible month, and a month that I will remember my entire life. Certainly, it moved me very deeply.

**Yamuna**: Srila Prabhupada usually lectured on The Nectar of Devotion in the evenings and the Srimad-Bhagavatam in the mornings, but sometimes he would change. We made him a small, very simple seat, just between the samadhi and bhajan kutir of Rupa Goswami. At that time there were still trees that went between these two buildings. Only one year later many trees were dug out and the area paved in marble and stone. But at that time there were still some trees there. One of the trees in the compound was another of the few sacred tamal trees in Vrindavan.

**Srila Prabhupada walks into a packed courtyard to deliver his lecture. People sit cross-legged, knee to knee. They even line the perimeter of the concrete patio. The monkeys swing to and fro in the branches of the mango tree, and they chatter until Prabhupada enters. Then, astonishingly, they shut up. Prabhupada sings from Bhaktivinoda Thakur’s Gitavali: “Jaya Radha-Madhava.” Everyone responds, and the courtyard echoes loudly in praise of Krishna. After this invocation, Prabhupada hands a copy of The Nectar of Devotion to Pradyumna and tells him to read from the Preface, where we’d left off this morning. Pradyumna sits very tall in lotus position and wears his glasses halfway down his nose. He looks very scholarly as he reads about the stages of devotional service.**

**— HAYAGRIVA DAS, VRINDAVAN DAYS**

**Yamuna**: *Srila Prabhupada preached during these programs mostly to his own disciples. He was also preaching to one goswami who was attending. His name was Hari Charan Goswami, and he was one of the sevaites from the Radha-Raman temple, one of the Six Goswami temples of Vrindavan. He faithfully attended Srila Prabhupada’s lectures each day. Others may have come for an occasional visit or when they were taking darshan of the Deities, but Hari Goswami was the only member of the Vrindavan community who attended on a regular basis, just like Prabhupada’s disciples. Therefore Srila Prabhupada sometimes directed his questions to him, breaking off from the lecture and saying, “What do you think, Goswamiji?” or “Do you agree?” Away from the lectures, Srila Prabhupada tried to encourage Hari Goswami to go to the Dallas gurukula and teach Sanskrit.*

*At the end of the discourse, Srila Prabhupada would regularly see that prasadam was distributed—either some fruits or some fried item. There are some classic kinds of prasadam which are to be distributed after this kind of program, and Srila Prabhupada requested that we obtain some of those savory items. They are called nimki, a hard white-flour dough rolled into thin disks, cut into triangle shapes and deep-fried in mustard oil. So he was really fond of seeing that prasadam was distributed to all of the people who came. Then either at the morning or evening programs kirtan was always held both before and after the program.*

Yamuna listened to The Nectar of Devotion discourses from 1972 over the years and was particularly moved by Srila Prabhupada’s emphasis on Vaishnava etiquette and the behavior of devotees.

**That is the sign of a devotee: appreciation. Narada Muni says that the devotee always appreciates the qualities of the other devotees. Yes, that is the sign, appreciation of the activities of devotees. A devotee who is actually freed from all contaminations does not find any fault with other devotees. He does not think himself that he’s a bigger devotee or greater devotee than others. He thinks himself as the lowest of all. As Caitanya-caritamrta's author Krishnadas Kaviraja says, “I am lower than the insect within the stool. I am a greater sinner than Jagai and Madhai. Anyone who takes my name—immediately all the results of his pious activities become vanquished.”**

**It is not imitation or any bluff. Any devotee who is actually advancing, he feels like that. Just like the great scientist, Sir Isaac Newton, used to say, “I’ve simply collected a few grains of sand from the ocean of knowledge.” Actually, that is a fact—everything is unlimited. So nobody should be proud falsely, that he has become a great devotee. Everyone should be very humble, trnad api sunicena taror iva sahisnuna, amanena manidena, kirtaniya sada harih. If one thinks that he has become very advanced devotee, then that is very dangerous.**

**— THE NECTAR OF DEVOTION DISCOURSE**

## Yamuna’s Initial Krishna-Balarama Deity Service

Yamuna was very much looking forward in Vrindavan to making the Deity arrangements for the Krishna-Balarama Temple. As she had been given this service by Srila Prabhupada, letters and discussions passed between them over the next two years. Srila Prabhupada was very specific in what he wanted, but this sometimes changed according to his assessment of the Krishna Consciousness of his disciples. Over the course of two years, he asked for Radha and Krishna, along with eight full-size gopis; Krishna and Balarama, large and small; and full-size PancaTattva Deities. Unfortunately, there was not room in the temple design to accommodate so many Deities. During one particularly disappointing time, Srila Prabhupada instructed Yamuna to simply put pictures up on the altar instead of installing any Deities. Ultimately, after a tsunami of difficulties, the Deities were made in the configuration in which They now appear. One thing he did not change was his desire for Krishna and Balarama to occupy the central altar in the temple, in commemoration of Their location in Raman Reti.

The first written instruction from Srila Prabhupada on Deity configuration for the Krishna-Balarama Temple was received on April 25, less than six weeks after Yamuna and Guru das arrived in Vrindavan.

**Regarding Yamuna’s questions, if possible, you can have all 8 gopis of 42" height, but it may be cumbersome. There is one Asta Sakhi temple there in Vrindavan; you may see how this is arranged there. Krishna may be black, Balarama of white, and the pose on the back of the BTG is very nice. You cannot get Lord Chaitanya with all five of His Associates? Formal seated pose of me can be there. Visakha has taken photos for that in Jaipur, but one thing: Is it possible to be made correctly? If not, it is no good.**

**— LETTER TO GURU DAS AND YAMUNA, APR. 25, 1972**

**Yamuna**: *We had a doll maker from Bengal come, and in this little courtyard space at Radha-Damodara Mandir, the first Krishna-Balarama prototypes for our temple were made with straw and mud. Prabhupada said They should be posed with Balarama’s hand resting on Krishna’s shoulder. Srila Prabhupada liked that pose very much. I believe They were modeled after the painting Bharadraja das did which was on the cover of Back to Godhead magazine. It was a difficult pose for the doll maker because of the hand positions, and later, as full-size Deities, it would be a challenge to have Their original Deity sringar made.*

*So Srila Prabhupada would sometimes go outside and supervise the doll maker, or he would wander into the courtyard to see how he was progressing. So after the doll maker covered the Krishna and Balarama prototypes in mud, he painted Them, then used whole wheat flour and water to tack on some jari trims.*

*Unfortunately, at the time the mice were particularly bad at Radha-Damodara, so when the prototype Krishna and Balarama Deities were stored in Srila Prabhupada’s kitchen, the mice, probably attracted by the wheat flour, gradually destroyed Them. Finally, Srila Prabhupada asked us to put Them in the Yamuna River and requested that another, smaller set be made. And so a second pair of Krishna-Balarama clay prototypes were then made. When They were done, those Krishna-Balarama clay Deities were placed in a little niche in Prabhupada’s cupboard. As a background to the niche I chose the color of madhurya rasa, which is bluish-black, and I did a little stencil behind Krishna and Balarama in the niche. Those beautiful little Krishna and Balarama Deities are still there.*

## Yamuna’s Famous Deity Book

On her arrival in Vrindavan, Yamuna had begun almost immediately to visit its principal temples and make detailed notes and drawings on the Deities’ sringar (clothing and jewelry) and standards of worship. She befriended the pujaris in the various temples and was often allowed into areas no female had ever been given access to. Of all the prominent temples in Vrindavan, Yamuna was most impressed with the seva at the Radha-Raman Mandir of Sri Gopala Bhatta Goswami. Even though there was a rotating lineage of goswamis who shared the seva of Sri Radha-Raman, the Deity standards always remained the same. Everything—from the style of dress, offerings, cooking and their many wonderful festivals—remained unchanged from year to year.

During his stay in Vrindavan, Srila Prabhupada asked Hari Charan Goswami (always referred to as Hari Goswami by Yamuna), a sevaite from the Radha-Raman temple who honored Srila Prabhupada by coming to his lectures and visitations, if Yamuna could learn their methods of Deity worship, and he agreed. Over the next year, Yamuna, in her usual meticulous way, carefully studied the art of Deity seva from Hari Goswami, and later from Padmanabha Goswami, who was always generous with his time. Yamuna’s detailed drawings and notes on observing the worship at Radha-Raman Mandir and the other principal temples in Vrindavan formed the basis for what became known as “Yamuna’s Deity Book,” a masterful look back at the ancient traditions of Deity worship in Vrindavan. Some of the drawings are included here, but we hope to publish it in its entirety.

## A Final Prayer Reflecting on Srila Prabhupada’s Vrindavan Stay

The prayer below was written by Yamuna during or after Srila Prabhupada’s visit to Vrindavan during the month of Damodara. Although it is undated, it could have been written in either 1972 or 1973.

*Dear Srila Prabhupada, I cherish these moments in Vrindavan with you. My deepest heartfelt prayer is that I never forget the sweetness you showed me, the instructions you gave to me and the chastisements you blessed me with. Most of all, may I become strong enough to appreciate them all equally.*
